name: Blombos Cave Drawing
desc: The earliest known drawing made by humans is generative. Ochre cross-hatching found at Blombos Cave in South Africa is the earliest known drawing yet found anywhere. “They qualify as generative because the placement of individual marks has not been decided by the artisan, but dictated by a manually executed symmetry‐based algorithm,” according to Philip Galanter . Casey Reas has spoken of how logical, systems thinking is “really essential for this medium.” What the Blombos cave art and many other similar, prehistoric tiling patterns reveal is the ancient, innate and unmistakably human origins of systems thinking in art. Blombos Cave’s symmetry-based tiling system may not universally be considered autonomous and thus generative. As I argue , the critical question to ask is: “Does the artist relinquish control to an external system at some point?” While a simple tiling system is deployed here, more complex versions will appear later in our story with Islamic tile art.

name: Oldest Evidence of Basket Weaving
desc: Oldest known evidence of basket weaving dates back to c. 24,000 BCE. Impressions of weaving on fired clay found in Moravia, Central Europe , predating settled life. Some studies suggest the practice could be much older and origins of the practice are unclear. This algorithmic process is widely considered a generative practice, for example, by Nettrice Gaskins . This ancient practice continues to inspire artists to this day.

name: First Known Author Is a Woman
desc: The first author known by name was a woman: Enheduanna (fl. ca. 2300 BCE), daughter of Akkadian king Sargon and high priestess at the temple of the moon god in Ur, southern Mesopotamia. Her collection of Temple Hymns bears an inscription that translates, roughly, to: “The compiler of this tablet is Enheduanna. That which I’ve created has never existed before.” -Sasha Stiles

name: Babylonians Begin Visualizing Mathematics
desc: Babylonians are first to understand applied geometry, using triangles to parcel farmland and track celestial bodies. The Greeks would build upon these concepts with roots in logic and eventually Euclid’s Elements .

name: I Ching Later Read as Binary
desc: First written between 1,000 to 750 BCE, I Ching , also known as the Book of Changes, is an ancient Chinese divination text. Some interpret the complex text to have introduced the binary system, based on its two symbols, the broken (yin) and solid (yang) lines, representing darkness and light respectively. This Western interpretation of the I Ching as binary may not be consistent with the document’s original meaning yet has impacted mathematics, philosophy and—thousands of years later—modern technology. In that sense, the I Ching was later read as an early form of binary. The formative figure and avid reader of Chinese texts, Gottfried Leibniz , who is also discussed later in this chapter, would go on to document the binary system in his 1703 paper, “ Explanation of Binary Arithmetic .” In the paper, through his perhaps flawed interpretation of the I Ching, Leibniz draws comparisons between his binary system and the Fuxi hexagram arrangement Bouvet sent him, citing it several times and employing its identifiable hexagrams. According to Dr. Andreas Schöter , I Ching’s system of symbols can be interpreted as binary representation. Schöter argues that the versatile system has inspired both historical and contemporary computational thinkers. Additionally, several prominent generative artists have been inspired by the I Ching throughout the previous decades, including John Cage , Manfred Mohr and Marius Watz .

name: Ancient Andean Textiles Weave Legacy of Identity
desc: For millennia, reaching back to at least 4200 BCE, Andean textiles have woven together stories of identity and ancestral beliefs. Predating written languages, textiles served as the predominant medium for conveying images and concepts, often including striking geometric patterns. These intricate cloth creations continue to hold profound significance to the Andean worldview to this day.

name: Oracle at Delphi
desc: Scholars and travelers flock to Delphi, the most important shrine in Ancient Greece , to ask questions about the future and await, in exchange for gold and gifts, enigmatic replies from the Pythia , priestess of Apollo. The deep-rooted impulse toward oracular dialogue, the intellectual exercise of deciphering the Pythia’s statements, and the cultural significance of such prophetic divinations lays a foundation for contemporary search engines and predictive text engines that tap into our collective consciousness, offering sometimes puzzling, sometimes profound answers. -Sasha Stiles

name: Pythagoras Popularizes Geometric Patterns
desc: Pythagoras credited with popularizing geometrical patterns, “the main feature of 1960s computer art. Computer artworks were frequently based on the golden section, Fibonacci numbers, and many other emblematic Pythagorean premises,” according to Grant Taylor .

name: Euclid’s Elements
desc: Considered one of the most influential and long-used textbooks of all time, Elements remains a key work in geometry’s logical development. Euclid ’s ancient Greek text consists of thirteen books that demonstrate how to make logical proofs to ascertain certainty and investigate the unknown. The books also include some of the earliest known algorithms. The concepts Elements introduced would be critical in the development of algorithms by Islamic mathematicians and throughout the European Middle Ages. The text would again prove vital in early modern science, influencing Copernicus , Kepler and Galileo among countless others. Its legacy throughout the millennia is unquestioned. Like the seminal advancements in binary systems from I Ching , Elements played a critical role in moving the field of logic forward. Binary systems and logic would prove foundational to modern attempts to design computing machines, including by Gottfried Leibniz later in this chapter.

name: Library of Alexandria Established
desc: Library of Alexandria is established around the mission of “holding in one place all of the knowledge ever accumulated by man,” the world’s “memory bank”; the Ptolemic dynasty grows the library by decreeing that any book brought into the city be immediately copied by scribes, and taking measures to preclude rivals from collecting books. -Sasha Stiles

name: Hero of Alexandria Invents Automata
desc: Hero of Alexandria , Greek mathematician and engineer, created a number of automata, including the aeolipile, a steam turbine, a fountain, a wind-powered organ and a puppet theater. Some of the earliest known mechanical devices, Hero’s automata demonstrated advanced knowledge of physics and engineering, paving the way for future developments in automation and robotics.

name: Emergence of Islamic Geometric Art
desc: Islamic geometric patterns, emerged in the 8th century during the Islamic Golden Age, influenced by Greek, Roman and Sasanian Persian mathematics and ornament. An example of a generative process predating the computer, Islamic artists used these complex geometric shapes to create intricate, symmetrical designs that were used to decorate buildings, manuscripts, textiles, and other objects.

name: Al-Khwārizmī’s Writes Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning
desc: The Persian Al-Khwārizmī 's Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning introduced zero, the decimal system and Hindu numerals to the Islamic and European world from India . Preserved only in its Latin translation, the text was likely based on Arabic translations of the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta ’s work. Al-Khwārizmī’s name, Algoritmi in Latin, later led to the term “algorithm" when the text reached European readers through twelfth-century Latin translations. It was also during this time of the Abbasid Caliphate, considered a “golden age,” that Islamic tiling and other abstract geometric forms flourished .
subjects: concerning the hindu art of reckoning

name: Ramon Llull Designs the “Logic Machine”
desc: Ramón Llull ’s logic machine was a device used to generate new knowledge by mechanically combining concepts and ideas. It anticipated the concept of computation, inspiring later philosophers and scientists to explore the potential of machines for generating new knowledge. The logic machine also had practical applications in fields such as language translation and cryptography. This device was highlighted in Cybernetic Serendipity as an important development in the history of the digital computer.

name: Richard of Wallingford Designs the St Albans Astronomical Clock
desc: Englishman Richard of Wallingford designs the St Albans astronomical clock, an early clockwork machine. An example of a generative process predating the computer, the art of creating clockwork figures became more refined during the Renaissance period, from the 15th to the 17th century, when some of the most complex and intricate automata were created.

name: Johannes Gutenberg’s Printing Press
desc: Johannes Gutenberg begins developing the mechanised moveable type printing press that would kick off Europe ’s Printing Revolution, capable of producing up to 3600 pages per day and significantly reducing the cost of publishing and distributing literature. This innovation would lead to the era of mass communication, enabling information and ideas to circulate widely and transcend the elite’s monopoly on literacy. -Sasha Stiles

name: Luca Pacioli publishes De Divina Proportione, illustrated by Leonardo da Vinci
desc: Luca Pacioli ’s book, illustrated by Leonardo, helped popularize the principles of mathematical proportion and beauty, known as the Golden Ratio, in art and architecture.

name: Albrecht Dürer Creates Engraving Melencolia I
desc: Packed with meaning and symbols, Melencolia I features a depiction of Dürer’s solid (the eight-faced stone to the left) whose points form the Dürer graph. The solid is a geometric shape discovered by Dürer and used in his art. It was instrumental to the development of perspective and proportion in art history as well as these mathematical concepts in geometry. In the top right we see the “magic square” where the numbers in each row, column, diagonal and quadrant all add up to 34. This work was highly influential to Vera Molnár . She developed systematic variations on the “magic square” from this piece. Molnár first encountered Dürer at the age of 14 or 15 and would say this about her experience to Hans Ulrich Obrist : “That was something very important to happen upon Dürer’s magic square in Melancholia. I was very young and was looking for a foundation, something that I could hold onto in making non-figurative painting." Here, Molnár reveals how Melencolia led her to abandon figurative work for good. Continuing , Molnár explains how her experience with Dürer led her to focus on the abstract, beginning a life-long love affair with the square: “I was looking for a rule, something hidden, a secret, and felt that I’d found it in the magic squares system.... The magic square was like that. I liked Dürer’s work very much. As I was courageous, hard-working and methodical, I said to myself that I would try with other magic squares.”

name: René Descartes Poses a Language Test for Machines
desc: Centuries before the Turing test , we have the Descartes test. In René Descartes' Discourse on the Method published originally in 1637, as the preface to three essays; an English translation followed in 1649. In its fifth part he imagines machines built to look and move like humans and gives two tests that would still expose them, saying: "For we may easily conceive a machine to be so constructed that it emits vocables, and even that it emits some correspondent to the action upon it of external objects which cause a change in its organs; for example, if touched in a particular place it may demand what we wish to say to it; if in another it may cry out that it is hurt, and such like; but not that it should arrange them variously so as appositely to reply to what is said in its presence, as men of the lowest grade of intellect can do." So Descartes had two tests. The first is language. Such a machine might respond in human-like ways but Descartes was skeptical that such a machine could ever arrange their responses generally. The second is versatility across all of life's tasks. Natural language processing and conversational programs dating back to Joseph Weizenbaum’s ELIZA and including today’s LLMs still answer to Descartes bar: replying sensibly to whatever is said.

name: Blaise Pascal Builds the Pascaline
desc: It was one of the first working mechanical calculators, performing addition and subtraction with an automatic carry between digits. Using a series of gears and wheels, the calculator revolutionized mathematics and engineering, paving the way for further development of machines that could perform more complex calculations. Pascal’s calculator was mentioned in the catalog of Cybernetic Serendipity as an important moment in the history of cybernetics.

name: Gottfried Leibniz Pioneers Computational Thinking
desc: Leibniz’s Dissertatio de arte combinatoria (“On the Combinatorial Art” 1666) was one of several cornerstone papers he would write throughout his life on concepts such as symbols, binary systems and formal logic. His voluminous writing and tinkering with machines would prove hugely influential to the development of computing. “On the Combinatorial Art” expanded his habilitation thesis at Leipzig. In it, he proposed a system of using symbols and rules to combine ideas and discover new knowledge. His system for arranging and manipulating concepts to find answers sounds remarkably similar to what we call algorithms. In addition to this seminal text, Leibniz decades later published the paper, “ Explanation of Binary Arithmetic ," in which he is credited for inventing the binary system. Leibniz also made important contributions to the field of formal logic before inventing several mechanical computational devices. His ability to synthesize knowledge throughout the ages to contribute to modern computing make him a singular figure in our story.

name: Gottfried Leibniz Builds the Calculating Machine
desc: Also known as the “stepped reckoner,” this was an early mechanical calculator, demonstrated in wooden model form to the Royal Society in 1673, designed to perform all four arithmetic operations. It was an important advancement in the field of computation, paving the way for further developments in the design and construction of calculating machines, including the development of digital computers.

name: Artificial Versifying by John Peter
desc: In John Peter’s book Artificial Versifying , the English mathematician describes a simple procedure that could be used to make generative poetry in Latin. Meant as fun for children, the procedure involved selecting letters in a way to produce grammatically and metrically correct poems without any prior knowledge of the language. This system stands as one of the earliest examples of generativity used in a creative endeavor. John Clark would go on to build the Eureka machine between 1832 and 1845, based on Peter’s Artificial Versifying .

name: Jonathan Swift publishes Gulliver’s Travels and includes a description of “the Engine”.
desc: In Gulliver’s Travels, “the Engine” is a device that shuffles words into new combinations, essentially serving as a prototype for a mechanical text generator. “The Engine” is one of the earliest references to a device resembling the modern computer. Benjamin Motte published the book in London in1726. The Engine appears in Part III, at the Academy of Lagado, where pupils turn iron handles to rearrange wooden blocks bearing words, so that “the most ignorant person” might write books. Sound Familiar?

name: Johann Philipp Kirnberger’s Musical Dice Game
desc: Known as Musikalisches Würfelspiel (“musical dice game”), this method first published by Johann Philipp Kirnberger was a monumental event in the history of art and chance. The game was a musical composition technique in which pre-composed measures were selected by rolls of dice. Serving as one of the earliest examples of aleatoric (chance) music, it stands as one of the earliest examples generally of art generated randomly by chance. Many subsequent, famous composers would experiment with musikalisches würfelspiel, including C.P.E. Bach and, by attribution, Mozart, who is still the most known practitioner. Musikalisches würfelspiel also begin the tradition of generative music developing prior to graphics, which continued into the twentieth century with Max Mathews at Bell Labs developing MUSIC I nearly a decade before computer graphics were exhibited as art.

name: Thomas Bayes develops Bayesian Inference
desc: Thomas Bayes developed this statistical framework, published posthumously by Richard Price , allowing for the quantification of uncertainty and the updating of probabilities based on new evidence. It has wide applications in fields such as artificial intelligence and data science. It contributed to the development of machine and deep learning when in 1964 Ray Solomonoff combined Bayesian probability-based reasoning and theoretical computer science to make predictions based on the past. Solomonoff and Andrej Kolmogorov would go on to expand upon information theory—discussed more in chapters 3 and 4—to develop Occam’s razor, a key concept to neural networks.

name: Karl Gottlieb von Windisch Publishes “Inanimate Reason”
desc: We've been trying to make human-like machines for centuries. In 1783 Karl Gottlieb von Windisch published letters describing exactly such a thing: a chess-playing automaton built by his friend Wolfgang von Kempelen for the Habsburg court in the decade prior. The machine, a life-size figure in Turkish dress seated at a cabinet, beat many challengers across Europe. Windisch's book, issued in German and French immediately and in English the next year as Inanimate Reason , praised it without claiming to know how it worked: “'Tis a deception! granted; but such an one as does honor to human nature.” The deception was apparently a strong human player hidden inside, which Edgar Allan Poe argued in his 1836 essay “Maelzel's Chess-Player.”

name: Joseph-Marie Jacquard Invents the Jacquard Loom
desc: The Jacquard loom used punch cards to control the weaving of patterns in fabric. It introduced the notion of a program stored outside the machine on punch cards, which would later result in generative weaving and modern computing. Charles Babbage would go on to utilize Jacquard’s method of punch card programming as one of computing’s earliest pioneers. “Computers did not pave the way for generative art; generative art helped to pave the way for computers,” according to Phil Galanter. Punch card programming would continue developing for the next century and a half before culminating in the use of mainframe computers and early languages such as FORTRAN . Additionally, textile design has continued to influence both fine art as well as generative art to this day. Examples include the Bauhaus weaving workshop ’s Anni Albers and Gunta Stölzl , the quilters of Gees Bend, Anna Lucia , Travess and Andreas Rau .

name: Mary Shelley Publishes “Frankenstein”
desc: As mechanization rose throughout the globe in the nineteen century, much like AI is today, we faced similar fears of humanity's power to construct its own intelligent beings. Thankfully, in the twenty-first century, that fear has entirely disappeared. Oh. Isaac Asimov would go on to name the fear the novel dramatizes the “Frankenstein complex.” We know about the fears of people two hundred years ago through their art and culture like, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus which was published anonymously in London in three volumes on January 1, 1818. Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley had begun it in the summer of 1816 near Geneva, when Lord Byron proposed that each member of his party, including Mary and her husband Percy Bysshe Shelley, write a ghost story. The story itself if well known. Scientist, Victor Frankenstein, assembles a living being and ultimately their relationship sours. The "monster" learns language by listening in secret and turns on its maker. Many further such stories have been told, including films like The Terminator and the Matrix. But humanity's ability to create its own destruction has been persistent fear in our psyche.

name: Nicéphore Niépce Produces the Earliest Surviving Camera Photograph
desc: ‍Photography’s impact on modern art is well established but its impact on digital and computer art more specifically is less examined yet central to this story. According to Herbert W. Franke , "The most significant stage on the path to the mechanization of the fine arts has been photography.” Further, art critic Frank Popper includes photography as the first of seven influences on the development of digital art. Digital generative artists such as Casey Reas , Margot Lovejoy and Terry Gips have all stressed the importance of photography to the development of computer art as well. Nicéphore Niépce produced the earliest photograph made in a camera obscura that survives today, using a pewter plate coated with bitumen. This breakthrough served as the basis for the continuation of developments in photography to this day. The invention of photography stands as a paradigm shift in art history. The camera’s ability to capture representations of the visible world would lead to painters losing interest in strict realism and spur the gradual abstraction of modern art. Photography, in addition to becoming its own art form, would also lead to cinema and video art, as art expanded from a handmade practice to include capture practices.

name: Charles Babbage Develops His Analytical Engine
desc: Foundational to the development of cybernetics, this unrealized mechanical computer aimed to use punch cards, inspired by the Jacquard Loom , to perform calculations. One of the earliest designs for a programmable computer, it also had a significant impact on the development of modern computers and programming languages.

name: Lady Lovelace's Objection
desc: In her 1843 notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine , Lovelace wrote that the machine could originate nothing and only do what it was ordered to do. Turing answers the objections by name in 1950. This prescient observation hints at the different paths computation would take from hard-programmed rules to learning models. People: Ada Lovelace .

name: Ada Lovelace Publishes the First Algorithm Written for a Machine
desc: Computer programming is born, as Ada Lovelace ’s 1843 notes on Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine set out a program for computing Bernoulli numbers, making her the first published computer programmer. Her work demonstrated the potential for computers to perform complex tasks, foreshadowing the development of modern programming languages. She even envisioned the computer’s ability to create programmed art. Inspired by the notion of combining science and art, Lovelace recognized the computer’s ability to extend beyond calculating numbers. She understood its potential to create complex images and music by translating basic rules into symbolic logic, carrying on the traditions of Euclid , Al-Khwārizmī and Leibniz. Lovelace foresaw a future where computers could be programmed to create beautiful and imaginative works of art, envisioning a creative partnership between humans and machines. This concept anticipated the field of computer-generated art by over a century. Her prescient ideas have inspired generations of computer programmers and artists. Lovelace would inspire future women pioneers in the field of programming such as Grace Hopper who introduced the use of natural language in programming in the 1950s . The "notes" accompany Lovelace's 1843 English translation of Luigi Federico Menabrea's French memoir on the Engine. However, the notes actually run about three times as long as the memoir.

name: Hugh Blackburn Describes the Harmonograph
desc: The Harmonograph, commonly agreed to be invented by Hugh Blackburn , is a mechanical apparatus that creates geometric drawings, typically Lissajous-type figures, through the use of pendulums. It stands as an early example of an autonomous system/machine that generates artistic forms, and as a precursor to later generative art and computer graphics.

name: Eureka Exhibited at London’s Egyptian Hall
desc: John Clark ’s Latin verse generating machine, Eureka, was a full mechanized version of John Peter’s book, Artificial Versifying , from 1677 and earlier in this Timeline . The machine generated Latin hexameter verse and stands as a precursor to the typewriter and other early mechanical devices. The inventor John Clark spent thirteen years building Eureka, from 1832 to 1845, which resembles a bookcase. This early automatic machine combined science, mechanization, computation, randomness and art in a way that is recognizable to contemporary digital generative art. The device stands as another example of the roots of generative poetry often stretching back further than generative graphics.

name: The Great Exhibition of London Lights Early Spark of the Arts & Crafts Movement
desc: Industrialization and Technology meet Art According to Frank Popper , “one can only speak of the direct influence of technology on art since the Industrial Revolution, and more particularly when its effects entered everyday life at the end of the 19th century through the progressive design movements known as Art Nouveau and its precedent, the Arts and Crafts movement, in England .” The first world’s fair, The Great Exhibition of London , kicks off the Modern Era of our Timeline due to its association with industrialization and its impact on the Arts and Crafts movement. The fair captured a world on the brink of a paradigm shift, the beginning of a new era in which technology and art would join and grow ever closer. Organized by Henry Cole , the legendary founder of the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, the fair’s showcase of poorly crafted manufactured goods with ornate Victorian design inspired backlash in the form of England’s Arts and Crafts movement. The event would inspire Arts & Crafts artists and designers to incorporate craftsmanship and traditional techniques into new technologies, ultimately leading to the development of both modern graphic and industrial design. In the coming decades, Arts and Crafts would usher in the era of technology impacting art which led to Art Nouveau and the Bauhaus . This moment is thus the spark that lit the fuse of the modern era of generative art with its criticisms, adjustments to and embrace of rapidly industrializing societies and new technologies in art.

name: George Boole Publishes “An Investigation of the Laws of Thought”
desc: The Boolean binary logic that underpins all of computation and thus contemporary society traces back to this 1854 book. George Boole published An Investigation of the Laws of Thought , while professor of mathematics at Queen's College, Cork. Largely self-taught, he stated his aim in the first sentence: “to investigate the fundamental laws of those operations of the mind by which reasoning is performed; to give expression to them in the symbolical language of a Calculus.” He treated logic as algebra over two values, 1 and 0, true and false. In 1937 Claude Shannon 's master's thesis showed that switching circuits obey Boole's algebra, and digital computers have been built on it ever since.

name: Gustave Courbet’s Pavilion of Realism
desc: In what Hans Ulrich Obrist considers the birth of Modernism, Gustave Courbet erected—at his own expense—the Pavilion of Realism in 1855, eight years prior to the Salon des Refusés . Courbet’s earlier rejection of Salon authority came after his works were excluded from the official Salon following a public dispute with Comte Nieuwerkerke, its influential superintendent of fine arts. The exhibition was either a bold act of defiance against the restrictive artistic norms of his time or the result of a petty beef. It was intentionally set directly adjacent to the prestigious Universal Exposition in Paris from which Courbet’s work was also rejected due to his spat with Nieuwerkerke. Within his Pavilion, Courbet showcased The Painter’s Studio, a monumental painting that exemplified his commitment to portraying the truth of contemporary life. Along with it was the equally scandalous masterpiece, A Burial at Ornans. Obrist explains the importance of the exhibition: “Courbet’s self-mounted exhibition inaugurated the modern period in painting, in which the artist, rather than [their] patron, became the protagonist of art.” [Ways of Curating, 37]

name: William Morris Founds Decorative Arts Firm Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co.
desc: The iconic firm was modeled on a craftsman’s workshop and took a pioneering stand against the non-functional role ascribed to art. The firm specialized in wallpaper designs with natural imagery but grew to manufacture furniture, textiles and stained glass as well. It stressed handcrafted production over the use of machine. Another important concept developed by Morris Co. was that the artist (or designer) should take a holistic approach, becoming involved in the entire creative process. These innovations would prove greatly influential to the upcoming Arts & Crafts movement. According to Frank Popper , this firm and the related Arts & Crafts movement were foundational in the development of the Bauhaus and even digital art, textile design and wallpaper patterns.

name: Édouard Manet’s Work Rejected by Paris Salon
desc: In what some consider to be the birth of Modernism in art, Manet’s Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe was flatly rejected by the Paris Salon for its unconventional style and subject matter. The painting, featuring a nude woman picnicking with clothed men, was considered scandalous at the time, as the nude woman was no longer cloaked under the legitimacy of Salon-approved topics such as mythology or history. This rejection prompted the state to open the Salon des Refusés , a monumental event in art history which kicked off the yet-to-be-named Impressionism movement. Some also consider this birth of Modernism but countering theories exist such as the Courbet’s Pavilion of Realism or my own that begins this chapter (the London World’s Fair of 1851 ). The industrialization and cultural conditions of the previous century gave rise to art based on personal experiences and non-realistic depictions of the world. A new avant-garde emerged that would go on to radically change the world of art for the next century.

name: The Salon des Refusés Opens in Paris
desc: The “exhibition of rejects,” a response to the rejection of many artists' works by the official Salon in Paris , begins. Since 1667, the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture held public exhibitions for their standout students. This exhibition came to be known as the Salon. For artists rejected from the conservative Salon’s jury, it meant patrons would be nearly impossible to find. In 1863, there was uproar after the jury selections and it took Emperor Napoleon III to order a separate exhibition to be organized for these rejected works. The simultaneous exhibition was called the Salon des Refusés (“Exhibition of the Rejects”). The Salon des Refusés featured the work of Manet, Cézanne and Pissarro yet the critical reception was poor with visitors only attending to ridicule the event. The exhibition radically challenged the established norms of the art world, sparking debates and paving the way for new artistic movements like Impressionism. The Salon des Refusés not only challenged the authority of the Salon jury but also contributed to a broader redefinition of artistic expression, marking a significant shift towards modern art and challenging traditional academic standards.
subjects: académie royale de peinture et de sculpture

name: James Clerk Maxwell publishes his theoretical analysis of Watt’s governor
desc: James Clerk Maxwell ’s “On Governors”, his theoretical analysis of Watt’s governor published in 1867 and 1868, a device used for regulating the speed of steam engines, was a significant contribution to the understanding of feedback control systems. It stands as a foundational moment in the history of cybernetics, as mentioned in the Cybernetic Serendipity catalog.

name: Samuel Butler Publishes “Erewhon”
desc: For further proof that our fear of producing intelligent machines that could one day overtake us is nothing new, see Samuel Butler 's satirical novel Erewhon; or, Over the Range . In the book, its narrator finds a hidden country whose people destroyed every machine invented in the previous 271 years, persuaded by a book that noticed machines were evolving faster than living things and might one day become conscious. Ring a bell?

name: The First Impressionist Exhibition
desc: This epochal event in art history, held in Paris , marked the emergence of the Impressionist movement, which challenged the cultural monopoly of the Paris Salon and paved the way for modern art. The exhibition was organized by a group calling themselves the “Anonymous Cooperative Society of Artists.” It featured around 175 works by 30 artists such as Monet, Renoir and Degas . The show was generally regarded as a failure, receiving infamously hostile reviews and poor attendance. There would be eight Impressionism exhibitions in total running from 1874 to 1886.

name: Impressionist Movement Named
desc: Critic Louis Leroy gave the Impressionist movement its name when he accused Claude Monet ’s Impression, Sunrise of being merely a sketch or “impression.” This was meant as insult by Leroy as it implied that Monet’s work was not a finished painting.

name: The Second Impressionist Exhibition
desc: The Second Impressionist Exhibition, held in Paris , was important in consolidating the Impressionist movement as a group and distinct style. Organized by the same anonymous cooperative as the first, the second exhibition featured 250 pieces by around 20 artists, including Monet’s The Japanese Girl and Caillebotte’s The Floor Planers. Still heavily ridiculed, the second exhibition actually generated enough in sales to cover costs and pay each artist a token amount.

name: Tulip and Rose by Morris & Co.
desc: Designed by William Morris and woven for Morris & Co. by the Heckmondwike Manufacturing Company, this was the first dateable Morris design for a woven furnishing textile, important for its budding abstraction. The piece features grid-like, symmetrical repeating patterns of natural forms, anticipating the upcoming Art Nouveau movement’s use of nature as well as as the early digital generative art structure. The work, as well as Morris & Co.’s growing interior design innovations were emblematic of what would become known as the Arts & Crafts movement. Art Nouveau and Arts & Crafts, both progressive design movements, were some of the earliest examples of how technology began influencing art during the first wave of industrialization.

name: Peacock Room by James Whistler
desc: James Whistler’s Peacock Room stands as an important example in the history of installation and immersive art, which has a rich tradition in digital art. But the room is also a an episode of art exceeding the bounds of commission, James McNeill Whistler transformed Frederick Leyland ’s dining room into what would become known as the Peacock Room, originally intended as minor touch-ups by the artist while architect Thomas Jeckyll was ill. Upon Leyland’s return, he discovered that Whistler had radically altered the space, painting over expensive leather wall coverings and embellishing the room with lavish gold and blue-green peacock motifs. The transformation culminated in Whistler adding a mural titled Art and Money; or, The Story of the Room, featuring two peacocks in a standoff, symbolizing the tension between artist and patron over the financial value of artistic labor. Hans Ulrich Obrist explains the rooms importance further: “It prefigured installation art, in which an artist works on the entire environment of a space, rather that simply decorating a part of it with a painting or sculpture.”
subjects: art and money; or, the story of the room

name: The Third to Eighth Impressionist Exhibitions
desc: The subsequent Impressionist Exhibitions began showcasing more distinct, experimental styles before ultimately fracturing. The exhibitions reached peak levels of artist-harmony as well as popular and critical acclaim by the Seventh exhibition. The Eighth saw the movement come to an inglorious end over internal turmoil.

name: Remington Releases the Standard Number 2 Typewriter
desc: One of the world’s first commercially successful typewriters, the Remington and Sons Standard Number 2 typewriter featured a QWERTY keyboard, which it helped to establish as the standard to this day. Its introduction revolutionized written communication. The typewriter would allow and inspire artists to create intricate, repetitive and pattern-based compositions through typed characters, offering a precursor to the digital generative art of today. The typewriter’s influence on artistic expression, particularly in the realms of concrete poetry and text-based art, helped shape the trajectory of generative art by introducing the concept of using machines and rules to generate visually striking and conceptually layered compositions.

name: Art Nouveau Is Born
desc: The term “art nouveau” first appeared in the 1880s in the Belgian journal L’Art Moderne to describe the work of Les Vingt. A significant moment in the history of modern art, Art Nouveau was characterized by intricate, flowing lines and organic, natural forms. It revolutionized the approach to architecture, furniture and graphic design, making use of the technological innovations of the turn of the century. Art Nouveau was an important precursor to modernism, which emphasized function over form and the elimination of superfluous ornament. Influenced by the ideas of the Arts & Crafts movement, Art Nouveau designers and artists sought to synthesize art and craft. The styles were similar as well with both emphasizing nature and the Gothic style. Both were interested in architecture and design’s power to reshape the human environment and, thus, experience.

name: Seurat Kicks of Post-Impressionism with Pointilism
desc: Seurat begins his best-known painting, A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, completed in 1886. This seminal work of Post-Impressionism is known for its innovative use of pointillism, “a highly systematic and scientific technique based on the hypothesis that closely positioned points of pure color mix together in the viewer’s eye.” It also exemplifies the movement’s interest in depicting people from different social classes’ everyday life through a modern, formalist lens.
subjects: a sunday afternoon on the island of la grande jatte

name: Founding of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers
desc: The organization would go on to become the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) in 1963. The IEEE would be foundational in its cultivation of an international network of early digital artists, according to Darko Fritz .
subjects: institute of electrical and electronics engineers (ieee)

name: “Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society” Officially Gives Arts & Crafts Movement its Name
desc: Founded in London and born out of the influence of William Morris and Philip Webb , the society’s objective was “to assert a new public relevance for the work of decorative artists.” Arts & Crafts sought to erase the distinction between fine art, design and craft, while uniting creativity and manufacturing. The society also officially gave the Arts & Crafts movement its name. This progressive design movement was one of the first to pose questions about the latest technology, mechanization and art. Arts & Crafts sought to harmonize the relationship between the artist, machines and art. Morris’s philosophical stand against poorly made manufactured goods would prove highly influential to Henry van de Velde , who brought Art Nouveau to Belgium and founded the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts . Walter Gropius would take over for van de Velde and the Arts and Crafts school would become the Bauhaus in 1919. Thus, a line can be drawn from the ideas of Morris directly to the founding of Bauhaus . Morris and this enormously important movement, according to Frank Popper , is the beginning of electronic art’s journey.
subjects: weimar school of arts and crafts

name: John Venn’s “graphical indication of randomness” Appears in The Logic of Chance
desc: English logician and mathematician John Venn constructed “a very fair graphical indication of randomness,” according to himself in the third edition of his seminal book, The Logic of Chance. A precursor to generative art and systemic art and thinking, Venn’s illustration consisted of a single, simple rule: Draw “a line which at every instant is as likely to take one direction as another.” From this simple rule, infinite possibilities of randomness can occur and a basic generative system was born. This book also ties together earlier moments in Chapter 1 that discuss logic and the visualization of mathematics. Here, Venn combines the two to visualize rules or as they’re more commonly referred to today, algorithms.

name: The Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society Holds its First Annual Exhibition
desc: These annual exhibitions by the newly formed Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society aimed to raise the cultural standing and awareness of craft work, such as ceramics, textiles, metalwork and furniture. According to the V&A , “for many years in Britain exhibitions mounted by the Society were the only public platform for the decorative arts, and were critical in changing the way people looked at manufactured objects.”

name: Henri Poincaré Publishes Seminal Paper on the Three-Body Problem
desc: Henri Poincaré 's work in the late 19th and early 20th century laid the foundation for the modern science of chaos and complexity, which has been critically influential on computer and generative art. The well-known three body problem concerned the difficulty of predicting the position of three celestial bodies in close proximity to another. Poincaré did not actually solve the problem but he did discover the butterfly effect which gave rise to the new field of chaos theory in the 1960s.

name: Paul Cézanne’s First Solo Exhibition
desc: The exhibition at Ambroise Vollard ’s gallery in Paris was significant for establishing Cézanne as a major artist of his time. The exhibition introduced Cézanne’s innovative style of using simplified forms and flattened space, laying the groundwork for the development of modern art’s journey to abstraction and movements such as Cubism.

name: Un coup de dés jamais n’abolira le hasard (A Throw of the Dice will Never Abolish Chance) by Stéphane Mallarmé
desc: This poem was one of the very first intimate and intense marriages of free verse and typographic freedom. It served as the precursor not only to twentieth-century avant-garde poetics (from Futurists and Constructivists, via Appolinarie and Dada to Surrealists then later to Visual, Concrete…) but also the birthplace of the artist’s book as well as concept albums. -Vuk Ćosić
subjects: a throw of the dice will never abolish chance
un coup de dés jamais n'abolira le hasard

name: Hermann Muthesius Inspired by visit to Great Britain
desc: German architect Hermann Muthesius , posted to London from 1896, was influenced by the Arts and Crafts Movement, including the latest developments in art and architecture. He brought ideas back to Germany , such as the importance of traditional craftsmanship, simplicity of design and the integration of art into everyday life. Muthesius would found the Deutscher Werkbund which had a major influence on Walter Gropius , founder of the Bauhaus and Le Corbusier . This explains how the ideas of the Arts & Crafts movement via Muthesius would go on to shape our concepts of art, architecture and design to this day.

name: First exhibition of Fauvism
desc: The shocking exhibition held in Paris at the Salon d’Automne, featured Fauvist work characterized by bold and experimental use of color, including Henri Matisse’s Woman with a Hat. Fauvism opened the door for more extreme approaches to abstraction. Artists, such as Matisse, innovated with color, inspiring countless others, including Kandinsky’s Blue Rider Group, Color Field painters and Expressionists. The movement’s incorporation of impulse and spontaneity also led the way for greater experimentation with randomness in art. This laid the groundwork for artists to further explore non-representational forms, where chance and randomness could play an even more prominent role.

name: Cézanne Begins His Mont Sainte-Victoire Series
desc: Beginning in the 1870s by the “Father of Post-Impressionism,” this series of forty-five watercolor and thirty-six oil paintings would have an outsized impact on art history. Significant for their challenging approach to landscape paintings, Cézanne broke from traditional conventions by flattening the space and using repeated forms to create a sense of depth. Cézanne famously believed that painters should “treat nature by means of the cylinder, the sphere, the cone,” one of the first breaths of abstraction in arts modernization. Cézanne also portrayed his subject matter, in this case Mont Sainte-Victoire, from diverse angles and points of view, highly influencing Picasso and Georges Braque ’s development of Cubism. “His innovations were tremendously influential for the masters of modernity, like Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso . Picasso even went so far as to call Cézanne ‘the father of us all.’”

name: Les Demoiselles d’Avignon by Picasso kicks off Cubism
desc: Cubism, one of the most influential movements of the twentieth century and inspired by Cézanne ’s use of basic geometric shapes, is born with Picasso’s Les Demoiselles d’Avignon. The painting preceded Picasso’s partnership with Georges Braque , who saw it later in 1907. Les Demoiselles is proto-Cubist. The first phase proper, Analytical Cubism, ran from 1908 to 1912, when Picasso and Braque broke objects down into their basic geometrical shapes, extending the ideas of Cézanne nearly to their logical conclusions. Cubism “brought different views of subjects (usually objects or figures) together in the same picture, resulting in paintings that appear fragmented and abstracted.” This marked a revolutionary departure from the Renaissance tradition of the illusion of space created from linear perspective. Cubism was not only a monumental step in modern art’s abstraction, it was crucial to digital generative art’s development as well. For instance, beyond its embrace of geometric forms, Cubism introduced a temporal, fourth dimension to visual art by presenting multiple perspectives of an object in a single composition. This shattered the notion of a fixed viewpoint and suggested the passage of time and movement within the artwork, anticipating Op and Kinetic art, two key predecessors of digital generative art.

name: Group IV, The Ten Largest, No. 7, Adulthood by Hilma af Klint
desc: Monumental works in the history of abstraction, Swedish artist Hilma af Klint created abstract paintings before the term “abstract art” was even coined. Group IV, The Ten Largest, No. 7, Adulthood is one of her most significant works, part of a series of ten large-scale paintings. The paintings are largely influenced the ideas of spiritualism and Theosophy, which were popular in the Western world at the time. The pieces challenge the Western art historical canon, pre-dating the work of male artists like Kandinsky and Mondrian who are typically credited with the invention of abstract art. Thus, the works are representative of the challenges women artists have faced throughout history. These colossal works in art history were kept privately underground for decades and rarely exhibited. Af Klint even stipulated in her will that the paintings could not be shown for twenty years after her passing. They would be essentially lost and forgotten until 1986. In 1988, The Secret Paintings of Hilma af Klint toured around Finland, Iceland and Norway in a small exhibition. New York ’s P.S.1 Contemporary Art Center showcased the works a year later in 1989 which finally drew broader public attention to the works. Af Klint’s work consistently toured around Europe for the next several decades but it was not until 2018 that af Klint received a major solo exhibition in the United States , Hilma af Klint: Paintings for the Future at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum .
subjects: hilma af klint: paintings for the future
the secret paintings of hilma af klint

name: Hermann Muthesius Founds the Deutscher Werkbund
desc: The Deutscher Werkbund in Munich, a crucially important and influential association, aimed at improving German design and industry in global markets by partnering product manufacturers with design professionals. Muthesius found inspiration for the Werkbund from his time spent in England , particularly from his time absorbing the Arts & Crafts movement. A member of the Werkbund, Walter Gropius , would advance the principles of the Werkbund further by later creating the Bauhaus school of design . Considered by Frank Popper instrumental in the development of digital art, the Werkbund also played a significant role in shaping modernist design principles, promoting the use of industrial production methods with traditional crafts.

name: Manifesto of Futurism Published by Filippo Tommaso Marinetti
desc: Marinetti’s manifesto called for artists to embrace the aesthetic language of technology and industrialization in their practice. Frank Popper considered Futurism (in addition to Dadaism and Constructivism) the most influential movement in the first quarter of the twentieth century on electronic art. Popper elaborates: “Futurism, besides its exaltation of dynamism and speed, attempted to find abstract equivalents for all the forms and elements in the universe and advocate the fusion of art and science.”

name: E. M. Forster's “The Machine Stops”
desc: There have always been twin views on technology and where it's leading us. Even a hundred years ago writers like H. G. Wells wrote of tech utopias while E. M. Forster was decidedly less optimistic. In Forster's story “The Machine Stops,” humanity lives underground in identical rooms, each person's needs met by a global Machine. This immediately recalls contemporary futuristic visions of this dystopia, like Fallout and Silo. It also eerily predicted more contemporary afflictions like video calls and blackboxes, as in Forster's story people rarely meet; they talk through screens and trade ideas second hand. When the Machine begins to fail and no one remembers how to repair it, a religion grows up around its manual. At least we have something to look forward to.

name: Georges Claude Invents the Neon Light
desc: The invention of neon tubing was a major development in the predecessor of electronic art, Lumino-Kinetic Art.

name: Der Blaue Reiter Exhibition
desc: The radical and provocative first exhibition of the Blue Rider Group, founded by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc , was a significant development in the abstraction of art. Influenced by Fauvism especially, the works emphasized color, form and spirituality over artistic tradition.

name: Sonia and Robery Delaunay Develop Orphism
desc: Inspired by the ideas of Cubism and Futurism, Sonia and Robert Delaunay sought with Orphism to create a new kind of abstract art. Their work emphasized the interplay of color and light, often using circular forms and contrasting hues to create dynamic visual effects. A key development in modern art’s abstraction, Orphism likened painting to music. Its musical inspiration explain the movement’s interest in expressing dynamism, inspiring future movements to embrace visual rhythms, optical effects and other dynamic relationship between elements, including digital generative art. These movements include Op art and Kinetic art, two important predecessors of electronic art.

name: Henry van de Velde Forms the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts
desc: Deeply influenced by William Morris ’s Arts and Crafts philosophy, Belgian architect and designer Henry van de Velde combined the Arts and Crafts School and the Academy of Fine Arts of Weimar to form the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts. Van de Velde would be rather short-lived in his tenure due to the approaching WWI. The impact of the school on human history, however, was profound. The school sought a harmonious solution to the problems posed at all levels of a rapidly modernizing life, specifically the machine-artisan-art triad. The school also attempted to articulate a socially committed, scientific aesthetic. Walter Gropius would later succeed van de Velde who was forced to resign in 1915, one year into WWI, due to his Belgian heritage. In 1919, the school, under Gropius, would become the Bauhaus .
subjects: academy of fine arts of weimar
weimar school of arts and crafts

name: Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 by Marcel Duchamp
desc: Rejected by the Cubists for appearing too Futurist, this proto-Dadaist painting applies a machine aesthetic to the human form, anticipating the dynamism of Kinetic Art that led to electronic art. Duchamp called this series of paintings “an organization of kinetic elements - an expression of time and space through the abstract presentation of movement…[But] we must bear in mind that, when we consider the movement of form in space over a certain time, we are entering the realm of geometry and mathematics in the same way as when we construct a machine.” Geometry, movement, mathematics, Duchamp’s massive impact on art history includes profoundly anticipating digital generative art well.

name: Leonardo Torres Quevedo Builds El Ajedrecista, a Chess-Playing Automaton
desc: Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo built the chess-playing automaton, El Ajedrecista (The Chess Player), in 1912 and presented it in Paris in 1914. Incapable of playing a full game from scratch, the machine played one specific endgame, its own king and rook against a human’s lone king. It could sense the pieces electrically and move its own with a mechanical arm. A 1915 Scientific American account reported Quevedo's claim that “an automaton can do many things that are popularly classed with thought.” A second version, built in 1920, moved the pieces with electromagnets under the board. This machine would even impact the budding field of cybernetics, when in January 1951 Quevedo's son Gonzalo Torres-Quevedo presented both machines at a Paris conference, where the 1920 machine defeated none other than Norbert Wiener .

name: Malevich Begins Developing Suprematism
desc: One of the key radical movements in modern art, abstraction and digital generative art history, Kazimir Malevich ’s use of geometric forms and limited colors in Suprematism has had a profound impact on art history. Malevich believed that Suprematism was “the culmination (in Russia at least) of Futurism’s interest in dynamism and Cubism’s reduced geometric forms.” Suprematism greatly influenced contemporary generative art’s abstract geometric aesthetic, particularly early computer art. Malevich would not display the work he was creating during this period until 1915.

name: 3 Standard Stoppages by Marcel Duchamp
desc: This revolutionary work of 1913 and 1914 remains one of the most famous examples of the use of chance in the history of art. Duchamp employed chance operations by dropping three one-meter threads, allowing them to take on random forms. He then traced and mounted these shapes as a commentary on the limitations of standard measurement systems. Duchamp’s exploration of chance and random processes questioned fundamental ideas such as artistic control and authorship, foreshadowing Dada as well as the embrace of generative algorithms in art creation. Crucially, his work gave legitimacy and recognition for chance operations in art, opening up possibilities for generative art and its algorithmic processes. This was part of Duchamp’s larger impact on conceptualism and shifting the focus from the artist’s hand to the underlying systems and concepts. This work, in the MoMA permanent collection, is thus one of the most foundation to this story of generative art history.

name: Bicycle Wheel by Marcel Duchamp
desc: This pieces stands as a precursor of both kinetic and conceptual art, another monumental work by Duchamp in the history of generative art. “In 1913 I had the happy idea to fasten a bicycle wheel to a kitchen stool and watch it turn.” -Marcel Duchamp

name: Prismes électriques by Sonia Delaunay
desc: Inspired by technological and mechanical innovations of the time, this key work of the Orphism movement sought to explore the effects of color and light in abstract art. Delaunay’s masterful command of color and her pioneering use of abstraction would prove to be enduringly influential.

name: Kazimir Malevich Stages “The Last Exhibition of Futurist Painting 0.10” in Petrograd
desc: A seminal moment in art history, this exhibition showcased Malevich’s Black Square , Dynamic Suprematism and other abstract works that rejected traditional representational art, marking the birth of the Suprematist movement. Suprematism’s exultation of pure form and geometry would become fundamental aspects of digital generative art.

name: Black Square by Kazimir Malevich
desc: This work of the Russian avant-garde, painted in 1915 though dated 1913 by Malevich, remains one of art history’s cornerstones. Black Square was instrumental in establishing “a new world of shapes and forms” that would eventually lead to digital generative art. This radical rejection of representation in art is one of the first instances of pure abstraction in painting. The lasting symbol of Malevich’s career and Suprematism, Black Square was an earth-shattering work, radically challenging thousands of years of artistic tradition and marking a turning point in the history of art.

name: Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings Found Dadaism
desc: By emphasizing chance, randomness and absurdity in art, Dada stands as a foundational movement in the development of digital generative art. Writer Hugo Ball and the poet and performer Emmy Hennings founded Dadaism in the midst of WWI’s disillusionment from their satirical nightclub in Zurich , the Cabaret Voltaire. From there he published a magazine in which Ball wrote, “will bear the name ‘Dada’. Dada, Dada, Dada, Dada.” Frank Popper acknowledged Dada, along with Constructivism and Futurism, as one of the first quarter of the twentieth century’s three most important movements. Dada eventually formed the basis of Surrealism, Conceptual art, Neo-Dada, Fluxus and the chance elements of generative art. It’s impact cannot be overstated.

name: Composition with Lines by Piet Mondrian
desc: This Early Modern oil on canvas was completed during Mondrian’s transition from Cubism to Neoplasticism. A. Michael Noll in 1965 would go on to conduct a famous early computer art experiment with Mondrian’s Composition with Lines. He asked colleagues their preference between the Mondrian piece and his computer-created Computer Composition With Lines . This was an early attempt to compare the creative hand of the artist to the creative power of a machine. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: Mondrian and van Doesburg Found De Stijl
desc: Founded by Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg originally as a publication, De Stijl means style in Dutch. It is believed that this magazine, De Stijl, was the first time the term “neo-plasticism” was used. The De Stijl movement sought to achieve a harmonious and universal visual language through the use of reduced geometric forms and primary colors. The movement’s emphasis on simplicity, primary colors and abstraction has resonated throughout generative art’s history. In addition to a clear aesthetic influence, De Stijl’s emphasis on grids and modular systems would impact future generations of generative artists.

name: “On Growth and Form” Published by D’Arcy Thompson
desc: The book by Scottish mathematical biologist D’Arcy Thompson showed how mathematical transformations could describe a variety of organic forms. Thompson thus pioneered the use of mathematics in biology which helped move forward mathematics in art. D’Arcy’s work greatly impacted computer art’s aesthetic in the second half of the century, particularly the artificial life movement.

name: Fountain by Marcel Duchamp
desc: Considered by many to be the first conceptual artwork, a key predecessor of digital generative art, this ready-made of a urinal remains one of the most important works in twentieth century art. Fountain exemplifies the irreverence of Dada and continues to influence any Deleuzian art form that challenges traditional conventions

name: Untitled [Squares Arranged according to the Laws of Chance] by Hans Arp
desc: This piece’s use of chance demonstrates an early example of an artist relinquishing control to challenge traditional art production techniques. Arp supposedly allowed random processes to determine the placement of the squares on the canvas. This act and the similar work of Duchamp marked a departure from traditional artistic control, serving as an early example of the element of randomness as a creative force. Arp’s work challenged the notion of the artist as a sole creator and laid the foundation for later developments in generative art, where algorithms and computational systems generate artworks. This piece remains foundational conceptually to not only Dadaism but to Surrealism and generative art.
subjects: untitled (squares arranged according to the laws of chance)
untitled [squares arranged according to the laws of chance]

name: Painterly Architectonic by Liubov Popova
desc: Helping to introduce Cubism and Futurism into Russian art after visits to France and Italy before WWI, this piece is part of a series that demonstrates Popova’s Suprematist style. Popova, a pioneer of geometric abstraction and Suprematism, treated planes “like solid material entities,” laying them atop one another to create a radically new artistic language. Around fifteen years later, this layered-plane style would reemerge as Concrete art.

name: Edouard Jeanneret [Le Corbusier] and Amédée Ozenfant form Purism
desc: The publication of Après le Cubisme (After Cubism) began the Purism movement, proposing “a kind of painting in which objects are represented as powerful basic forms stripped of detail.” Purism relates to electronic and digital generative art due to its embrace of technology and a timeless machine aesthetic.

name: Red and Blue Chair by Gerrit Rietveld
desc: A canonical artefact of art history and one of the most important pieces of furniture ever built, the chair, designed in 1918 and painted about 1923, composed of 13 square-profiled battens, two rectangular panels and two armrests, was stripped of its volume to emphasize functionality. It stands as a representation of the De Stijl movement’s principles of abstract simplicity and functionality.

name: Walter Gropius founds Bauhaus
desc: The revolutionary art school aimed to bring art into contact with everyday life, leveling the distinction between fine and applied art. It was formed by Walter Gropius after he succeeded Henry van de Velde as the head of the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts . This school, as the name implies, was heavily influenced by the British Arts & Crafts movement of the late nineteenth century. Instructors included modern art titans, including Anni and Josef Albers , Gunta Stölzl , Wassily Kandinsky , Paul Klee , László Moholy-Nagy and Johannes Itten . The school, which would become heavily influenced by the ideas of Constructivism due to Moholy-Nagy and Kandinsky in particular, emphasized the integration of art with design and technology. Bauhaus teachings also encouraged experimentation, with new materials and techniques. These principles laid the foundation for the development of not only modern art and design but generative art as well. Additionally, the school’s approach to abstract geometric forms as well as the reduction of art to its essential elements have influenced generative art’s aesthetics. Finally, the Bauhaus’s progressive and holistic approach to art education along with its focus on the fusion of art and craft had a lasting impact on art and technology.
subjects: weimar school of arts and crafts

name: LHOOQ by Marcel Duchamp
desc: Along with Fountain , this Dada classic of a crude comment below the Mona Lisa on which Duchamp drew a mustache and beard, remains a classic example of irreverence towards traditional art. Although Duchamp never associated himself with any particular movement, his legacy has impacted several; in this case, its Dada.

name: “Tradition and the Individual Talent” by T.S. Eliot
desc: T.S. Eliot publishes “ Tradition and the Individual Talent ,” a critical essay that argues for greater understanding of the influence of canonical texts on any single writer and seeks to place the personality of the poet within a far greater tradition of literary voices and cultural ideas – prescient concepts that suggest ways in which AI may become valuable to writers. Three years later, in 1922, T.S. Eliot publishes The Waste Land , a landmark poem that freely interpolates material from a wealth of external sources, anticipating the synthesizing powers of large language models and deeply influencing the automated writing techniques of authors such as William Burroughs . -Sasha Stiles Image: Eliot in 1923 by Lady Ottoline Morrell (Public Domain)

name: Marcel Duchamp and Man Ray create Rotary Glass Plates [Precision Optics]
desc: An early example of Lumino-kinetic art, progenitor of electronic art, this piece consisted of painted glass plates rotating on an electric motor to create optical illusions. One of Ray’s and Duchamp’s experiments with machines and motion, Rotary Glass Plates shattered traditional notions that art had to be static. It also questioned optical perception, an important predecessor to the Op Art movement.

name: First Dadaist Fair Held in Berlin
desc: A pivotal moment in the history of avant-garde art, the First International Dada-Fair showcased Dada’s anti-art and anti-establishment philosophy of absurdity and provocation to the world for the first time. It featured works from some of Dada’s most prominent participants, including Hans Arp, Max Ernst and Hannah Höch .

name: Obstruction by Man Ray
desc: Along with Constructivists Rodchenko and Tatlin, Ray pioneered the use of mobiles (this one composed of 63 coat hangers), paving the way for future kinetic art and eventually all electronic art. This moment serves as a key example in art’s impulse towards kineticism in the early twentieth century. Artists, in an attempt to break free from the restraints of the static canvas, pushed to make art more dynamic and interactive, a huge leap along the path towards digital art.

name: Bauhaus Weaving Workshop Initiated by Gunta Stölzl
desc: After Gunta Stölzl asked for a class for women to be set up, the weaving workshop was created by the women themselves and taught by Helena Börner. This was the only workshop available to the women students at Bauhaus as all other workshops, from wood to metal, were open only to male students, and the Bauhaus had no architecture course until 1927.

name: Dada Head by Sophie Taeuber-Arp
desc: The pioneering abstract artist’s sculptures of abstract heads are now considered icons of the Dada movement, a vital predecessor to generative art.

name: Random Poetry (generation) by Tristan Tzara
desc: Possibly the most influential among the avant-garde experimentalist giants, Tzara says in his own words, in a 1920 manifesto later collected in Seven Dada Manifestos : "Take a newspaper. Take a pair of scissors. Choose an article as long as you are planning to make your poem. Cut out the article. Then cut out each of the words that make up this article and put them in a bag. Shake it gently. Then take out the scraps one after another in the order in which they left the bag. Copy conscientiously. The poem will be like you. And here you are a writer, infinitely original and endowed with a sensibility that is charming beyond the understanding of the vulgar." Burroughs spoke of its influence on him in “The Third Mind interview” (1977) as have many others. -Vuk Ćosić

name: Karel Čapek's play “R.U.R.” Names the Robot
desc: It was around this time that automaton started losing the verbal fight with the term, a hundred years later, we still use today: robot. And to be honest, not a great start for our relationship. Karel Čapek 's play R.U.R. ( Rossum's Universal Robots ) was published in Prague in November 1920 and first staged in January 1921. Its robots are artificial workers made from synthetic organic matter and built to free people from labor. Ah but they rebel and wipe out humanity. The word robot came from the Czech robota , forced labor. In proof that art is always relevant (wink), Karel credited his brother, the painter Josef Čapek , with suggesting the name. It would take several years for the word to gain widespread acknowledgement let alone popularity. In 1922 the play had gone to New York and was in London in 1923, along with an English translation. From there, the word spread from English into dozens of other languages. And here we are today still using it.

name: Tatlin and Rodchenko Found Constructivism
desc: Named by 1921 and led by Vladimir Tatlin and Alexander Rodchenko , Constructivism is arguably the most influential movement of the first half of the 20th c. on digital and generative art. Influenced by Picasso’s Cubist constructions and the techo-inspired Manifesto of Futurism , Tatlin and Rodchenko believed art should directly reflect the modern industrial world. Besides its importance in the development of kinetic and electronic art, Constructivism was highly influential on early, particularly European, computer art and Herbert W. Franke . Franke recognized that Constructivism’s visual language of lines and basic geometric forms lent itself naturally to code-based and computational art. Franke wrote that “the aim of many supporters of constructivist tendencies - a rejection of the personal element; a crystal-clear, objective presentation; the maximum precision - can be realized by the computer in a hitherto unparalleled degree.” Beyond Franke, computer pioneer researchgate.net : “I (that is, Ernest Edmonds ) had been committed to painting since my early-teenage years, strongly influenced by the constructivists. I started to use a computer in my artwork in 1968, when I wrote a program that searched for an arrangement, a layout, of a given set of picture elements.” An example of the Constructivist machine aesthetic can be found in Auro Lecci ’s computer-generated Slant One .

name: Students Responsible for Teaching Themselves at Bauhau Weaving Workshop
desc: Master of form Georg Muche “swore never to take a thread in his hand: He did not want to be associated with the feminine aura of weaving.” This led to Gunta Stölzl and Benita Otte taking courses at a technical school to teach their fellow classmates the technical aspects of working a loom.

name: K VII by László Moholy-Nagy
desc: Characterized by ordered, geometric forms, the work was completed one year before Moholy-Nagy began teaching at the Bauhaus . “Moholy-Nagy’s appointment signalled a major shift in the school’s philosophy away from its earlier crafts ethos towards a closer alignment with the demands of modern industry, and a programme of simple design and unadorned functionalism.”

name: Thomas Wilfred Begins His Lumia Public Performances
desc: Lumia is an Lumino-kinetic art form invented by Wilfred and performed on a device called a clavilux or “color organ.” These compositions of light were infinitely changing and had the appearance of a colorful aurora borealis. Lumia made Wilfred one of the most famous American artists of the 1920s. He would continue perfecting his craft for decades and was exhibited at MoMA in the influential 15 Americans (1952). Wilfred’s work with light was decades ahead of its time, paving the way for electronic, video and digital generative art, including the work of Nam June Paik .

name: Rayograph by Man Ray
desc: Rayographs, photographs made by placing objects directly on sensitized paper and exposing them to light reflected Dada’s interest in chance and the nonsensical. “The random objects leave behind a shadowy imprint that dissociates them from their original context.” These works stand as critical examples of early generative as well as experimental photography.

name: Oskar Schlemmer premières Triadisches Ballett
desc: The Constructivist Bauhaus teacher’s most famous work, this avant-garde artistic dance transformed dancers into geometrical shapes. Schlemmer’s aesthetics would go to influence Japanese Jikken Kobo. The following year, Schlemmer was hired as master of form at the Bauhaus theater workshop. Due to the popularity of performance, as the ballet toured, it helped to spread the word of Bauhaus around the world.

name: László Moholy-Nagy Begins Teaching at Bauhaus
desc: Moholy-Nagy remained at the Bauhaus until 1928, where he focused on painting, lithographs, montage, assemblage and photography. The pioneer of experimental photography, heavily inspired in later years by the upcoming Constructivism, advocated for a fusion of art and technology. His ideas about the role of art in modern society influenced the development of the Bauhaus and subsequent modernist movements.

name: Construction in Enamel by László Moholy-Nagy
desc: Moholy-Nagy’s piece, which he described over the telephone to a local enamel factory in Weimar, would go on to influence the Japanese Jikken Kobo movement, particularly Katsuhiro Yamaguchi ’s “order art.”

name: Composition 8 by Wassily Kandinsky
desc: While at the Bauhaus , Kandinsky further developed his Constructivist aesthetic by investigating the use of color, form, and composition to convey emotional and spiritual themes. One of Kandinsky’s most well-known works, Composition 8 also presages the dominant role of circles in his later work.

name: Bauhaus Repositions
desc: Originally conceived of to unify arts and crafts, the Bauhaus under Gropius began pivoting to design for mass production, adopting the slogan “Art into Industry.”

name: First exhibition of Bauhaus, Weimar
desc: This exhibition showcased the interdisciplinary nature of the school, highlighting works of painting, textiles, sculpture, design, architecture and graphics. It was important in establishing the school’s reputation as a center of modernism and its influence on the development of modern art and design.

name: Bauhaus Weaving Workshop Developes New Aesthetic
desc: Gunta Stölzl leads the women in the Bauhaus weaving workshop to alter its aesthetic, emphasizing tapestries based on abstraction and countering the previous Art-Nouveau narrative.

name: Constructivists Publish Their Manifesto in “Lef”
desc: Constructivism’s manifesto espoused the belief that art should directly reflect the modern industrial world: “The material formation of the object is to be substituted for its aesthetic combination. The object is to be treated as a whole and thus will be of no discernible ‘style’ but simply a product of an industrial order like a car, an aeroplane and such like. Constructivism is a purely technical mastery and organisation of materials.” Constructivism emphasized the integration of art and technology, seeking to create practical, functional objects that embodied the principles of modern industrial society. These ideas would also prove hugely influential to the Bauhaus . Tatlin aimed to bridge the gap between art and everyday life, embracing materials such as metal, glass, and other industrial materials. Constructivism focused on the notion of art as a social and political force for change, emphasizing collective creativity and the importance of utility and construction.

name: Mavo movement founded in Japan
desc: Led by Tomoyoshi Murayama , this radical Japanese art movement promulgated an interdisciplinary array of performance art, painting, illustration and architecture to communicate anti-establishment messages to the mainstream. Reacting to Japan ’s rapid modernization and industrial development, the Mavo group’s works focused on crisis, peril and uncertainty. Mavo sought to reintegrate art into daily life, a concept predating New Tendencies and GRAV by 40 years. Mavo thus was critical to the advancement of audience participation in art, an important concept in digital art.

name: André Breton Writes the “Surrealist Manifesto”
desc: One of the most important predecessors of generative art due to its use of chance, Breton called for artists to bypass reason and rationality by accessing their unconscious mind. Contemporary language artist, Sasha Stiles details its importance: “The French poet, critic and editor André Breton publishes the Surrealist Manifesto , in which he lays the groundwork for subsequent automated and aleatory writing techniques by defining Surrealism as ‘Psychic automatism in its pure state, by which one proposes to express…the actual functioning of thought…in the absence of any control exercised by reason, exempt from any aesthetic or moral concern.’”

name: Counter Composition V by Theo van Doesburg
desc: The signature work of van Doesburg features a simple composition of geometric shapes and colors arranged in a dynamic and asymmetrical pattern. The piece exemplifies the principles of De Stijl, seeking to create a universal language of form and color that could be applied to all aspects of art and design.

name: “The Isms of Art” by Hans Arp and El Lissitzky
desc: A critical publication by the leaders of the Dadaist and Constructivist movements documenting the turbulent developemtns of the art world in the first quarter of the twentieth century. The book opens with definitions of each movement by leading artists, followed by photographic plates surveying the isms of 1914 to 1924, among them Dadaism, Constructivism and Futurism. It serves as a visual exploration and representation of the diverse artistic movements of the early 20th century, showcasing their different ideologies and aesthetics.

name: Bell Labs Founded
desc: One of the most important developments in digital and generative art’s history, Bell Labs would go on to become instrumental in the development of computational art and animation. The list of pioneering engineers and artists with connections to the Lab is astonishing. The list includes: Billy Klüver , Kenneth Knowlton, A. Michael Noll , Béla Julesz , Edward Zajec , Leon Harmon , Claude Shannon , Stan Vanderbeek, Lillian Schwartz , Nam June Paik and Max Mathews . Their innovative work in the 1960s and 1970s was absolutely critical to the development of art and technology, laying the groundwork for the digital art revolution that would follow. In fact, Bell Labs’s Billy Klüver would co-found Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.) with Robert Rauschenberg in the ’60s. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: International Exposition of Modern Industrial and Decorative Arts, Paris
