desc: A key event in the fusion of art and industry, the exhibition saw avant-garde ideas from around the globe presented for the first time. It was instrumental to the development of modern design and architecture. The term Art Deco derives from this exhibition but was only coined in the 1960s.
subjects: international exposition of modern industrial and decorative arts

name: The Bauhaus Moves to the Iconic Dessau Campus
desc: Moving from Weimar to Dessau, this Walter Gropius designed building for the Bauhaus was envisioned as a “Gesamtkunstwerk” (comprehensive artwork). “The building contained many features that later became hallmarks of modernist architecture, including steel-frame construction, a glass curtain wall, and an asymmetrical, pinwheel plan,” according to the Met.

name: Bauhaus Weavers Revolt
desc: Following the move to Dessau , the weaving workshop relocated to a large studio with new looms. With Georg Muche , the workshop’s master of form, lacking the knowledge to operate the new equipment, the weavers demanded Gunta Stölzl take over. The demand led to unrest throughout the school and a reexamining of the masters.

name: Surrealists Experiment with Rules-Based Chance
desc: Based on parlor games, the group began creating “exquisite corpses,” which involved collaborative and random creations based on a set of rules. This technique was a precursor to rules-based systems producing random results.

name: Gunta Stölzl Named Director of Bauhaus Weaving Workshop
desc: Made head of workshop in 1927 and formally Jungmeister in 1928, holding the post until 1931, Stölzl became the first woman to fill a senior position at the Bauhaus due to the wide support of her students. It was after Stölzl took charge of the workshop that its importance and innovation increased.

name: Kazimir Malevich Publishes “The Non-Objective World”
desc: One of the most important theoretical sources in the development of abstract art, the book articulated the principles of Suprematism, which rejected representation in favor of pure abstraction. Suprematism sought to transcend materiality and represent the spiritual essence of art. Malevich advocated for non-objective art, stripping down forms to their basic geometric elements, primarily focusing on squares, circles and lines. Suprematism aimed to evoke a sense of pure aesthetic experience, emphasizing the supremacy of pure feeling and perception over representational content. The book articulates Malevich’s rejection of utilitarianism and focus on the exploration of geometric abstraction as a means to access universal truths and transcend the physical world. In contrast to Malevich’s Suprematism, Tatlin’s Constructivism aimed to combine art with utility, integrating art and technology. Constructivists sought to create practical, functional objects that embodied the principles of modern industrial society. While Constructivism emphasized functionality, industrial materials and the integration of art and society, Suprematism embraced non-objectivity, geometric abstraction and the pursuit of spiritual and universal truths.

name: Max Ernst Develops Pioneering Method of Chance in Painting, Grattage
desc: A fundamental development in the inclusion of chance in abstract art, grattage involves scraping or scratching the surface of a canvas covered with layers of paint, revealing the textures and patterns created by the different layers. Ernst used this experimental technique in his surrealist paintings, allowing chance and improvisation to guide the creation of the final image.

name: Philo Farnsworth Invents the “Image Dissector”
desc: One of the most celebrated and prolific inventors of all time, Farnsworth was the quintessential “mad scientist” and inspiration for Professor Farnsworth on TV series Futruama. His “image dissector” was an early television transmission tube that focused light on a detector in front of a tube, which could convert electrons into electrical signals visible by a television receiver. This tube was also the center of a longstanding legal battle between Farnsworth and RCA over the invention of the television. While Farnsworth won the battle, RCA ended up winning the war in the long run despite technology inferior to Farnsworhth’s.

name: Vannevar Bush constructs his Differential Analyser
desc: Mentioned in the Cybernetic Serendipity catalog as an important development in the history of cybernetics, the Differential Analyser was an early mechanical computer, invented by the American engineer, used to solve complex mathematical problems. With rotating gears and shafts, it performed calculations and allowed researchers to model physical phenomena such as the motion of planets and the behavior of fluids. Bush’s invention had a significant impact on cybernetic devices and the development of modern computers.

name: The Bauhaus Opens Workshops to All Students
desc: Under new director Hannes Meyer , women at the Bauhaus are allowed to choose their own workshops and admitted to study architecture. This long-overdue step towards greater gender inclusivity meant that the women students were no longer confined to the weaving workshop only.

name: Highway and Byways by Paul Klee
desc: Highways and Byways, a painting by the Swiss artist Paul Klee , is significant for its synthesis of Klee’s interests in geometric abstraction and music. Klee uses color to evoke a sense of movement and rhythm. It represents a high point in Klee’s career and exemplifies the artist’s innovative approach to painting, which influenced generations of artists in the 20th century, including Vera Molár.

name: Arithmetic Composition by Theo van Doesburg
desc: A work which presages the mathematics-based, geometric compositions of contemporary generative art, van Doesburg’s piece stands as an example of the De Stijl movement’s attempt to create a new visual language based on geometric forms and primary colors. Its diagonal composition reflects van Doesburg’s interest in the relationship between art and technology.

name: Light Prop for an Electric Stage by László Moholy-Nagy
desc: One of the first electrically powered kinetic sculptures, this kinetic light sculpture is an important example of the historical lineage connecting early Lumino-Kinetic Art to Op and Kinetic art, which led to the development of digital art. Created two years after Moholy-Nagy left the Bauhaus , this piece synthesizes his experiments there, incorporating light, technology and industrial materials.
subjects: light prop for an electric stage

name: Composition with Red Blue and Yellow by Piet Mondrian
desc: An iconic example of Mondrian’s Neo-Plasticism, characterized by simple geometric, rectilinear forms and primary colors, the piece explores asymmetry, pure planes of color and relational opposites. It represents a shift towards abstraction and a rejection of naturalism in art, becoming a seminal work in the development of abstract art and modernism.
subjects: composition with red, blue and yellow

name: Concrete Art Coined by Theo van Doesburg
desc: One of the foundational movements in the history generative art, the Dutch artist and architect’s term describes abstract art based on mathematic or scientific principles with an emphasis on planes and color. Concrete art to van Doesburg was not abstraction based on reality but was reality itself with a focus on the immediate materiality of art.

name: Color Structure by Joaquín Torres-García
desc: The father of South American geometric abstraction’s seminal work. Color Structure was critical to the development of modernist art in Latin America . Its grid-like composition of colorful geometric shapes was intended to express Torres-García’s philosophy of universal constructivism. The piece also demonstrates his interest in the principles of Neo-Plasticism also evident in the work of Piet Mondrian .

name: Gunta Stölzl Departs the Bauhaus
desc: Gunta Stölzl , pioneering weaver and textile artist, left the Bauhaus due to conflicts with its male-dominated administration, her support for left-wing politics and rising anti-semitism in Germany . Her departure was a significant loss for the school but Stölzl would continue to be a leading figure in the development of modernist textile art and design. She would become the first woman to be exhibited for textiles at MoMA .

name: Nazis Permanently Close the Bauhaus
desc: The Nazis permanently closed Bauhaus due to their opposition to its modernist and internationalist principles, which they saw as incompatible with their vision of a “pure” and traditional German culture. Many Bauhaus artists and designers were persecuted or forced to flee Germany as a result with many relocating to the United States , where Josef and Anni Albers joined Black Mountain College in North Carolina and Moholy-Nagy opened the New Bauhaus in Chicago .

name: George David Birkhoff Proposes the “Aesthetic Measure”
desc: This important development in the twentieth-century attempt to measure aesthetics described aesthetic effectiveness by its degree of complexity and order.

name: Black Mountain College Opens
desc: Black Mountain College was founded in North Carolina as an experimental liberal arts college with a focus on the arts, including music, visual arts, and creative writing. It became a seminal institution in the development of modernist art and education, hosting influential artists and thinkers such as John Cage , Anni and Josef Albers , Cy Twombly and Robert Rauschenberg . Several former Bauhaus faculty members, such as the Alberses, joined the Black Mountain College faculty. The college adopted many of the Bauhaus’s principles of interdisciplinary collaboration, experimentation, and the integration of art and technology.

name: Abstract Composition by Jean Hélion
desc: Vera Molnar saw this piece and was encouraged to create her own abstract, constructivist-inspired art, the computer art pioneer told Hans Ulrich Obrist . A vibrant and dynamic abstract painting, Hélion’s work was a challenge to traditional notions of representation and perspective.

name: Endless Rhythm by Robert Delaunay
desc: Endless Rhythm focuses on geometric shapes and contrasting color, indicating Delaunay’s move towards total abstraction. Delaunay’s work would go to influence the development of Op Art and Kinetic Art, key predecessors of digital art.

name: Joaquín Torres-García Brings Geometric Abstraction to Latin America
desc: After forty years abroad, the Uruguayan-SpanishTorres-García brought the ideas of geometric abstraction to Latin America in order to reconcile his affinity for the movement with the region’s own cultural traditions. His new style was known as Universalismo Constructivo (Constructive Universalism) and aimed to inject emotion and humanity into the austere aesthetics of De Stijl and Constructivism.

name: The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even (The Green Box) (La Mariée mise à nu par ses célibataires, même [Boîte verte] ) by Marcel Duchamp
desc: A paramount work in the intersection of chance and art, The Green Box consists of ninety-four loose documents that all related to the idea of chance. Arranged in no particular order, the viewer is free to explore the unbound pieces randomly, an important development to the increase of audience participation in the coming decades.
subjects: the bride stripped bare by her bachelors, even

name: Alan Turing Describes the Turing Machine
desc: Considered foundational to the development of computer science, Turing ’s “automatic machines” were computational devices consisting of readable and writeable tape that could implement computer algorithms.

name: Exhibition of Cubism and Abstract Art, MoMA
desc: A groundbreaking event in the history of abstraction and modernism in North America , this exhibition developed the narrative that adventurous artists were rejecting representation due to having grown “bored with painting facts.” The exhibition marked a shift in the global center of the art world from Europe to New York . This trend would dramatically accelerate during and after WWII, which was in its early phases in Asia . This instrumental exhibition’s weight can still be felt today as the narrative it created (proposed by MoMA ’s founding director Alfred H. Barr, Jr.) continues to shape how modernism is presented.

name: László Moholy-Nagy founds the Chicago Institute of Design
desc: Originally known as the New Bauhaus in Chicago , the school attracted former staff from the original Bauhaus such as György Kepes . The creation of an American Bauhaus played a role in tilting the global center of modernism to North America and carried on the original’s attempt to create a holistic aesthetic congruous with a modern industrial society.

name: Konrad Zuse Creates the Z1
desc: Zuse would finish the motor-driven, mechanical computer in 1938. The first freely programmable binary computer, the Z1 laid the groundwork for modern computers by using Boolean logic and incorporating program control. The Z1 used moving rods and plates to represent 1s and 0s, reading instructions from punched tape.

name: Konrad Zuse Completes the Z3
desc: The world’s first functioning programmable, digital computer, the Z3 paved the way for future advancements in computer science. Zuse built the Z3 in his parents’ Berlin apartment. The device was destroyed by the Allied bombing of Berlin in 1943.

name: Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil Patent Frequency Hopping
desc: Hedy Lamarr was one of Golden Age Hollywood's most sought after stars. But she was also an inventor. With all hands on deck during WWII on August 11, 1942, Lamarr and composer George Antheil received a US patent for a “Secret Communication System.” Known as frequency-hopping, the technique kept radio-guided torpedoes from being jammed. The transmitter and receiver would jump together between 88 frequencies, synchronized like a player piano. Although ultimately not used during the war, frequency hopping later became relevant with wireless communication. As such, Lamarr entered the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2014.

name: Abstract Expressionism Begins
desc: The first American avant-garde movement and deeply influenced by the Surrealist focus on tapping into the unconscious, Abstract Expressionism marked a transition from the hard-edged abstraction of the early twentieth century towards a more spontaneous and emotional form of self-expression. The movement is thought to have begun when Peggy Guggenheim commissioned Jackson Pollock ’s Mural for her apartment.

name: Exhibition by 31 Women at Peggy Guggenheim’s The Art of this Century
desc: Juried by Peggy Guggenheim and Marcel Duchamp , the exhibition was one of the first at Guggenheim’s The Art of this Century. The all-woman exhibition was a direct response to the male-dominated art scene and provided a platform for female artists to showcase their works. The show highlighted the critical role that female artists played in the development of Surrealism and abstract art.

name: Warren S. McCulloch and Walter Pitts publish “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity”
desc: This influential paper holds immense importance in the development of artificial intelligence (AI), showing that neural networks could perform logical operations and suggested that the brain might work like a digital computer. The paper presented a formal model of neural networks, demonstrating how complex cognitive processes could be understood through logical and mathematical principles. Their work proved foundational to the field of computational neuroscience, inspiring subsequent research in AI and machine learning. By bridging the gap between biology and computation, McCulloch and Pitts provided a framework for simulating intelligent behavior, influencing the development of AI algorithms and architectures. In papers from 1945-1952, McCulloch and Pitts would continue developing the mathematical theory of the mind.
subjects: a logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity

name: Arturo Rosenblueth, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow Publish “Behavior, Purpose and Teleology”
desc: The roots of cybernetics lie uncomfortably in the terrain of autonomous weapons and the military industrial complex. After all, the ideas grew smack in the middle of WWII. In January 1943 Arturo Rosenblueth of Harvard Medical School, Norbert Wiener of MIT and Julian Bigelow published “Behavior, Purpose and Teleology” in Philosophy of Science . Working on anti-aircraft fire control, Wiener and Bigelow conclude that voluntary action depends on feedback. The essay applied one scheme to animals and machines, citing a target-seeking torpedo: “All purposeful behavior may be considered to require negative feed-back.” Rosenblueth supplied the medical parallel, a patient with cerebellar disease whose hand oscillates more and more as it carries a glass of water to his mouth. He had presented the ideas at a 1942 Macy Foundation meeting in New York attended by Warren McCulloch. One of technology's original sins which this moment highlights is the inexorable tie between technology and weapons. It's all the more unsettling how long we've been trying to make weapons more responsive and lifelike.

name: “Language of Vision” by György Kepes
desc: Kepes, an artist, designer and theoretician, analyzes the effect of visual language on the structure of human consciousness. The book’s explored the concept of visual language and how elements such as line, color and form could be used to create new visual structures. In addition to influencing the post-war Japanese avant-garde, the book also provided a theoretical foundation for the creation of generative art. It outlined principles of composition as well as encouraging experimentation and innovation with basic forms, a task perfectly suited to algorithmic art.

name: Arturo Births Madí and AACI
desc: Termed “an essential document in the bibliography of 20th-century history” by Jorge Glusberg , the modest abstract art magazine’s first and only issue in 1944 was printed in the Buenos Aires Caballito district. The single issue, with a cover by Tomás Maldonado , is credited for birthing both the Asociación Arte Concreto-Invención (AACI) in 1945 as well as Gyula Kosice’s Madí in 1946. Both groups were inspired by the prominently featured work of Joaquin Torres García, founder of Latin American Constructivism, as well as the magazine’s advocacy for the societal benefits of geometric art.

name: Birth of Art Informel in France
desc: Responding to the horrors of WWII, European artists rejected the artistic traditions of figurative and geometric work in favor of anti-compositional forms and gestural techniques. Along with the movement’s stylistic relative in North America , Abstract Expressionism, Art Informel espoused spontaneity and expression.

name: Three Spheres I by M. C. Escher
desc: A master of celebrating mathematics, especially geometry, by incorporating it into his art, Escher’s work anticipates the use of a computer to visualize mathematics using algorithms.

name: ENIAC Developed
desc: ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), unveiled in February 1946, was the prototype from which modern computers evolved. Developed by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert of the University of Pennsylvania, ENIAC is commonly called the first general-purpose electronic and digital computer. Laying the foundation for modern computing, ENIAC demonstrated that high-speed digital computing was possible with vacuum tubes. Considered “the first digital computer, [it] weighed over thirty tons, consumed 200 kilowatts of electrical power, and contained around 19,000 vacuum tubes that got very hot very fast, and as a result constantly burned out, making it very unreliable.” Commissioned in 1943, ENIAC was financed by the United States Army, Ordnance Corps during WWII to calculate artillery firing tables. Thus, the history of computing coincides with the military and warfare, which will continue for the several decades. It would not be until the late 1970s that computers would lose the air of mystery and fear that largely surrounded them with the advent of personal computers and video games. Famously it was six women who programmed it, known as the ENIAC Six: Kathleen McNulty, Jean Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Frances Bilas and Ruth Lichterman. They set up the trajectory calculation shown at the February 1946 unveiling despite not even being introduced at the event.

name: The Asociación Arte Concreto-Invención (AACI) Founded
desc: Argentine artist Tomás Maldonado and poet Edgar Bayley founded AACI with their 1945 exhibition and manifesto. This movement’s emphasis on geometric abstraction and rejection of representation would go on to influence art in South America while laying the groundwork for a generative art aesthetic.

name: Grupo Madí Movement
desc: Formed by artists including Gyula Kosice , Carmelo Arden Quin , and Rhod Rothfuss , Madí embraced concrete art and sought to create a new visual language using abstract shapes and colors, considered an important part of the history of Concrete Art in Latin America .

name: Luminous Structures by Gyula Kosice
desc: The earliest attempt to use neon light as the principal material in a sculpture. Neon art was foundational in the development of lumino-kinetic art and, therefore, electronic art.

name: Birth of Early Digital Tools
desc: This year saw three key developments in the technology that would enable computer art. • The first point plotters begin development: Electronics Associates, Inc. • “Light Gun,” precursor of the light pen, is developed by the military for the Whirlwind project.

name: Molnár’s Paris: Vera Molnár Moves to Paris
desc: Veronika “Vera” Gács arrived in Paris on December 10, 1947, with her soon-to-be husband, François Molnár . “I was obsessed with the desire to see modern art, and for me that could only mean Paris,” she later recalled.1 The twenty-three-year-old Vera stayed with François at a hotel on Rue de l’Hirondelle, her first place of residence in the city. There she would produce her first creative expression in Paris, drawing the house across the street from her hotel window. The Hungarian expat would call the city home for the next seventy-six years.

name: Jean-José Marchand and Georges Mathieu coin the term “lyrical abstraction”
desc: A substyle of the European Art Informel, Lyrical Abstraction favored anti-compositional forms and loose gestural techniques. It was related to the American Abstract Expressionism and influenced by Surrealism’s spontaneity and irrationality.

name: Bell Labs Team Discovers the Transistor
desc: Replacing the vacuum tube-concept of ENIAC , the discovery of the transistor by the team of Shockley, Bardeen and Brattain at Bell Labs sparked a revolution in electronics. In just a few short years electronic devices including radios and computers could be produced much more reliably due to transistors.

name: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Established
desc: This non-profit professional membership group was the first association for computing. In 1969 it would produce the offshoot Special Interest Group on Graphics and Interactive Techniques ( SIGGRAPH ), whose annual conference began in 1974 , which to this day plays a critical role in organizing events and maintaining a database of computer graphics developments. ACM would organize an annual Computer Arts Festival onwards from 1968.

name: Kathleen Booth Writes an Early Assembly Language
desc: Assembly language, a complex computational layer just above binary that every higher-level language leverages, is thus foundational. Along with the ENIAC Six , another often overlooked woman in the history of programming is the English mathematician Kathleen Booth . At Birkbeck College in London, Booth worked with husband Andrew Donald Booth on their Automatic Relay Calculator, writing Coding for A.R.C. in 1947. It set out a symbolic notation for instructions that stood between the programmer and the machine's raw numbers and counted among the first assembly languages. The Booths went on to build the APE(X)C computers in the early 1950s, with Kathleen Booth later writing one of the first books on programming, Programming for an Automatic Digital Calculator (1958).

name: Cybernetics Is Born
desc: Norbert Wiener’s Cybernetics was published the same year as Claude Shannon ’s " A Mathematical Theory of Communication .” Max Bense would apply both their works to aesthetics in his pioneering work, Aesthetica (1965) , which laid the theoretical foundations of digital and AI art with computer art. Cybernetics thus played a vital role in both the birth of digital art and artificial intelligence, thus making it one of the single most important moments on the timeline. Max Bense and his role at the University of Stuttgart explains the connection to computer art, specifically. He taught the first European computer artists, Georg Nees and Frieder Nake , leaving an indelible marks on their thinking that last to this day, as this 2018 talk by Nake demonstrates. For artificial intelligence, cybernetics was an early attempt to unite machines and organic beings in a functional way, as it sought a theory of control, feedback and communication applicable to machines as well as animals. In the book Art in the Age of Machine Learning, author Sofian Audry argues that the concept of machine learning dates back to cybernetics. According to the writer Jack Burnham , curator of the legendary Software exhibition : “One of the landmarks in the history of science occurred in 1947 when the M.I.T. mathematician Norbert Wiener along with his colleague Arture Rosenblueth of Harvard, coined the word Cybernetics.”
subjects: art in the age of machine learning

name: Claude Shannon Develops Information Theory with “A Mathematical Theory of Communication”
desc: Claude Shannon ’s "A Mathematical Theory of Communication” was published the same year as Norbert Wiener’s Cybernetics . Max Bense would apply both their works to aesthetics in his pioneering work, Aesthetica (1965) , which laid the theoretical foundations of digital and AI art with computer art. Cybernetics thus played a vital role in both the birth of digital art and artificial intelligence, thus making it one of the single most important moments on the timeline. Max Bense and his role at the University of Stuttgart explains the connection to computer art, specifically. He taught the first European computer artists, Georg Nees and Frieder Nake , leaving an indelible marks on their thinking that last to this day, as this 2018 talk by Nake demonstrates. Written at Bell Labs , Shannon’s paper “defined in mathematical terms what information is and how it can be transmitted in the face of noise. What had been viewed as quite distinct modes of communication--the telegraph, telephone, radio and television--were unified in a single framework.” Shannon’s earlier work from 1937 included an early design of a digital circuit around the same time as Konrad Zuse began working on the Z3 and his own digital circuits.

name: Molnár’s Paris: Vera and Francois Molnár Marry and Find Studio Space
desc: Married and now named Vera Molnár , the young couple left their Parisian hotel to live with her affluent Franco-Hungarian family in the suburbs of Ermont-Eaubonne. The newlywed couple spent a year living in a small caretaker’s lodge on the property. The Molnárs had access to a studio on the estate, which delighted the young artists and made their visiting artist friends extremely jealous. This idyllic situation, however, would not last long, as a minor family scandal forced them to relocate. It was around this time in the late ’40s that Vera began experimenting with abstraction, after encountering the work of Albrecht Dürer .

name: The Mathematical Basis of the Arts by Joseph Schillinger
desc: This book, influential to later computer artists, promoted the concept that codified mathematical language could generate art when combined with a machine.
subjects: the mathematical basis of the arts

name: CoBrA Formed
desc: Asger Jorn organized CoBrA with Karel Appel , Constant, Corneille , the writer Christian Dotremont and Joseph Noiret ; Pierre Alechinsky joined the following year. Named after the first letters of the capitals of the founders’ home countries ( Copenhagen , Brussels and Amsterdam ), CoBrA rejected rationality, individualism and classicism in art. Embracing collaboration and Surrealism, CoBrA also rejected the notion of the lone-genius artist, a stance echoed in the following decade by Victor Vasarely and GRAV.

name: Jean Dubuffet’s Art Brut
desc: Dubuffet founded the Compagnie de l’Art Brut to promote the study of Art Brut. A French term that translates as “raw art”, Art Brut rejected “art culturel” (cultural art) and embraced forms such as graffiti or naïve art made outside the academic tradition of fine art. This movement serves as a predecessor to early computer-generated art of the upcoming decades which also largely rejected formal art training.

name: William Grey Walter Constructs the First Electronic Autonomous Robots
desc: Built across 1948 and 1949, this self-navigating, pathfinding robot was an important development in cybernetics (and robotics), as it could react to external factors and changing conditions like a biological system. This work prefigured the cybernetic sculpture of the ’60s and ’70s.

name: Yoru no Kai Founded
desc: “The Night Society” in English, Yoru no Kai, founded by Taro Okamoto and Kiyoteru Hanada , played a preeminent part in forming Japan ’s post-war avant-garde. It influenced the development of the highly experimental Jikken Kobo and Gutai movements, both critical to the development of Japanese media art.

name: Jack Kerouac Introduces Phrase “Beat Generation”
desc: Writing in response to the atrocities of WWII, the Beat Poets (including Allen Ginsberg and Lawrence Ferlinghetti ) rebel against convention and seek to expand consciousness via experiments in automated writing, including hallucinogenics, spiritual rituals, and aleatory techniques meant to empower spontaneity and unfetter truth from the constraints of human reason.

name: Klára Dán von Neumann Codes the First Monte Carlo Simulations on ENIAC
desc: Machines leveraging chance with stored programs, the roots actually extend to just after WWII with the story of Klára Dán von Neumann . Besides how often overlooked early women programmers were, the story of Klára Dán von Neumann also reminds us (again and again) of the uncomfortable and unrelenting connection between computers and the military, including weapons as unsavory as the atomic variety. In the spring of 1948 Klára Dán von Neumann (wife of John von Neumann ) wrote and ran the code for a series of Monte Carlo simulations of nuclear chain reactions for Los Alamos on ENIAC . The machine had only just been converted to run programs stored in memory. The method, devised by Stanisław Ulam and John von Neumann with Nicholas Metropolis , answered questions too complex to calculate directly by following thousands of random paths and counting the outcomes. Her programs were among the first to use a modern, stored-program design. Chance put to work by a machine, the same principle runs through generative art from Georg Nees , Vera Molnár and onward.

name: Norbert Wiener Publishes “Cybernetics”
desc: Norbert Wiener , the MIT mathematician whose significance is covered extensively on this timeline, published Cybernetics: or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine in 1948. Cybernetics as a term comes from the Greek for steersman, and named a science of feedback. It described how systems, living or mechanical, measure the effects of their actions and correct themselves. Wiener drew on his wartime work on anti-aircraft prediction, mentioned previously in this Timeline and on meetings with Warren McCulloch, Walter Pitts , John von Neumann and others. The impact of cybernetics on computation and AI is foundational to both. So, it's pretty important. For art, its ideas reached artists through Max Bense in Stuttgart and Jasia Reichardt 's 1968 exhibition Cybernetic Serendipity .

name: W. Ross Ashby Builds the Homeostat
desc: From the history of automatons to early robots, but especially around this time post WWII, people started dreaming of "Thinking Machines." Not just "mindless" instruction followers but machines capable of their own thought like the human brain. That includes adaptability. The homeostat was one of the first devices capable of adaptation by mimicking supposed brain functions by reaching equilibrium with pivoting magnets. At Barnwood House, a psychiatric hospital in Gloucester, England , W. Ross Ashby and his laboratory assistant Denis Bannister completed the homeostat in March 1948 from four ex-RAF bomb control units. Again we see technology and war's close ties. Ashby himself was a central figure of the post-war British cyberneticists. Each unit carried a pivoted magnet and fed its output to the other three. When a magnet swung too far, a stepping switch gave its unit new circuit values, drawn from a table of random numbers, until all four magnets settled at the center again. Ashby called this ultrastability . In January 1949 Time called the machine “the closest thing to a synthetic brain so far designed by man.” Ashby set out the theory in Design for a Brain (1952). While the homeostat's complicated and esoteric functioning no longer persists mechanically, the ideas that the machine pointed to would become some of the most relevant and important in the decades to today.

name: "Anni Albers: Textiles” Exhibition at Museum of Modern Art
desc: This landmark exhibition was the Museum of Modern Art’s first devoted to the work of a single textile artist. The exhibitions tour over the next four years would establish Albers as one of the most important artists of her day.

name: Composition by Kenneth Martin
desc: This abstract painting in the Tate collection serves as an important example of material (non-digital) generative art. This work marked Martin’s move towards “pure invention” and rules-based work. He was influenced during this period by D’Arcy W Thompson’s On Growth and Form .

name: Yomiuri Indépendant Begins
desc: More commonly referred to as Yomiuri Anpan, the annual non-juried exhibition played a crucial role in the birth of Japanese postwar avant-garde art. Famously democratizing, anyone could show their work by paying the fee in an attempt to promote freedom of expression and thought. Supervised by Japanese Surrealist icon Shuzo Takiguchi , instrumental in the formation of Jikken Kobo, Yomiuri Anpan offered an ideal space for independent artists and the most experimental works (even judged by today’s standards).

name: Donald Hebb Publishes “The Organization of Behavior”
desc: It was around this mid-century turn in history when the advancements in neuroscience provided scientists in many different fields, a better understanding of the inner-workings of the human brain, neurons. This is critical because science and technology influence each other. And this work would provide future computer scientists (see Rosenblatt below) a brain-based model on which to inspire their work. The paper itself was by McGill University psychologist Donald O. Hebb , who published The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory . He proposed that when one nerve cell repeatedly takes part in firing another, some growth process or metabolic change makes the first more efficient at firing the second. Frequently repeated stimulation would build groups of such cells, which he called cell assemblies, and he described a series of their actions as the thought process. Early AI researcher Frank Rosenblatt named Hebb’s work as an inspiration for his 1958 perceptron. The slogan “cells that fire together, wire together” came later, from the neurobiologist Carla Shatz in a 1992 Scientific American article.

name: Alan Turing Proposes the “Turing Test”
desc: Originally called the imitation game, the Turing test is meant to determine whether a computer or AI can think like a human being. The test consists of a human interviewing both a person and machine. The machine passes the Turing test if the interviewer cannot correctly identify which is the machine and which is the person.

name: Ben Laposky Makes the First Oscillons
desc: Ben Laposky produces the first graphics generated by electronic machines, a critical step on the way to the digitization of generative art with proto-computer art. Using an oscilloscope in 1950, Ben F. Laposky originated the concept of graphics generated by electronic machines, creating his now legendary oscillons. These “electrical compositions” are regarded as among the first electronic graphics. Image is copyrighted by Ben Laposky and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection .

name: Molnár’s Paris: Molnárs Move to Belleville
desc: The Molnárs were forced to leave Vera’s bourgeois family estate to make room for a relative and his young girlfriend, who had an unexpected pregnancy and needed to marry right away. Given some money for rent, Vera and François were confronted with the harsh realities of Parisian real estate. They found a one-room apartment in Belleville “with a tiny kitchen and the toilet on the landing. Horrible. But we still drew and it still worked. We survived,” she later recollected. When asked at the time where she lived, Vera replied, “You wouldn’t believe me; it’s horrendous. Belleville.”

name: Alejandro Otero Begins His Collage Work
desc: This major Venezuelan kinetic artist and abstract geometric painter began his collage work with found materials inspired by Mondrian. These would lead to one of his significant contributions, Coloritmo (Colorhythms).

name: Jesús Rafael Soto Settles in Paris
desc: A seminal figure in the development of Kinetic Art, Soto’s arrival in Paris put him in contact with Victor Vasarely , Yaacov Agam , Jean Tinguely and others connected with the Salon des Réalités Nouvelles. The pioneer of kinetic and optical art, characterized by geometric shapes and movement, used simple shapes and colors to create visually engaging artworks, paving the way for computer-generated art.

name: Early Computers Play Tic-Tac-Toe, Nim, Chess and Draughts
desc: Popularized in today's imagination by DeepMind 's AlphaGo, machine intelligence and games has a long history. In fact, in the early 1950s, very early computers around the world started playing basic games, like tic-tac-toe with real people. First was the 1950 Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto , where Josef Kates’s Bertie the Brain played tic-tac-toe against visitors. Then in 1951, Ferranti’s Nimrod played nim at the Festival of Britain’s Science Exhibition in London. Both machines were built for that one specific game only, though. In contrast, Dietrich Prinz used the general-purpose Ferranti Mark I at the University of Manchester to solve simple mate-in-two chess problems in November 1951. Finally, between 1951 and 1952 Christopher Strachey (of love-letter fame) wrote a draughts program that looked a few moves ahead and valued positions by the pieces left on the board. Given wrong input, it printed “I REFUSE TO WASTE ANY MORE TIME. GO AND PLAY WITH A HUMAN BEING.” We have always welcomed the challenge from machines, particularly as they wobbled clumsily in their early days. Now, in the second quarter of the twenty-first century, artificial intelligence can beat humans at essentially any digital task or game. The test has turned to robotics as the next human vs machine game frontier.

name: Edmund C. Berkeley Begins Publishing “Computers and Automation”
desc: Beginning in September 1951, Edmund C. Berkeley published Computers and Automation, the first magazine dedicated to the computing revolution. Next decade, Computers and Automation would play a vital role in the development of computer art with its “Computer Art Contest” beginning in 1963 .

name: John von Neumann Devises Cellular Automata
desc: The Hungarian-American mathematician von Neumann’s conception of cellular automata (CA), suggested by Stanislaw Ulam , demonstrated the potential for simple rules to give rise to complex and unpredictable behavior. CA has been foundational to the development of generative art as CA profoundly influenced fields such as artificial life, complexity science, and computer graphics.

name: Ivan Moscovich Begins Experimenting with Mathematical Forms
desc: Mathematician Ivan Moscovich experimented with different mechanisms to create complex curves and shapes based on mathematical formulas. His work demonstrated the potential of algorithmic processes to generate intricate and visually appealing designs. Moscovich’s work was an early example of the intersection between mathematics, computer programming, and art.

name: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds Build the SNARC Neural Network Machine
desc: SNARC (Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator), the first artificial neural network, was composed of simple electronic circuits that could learn from their environment and adjust their behavior accordingly. Using 3,000 vacuum tubes to simulate a network of 40 neurons, it paved the way for the development of modern machine learning and artificial intelligence.

name: The Ferranti Mark I Is the First Commercially Available Electronic Computer
desc: Based on its prototype, the legendary Manchester Mark I, the Ferranti Mark I was the world’s first commercially available general-purpose digital computer.

name: Jikken Kobo Begins
desc: Meaning “Experimental Workshop” in English, Jikken Kobo was a radically experimental Japanese art collective, with a highly Deleuzian approach to art and the technology of the time. They created groundbreaking works that integrated technology, music, performance and visual art, using electronic devices and new media to create innovative and immersive experiences for their audiences. At the time in the early ’50s, this was one of the most radical art movements in the world.

name: Imaginary Landscape No 4 by John Cage
desc: The singular pioneer of generative music, John Cage began to utilize chance in his compositions around this time with “Imaginary Landscape No 4″ and “Music of Changes.” In “Imaginary Landscapes,” twelve radios were played at once with their broadcasts determined by chance and out of Cage’s control.

name: Spectrum Colors Arranged by Chance by Ellsworth Kelly
desc: Composed during his time in France , this part of a series of chance-arranged spectrum collages marked the shift of Kelly’s work towards chance methodologies as well as work on a grid. Inspired by Dadaism and Surrealism, this preeminent example of chance in art has strongly influenced later generations of generative artists as well as bearing conceptual and form resemblance to the color chart work of Gerhard Richter .

name: Around Is Around by Norman McLaren
desc: A pioneering work in the development of proto-computer abstract animation, Around Is Around, made with Evelyn Lambart and Chester Beachell , is a ten-minute long animated film that was groundbreaking for its time. It used an oscilloscope to produce certain abstract images, one the first published animations to do so. The British Film Institute expounds : “This experiment blazes so many trails that we need to list them before considering which is merely a picturesque by-path, and which may be expected to lead some where. Among the more important novelties exemplified are: (i) Three-dimensional abstract form. (ii) Abstract form plus stereophonic music. (iii) Abstract form produced from hand-drawn track photographed frame-by-frame. (iv) Abstract form produced by normal-speed cinematography. (v) Three-dimensional form produced by synthesis from a series of two-dimensional images.”

name: MIT Demonstrates the Whirlwind Computer
desc: Begun in the mid-1940s under Jay Forrester at MIT to drive a programmable flight simulator for the Office of Naval Research, Whirlwind was demonstrated processing live radar data in September 1950. The Whirlwind is a significant step in the evolution of computing technology as it was the first computer that could display real-time graphics and text with its oscilloscope screen. The computer would last until 1959 when it was finally shut down due to its large costs.

name: Theater Piece No. 1 by John Cage
desc: Kicking off the Neo-Dada movement and critical to the development of performance art, Cage’s Theater Piece No. 1 paved the way for the movement’s collaborative, multimedia and chance-based nature. The piece included several simultaneous, improvized performance elements including a poetry reading, music, dance, photography, film and plastic work (four panels of Robert Rauschenberg ’s White Paintings hung from the ceiling). Other than assigning the mediums, Cage “let each individual artist determine the specifics of their role within the performance, emphasizing the function of chance in determining the course of the event.”

name: Love-Letters by Christopher Strachey
desc: A landmark in the history of computer-generated text, Strachey’s love letter algorithm (or M.U.C.) created generative poems by combining words selected from a database via the random generator of the Ferranti Mark I . It anticipates the combinatorial procedures the computer artists of the ’60s, among them Noll, Nake and Nees, would arrive at independently. Besides its massive importance in the development of information theory and the computer art of the ’60s, Love-Letters remains pivotal to how we think about digital generative art today. Sasha Stiles writes of this event’s importance: “In collaboration with Alan Turing , programmer Christopher Strachey creates an automated love-letter generator for the Manchester Mark I computer [the Ferranti Mark 1] – the world’s first experiment in text-generating software.” Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: Founding of the Independent Group (IG)
desc: The Independent Group (IG), a collective of British artists, critics, and designers who came together in the early 1950s, explored the intersection of pop culture, mass media imagery, and art in technology. They sought to bridge the gap between high art and popular culture and were interested in the impact of new technologies on art and society. IG members Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi would go on to infulence computer art again in the early ’70s influence Slade to adopt technology in art’s teaching. Thus, they were a principal group in the surge of participatory and technological art of the ’50s and ’60s whose influence extends far beyond. The group’s members, including Hamilton, John McHale , Paolozzi and Alison and Peter Smithson , even paved the way for the Pop Art movement and influenced contemporary art and design. Hamilton, McHale and Paolozzi were in particular interested in art’s mechanization. IG’s collage work juxtaposed art and technology in a way that was revelatory and radical at the time. The group’s vision to anticipate both mass media and digital art make them critical touchstones in the history of the mechanization of art and, thus, on-chain generative art.

name: Abstronic by Mary Ellen Bute
desc: Pioneering work of abstract electronic animation Using an oscilloscope, Bute was the creator of some of the earliest electronically generated images. In 1952, she created the landmark experimental film Abstronic, (a portmanteau of the words “abstract” and “electronic”). Her abstract animations anticipated the upcoming aesthetic language of computer art by incorporating Lissajous curves and geometric abstraction. Bute was captivated by the proposition of drawing with light. She revealed that with only knobs and switches “I can ‘draw’ with a beam of light with as much freedom as with a brush.” In fact, she “would rather use light to draw with instead of making thousands of drawings.” Bute was one of the first people in history to recognize that when a human and electronic instrument collaborate, “the creative possibilities are limitless.”

name: Birth of Neo-Dada
desc: While not formally named until the early 1960s by Barbara Rose , we consider the birth of Neo-Dada to have occurred in 1952 with John Cage’s Theater Piece No. 1 . This seminal, multi-media, collaborative work of performance art involved unscripted poetry, music and Robert Rauschenberg ’s White Painting (1951), four panels of which hung above the performers. These elements would all become hallmarks of the Neo-Dada movement in the coming years. Paving the way for Pop Art, Minimalism and Conceptualism, the term Neo-Dadaism was applied to the works of artists such as Jasper Johns , Merce Cunningham , John Cage , Robert Rauschenberg and Allan Kaprow . Marcel Duchamp ’s arrival in New York and increasing influence can partially explain the movement’s genesis. Neo-Dada artists are known for their usage of mass media, found objects and performance. Most importantly for generative art, Neo-Dada was known for its embrace of chance, from Kaprow (performance) to Cunningham (dance) and Cage (music). In this sense, Neo-Dada was profoundly impactful on contemporary generative art. It was also a predecessor to the digital mass media art of the ’80s and ’90s, which, according to Casey Reas was one of the pre-conditions for NFTs.

name: Electronic Abstractions by Ben Laposky
desc: The Origins of Computer Art This series of experimental artworks by Ben Laposky was generated on analogue equipment by photographing oscilloscope patterns created by electronic circuits. He called these resulting images “Oscillons.” These works are among the earliest examples of electronically generated images. In 1953, Laposky exhibited fifty Oscillons as photographs, kinetic oscilloscope displays, light boxes and movies at the Sanford Museum in Cherokee, Iowa.

name: Arthur Samuel’s Checkers Program Learns from Experience
desc: It's not hard to understand why DeepMind 's first thought with AI was games. As several ( El Ajedrecista ) other ( the chess-playing Turk ) moments ( the first game programs ) have mentioned, games and machine learning have a long history. But in the early '50s it's remarkable these machines could even approach playing a game like checkers, several decades before Deep Blue started beating chess world champions. Legendary ML computer scientist Arthur Samuel, who IBM credits with coining the term machine learning, wrote his first checkers program for the IBM 701 in 1952. His paper “Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers,” in the July 1959 IBM Journal of Research and Development , described two methods: saving positions the program had scored and adjusting its scoring formula’s weights. Those weights changed as one copy, Alpha, played another, Beta. A computer, Samuel wrote, “can be programmed so that it will learn to play a better game of checkers than can be played by the person who wrote the program.”

name: Grace Murray Hopper Invents General Programming Languages
desc: Grace Hopper is one of the most important pioneers in the development of computer programming. Hopper pioneered the concept of automatic programming and in 1952 she developed the first compiler (A-0). Most critically, Hopper was the first to write programs in words rather than symbols. By 1957 she had completed FLOW-MATIC (B-0), the first English-language business data processing compiler. FLOW-MATIC became the main model for COBOL, specified in 1959 by a committee drawn from computer manufacturers and the Pentagon on which Hopper served as technical adviser, as a language capable of operating on different types of computers. Hopper thus enabled general computer languages, which would profoundly and irrevocably impact computer technology in the long-term. In the short-term, it also helped to significantly expand the number of people who could interact with computers.

name: Antennae with Red and Blue Dots by Alexander Calder
desc: This important example of kinetic sculpture, dated c.1953 by Tate , was created using a set of rules (i.e. “the smallest black elements should hang as far from the largest black elements as possible, not directly beneath them”) to create random motion. Kinetic sculpture was a critical predecessor to the digital motion of electronic (generative) art.
subjects: antennae with red and blue dots

name: Mood Contrasts by Mary Ellen Bute
desc: Bute’s oscillograph-made, pioneering abstract film saw Rimsky Korsakov’s “Hymn to the Sun” and “Dance of the Tumblers” visually interpreted by an array of Surrealist visual images.

name: Oscillons 34, 26, 14, 47 by Ben Laposky
desc: These pivotal works of proto-computer art serve as a link between analog and the upcoming digital art-making devices. Image is copyrighted by Ben Laposky and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection .

name: Plans mobiles by Pol Bury
desc: Plans mobiles (Mobile Planes), made from 1953 to 1955, perfectly illustrates a “new energy from the possibility of movement” in art. These reliefs of flat metal and painted wood mounted on pivots, turned by hand, serve as an important step in the development of interactive art.

name: Jikken Kōbō’s Fifth Presentation Introduces the Autoslide Works
desc: As proto-video art, this exhibition was an important precursor to electronic art. It combined experimentally composed music with surrealistic visuals. As told by Jikken Kōbō co-founder, Yamaguchi Katsuhiro: “Asahigraph editor Izawa Tadasu introduced Kōbō to the Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation (later SONY), which had developed an “autoslide projector,” a slide projector with synchronized sound. The group established a relationship with the company, and the Kōbō members worked together to create an audiovisual piece for this device.”

name: Musicolour (1953–57), Gordon Pask
desc: Exhibited at Cybernetic Serendipity , this ahead of its time cybernetic sculpture anticipated interactivity in electronic art. An interactive installation that translated musical input into visual displays of colored lights, Musicolour utilized sensors to detect the pitch, rhythm, and dynamics of the music, generating a real-time visual representation of the audio. Musicolour blurred distinctions between music and visual art, pioneering the concept of synesthesia and the integration of different sensory modalities in artistic experiences. This groundbreaking work inspired subsequent generations of artists and researchers to explore the intersection of sound and visuals, leading to the development of generative art practices that create dynamic and interactive audio-visual compositions. Musicolour’s influence can be seen in the use of real-time data and the integration of multiple sensory inputs in contemporary digital generative art.

name: Roald Dahl's “The Great Automatic Grammatizator”
desc: That language is mathematical and conceivably can be automated like a calculator is no new thought as many pre-Modern language "versifiers" and other tools have taught us. But still something is particularly prescient about this Roald Dahl mid-century description of something approaching an LLM. Dahl's collection of short stories Someone Like You , published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York in 1953, includes ours of interest: “The Great Automatic Grammatizator.” Its hero, Adolph Knipe, an engineer who has helped build a giant computing machine, decides that English grammar follows rules almost as strict as mathematics and builds a machine that writes stories and novels to order. He and his employer, Mr. Bohlen, flood the market, then pay real authors to put their names to machine-written books and stop writing. In a tragic twist, the narrator, a writer, is one of the few who refuses, and his children go hungry. It's a bleak tale of an author's insecure anxieties decades too soon. But it seems to be coming truer by the day in the 2020s.

name: Pierre de Latil Publishes Thinking by Machine
desc: It's almost comforting that over seventy years ago, we were similarly tantalized by the seductive power of machinic intelligence. As soon as it became clear that machines were excellent at following instructions, we seemed to expect them to also be able to think, on their own. We can see this impulse from a book in France that helped bring the ideas of cybernetics to the continent and, globally, popularize the idea that machines were somehow capable of thinking. The French science journalist Pierre de Latil published La Pensée artificielle with Gallimard in 1953; it appeared in English in 1956 as Thinking by Machine: A Study of Cybernetics . Writing for general readers, de Latil explained the new science of feedback and control through the machines of its founders, among them W. Ross Ashby 's homeostat and W. Grey Walter's electronic tortoises, and asked whether such devices could be said to think. The American edition even carried a foreword by Isaac Asimov. Are machines really intelligent, really thinking or just fooling us into believing they are? These are persistent questions stretching back decades. Are we closer to an answer today?

name: Gutai Movement in Japan
desc: Founded by Jiro Yoshihara , Gutai was a radically experimental movement even by today’s standards. Its experimental approach to art-making combined with its interest in technology, participation and conceptual art paved the way for later artists in Japan to explore generative processes and techniques.

name: Max Bense Begins Publishing Aesthetica
desc: Bense’s Aesthetica, foundational to computer art history, established the theoretical foundation of computer art. Bense proposed a systematic approach to analyzing the form and structure of art, emphasizing the importance of mathematical and logical principles. Bense’s ideas would later greatly influence his students, Georg Nees and Frieder Nake , as well as the direction of the computer art pioneers’ work.

name: Ivan Serpa Founds The Grupo Frente
desc: The Brazilian movement rejected strict adherence to the orthodoxy of purity, science, and math. Grupo Frente was interested in representing organic, nonfigurative forms. They promoted increased creative intuition in geometric abstraction. The movement was instrumental in the development of Concrete Art and geometric abstraction, particularly in Latin America .

name: Molnár’s Paris: Rue de Gergovie Apartment and Studio
desc: With both young artists desperate to leave Belleville, they got creative. “This can’t go on; we can’t live there any more; it’s filthy; we’ll find a studio,” Vera remembers François remarking at the time. Leveraging the area’s bad reputation, they orchestrated a flat swap with “drunks” eager for proximity to bars. The move landed them in a seventh-floor Rue de Gergovie apartment with a studio and panoramic Paris views. Together, Vera and François, dubbed a “two-headed painter,” collaborated until 1960, when François shifted to a research career. In the late '50s and early '60s, Vera explored solo creativity, first investigating the machine imaginaire .

name: Whirlwind and SAGE Initiatives by US Military Funding Spark Computing Innovations
desc: In 1954, Douglas Ross created the “Scope Input Program.” This program made for Whirlwind computers was the first example of hand-drawing with a computer. In 1951, the Whirlwind began operating at MIT as part of the first demonstration of a graphics display on a vectorscope screen. It was thus the first computer that operated in real time. SAGE operators selected targets with a light gun, a pointing device carried over from Whirlwind. This enabled a form of rudimentary hand drawing on a computer. IBM built a duplexed AN/FSQ-7 computer, descended from MIT’s experimental Whirlwind, for each SAGE direction centre. These two projects were significant to the development of computing and digital generative art as they demonstrated the viability of cathode-ray tube displays.

name: Margaret Masterman Founds the Cambridge Language Research Unit
desc: Computerized text and language games have gone hand in hand with the systems and generative art for centuries. But a big step took place in 1954 when philosopher Margaret Masterman founded the Cambridge Language Research Group to study machine translation, then outside the curriculum of every English university. The informal circle became the Cambridge Language Research Unit (CLRU) in 1956. Early members included the plant scientist Richard H. Richens, the mathematician Lady Hoskyns and the linguist M. A. K. Halliday. In 1968 Cybernetic Serendipity showed Masterman's Computerized Japanese Haiku , made with Robin McKinnon Wood at the CLRU: a poem frame whose slots an operator filled, sometimes from the thesaurus.

name: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky & Claude Shannon Introduce World to AI
desc: John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky , along with Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon , organized the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence. This seminal event marked the birth of AI as a field of study. The conference itself did actually take place in 1956, as proposed. The now legendary proposal and subsequent conference by the titans of the field asserted that machines could simulate every aspect of learning and intelligence, laying the foundation for decades of AI research—and winters. The term “artificial intelligence” was coined with this document and the project brought together leading minds to explore machine learning, neural networks, and more, setting the stage for the scientific and artistic explorations of a field at its birth.
subjects: dartmouth summer research project on artificial intelligence

name: Victor Vasarely’s Yellow Manifesto Lays Generative Art’s Conceptual Foundation
desc: Victor Vasarely ’s seminal Yellow Manifesto envisioned a synthesis between art and technology to enhance art’s accessibility through mass production. His manifesto links the Constructivist research of the Bauhaus to Op Art, Kinetic Art, New Tendencies and contemporary generative art. Vasarely believed that technology could spearhead the accessibility of art by rejecting the concept of a single work. Instead, Vasarely proposed making art more reproducible. This move played an important role in the gradual dematerialization of art, a critical step in the development of electronic, performance and conceptual art. The concept of mass produced art would also greatly influence Pop Art and remains central to the broadening collector base that generative art today enjoys. Vasarely also questioned the “lone genius” artist which would inspire the New Tendencies groups of the ’60s, especially Group de Recherche d’Art Visuel ( GRAV ). GRAV was significantly influenced by Vasarely’s Yellow Manifesto and included two of generative art’s most timeless icons: Vera Molnár and François Morellet . Other members included Yvaral Vasarely (Victor’s son) and Julio Le Parc .

name: The Term “Artificial Intelligence” Is Coined
desc: John McCarthy coined the term “artificial intelligence” in a proposal for a Dartmouth College study written with Marvin Minsky (Harvard University), Nathaniel Rochester (IBM) and Claude Shannon (Bell Telephone Laboratories). According to the proposal, “the study is to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.” The proposal also included an early hypothesis on the connection between randomness, intuition and creativity: “A fairly attractive and yet clearly incomplete conjecture is that the difference between creative thinking and unimaginative competent thinking lies in the injection of some randomness. The randomness must be guided by intuition to be efficient. In other words, the educated guess or the hunch include controlled randomness in otherwise orderly thinking.” The workshop took place the following year and is considered the official beginning of the field.

name: “Le Mouvement” Is First Post-War Kinetic Exhibition
desc: The April 1955 exhibition at the Galerie Denise René, in which Vasarely was central, launched both Op and Kinetic Art, while inspiring the New Tendencies group GRAV . It’s thus a pivotal moment in the history of generative art. Le Mouvement included Yaacov Agam , Pol Bury , Alexander Calder , Marcel Duchamp , Robert Jacobsen , Jesús Rafael Soto, Jean Tinguely and Victor Vasarely . The exhibition corresponded to the principles laid out in his “ Yellow Manifesto .” An intense period of experimentation in media and production choices followed the exhibition. The manifesto and this exhibition helped lay the groundwork for both electronic art and the digitization of generative art.

name: “Experimental Outdoor Exhibition of Modern Art to Challenge the Midsummer Sun” by Gutai
desc: This legendary outdoor exhibition featured radical concepts that were a decade ahead of their time. The central innovative concept that concerns generative art’s development was the direct encouragement of audience participation and interactivity. GRAV would not bring this concept to European audiences until the mid ’60s.
subjects: experimental outdoor exhibition of modern art to challenge the midsummer sun

name: Ben Laposky Releases Colored Electronic Image
desc: In a follow up Electronic Abstractions , Laposky released a colored version of his electronic images, Oscillons. These early colored analogue graphics were created with an oscilloscope by manipulating electronic waves. Image is copyrighted by Ben Laposky and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection .

name: Herbert W. Franke Begins Creating Art with an Oscillograph
desc: Franke’s Pendular Oscillogram, made with a cathode ray oscillograph built by his friend Dr Franz Raimann , is considered, along with Laposky’s Electronic Abstraction , to be one of the first pieces of (analog) computer art. Image is copyrighted by Herbert W. Franke and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: CYSP 1 by Nicolas Schöffer
desc: This mobile kinetic sculpture is considered the first cybernetic sculpture. CYSP is short for “CYbernetic SPatiodynamic.” The piece, whose electronic brain was built by engineers at Philips, used microphones, wheels, motors and cells that responded to their environment. The structure could, for instance, navigate between obstacles. Schöffer’s work sought to merge the theories of cybernetics with artistic creation. His Lumino-Kinetic sculptures used light, movement and sound to demonstrate kinetic principles.

name: “The New Landscape in Art and Science” by György Kepes
desc: A precursor to C. P. Snow’s “two cultures” thesis of 1959 , The New Landscape in Art and Science was a book that attempted to combat the growing pessimism in the art world towards the mixing of art and science. Kepes, the prominent figure in the development of computer and digital art, explored the intersections between art, science and technology. He sought to focus on where science and art intersected, laying out ideas about visual perception, patterns and the relationship between art and nature. The publication was poorly received by his contemporaries yet, critically, it illustrated the growing rift between science and art.
subjects: the new landscape in art and science

name: 2nd Gutai Outdoor Exhibition in Ashiya Park
desc: Following the first exhibition , the group continued to enhance audience participation. It even anticipated the communal drawing practices of the net art community. It was an additional important contribution by Gutai to the development of interactive art as well.

name: Electric Dress by Atsuko Tanaka
desc: The Gutai member’s best known work was constructed by fashioning vividly painted light bulbs into a dress. The piece consists of only light bulbs and their cords. A re-imagination of the traditional kimono, Electric Dress represented modern Japan ’s embrace of the new in society as well as art. This aligned perfectly with the aims of the Gutai group, seeking a radical departure from the past, which had been largely marked by turmoil and war for decades. The group also sought to blur the lines between everyday life and art, another way Tanaka’s Electric Dress exemplifies the movement. It would not be for several more years before European groups like New Tendencies began making such calls. An important predecessor to electronic art, the dress embraced elements central Tanaka’s career and Gutai: change, movement and interactivity. It was also an important step in the development of electronic art as an interactive Light sculpture.

name: Suite for Five by Merce Cunningham
desc: A hugely important moment in Chance Dance and with a score by John Cage , Suite for Five is a Neo-Dada classic. According to the Art Story : “Cunningham and Cage relied heavily upon chance in the creation of this work, citing that both the score and the choreography were determined by random operations like counting the imperfections in a piece of paper.”

name: Allen Newell, Cliff Shaw and Herbert Simon Build the Logic Theorist
desc: The quest for machines that did more than just blindly follow instructions in binary determinacy, for machines that actually think, is a long one, covered many times on this Timeline ( Lady Lovelace’s Objection , the Turing Test , the Homeostat ). For instance, in January 1956 Herbert A. Simon told his class, "Over Christmas Allen Newell and I invented a thinking machine." With Cliff Shaw at the RAND Corporation in Santa Monica, they had built the Logic Theorist, a program that searched for proofs in symbolic logic using heuristics modeled on human problem solving. At the now legendary Dartmouth workshop that summer, where the term "artificial intelligence" was coined, the three described IPL, the list-processing language in which they wrote it. By 1957, running on RAND's JOHNNIAC computer, the Logic Theorist had proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in chapter 2 of Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell's Principia Mathematica . Logic with learning would prove a valuable combination in the decades ahead.

name: John Backus Releases FORTRAN
desc: Conceived in 1954, the programming language of early computer art, Fortran (FORMula TRANslator) is one of the oldest high-level programming languages. It made code more comprehensible to scientists, mathematicians and, of course, artists. Originally developed by IBM, it became the first computer language standard and is one of the most influential software products in history. It is still in use today. Fortran was also essential to the early development of computer art. Early pioneers like Vera Molnár , Manfred Mohr and many others used the language to create algorithmic art in the 1960s and 1970s. The Victoria and Albert Museum on Fortran: “Fortran is used in works including Dominic Boreham ’s IM21 (B5) P0.5 3.X.79. Early computer programmes were stored on punched cards, including Manfred Mohr’s P032 (Matrix Elements). Written by the artist in Fortran, this programme instructed a plotter device to produce the drawing P-32 (Matrix Elements ) .”

name: “An Experiment in Musical Composition” is Published
desc: This consequential paper by Brooks, Hopkins, Neumann and Wright outlines how a computer can be used as a system to create art.

name: “Syntactic Structures” by Noam Chomsky
desc: Chomsky’s epochal book influenced both mid-century computational theory and artificial intelligence by introducing the concept of Transformational-Generative Grammar, “the most significant development in linguistic theory and research in the 20th century.” Generative Grammar seeks to explain how humans are able to produce and understand an infinite number of grammatically correct sentences. The theory proposes that language is innately hardwired into the human brain and that there are underlying rules or structures that govern the way in which sentences are formed. It has had a significant impact on computational theory. The theory has inspired the development of algorithms and computational models that attempt to simulate the way in which humans generate and understand language.

name: ZERO Forms in Düsseldorf
desc: Founded by Otto Piene and Heinz Mack in Düsseldorf, four years before New Tendencies , Zero was inspired by the notion of starting over (hence the name). The group grew throughout the ’50s and early ’60s into an international movement of artists and architects who sought to create a new form of art that was both rational and objective, focusing on a work’s materials. Also associated with the Gutai movement in Japan , Zero rejected traditional art forms and embraced new technologies, focusing on geometric abstraction and kinetic art. As Margit Rosen would write on the connection between New Tendencies and computer art: “New Tendencies’ idea of art as research, the endeavor to enforce a constructive, rational, demystified art and to overcome the gap between current art practices and processes in science and technology, as well as the wish to stop the art market from defining artistic aims and methods, made it possible to open this art movement to the world of computing technology and its own band of practitioners.”

name: Black Mountain College Closes
desc: The spiritual successor to the Bauhau closed after 24 years primarily due to financial difficulties. It had been opened in 1933 by John A. Rice , who hired the Bauhaus ’s Josef Albers. The college’s faculty and staff over the years included some of the most impactful artists of the twentieth-century such as Anni and Josef Albers, Walter Gropius , Merce Cunningham , John Cage , Robert Motherwell , Dorothea Rockburne , Cy Twombly , Robert Rauschenberg , Susan Weil , Franz Kline , Aaron Siskind , Willem and Elaine de Kooning and Mary Caroline Richards .

name: Richard Hamilton Lists the ‘Characteristics of Pop Art’
desc: According to Hamilton, an early progenitor of Pop Art: “Pop Art is: Popular (designed for a mass audience), Transient (short-term solution), Expendable (easily forgotten), Low cost, Mass produced, Young (aimed at youth), Witty, Sexy, Gimmicky, Glamorous, Big business” Similar words have been used to derisively describe the on-chain art of today.

name: Allan Kaprow Begins Making ‘Environments’
desc: Environments, precursors to “happenings” as well as the Performance and Installation Art of the ’60s-’70s, were large-scale, immersive installations intended to engage all of the senses of the viewer. Kaprow believed that art should be experienced rather than observed, and his Environments were designed to create an interactive and participatory experience for the viewer.

name: Duchamp Gives His Famous Talk, “The Creative Act”
desc: In this talk, Duchamp explained the importance of chance in the creative act. He deemed that both the artist and the participant partook in chance creation, anticipating the work of Eco several years later “The Open Work” by Umberto Eco . “All in all, the creative act is not performed by the artist alone; the spectator brings the work in contact with the external world by deciphering and interpreting its inner qualifications and thus adds his contributions to the creative act.”

name: Max Mathews Develops MUSIC I
desc: Mathews, computer music pioneer, developed the computer music composition language on an IBM 704 while at Bell Labs . MUSIC I was the first demonstration of computer synthesized music. Mathews himself described the development: “Computer performance of music was born in 1957 when an IBM 704 in NYC played a 17 second composition on the Music I program which I wrote. The timbres and notes were not inspiring, but the technical breakthrough is still reverberating.”

name: Voyage II, Frank Malina
desc: This piece by Malina, pioneer of Lumino-Kinetic art, demonstrates the development of the Lumino-Kinetic movement towards electronic art.

name: A. P. Rich Writes Program for the Design of Wave Patterns for Textiles
desc: Rich, of the Applied Physics Laboratory, Johns Hopkins University, wrote one of the earliest examples of using a computer program for graphic design, according to Herbert W. Franke . This was of wave patterns for textiles.

name: “Theorie de l’information et perception esthetique (Information Theory and Esthetic Perception)” by Abraham A. Moles
desc: Information Theory and Esthetic Perception by Abraham A. Moles, later professor at Strasbourg University, was an early, important work on information aesthetics. Moles combined Shannon’s information theory with aesthetics. While Bense’s generative aesthetics focused on an artwork’s aesthetic value, Moles was interested in models of perception and semiotics or symbolic communication. This book posits that pleasure, beauty, and artistic response are the result of informational processes, which can be mathematically analyzed and understood. According to Margit Rosen , “it inspired the development of strategies to develop procedures of programming as a precondition for the production of art.”
subjects: théorie de l'information et perception esthétique

name: Fontana Mix, John Cage
desc: This landmark, hugely influence piece of chance music consists of a graphic score of transparent sheets the performer superimposes to derive a realisation. Cage remains the composer most willing to explore “chance operations” in the composition and performance of music.

name: John Whitney Sr. Makes the Vertigo Titles with an Analog Computing Device
desc: After Hitchcock hired John Whitney to create the opening animation for his film, Vertigo, Whitney used a WWII-era “M5 gun director” targeting computer that required five people to operate. This device was used because it could rotate endlessly and was thus able to move in relation to a pendulum that was generating the spiral compositions. Saul Bass collaborated with Whitney to design the analog-computed animated sequence.

name: Méta-matic No. 8 by Jean Tinguely
desc: Foreshadowing the plotter, the Swiss kinetic sculptor’s key piece in the history of chance in art, Méta-matic No. 8, was an animated sculpture made from found material. The piece was exhibited at the legendary The machine, as seen at the end of the mechanical age . link This piece itself was actually a drawing machine, constantly producing an abstract drawing on its own. Tinguely said: “The machine is above all an instrument which permits me to be poetic. If you respect the machine, if you enter into a game with the machine, then perhaps you can make a truly joyous machine; by joyous I mean free.” The piece, like much of Tinguely’s work, also questioned the role of the artist’s hand in an artwork’s production and the art object itself. This work also further demonstrates the role of Kinetic Art in the development of computer art as well as an example of proto-digital generative art.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Jack St. Clair Kilby at Texas Instruments and, independently, Robert Noyce at Fairchild Arrive at the Integrated Circuit
desc: Kilby demonstrated his device in 1958, Noyce’s design following in 1959. The integrated circuit was a breakthrough in electronics that sparked the miniaturization of the industry. The large size of previous circuit iterations, such as tubes and transistors, caused frequent faulty connections and failures. The entire circuit of a computer (transistors, capacitors, resistors, wires, …) could now be made with silicon and could fit on a single board.

name: I. J. Good Speaks on Machine Judgment at the Gaberbocchus Common Room
