desc: As described by Jasia Reichardt herself at Le Random ( “The Ultraintelligent Machine and Gaberbocchus Common Room ” ), on January 14, 1958, the mathematician I. J. Good , a one-time colleague of Alan Turing , spoke at the Gaberbocchus Common Room in London . Franciszka and Stefan Themerson had opened the club in 1957 in the Maida Vale basement of their Gaberbocchus Press so that artists and scientists could meet. Good asked whether a machine could make probability judgments. He imagined one built from partly random networks of model neurons, rewarded for a correct judgment with a chemical that lowered the thresholds of the neurons it had just used. Computers and Automation printed the talk in 1959. In a 1965 paper Good called such a machine "ultraintelligent." He wasn't far it seems.

name: Frank Rosenblatt Introduces the Perceptron
desc: Depending on how it goes with AI, the perceptron could end up being one of history's most important concepts, well, ever basically. Frank Rosenblatt 's perceptron is essentially the first neural network and a monumental step in the story of deep learning AI art. The perceptron is also a bit of a tragic tale. A decade later, deep learning AI's anti-hero Marvin Minsky published Perceptrons , a book that critics of neural networks would point to in order to discredit the field or deny funding. It was thought of as proof that those pesky neural networks just didn't work. Machines couldn't learn (at least not that way). So the perceptron itself marks the beginning of neural networks and also partly explains why if this idea came out in 1958, it only really exploded around 2010. There are many reasons why like data and compute needing to catch up with theory. But that theory barely even existed, largely because of Minsky and his dividing of the AI field from about 1969 to 2010. Rosenblatt himself though was a research psychologist at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York. He described the perceptron in a 1957 report and in Psychological Review in 1958. It modeled the brain as sensory, association and response units that learn to sort shapes into classes. In July 1958 the U.S. Office of Naval Research (And, yes, you knew the military industrial complex was going to be involved, didn't you?) demonstrated it on an IBM 704: after 50 trials, the computer taught itself to tell cards marked on the left from those marked on the right. In other words, it was already demonstrating some very early effectiveness. Rosenblatt called it "the first machine which is capable of having an original idea." The human idea itself was certainly original.

name: Minimalism Emerges with “16 Americans” at MoMA
desc: A rebuke of gestural art and extension of modern art’s abstraction, Minimalism emerged in the late ’50s with exhibitions such as Frank Stella ’s Black Paintings at the Museum of Modern Art in New York . But Dorothy Miller ’s 16 Americans, also at MoMA , established the importance of the young movement.

name: Béla Julesz Invents Random-dot Stereograms
desc: Julesz’s “Two Image Random Dot Stereograms” were 2 side-by-side randomly generated dot images. When viewed through a stereoscope they created the sensation of depth. Julesz displayed these patterns on a screen and developed the procedure at Bell Labs .

name: Raymond Scott Builds the Electronium, an Instrument for Generative Composition
desc: Scott developed this important proto-digital generative art (in this case music) with his Electronium. This device was an early synthesizer combined with algorithmic compositions which produced generative music.

name: Herbert W. Franke’s “Experimentelle Ästhetik” Exhibition
desc: The exhibition was held at the Museum of Applied Arts in Vienna , presenting the experimental images of the then physicist-artist, Herbert W. Franke . Franke experimented with a variety of machines and technical methods including, analog computers, oscillograms and X-ray machines.

name: CalComp 565 Drum Plotter Released
desc: One of the earliest computer graphics output devices sold and the first drum plotter printer, the CalComp 565 could produce large-scale drawings with precise lines, becoming a popular tool for computer artists. CalComp would come to dominate the plotter market by the end of the next decade, proving to be indispensable to the development of computer art.

name: Gustav Metzger Begins Creating “Auto-Destructive Art”
desc: To protest nuclear war and showcase his values of spontaneity and randomness, Metzger creates his first acid paintings. This form of material generative art is created by spraying acid onto sheets of nylon. This produces rapidly changing shapes as the nylon dissolves. The work is thus auto-creative as well as auto-destructive. Metzger along with Max Bense was instrumental in the development of generative art. He and Bense “envisioned art as a laboratory for imagining how computers could defy their militaristic origins and be structured according to alternative logics—the eruptive spontaneity of the creative act, for example, or the mutually beneficial, horizontal processes of communication and collaborative action.”

name: “The Two Cultures” Lecture by C.P. Snow
desc: C.P. Snow ’s “Two Cultures” lecture was a call to bridge the divide between the sciences and the humanities, embodied by the multi-disciplinary computer art. Snow argued that this gap, and the lack of understanding between the two groups, was detrimental to society’s progress. In the 1960s and 1970s, “The Two Cultures debate framed much of the early criticism and reception of computer art.” Early computer artists were primarily from a scientific background and viewed art from a technical perspective, leading to their work being dismissed by traditional artists and critics.

name: 18 Happenings in 6 Parts by Allan Kaprow
desc: Kaprow’s seminal exhibition was the first Happenings and coined the term as art form. Happenings were avant-garde, interactive art events that paved the way for Performance Art and Fluxus . The exhibit itself consisted of a sequence of 18 loosely scripted events or “happenings” that took place in six different areas of the Reuben Gallery in New York . The happenings, designed to be experienced by a small audience, also encouraged audience interaction in the work. In one section of the exhibit, actors walked around the space holding umbrellas and chanting a series of words and phrases. In another section, performers created a large wall made of newspapers, which the audience was invited to tear down. Along with Gutai in Japan and GRAV in Paris , happenings anticipated many concepts of the contemporary digital generative art space: the work was designed to challenge traditional notions of art and spectatorship, breaking down barriers between art and everyday life. It was also a participatory and immersive experience with audience members becoming active collaborators in the creation of the art.

name: “Manifesto Neoconcreto” by Ferreira Gullar
desc: Gullar’s manifesto advocated for a new kind of art that rejected the formalism of traditional concrete art and embraced a more humanistic, participatory approach. It called for a more organic, intuitive, and emotional art that engaged the senses and emotions of the viewer, serving as an important development in the histroy of South American geometric abstraction.

name: Theo Lutz produces Stochastic Texts
desc: This key development in the pre-history of computer-generated literature was an early use of a computer to generate text. Lutz’s “stochastic texts” were produced at Stuttgart when Max Bense was there developing Aesthetica . The texts were determined by a syntactical scheme, random generator and frequency criteria on a Z22. Lutz’s usage of stored words provided Bense with ideas for Aesthetica.

name: Tête barbue (Bearded Head) by Jean Dubuffet
desc: This important example in the history of chance in art consists of simply a found piece of driftwood that happened to look like something else. Dubuffet noticed the piece after thinking the natural shape resembled a head and the barnacles resembled hair. He burned a few additional holes and placed the work on a pedestal. Dubuffet believed that natural forms, simplicity and rawness endowed his work with greater authenticity.

name: Vera Molnár Develops Her “Machine Imaginaire”
desc: Meaning the “imaginary computer,” Molnár’s “machine imaginaire” is the now famous concept that she developed to imagine a computer to expand her creative process. The hypothetical machine allowed her to systematically create works that included all the possible combinations of forms she wished. Now based in Paris , It would take nearly another decade, 1968, before Molnár would gain access to an actual computer .

name: John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky Found the MIT Artificial Intelligence Project
desc: The heart of AI has been tugged by academia, industry and most worryingly the military for the entirety of its existence. Here we see that pattern play out in action as McCarthy and Minsky's legendary AI research lab had roots in academia before jettisoning to DARPA and the military industrial complex. In 1959 John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky founded the Artificial Intelligence Project at MIT, the institute's first coordinated AI research, within the Research Laboratory of Electronics and the Computation Center. AI was vague from the start, as no written proposal was ever made. When the laboratory's director, Jerome Wiesner , asked what they needed, McCarthy recalled, "we asked for a room, two programmers, a secretary and a keypunch." Wiesner also had them supervise some of six mathematics graduate students. But this was a huge development as McCarthy's LISP was implemented there. Later, in 1963, the lab joined the DARPA-funded Project MAC. The MIT AI Lab later split off from Project MAC and in 2003 merged with the Laboratory for Computer Science to form CSAIL.

name: Oliver Selfridge Proposes Pandemonium
desc: Back at MIT, Oliver Selfridge of its Lincoln Laboratory, presented "Pandemonium: A Paradigm for Learning" at the Symposium on the Mechanisation of Thought Processes at the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington, England , in November 1958; the proceedings appeared in 1959. It was an exciting time for computing, before it had really been pigeonholed into less experimental roles from the late '60s onwards (until maybe around 2010 with the advent of deep learning proper). Selfridge's model for learning to recognize patterns had four levels of "demons." Data demons stored the image and computational demons computed features from it. Cognitive demons weighed that evidence and shouted; a decision demon picked the loudest. It learned by adjusting the weight given to each feature and by culling and breeding its feature demons through a kind of natural selection. Not neural networks but "demons," one can still see how prevalent statistical weights are in machine learning.

name: The National Physical Laboratory's Mechanisation of Thought Processes
desc: The UK's answer to the 1956 Dartmouth AI conference, this symposium continued the budding field's momentum and mostly open-minded spirit, as one of the first international meetings on artificial intelligence after Dartmouth. As for the event itself, it took place in November 1958 at Britain's National Physical Laboratory in Teddington. The conference took place over four days and its theme was the Mechanisation of Thought Processes. Her Majesty's Stationery Office would go on to publish its proceedings in two 1959 volumes. John McCarthy presented “Programs with Common Sense,” proposing a program that would reason from stated facts, and Oliver Selfridge presented Pandemonium, a model of pattern recognition by competing units, mentioned previously on this timeline. It was a veritable all-star lineup with Marvin Minsky , Grace Hopper , Donald MacKay and Albert Uttley all speaking. The late-50s weren't entirely free as it was still a bit political who even got invited to these conferences with certain regrettable omissions, chiefly Rosenblatt. However, these were still mostly drama-free days in AI research. But drama would plague the field in ten years' time with Minsky's Perceptrons book all but splitting the field ideologically into connectionist and symbolic camps.

name: Eduardo Mac Entyre Founds the Pintura Generativa Group
desc: Arte Concreto's rich legacy of geometric aesthetics in South America (Brazil in particular) from the 1950s reflected the change of a continent rapidly industrializing. But by the early 1960s, the movement's rigidity, "focus[ing] solely on the principles of color, line, and shape," according to MoMA , began frustrating artists like Lygia Clark and Lygia Pape. These artists took the movement in more experimental directions in Brazil. But this experimental rejection of Arte Concreto's rigidity has roots in Brazil's neighbor Argentina as well. Buenos Aires native Eduardo Mac Entyre co-founded the transformative Pintura Generativa group alongside Miguel Ángel Vidal and mentor Ignacio Pirovano. This group's view of "generative" differs (but is commonly mistaken) from this Timeline's. We mean art using autonomous systems. Mac Entyre meant his more dynamic visual language that pulsated with motion. The group chose the term “generative” because it aptly described their intention to transform static elements into dynamic, evolving forms. Mac Entyre vividly demonstrates the group’s signature aesthetic in his Seis Formas en Dos Circunferencias (1966).

name: Kurd Alsleben and Cord Passow Make Analog Computer Drawings
desc: Artist Kurd Alsleben in collaboration with physicist Cord Passow used an analogue computer (EAI 231 R) in Hamburg to create parametric generative art. The analog computer, combined with a mechanical drawing mechanism, produced graphical works of waves and lines based on the changing results of an equation. By adjusting the parameters of the equation, the outputs varied in visual form.

name: Karl Otto Götz Manually Anticipates Digital Generative Art
desc: Karl Götz’s Statistisch-metrische Modulation (Statistical-metrical Modulation) is a series of hand-drawn Raster Pictures of 2 x 2 cm black and white squares on pieces of variously-sized cardboard. Götz was fascinated by the dematerialization of the art object that computers were enabling. He believed this was a paradigm shift. Statistisch-metrische Modulation was an attempt to explore this digital aesthetic (manually) before it was possible electronically. But Götz could clearly see what was coming: “When one thinks how much ‘easier,’ or less taxing, it would be to realize such [raster] pictures electronically, that is to say, that they would appear on the screen. It is obvious that these technical means will be used”(1963).

name: John Whitney Sr. Founds “Motion Graphics Incorporated”
desc: John Whitney Sr., pioneer in the field of computer-generated art and animation, founded Motion Graphics Incorporated. It became one of the first companies to use computers for creating graphics and animation. Whitney’s work and innovations would normalize the use of computers in the creative arts and had a profound impact on the development of computer generated images. The work at Motion Graphics was largely completed by a mechanical analog computer built by Whitney himself that controlled cameras above the artwork, a technique he used for the film Vertigo in 1958 . He used this invention to create other film and television title sequences and commercials. While mechanical, Whitney’s machines anticipated future computer software.

name: Vera Molnar Co-Founds Centre de Recherche d’Art Visuel, (later Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV))
desc: Playing a significant role in the development of Kinetic and Op Art, the Parisian collective aimed to explore the relationship between art, science and technology to create works that empirically engaged with new materials and challenged traditional notions of art. The fusion of science and art would be a pivotal feature of computer art as well as digital generative art. Founded by Hector García Miranda , Horacio García Rossi , Hugo Demarco , Julio Le Parc , Vera Molnár , François Molnár , François Morellet , Sergio Moyano , Servanes (Simone Revoil), Joël Stein , Francisco Sobrino , and Yvaral (Jean-Pierre Vasarely), Centre de Recherche d’Art Visuel was “a center for visual research where the artists could work together towards the realization of their common formal and theoretical goals. In the summer of 1960, the young artists rented a small garage in the Marais district of Paris , which provided them with a common meeting and exhibition space.” The group would change its name to Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel ( GRAV ) in July 1961. GRAV artists used light, motion and other perceptual elements to create immersive and interactive artworks that required the viewer’s participation. These would all be crucial concepts to the development of electronic art. Their work explicitly built upon the ideas of Victor Vasarely’s Yellow Manifesto ., while implicitly building upon previous, even more radical movements such as Gutai in Japan and Allan Kaprow ’s happenings in New York. Further, Vera Molnar’s time as a member of GRAV was instrumental in shaping her approach to art. While she was initially focused on traditional forms of art such as painting and drawing, her time with GRAV exposed her to new techniques and approaches to art-making. Through her involvement with the group, Molnar became interested in exploring the relationship between art and technology, which would lead her later in the decade to experiment with computer-generated images. She began creating algorithmic art using early computer programming languages such as FORTRAN . Although she had a disposition toward abstraction since childhood, her work became increasingly focused on the use of geometry and pattern. Molnar’s time with GRAV also had an impact on her aesthetic sensibilities, influencing her interest in the use of repetitive forms, simple shapes and bold colors. She continued to explore these themes in her later computer-generated artworks, creating intricate and mesmerizing geometric patterns that play with the viewer’s perception, beginning in 1968. Overall, Molnar’s time with GRAV helped to shape her approach to art and technology, which along with her concept of the “Machine Imaginaire” (Imaginary Computer) led to her becoming one of the great pioneers of computer-generated art. From the Bright Moments Buenos Aires Timeline Poster: Argentine painters Horacio García Rossi and Julio Le Parc, alongside luminaries like François Morellet and Vera Molnár, founded the Centre de Recherche d’Art Visuel, renamed GRAV in 1961, the profoundly important collective that helped bridge the analog and digital art worlds as part of the New Tendencies movement. Initially, the group was rooted in op and kinetic art, two critical predecessors of electronic art. Like Mac Entyre’s Pintura Generativa , the group aimed to liberate art from the static canvas.

name: Music from Mathematics, the First Computer Music Issued on Record
desc: The first commercially issued recording of computer generated music, Music from Mathematics ( full album ), created by John R. Pierce and Max Mathews at Bell Labs . This work is not only some of the earliest digital electronic music ever produced, it also some of the earliest digital generative art and digital art, generally. According to the New York Times : “While not the first person to make sound with a computer, Max was the first one to do so with a replicable combination of hardware and software that allowed the user to specify what tones he wanted to hear.” The Times article goes on to add how Mathews’s early attempts to create computer-generated music, “laid the groundwork for a revolutionary advancement in music, the reverberations of which are felt everywhere today.”

name: Konkrete Kunst: 50 Jahre Entwicklung, Helmhaus Zürich
desc: This iconic exhibition featured Concrete art of the last fifty years, an exhibition that by itself could nearly tell the story of this movement to this point in 1960. It featured works by a veritable who’s who of twentieth century abstract art, including Kandinsky, Malevich, Mondrian, Moholy-Nagy and Taeuber-Arp. Perhaps most interesting for our story, one such piece, Effet esthétique de l’inversion des fonctions par la fluctuation de l’attention, appeared at this incredibly prestigious, landmark exhibition by a relatively unkown thirty-six year old Hungarian artist, Vera Molnár .

name: William Fetter Creates the First Computer Graphics
desc: At the Wichita Branch of the Military Aircraft Systems Division of Boeing , William Fetter coined the term “computer graphics” to refer to his plotter drawings. He created visualization on a computer “to help airplane designers and engineers envision on a computer screen the diverse human body shapes and a pilot’s limited vision in a cockpit as a plane lands.” These were among the first true perspective drawings produced by a computer. These historic artifacts are some of the beginnings of the computer graphics industry and would later in the ’60s be displayed as Boeing Man .

name: John McCarthy Introduces LISP
desc: John McCarthy at MIT introduced the programming language LISP (List Processing) in 1960. He published the language in his seminal paper in on recursive functions in programming. LISP would go on to be used in Symbolics graphics computer. Nearly twenty years later, Peter Beyls would use LISP to create some of his early computer-generated work. Harold Cohen would also use LISP in his work with AARON . LISP thus significantly influenced digital art by introducing a programming environment conducive to creative expression and generative processes. LISP’s unique symbolic manipulation capabilities enabled artists to more easily represent artistic concepts as code. Along with John Backus’s FORTRAN (1957) and John G. Kemeny and Thomas E. Kurtz’s BASIC (1964) , LISP was one of the most significant early digital software developments in programmed art.

name: Bernard Widrow and Marcian Hoff Introduce ADALINE
desc: ADALINE (Adaptive Linear Neuron or Element) was a foundational single-layer artificial neural network. But don't be fooled into thinking it was simple, as it was surprisingly modern. Its architecture had inputs, weights and bias; its learning rule, Least Mean Squares (LMS) algorithm, was even based on stochastic gradient descent. Where Rosenblatt's Perceptron ( see earlier on the timeline ) learned only from a right-or-wrong verdict, ADALINE learned from how far off its score was before the yes/no call was made. Electrical engineer Bernard Widrow and his first graduate student, Marcian “Ted” Hoff created ADALINE at Stanford University , describing it in their 1960 paper “Adaptive Switching Circuits.” The lunch-pail-sized machine read crude letter patterns set on a four-by-four grid of toggle switches and learned to sort them. After each example, all 17 of its weights moved by equal amounts to bring the error to zero. This is the famous LMS rule mentioned above, following the error downhill one example at a time. To this day, the Smithsonian holds two ADALINEs.

name: Lygia Clark Begins Her Bichos
desc: Today, interactive work that involves full-body experience is normal, almost expected in contemporary art. But in 1960, participation and interaction were much more radical. A big step in the direction towards more interactive art in the coming decades was the Brazilian artist Lygia Clark's Bichos (Critters), sculptures. The artworks consisted of flat metal plates joined by hinges that viewers were meant to handle and refold. Each Bicho has many possible configurations and none is considered final: the work is completed by the person moving it. They aren't just conceptually completing the work in the Duchampian sense; they are physically altering the work. Clark had signed the Neo-Concrete Manifesto in Rio de Janeiro in 1959, which rejected the rigid rationalism of Concrete art for works that involved the body and its fluidity.

name: Grand tir–séance Galerie J by Niki de Saint Phalle
desc: This convention-defying work of chance art saw Saint Phalle create an assemblage of white, found objects, surrounded by sacks of colored paint. She would then fire a rifle at the paint sacks to explosively create the work. A fascinating example of the ingenuity and breadth of generative art, the rifle plays a decisive role in the system that ultimately creates the art and could thus be considered an autonomous system.

name: “Automat und Mensch Kybernetische Tatsachen und Hypothesen” by Karl Steinbuch
desc: Steinbuch’s books introduced the concept of “information processing” as a core function of machines and computers. This idea laid the foundation for the development of artificial intelligence and cognitive science. According to Gottfried Jäger , the book “was seminal for my way of thinking.” The book attempted to explain intellectual functions in terms of information transfers and science. Automat und Mensch taught Jäger that “a human brain and a hand weren’t necessary anymore for artistic expression. It could be also a technical apparatus. A camera or a computer were capable of achieving intellectual results.” Thus, the book significantly influenced the way we understand the relationship between humans and machines. Steinbuch’s work helped to shape the field of cybernetics and inspired further research in the field of computer science, leading to the upcoming digital revolution in art.
subjects: automat und mensch: a history of ai and generative art

name: George Maciunas’s “Bread & AG” Opens in New York, the First Fluxus Event
desc: The Lithuanian-American artist and curator, Maciunas founded and organized the Fluxus (“flowing” in English) movement’s first event. The event, which would be the first of a brilliant, art-chaning series, included readings by poet Frank Kuenstler . Fluxus, an international avant-garde movement, rejected traditional artistic mediums and emphasized performance, humor and experimentation. The movement has strong ties to Dada’s anti-art sentiment and is considered to be part of a broader Neo-Dada movement that emerged around this time. Fluxus has strong ties to both computer and generative art, particularly regarding the dematerialization of art and the rise of conceptual art which the movement propels. Fluxus also often features elements of rules-based practice. Additionally, it is multi-disciplinary with collaboration and audience participation encouraged, two further hallmarks of the rise of electronic art. Chance and randomness also play an important role in Fluxus performances. The focus was on process and concept rather than a unified finished art object, a tradition that continues today in many circles of digital generative art, particularly within academia. Like GRAV, Fluxus artists sought to diminish distinctions between art and everyday life with Deleuzian work often incorporating non-traditional materials and methods.

name: “Nove tendencije” the first New Tendencies exhibition opens at the Gallery for Contemporary Art, Zagreb
desc: Dissatisfied with 1960 Venice Biennale , Brazilian artist Almir Mavignier and art critic Matko Meštrović sought to organize a new exhibition that showcased “new tendencies” in art not yet supported by the establishment. The exhibition was held at the Gallery for Contemporary Art, Zagreb . The New Tendencies movement was hugely important for the development of computer and digital art. Technology was central to the movement’s goals: “Many followers of the NT [New Tendencies] have tried to give their work the habit of the machine or else they have based their procedures on the use of mechanical or electrical devices; they have all dreamt of the machines—and now the machines have arrived,” said critic Radoslav Putar . Nove tendencije, the exhibition, featured work of Concrete Art that blurred the lines between painting and sculpture. GRAV member François Morellet ’s work was described as “programmed painting.” Artists from the Zero Group also presented work in their Lumino-Kinetic style. These exhibitions and groups serve as the extension in the genealogy of generative art of the lumino-kinetic tradition, which leads ultimately later in the decade to the development of electronic art.

name: Invention of the Zuse Graphomat Z 64
desc: Presented for the first time at the Hanover Fair, this revolutionary drawing machine would be used by early computer pioneers such as Georg Nees and Frieder Nake . Designed by the prolific German engineer Konrad Zuse , the Z 64 was one of the first computer-driven plotters, allowing artists to create precise geometric shapes and patterns on paper, translated from computer code. The Graphomat Z 64 was particularly important for computer art because it allowed artists to create complex and precise works without the need for manual labor. This made it possible to create large-scale works that would have been impossible with traditional artistic methods. The Graphomat Z 64 helped to pave the way for the development of computer art and inspired a generation of artists to explore new forms of digital expression, enabled by the Graphomat.

name: “Symbols, Signals, and Noise” by John R. Pierce
desc: This book played an important role in the development of cybernetic theory, stating that “art was clearly a communication phenomenon,” according to Grant Taylor . This echoed Abraham Moles , whose Théorie de l’information et perception esthétique (1958, translated 1966) attempted to objectively formalize communication in art. John R. Pierce also collaborated with Max Mathews at Bell Labs on the earliest electronic music, Music from Mathematics .
subjects: théorie de l'information et perception esthétique

name: “An Approach to Cybernetics” by Gordon Pask
desc: An Approach to Cybernetics by Gordon Pask is a foundational text in the field of cybernetics, which explores the principles of information and control in complex systems. Pask presents the concept of “learning machines” in the book. These are machines capable of acquiring knowledge and modifying their behavior based on that knowledge, similar to a pupil-teacher relationship. Pask argues that these machines should not be designed as fixed, predetermined systems, but rather should be allowed to learn and adapt in response to feedback from their environment. The book also covers the main areas of cybernetics such as feedback, communication, and learning, and argues that these concepts are fundamental to understanding both natural and artificial systems. The book is based on Pask’s own experience designing the responsive machines he describes, such as the Musicolour (1953–57) .

name: Variations luminodynamiques by Nicolas Schöffer
desc: The founder of Cybernetic Art, Schöffer’s pioneering work of video art was an experimental program broadcast on French Television. The Surrealistic 9 min and 10 second film is in the permanent collection of the Centre Pompidou .

name: Epidauros II by Barbara Hepworth
desc: This giant of modernist sculpture, Hepworth’s Epidauros II and its “pure form” would influence Roman Verostko ’s work at that time and throughout his career.

name: Dragons Emerging from the Forest by Kazuo Shiraga
desc: This work by a key member of the Japanese Gutai movement serves as an example of their groundbreaking use of chance. Shiraga swung, slipped and spun back and forth from a rope attached to the ceiling with wet oil paint on his feet. As he swung, his feet would come in contact with the canvas on the floor, creating the piece. This could be considered a work of material generative art with the rope-swing-body-paint-motion combination forming the autonomous system.

name: Bridget Riley Paints Movement in Squares
desc: A rule-based work of art is, simply put, one of the most famous paintings in history, let alone Op Art. In 1961 Bridget Riley painted Movement in Squares , a black-and-white checkerboard whose columns of squares narrow progressively toward one side until the flat surface seems to fold. The masterpiece is built from a single unit and a strict rule of change, resulting in the appearance of movement and depth in the eye of the viewer. It began the black-and-white works that made Riley a leading figure of Op Art. Her painting Current (1964) would later appear on the catalogue cover of MoMA's exhibition The Responsive Eye in 1965. Today, Movement in Squares is in the Arts Council Collection, London.

name: A. Michael Noll Creates some of the First Creative Graphics with a Digital Computer; Terms Phrase Programmer-Artist
desc: The First Computer Art Experimenting on the side with computer-generated creative expression while at Bell Labs , Noll avoided calling the works he documented and produced “art.” He referred to them instead as “patterns” in order to avoid controversy. Patterns by 7090 , as Noll named them, are among the first known algorithmically generated art on a digital computer. These are among the first-known digital generative graphics. These were programmed on FORTRAN with an IBM 7090 mainframe computer. Noll printed the patterns on a Stromberg-Carlson 4020 Microfilm Printer. In a 1962 Technical Memorandum describing the process and showcasing the pieces, Noll coined the term “programmer-artist.” In the Technical Memorandum, Noll speculated that with greater study, “the programmer-artist might be better prepared to produce not just haphazard patterns, but ‘true art.’” Thus, these experiments paved the way for further exploration, particularly at Bell Labs. Noll would go on to display the work publicly three years later, at the Howard Wise Gallery in April 1965 . Le Random’s Monk Antony has interviewed Dr. Noll about this series and the decade of the ’60s. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) . Image is copyrighted by A. Michael Noll and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: The US Company (USCO) Garners Interest for Science and Technology in Art
desc: This group, which formed in 1962, played a critical role in expanding interest in science and technology in art in the United States . The group toured widely with multimedia performances, championing technology in art.

name: Umberto Eco Coins “Programmed Art”
desc: Eco used the term “programmed art” for the Italian kinetic works shown at Olivetti by Gruppo T, Gruppo N, Enzo Mari and Bruno Munari . Programmed art extended the aesthetics and concepts of Constructivism and Neo-Plasticism. According to Grant Taylor , “computer art appealed to the same concepts of objectivity and the will to detach the art object from the idea.” This work thus played an important in calling for the dematerialization of art, which was a profound leap that art undertook, in this time period.

name: American Pop Art Bursts onto the Scene
desc: With no prior personal relationships and independently from one another, American Pop Art exploded in 1962 with four monumental exhibitions. Roy Lichtenstein had his first show of paintings based on comic-book panels at the Castelli Gallery ( New York City) in February. Andy Warhol had his first solo Pop art show, 32 Campbell’s Soup Cans at the Ferus Gallery ( Los Angeles ) in July. James Rosenquist had his first solo show at the Green Gallery (New York City). Lichtenstein, Warhol, Ed Ruscha and Wayne Thiebaud opened the group exhibition New Painting of Common Objects at the Pasadena Art Museum in September. Pop Art played an important role in the development of digital generative art with its emphasis on collaboration, process and mass production. Warhol’s prints also have much in common with digital generative art collections with a unified theme but individual random variation. Casey Reas has spoken of the importance of the mass production of art as a prerequisite for NFTs. This is a monumental step in that direction.

name: “Augmenting Human Intellect” by Douglas Engelbart
desc: In this seminal report for the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Engelbart proposed the idea of using technology to enhance human cognitive abilities. He argued that by developing tools that amplified human intelligence, we could better address complex social and environmental problems, creating a more equitable and sustainable world. His ideas were influential in the development of modern computing, user interface design and collaborative work systems. This vision of the computer as a tool for enhancing human intellect would be echoed by Vera Molnár in her views that the computer enhanced human intuition.
subjects: air force office of scientific research

name: “The Open Work” by Umberto Eco
desc: The Open Work, a book by Umberto Eco , proposed the idea of art as a process of interaction between the artwork and the viewer, rather than a fixed object. This concept has been highly influential in contemporary digital generative art and has expanded the possibilities for audience engagement and participation in the creative process. Casey Reas included this book in his suggested reading list for his talk “ The Thing that Makes the Thing is More Interesting than the Thing .”

name: “The Great Experiment: Russian Art, 1863-1922” by Camilla Gray
desc: The first English-language book about the Russian avant-garde covers the Constructivist and Suprematist movements of the early twentieth-century. The book brought more attention to these movements, particularly outside of Russia , and made their techniques more commonly known. The book, therefore, was an important influence on the Minimalism movement with artists such as Flavin, Morris and Judd all referencing Tatlin, Rodchenko and/or Malevich in their careers.

name: Lee Harrison III Builds ANIMAC
desc: ANIMAC, a hybrid graphic animator and precursor to Scanimate was an early motion capture system. It featured sensors mounted on a person that were captured on a screen. This was an important development in the history of computer video art, particularly attempts to capture human motion such as generative dance and choreography.

name: Clark and Molnar Invent the LINC
desc: Considered the first individual computer work station, the LINC (Laboratory INstrument Computer) was an important forerunner of the personal computer developed by Wes Clark and Charles Molnar at the MIT Lincoln Laboratory. The LINC is a key development in computer science as well as on-chain digital generative art history. LINC represented a key jump in the shrinking of computer sizes, culminating in today’s smartphone-enabled NFTs.

name: “Pour une peinture expérimentale programmée,” in Groupe de recherche d’art visuel (Paris: Galerie Denise René; GRAV)
desc: In the catalogue for this early GRAV exhibition, Morellet would spell out the group’s relevance to the programmed, digital generative art of today. Morellet wrote of the ability of “programmed experimental painting,” essentially today’s digital generative art, to be used in order to experimentally “demystify art.” He believed that generative techniques could produce thousands of works of art at a time for aesthetic experiments. Morellet was proposing a new science of art that he hoped could reveal insights into questions of aesthetics. To conduct his aesthetic experiments, he produced a multitude of works following a program. He called this early material generative art, “programmed experimental painting.” By producing many generative iterations, Morellet sought to gain more data points for his scientific investigation into aesthetics. He aimed to satisfy “the need on the part of a section of the public who wants to share in the “creation” of works of art, and who are interested in demystifying art and in better understanding it.” In other words, Morellet used generative techniques as a tool to better understand art’s underlying aesthetic concepts.

name: Viktor Glushkov Proposes OGAS, a Soviet Computer Network
desc: In 1962 Viktor Glushkov, director of the Institute of Cybernetics in Kyiv, proposed OGAS with Anatoly Kitov and others, a nationwide computer network to manage the Soviet command economy. At its most ambitious, up to twenty thousand computer centers were planned to feed several hundred regional centers and one center in Moscow. Glushkov imagined OGAS, as a “brainlike” network. But the project would stall in bureaucratic limbo for nearly a decade. It reached the Politburo on October 1, 1970, a year after ARPANET went online. The 1971 Party Congress even approved the network and 1,600 factory control systems but OGAS was stripped of its more experimental design, becoming a purely technical network.

name: I. J. Good Edits The Scientist Speculates
desc: In 1962 the British mathematician I. J. Good , who had worked with Alan Turing at Bletchley Park, edited The Scientist Speculates: An Anthology of Partly-Baked Ideas for Heinemann in London. It collected short speculative pieces by scientists on questions they could not yet test, from the nature of mind and consciousness to machine intelligence and life elsewhere in the universe. Good's interest in machines that could improve themselves led three years later to his essay on an “ultraintelligent machine,” an early statement of what is now called the intelligence explosion. The seminal Jasia Reichardt describes the ultraintelligent machine and its story in our Editorials: “The Ultraintelligent Machine and Gaberbocchus Common Room ” .

name: Frank Rosenblatt Publishes Principles of Neurodynamics
desc: Ah, the perceptron, one of the most (in)famous words in AI history. As mentioned previously in this timeline , Frank Rosenblatt first described the Perceptron in 1958. In 1962 Spartan Books in Washington published Frank Rosenblatt's Principles of Neurodynamics: Perceptrons and the Theory of Brain Mechanisms . This 616-page tome was an account of the perceptron research he had begun at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in 1957. The book set out the theory and experiments behind networks of simple neuron-like units that learn to classify patterns by adjusting their connections after each error, and it proved that such learning succeeds whenever a solution exists. Rosenblatt also discussed networks with more than one layer of adjustable units, which he could not yet train reliably. Due to this unreliability in multi-layer perceptrons especially, seven years later in 1969 Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons supposedly disproved the effectiveness of perceptrons and thus neural networks. The impact of this cannot be overstated, as it essentially split the field into connectionism, favoring neural nets and Rosenblatt's perceptron, and symbolism, favoring hard-coded expert systems. It was the learning versus rules AI split that wouldn't really resolve until around 2010. For decades, neural networks were disavowed and denied funding, largely because "Oh, hadn't they already been disproven by Minsky?" They weren't and, of course, as you know. The connectionist/perceptron/neural net/Rosenblatt "side" would end up "winning" and is known today as deep learning.

name: Daphne Oram Develops Oramics, Sound Drawn by Hand
desc: Have you ever wanted to make sound by drawing? Daphne Oram did. Oram co-founded the BBC Radiophonic Workshop in 1958 before leaving the following year to work on her own. With a grant from the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation in 1962 she began building Oramics, a machine that turned drawing into sound. How exactly in 1962 was this possible you ask? Shapes painted on ten strips of 35 mm film were read by photocells as the strips moved. This controlled a sound's pitch, volume and timbre. It was among the first ways to compose electronic music by drawing, a graphic score that the machine played directly.

name: Ivan Sutherland Invents “Sketchpad”
desc: One of the first graphical user interfaces, Sketchpad was the first interactive computer graphics programs.

name: Henry Flynt Coins “Concept Art”
desc: “’Concept art’ is first of all an art of which the material is ‘concepts.’” -Henry Flynt in “Concept Art” Flynt, an American philosopher, musician and artist, coined the term “concept art” in his 1961 essay “Concept Art”, published in An Anthology in 1963. In the essay, Flynt argues that art should be based on ideas rather than aesthetics. He claims that artists should focus on creating thought-provoking works rather than visually appealing ones, a key tenet of post-modernism. Conceptual art shares generative art’s interest in the process of creation, as the term “concept art” was later adopted by other artists, including Sol LeWitt , a progenitor of material generative practices. In many ways, computer art specifically can be seen as an extension of conceptual art, according to Frank Popper and Grant Taylor . In addition to aesthetic overlap, both movements emphasize the importance of ideas over materials and use can use algorithmic procedure, text, and other non-traditional mediums to convey their ideas. Conceptual artists like Sol LeWitt produced instructions for other humans to carry out. Computer artists like Manfred Mohr produced algorithms for a computer plotter to carry out. This was another hugely important step in the dematerialization of art.

name: Military Agencies Create Early Computer-Generated Art
desc: These objects are some of the first creative computer-generated imagery along with A. Michael Noll’s Patterns by 7090 from a year earlier in 1962. They may, however, be the first objects created with the intention of being fine art by a digital computer. Noll considered his work “patterns” at the time to avoid scrutiny. But as of 2023 in a conversation with me, he declared Patterns by 7090 to certainly be works of art. We will share this conversation with Dr. Noll soon. Splatter Pattern won first prize and Stained Glass Window second in the Computers and Automation computer art contest of 1963 , both plotted on an Electronic Associates DATA PLOTTER. The United States Army Ballistic Research Laboratories (BRL) was a scientific research institution established in 1938, primarily focused on the development of ballistic technology for the U.S. military. During and after WWII, it would also be a key contributor to the computing revolution. In the 1960s, the BRL became involved in the development of computer graphics and, thus, digital art, with its attempts to visualize missile trajectories. The creations were produced just one year after the Cuban Missile Crisis. One of the BRL’s contributions to the field of computer art was the creation of the “splatter pattern” technique. This technique involved using a computer program to randomly generate patterns of dots and lines, which were then printed out on a large format plotter. It’s telling that some of the first machines capable of creating digital computer art were used to do so. BRL not only helped to establish computer-generated images as a viable form of artistic expression, it also paved the way for the development of the computer, computer graphics and animation. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .
subjects: united states army ballistic research laboratories

name: “Computers and Automation” Births “Computer Art”
desc: “Computer art” is born! The trade journal Computers and Automation significantly impacted the infancy of computer art. The magazine was the first to use the phrase “computer art,” which it used on the title page of the January 1963 edition. This would help to popularize the term as well as the movement for another decade. Crucially, it also started the pivotal “Computer Art Contest.” The contest helped to popularize the concept of using computers as a tool for artistic expression. The magazine also provided a forum for artists and technologists to exchange ideas and discuss the potential of computer art. Computers and Automation helped to establish a community of artists and technologists who were interested in exploring the creative potential of the computer. It providing the foundation for the movement in the coming years.

name: Condensation Cube by Hans Haacke
desc: Condensation Cube (1963–65) is a sealed transparent acrylic cube containing a small quantity of water. The temperature differential between the inside of the cube and the room causes water vapour to condense and run down the inside walls in continually changing patterns. The rate of condensation and evaporation is affected by the temperature and humidity of the environment, resulting in an ever-changing and unpredictable pattern of water droplets. The work emphasizes the role of natural processes and chance in the creation of art, demonstrating the potential of generative art to create dynamic and evolving artworks beyond the digital realm. It is also a key example of material generative art. While a canonical example of material generative art, the piece does highlight the at-times lacking conceptual foundation of some generative practices.

name: Gaussian Quadratic by A. Michael Noll
desc: One of the most iconic works of early computer art, Noll’s Gaussian Quadratic is a computer-generated artwork consisting of a series of connected lines generated by mathematical algorithms, Noll created while working at Bell Labs . The piece was one of the first artworks to be created entirely by a computer, demonstrating the potential of computers as a tool for artistic expression and inspiring future generations of artists to experiment with computer-generated imagery. Noll himself describes it: “Ninety-nine lines connect 100 points whose horizontal coordinates are Gaussian. Vertical coordinates increase according to a quadratic equation. As a point reaches the top, it is reflected to the bottom to continue its rise. The exact proportions of this pattern were chosen from many other examples. This particular proportion is vaguely similar to the painting Ma Jolie by Picasso.” Derived from Noll’s 1962 experiments, the piece today is in the collection of the V&A Museum as well as Spalter Digital . The piece would go on to be displayed at the first public exhibition of computer art in the United States , at New York’s Howard Wise Gallery in 1965 as well as Cybernetic Serendipity (1968) . Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) where he mentions Gaussian Quadratic as his personal favorite piece. Image is copyrighted by A. Michael Noll and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Thomas Wilfred, Lumia Suite, Opus 158
desc: Commissioned by the Museum of Modern Art, this piece went on view at the museum’s 1964 reopening and stayed on display until 1981 before being disassembled. It was created by kinetic light artist Thomas Wilfred who pioneered the “lumia” art form in the 1920s. The extremely complex work was created on a device consisting of metal, fans, electric motors and light.

name: compArt ER 56 series and Random Polygon Move Signal Frieder Nake’s Entrance into Computer Art
desc: 1963 marks the year that Nake, the computer art pioneer, began making computer art. His compArt ER56 series refers to the program created to produce his work from 1963 to 1965. Random Polygon Move, the earliest catalogued example dating from July 1964, is an early plotter drawing similar in style to Noll’s Gaussian Quadratic with lines connecting points determined by a random number generator. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: “Exposition of Music—Electronic Television” Exhibition by Nam June Paik
desc: Paik’s first exhibit, at Galerie Parnass in Wuppertal in March 1963, marked the birth of video art and represented turning point in the dematerialization of art. The pioneering Korean artist, then working in Germany , transformed thirteen televisions into a multimedia installation that incorporated music, moving images and electronic sound. He combined technology and art in a novel way, using television sets as a canvas to create a new medium of artistic expression, helping to free art from the confines of the static canvas and anticipating much of today’s animated art. Paik’s work showed how technology could be used to create art accessible to the masses through the use of electronic media. It was thus an important example of both mass-media art and the dematerialization of art, two of Casey Reas ’s preconditions for NFTs.

name: Simulation of a Two-Gyro Gravity-Gradient Attitude Control System by Edward E. Zajac
desc: Constructed by Zajac at Bell Labs , this is frequently credited as the first computer animation. Zajac’s Gyro Gravity Gradient Attitude Control System is a study of satellite motion, showing how one could always have a side facing earth during orbit. Zajac programmed the frames in Fortran on an IBM 7090, the same Device A. Michael Noll used to produce his early plotted works. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) . Image courtesy of the artist and SIGGRAPH .

name: ASCII Adopted as Standard
desc: ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) was adopted as a standard in 1963. This code is a character encoding system that assigns unique numbers to represent each letter and character of the alphabet. ASCII has played a significant role in both computer and digital art. In computer art, ASCII characters have been used to create images, designs, and animations, with artists utilizing the unique visual properties of ASCII characters to create often abstract works. Well known examples include Vuk Ćosić ’s Deep ASCII (1998) . Kenneth Knowlton and Leon Harmon ’s Computer Nude (Studies in Perception I) (1966) is an often-cited forerunner, built from small symbols standing for shades of grey rather than ASCII characters. In digital art, ASCII has been used as a tool for text-based art with artists using characters to create intricate typographic compositions and designs. Overall, ASCII has provided artists with a powerful tool for creating digital works that are both visually unique and highly flexible. In terms of its importance at the time, ASCII allowed computers to communicate with each other in a standardized way, regardless of manufacturer or operating system. This meant that data could be easily transferred between different computers and devices, which helped to facilitate the growth of the digital age.

name: “Inventing the Future” by Dennis Gabor
desc: In his book Inventing the Future, Gabor discusses the role of science and technology in shaping the future of society. He argues that technological progress is essential for the advancement of civilization and that scientists and engineers have a responsibility to use their knowledge for the betterment of humanity. Gabor was a strong advocate for the use of technology in creative fields, believing that advancements in science and engineering had the potential to transform art and culture. His ideas helped shape the growing debate in society at the time about whether technology was a net positive or negative for humanity.

name: Roy Ascott’s First Show: “Diagram-boxes and Analogue Structures”
desc: Ascott, British cybernetic and telematics arts pioneer, had his first exhibition at the Molton Gallery, London , in February 1963 with Diagram-boxes and Analogue Structures. The exhibit itself featured “change-paintings and other works in wood, Perspex and glass.” Ascott himself would say about the exhibition: “My first London show at the Molton Gallery in 1964, Analogue Structures and Diagram Boxes, was the breakthrough exhibition, in which I exhibited work based on my enthusiasm for cybernetics that serves as the starting point of al my subsequent essays into interactivity, and my play with the metaphors of science.” He has been asked which project in his career he wanted to be remembered by: “It would be the Molton show, because it seeded ideas that have had legitimacy and relevance beyond the analogue structures I then employed, and informs the practice and theory of the ‘new media’ arts,” Ascot told Melentie Pandilovski.

name: Kenneth C. Knowlton develops BEFLIX
desc: Knowlton, a pioneer of computer art and animation, at Bell Labs developed BEFLIX, the first general-purpose programming language for computer animation. BEFLIX is short for “Bell Flicks” and was written in macro FAP, the Fortran Assembly Program. BEFLIX was used by artists, including Stan Vanderbeek to make some of the earliest experimental, abstract films in collaboration with Knowlton. Image is copyrighted by Ken and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Charles Csuri Begins Experimenting with Computers and Art
desc: Charles “Chuck” Csuri began exploring the possibility of applying computer graphics to art in 1963, while a professor teaching painting at The Ohio State University (OSU). Originally a painter in the 1950s who canoodled with New York’s avant-garde scene, Csuri became increasingly fascinated with the computer and its potential for art making while at OSU from 1960. In 1963, he began with analogue "computational" processes with his work After the Artist . He made the work with a device he built to process drawings, working like a pantograph. It changed the length of one or more of its parts, redrawing the traced image in a transformed state. In 1964 he drew a devil holding a punch card, a jab at the technology of the day. Within three years he was programming a mainframe with the mathematician James Shaffer , where he would produce his most famous early computer art, including Sine Curve Man , Random War and Hummingbird .

name: Doug Engelbart Designs the First Computer Mouse
desc: Doug Engelbart, a computer engineer, conceived the first computer mouse, which his engineer Bill English built from wood with one button. Engelbart’s invention was a significant contribution to the development of modern computing and the tools that would enable digital art. It revolutionized the way users interacted with computers, making it easier and more intuitive to navigate through graphical user interfaces.

name: Hiroshi Kawano Publishes His First Algorithmic Images
desc: Kawano, an information aesthetics scholar and one of the earliest pioneers in using computer algorithms to create artistic compositions, placed the computer at the center of artistic generation. He engaged with computer art on a philosophical level, believing artists created the “art computer” which had its own “artificial creativity.” He published his first computer-generated images in September 1964, going on to computer-generated literature and music. Image is copyrighted by Hiroshi Kawano and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: The First Man (Boeing Man) by William Fetter
desc: At Boeing in Seattle, where Fetter moved in 1963, he and his team were the first to draw a human figure using a computer. Fetter had previously worked at Boeing to create some of the earliest computer graphics of a flight simulation in 1960 . This 3D image of the human body with computer graphics was groundbreaking for its time and is still known famously as Boeing Man.

name: Molnár’s Paris: Rue Hallé Permanent Home
desc: In 1964, the Molnárs planned and constructed their own three-story home and studio on Rue Hallé. Vera later reminisced, “It was the Morellets who lent us money, plus the family and the bank, which meant that we were poor all our lives.” Despite this, it was a spacious and comfortable dream home, profoundly influencing Vera’s artistic journey. Reflecting on the past, she marvels, “Did I already have a table? My own? Which wasn’t half for me, half a desk for François, where I could leave my stuff? There were things I couldn’t do [before] that time because I didn’t have a table.”

name: First Piece of Computer Art Criticism by Arnold Rockman and Leslie Mezei
desc: Arnold Rockman , art critic, and Leslie Mezei, computer scientist, together wrote: “the first recognizable piece of computer art criticism. Appearing in Canadian Art and entitled “The Electronic Computer as an Artist.” This seminal article possessed all of the basic elements of art criticism: historical context, stylistic analysis, and, most importantly, evaluative judgment,” according to Grant Taylor . Note from the title of the article, “The Electronic Computer as an Artist,” how even the earliest forms of computer art asked questions about authorship and the computer’s creative role.
subjects: the electronic computer as an artist

name: US Army’s BRL Wins Computer Art Content Top Prize for Second Straight Year
desc: The United States Army Ballistic Research Laboratories won the Computers and Automation “Computer Art Contest” first prize for the second straight year with Trajectories of a Ricocheting Projectile.
subjects: united states army ballistic research laboratories

name: Leslie Mezei Gives the First Lecture on Computer Art
desc: Canadian Leslie Mezei, computer art pioneer and scholar, played a hugely important and influential role in the development of computer graphics. The lecture was held, according to Grant Taylor , “at the fourth meeting of the Computing and Data Processing Society of Canada .” Taylor continues, describing how Mezei spoke about “the possibility for formulating general laws of aesthetics that could aid in artistic design,” influeced by George David Birkhoff’s 1933 Aesthetic Measure . His interdisciplinary accomplishments cannot be overstated. In his own words: “In 1965 I became an Associate Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto . I taught the first Artificial Intelligence course in Canada in 1967, and in the same year, established the Computer Graphics Group, which became the Dynamic Graphics Project (DGP). [I had] an annual Bibliography from March 1967, and a regular column in ArtsCanada from April 1968 for two years. I started producing my own computer art in 1967, exploring geometric, mathematical and random transformations, and early representational images, using my SPARTA language, and animations with ARTA. They have been included in many exhibitions and published in many catalogues, articles and books.”
subjects: computing and data processing society of canada

name: “monument” for V. Tatlin by Dan Flavin
desc: The first of Flavin’s homages to Vladimir Tatlin , co-founder of Constructivism, alludes to the Constructivist focus on modest industrial materials. Flavin’s modest industrial materials are, of course, fluorescent light tubes which he arranges to resemble Tatlin’s Tower. This never-built but highly influential structure was a monument to the ideals of the communist revolution. Flavin’s monument, in addition to materials, also pays homage to Tatlin’s futuristic, utopian ideals. This series demonstrates Constructivism’s influence on Minimalism, both of which were highly influential to digital generative art aesthetic.

name: Time Popularizes “Op Art”
desc: Despite Victor Vasarely spawning the movement nearly a decade earlier with the manifesto and subsequent exhibition, Le Mouvement , the term “Op Art” was popularized in 1964 by Time Magazine, though its coinage is contested. Op Art and the related Kinetic Art were both focused on motion, perceived or real. Both precipitated the popularization of cybernetic art and the digital motion upcoming with computer-generated art. The culmination of the intersection between Op Art, cybernetic art and proto-digital art emerged at The Responsive Eye at MoMA the following year (1965).

name: 23-Ecke by Georg Nees
desc: 23-Ecke (Polygon of 23 Vertices) is believed to be the pioneer Nees’s first work. It was shown the following year at Computergrafik , the first ever computer art exhibition, organised by Max Bense in Stuttgart . Nees said after seeing this work plotted out by the Graphomat: “Here is something that will not vanish again. Look artists, one can make abstract art en masse! Why should an artist not let himself be helped by the computer?

name: First version of BASIC Released
desc: John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz released version 1 of the programming language, BASIC (Beginner’s All-Purpose Symbolic Instruction Code). Designed for beginners, BASIC made computer programming accessible and increased its overall use, including in the arts.

name: Marshall McLuhan Published Book "Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man”
desc: The book that coined the phrase “the medium is the message,” Understand Media is a significant work in media theory and art history. The book expressed McLuhan’s highly influential ideas about media and its effects on human culture and behavior, still relevant today. McLuhan’s ideas would be further explored and greatly inspirational to artists in the second half of the ’60s that would begin experimenting with this new media technology (television, film, computers, audiotape, etc). This would include Robert Rauschenberg , Yvonne Rainer , John Cage , Andy Warhol , and Stan VanDerBeek who would collaborate with engineers from Bell Labs like Billy Klüver , later a founder of EAT. McLuhan argued that the medium through which information is conveyed shapes how people perceive and understand the world around them. It also popularized the idea of the global village. He introduced the concepts of “hot” and “cool” media, and how they influence people’s level of participation and engagement. His ideas also paved the way for later studies on the impact of technology on society, including the internet and of course art.
subjects: understanding media: the extensions of man

name: Computer Composition with Lines by A. Michael Noll
desc: One of the computer art pioneer’s legendary pieces, Computer Composition with Lines won Computer and Automation’s first prize in 1965. Most famously, Noll used the piece in his Mondrian experiment, seeking to pit a machine’s creative power against a human artist’s. He placed his own Computer Composition with Lines alongside Mondrian’s Composition with Lines and asked his colleagues which they preferred between the two. According to Noll himself : “The conclusion of these investigations of computer-generated two-dimensional pictures is that the exciting potential of computers in art consists in their capability of producing mixtures of random elements with mathematically specified formulae for order.” Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) . Image is copyrighted by A. Michael Noll and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Yoko Ono Publishes Grapefruit
desc: One of the greatest and most referenced works of instruction-based art, Grapefruit remains a canonical example of the dematerialized art object popularized at the time by Lucy Lippard . Ono published the book on July 4, 1964 in Tokyo, itself consisting of instructions for paintings, music, events and objects, printed in an edition of 500. A work such as “Painting to Be Stepped On” exists as a written instruction that anyone can carry out and each performance of it differs. While perhaps Ono's most well-known work, the conceptual artist had written instruction pieces since the mid-1950s, which sat close to the early Fluxus event scores of George Brecht and La Monte Young. Artworks as sets of rules executed by others is the principle that later links conceptual art to code and technological art, as explored in “Living Aesthetics: A Grammar of Protocol Art and Worldbuilding” .

name: The Foundational “Aesthetica” Published by Max Bense is Finished
desc: This 348-page tome by Max Bense , Aesthetica. Einführung in die neue Aesthetik, contained four volumes and a manifesto. Bense published the four volumes between 1954 and 1960 ; the 1965 edition collects them and adds the manifesto. The works “anticipated the principles of computer art” and were foundational to the development of cybernetics. Bense was one of the first theorists to recognize the potential of computer technology as a medium for art. In Aesthetica, he introduced the concept of “generative aesthetics,” and the ability to “program the beautiful” which emphasized the use of algorithms to create surprising and novel artistic forms. This idea inspired artists and programmers to experiment with computer-generated art, leading to the birth of computer art as a distinct genre in the 1960s, where Bense’s impact was felt particularly in Europe at the University of Stuttgart with students Georg Nees and Frieder Nake , who would make some of the earliest computer art. Bense’s work helped establish the theoretical foundations for computer art and its potential as a medium for artistic expression. From a previous entry on the importance of cybernetics : Cybernetics would play a vital role in both the birth of digital art and artificial intelligence, thus making it one of the single most important moments on the timeline. Max Bense and his role at the University of Stuttgart explains the connection to computer art, specifically. He supervised Georg Nees’s doctorate and Frieder Nake sat in on his lectures, leaving an indelible marks on their thinking that last to this day, as this 2018 talk by Nake demonstrates. For artificial intelligence, cybernetics was an early attempt to unite machines and organic beings in a functional way, as it sought a theory of control, feedback and communication applicable to machines as well as animals. In the book Art in the Age of Machine Learning, author Sofian Audry argues that the concept of machine learning dates back to cybernetics.
subjects: art in the age of machine learning

name: The World’s First Computer Art Exhibition: “Georg Nees: Computergrafik”, Studiengalerie der TH Stuttgart
desc: Opening 4 February and running from the 5th to the 19th, Computergrafik was the first of the three 1965 computer art exhibitions globally. Invited by Max Bense to show the graphical work Georg Nees had been working on, Computergrafik was held in the Studiengalerie of the Technische Hochschule Stuttgart . Nees was the only artist on display. The February exhibit was the first gallery exhibition of graphic works created by a digital computer, though a one-day showing of computer-generated images programmed by Joan Shogren at San Jose State College on 6 May 1963 preceded it. It opened just months before the Howard Wise show in New York (April) . It would go on to greatly influence another exhibition several months later in November of the same year with Frieder Nake . The reaction from the general public and from the artistic community upon seeing the first computer art was negative and bordered on hostile.

name: Computer-Generated Pictures, Howard Wise Gallery
desc: On display in April 1965, the legendary Computer-Generated Pictures introduced computer art to the broader public, especially in the United States . The second of the three computer art exhibitions of 1965, Computer-Generated Pictures was the first in North America and the first held in a commercial gallery. The show was held by artist-researchers A. Michael Noll and Béla Julesz spanning several years of their research from Bell Labs . Howard Wise was an industrialist and art lover, particularly Op and Lumino-Kinetic Art. An Op art lover, Wise was particularly interested in the pair’s work with 3D depth perception. Julesz exhibited his random-dot stereograms , consisting of computer-generated patterns that gave the illusion of “binocular depth perception.” Today these are known as “magic eye” pictures. Meant to be viewed in 3D, they handed out glasses to visitors to view the works. The show featured Noll’s stereographic (3D) works as well (1964 link), along with his now legendary: Patterns by 7090 Gaussian-Quadratic Computer Composition With Lines Vertical-Horizontal Number Three Ninety Parallel Sinusoids Famously, not a single work sold; the public reception was cold to indifferent. The show was another example in art history of a visionary exhibition too far ahead of its time to be recognized or understood by contemporaries. Computer-Generated Pictures was a landmark development in the gradual acceptance of the computer’s role in art-making. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) . Image is copyrighted by The Artists and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.
subjects: ninety parallel sinusoids with linearly increasing period

name: computer grafik by Georg Nees and Frieder Nake at Galerie Wendelin Niedlich in Stuttgart (Germany)
desc: Opening November 5, 1965, computer grafik was Europe ’s first computer art exhibition outside of a university and third ever public show. It was the third and final of the three famous 1965 shows. Nake’s first ever exhibition, the show was highly influenced by the thinking of Max Bense and his views on generative aesthetics. Nees took his doctorate under Bense, writing his thesis on computer art, and Nake sat in on Bense’s lectures. The exhibition was extremely optimistic about the creative possibilities of computers and art. It asked questions about technology and art, as well as artificial intelligence, envisioning the out-sized creative possibilities that programmed art promised. While some of these works actually sold for very small prices, public sentiment was muted at best. This author, Peter Bauman spoke to Frieder Nake about the beginnings of computer art and more in “Frieder Nake on “Machinic” Miracles” at Le Random Editorials.

name: Giorno Poetry Systems Founded
desc: John Giorno ’s Poetry Systems , “a nonprofit production company designed to introduce new, innovative poetry to wider audiences,” reflects Giorno’s belief that poetry, within the context of Pop-Art ideas, lagged behind other art forms in terms of media and inventiveness. He sought to innovate poetry by using modern communication technologies as a performance and publication space, leveraging telephones, televisions and records to connect with readers. Giorno would go on to collaborate with William Burroughs and Brion Gysin , among others. -Sasha Stiles *Image credit: John Giorno at Hotel Chelsea staring into Brion Gysin’s Dream Machine, 1965. Courtesy of the John Giorno Foundation

name: “The Responsive Eye”, MoMA
desc: The exhibition by William C. Seitz at The Museum of Modern Art ignited Opto-Kinetic Art and even inspired Vera Molnár shortly after. This landmark exhibition of Op/Kinetic Art popularized the movements as well as the alliance between science, technology and art. The exhibition showcased some of the most influential artists of the twentieth-century, including Bridget Riley , Josef Albers , Ellsworth Kelly , Frank Stella and Victor Vasarely . It also featured a large number of the newly dubbed “ New Tendencies ” movement which included Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel ( GRAV ). Computer art legend Vera Molnár was a member of GRAV as well as François Morellet . The exhibition emphasized the role of technology and movement in the creation of new forms of artistic expression. By linking Op Art and Kinetic Art together, the exhibition showed that art did not have to be a static image. The Responsive Eye paved the way for innovative work that incorporated technology and science: namely, computer art and digital generative art. Three years later, Molnár would use a computer to create “ Interruptions ,” a work with a clear aesthetic nod to "The Responsive Eye.” Casey Reas mentions The Responsive Eye to Le Random when discussing significant moments in generative art history.

name: 13/9/65 Nr. 2 (“Hommage à Paul Klee”) by Frieder Nake
desc: One of the most cited and recognized works among the earliest computer art, Homage to Paul Klee (in English) draws inspiration from Klee’s Hauptweg und Nebenwege (1929) without Nake directly attempting to reproduce it algorithmically. Image is copyrighted by Frieder Nake and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Five Screens with Computer by Gustav Metzger
desc: Hearing the words “five screens with computer” today, our minds automatically think of a laptop or desktop computer’s “screen” or digital display. As such screens did not exist in 1965, this piece’s “five screens” were actually “made of stainless steel, about thirty feet high, forty feet long and three feet deep,” according to Gustav Metzger himself in the Cybernetic Serendipity catalog. In this unrealized project, a computer would eject the screens’ elements one by one until the site was empty, a process that would take ten years. This “auto-destructive” art was a critique of the “rationalism” of computers and technology and backlash to their militaristic roots.

name: “Portrait of the Machine As a Young Artist” by John R. Pierce in Playboy One of the Earliest Computer Art Essays
desc: This landmark essay in the popular magazine for men helped nudge computer art into mainstream culture. Written by Bell Labs ’s John R. Pierce , the title refers to the James Joyce novel, alluding to the computer as a maturing artist. The article encouraged the use of artistic experimentation with computers and technology with a staunchly pro-technology argument.
subjects: portrait of the machine as a young artist

name: “Electronic Art" Exhibition by Nam June Paik at Galeria Bonino (New York)
desc: This early Paik exhibit sought to establish the television as an artistic medium. Along with another of his exhibitions at Bonino (1968), these would establish the artist as a pioneer of video art. The exhibitions would also garner Paik critical attention, especially the piece Magnet TV , which featured a TV screen distorted by a large magnet, an example of material-digital generative art.

name: Four Self-Distorting Grids by François Morellet
desc: Exemplifying the influence of Kinetic Art on Op art, this motorized, kinetic structure demonstrates that Op Art did not have to solely rely on virtual movement. This also indicates the extent to which VIctor Vasarely’s ideas, particularly from his Yellow Manifesto , influenced Morellet.

name: Four-Dimensional Hyperobjects by A. Michael Noll
desc: Made by Noll at Bell Labs , this stereoscopic film of a “hypercube” is one of the earliest 3D computer graphic films. Images were printed side-by-side, frame-by-frame and are meant for 3D freeviewing (like a “Magic Eye”). The work is similar to what Noll and Julesz exhibited at Howard Wise that year . The video can be viewed in the same way as a Magic Eye by relaxing the eye without the need for 3D glasses. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: nul 1965, Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam
desc: As Gutai gained fame in Europe , Jiro Yoshihara , accompanied by his son Michio, was invited to exhibit in Amsterdam . Only three-dimensional and new works were allowed with no paintings. Yoshihara presented nine previously well-received pieces and two new ones by Michio, impressing the audience and solidifying Gutai’s reputation outside of Japan as an exceptional avant-garde art group. This exhibition also featured new European avant-garde groups that had been inspired by the radical ideas of Gutai, including Nul and ZERO .

name: “Computer-Produced Movies” by Kenneth C. Knowlton
desc: The article in which Knowlton explains BEFLIX and his early computer animation techniques, which he developed at Bell Labs . Knowlton writes in the article: “An automatic, electronic microfilm recorder can plot points and draw lines many orders of magnitude faster than a human draftsman can. This machine and the electronic computer which controls it promise to facilitate the production of animated movies for a wide range educational and research purposes.” Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A.
