Michael Noll ( transcript ) , where he discusses Knowlton, BEFLIX and the early days at Bell Labs.

name: DENDRAL Project Begins at Stanford
desc: Much of this Timeline's history of AI will focus on the cybernetic-connectionist-deep learning thread. However, we will from time to time highlight major advancements in symbolic, expert systems. One of the earliest hard-coded AI expert systems used for scientific reasoning was DENDRAL. In 1965 at Stanford University , computer scientist Edward Feigenbaum asked Nobel laureate Joshua Lederberg for a scientific problem to study hypothesis formation. Lederberg, involved in NASA ’s search for life on Mars, suggested identifying unknown molecules from mass spectrometry data. And they did and they created DENDRAL, a program that generated every chemically valid arrangement of a molecule’s atoms and pruned the list with chemists’ "expert" rules of thumb. The team asked chemist Carl Djerassi, “What do you know about this problem that the program does not know?” Bruce Buchanan and Georgia Sutherland turned the answers into rules, working with Djerassi’s colleague Alan Duffield. It was precisely this kind of expert system that would gain in popularity in the '70s and '80s while neural network AI experienced a prolonged winter.

name: I. J. Good Predicts an Intelligence Explosion
desc: For ages, it was easy to imagine and fear but impossibly difficult to concretely understand the capabilities of an "ultraintelligent machine" or what the ramifications would be for humanity, if we did indeed make one. Back in the 1950s and '60s, statistician I. J. Good all too presciently did the imagining part. In 1965, Good, who had worked with Alan Turing at Bletchley Park, published “Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine” in Advances in Computers . Such a machine, able to far surpass the intellectual activities of any person, could also design better machines, setting off what Good called an intelligence explosion. “The first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make,” he wrote, provided it told humans how to keep it under control. Good also consulted on Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey , whose shipboard computer HAL kills most of the crew. Personally, I find it comforting to find contemporary fears perfectly mirrored in decades past. It defangs our current fears a bit, or perhaps only confirms them. Jasia Reichardt , writing for Le Random, wrote about Good and the ultraintelligent machine: “The Ultraintelligent Machine and Gaberbocchus Common Room ” .

name: Alexey Ivakhnenko and Valentin Lapa Train Multilayer Networks
desc: The story of deep learning's ascendance in AI research over decades is a long and twisting tale. But it's remarkable how quickly its theory and potential were recognized. In their 1965 book Cybernetic Predicting Devices , Soviet scientists Alexey Ivakhnenko and Valentin Lapa set out a way to train networks with many layers. The approach, known as the Group Method of Data Handling (GMDH), grew a network one layer at a time. Each unit fitted a simple curve to its inputs and any unit that did poorly on fresh test data was dropped. Ivakhnenko likened it to plant breeding. In 1971, at the Institute of Cybernetics in Kyiv, Ivakhnenko described a GMDH network eight layers deep. Jürgen Schmidhuber ’s 2015 survey of deep learning calls such networks “perhaps the first” deep learning systems of the multilayer perceptron type. No big deal.

name: Warren S. McCulloch Publishes Embodiments of Mind
desc: Embodiments of Mind is a collection of essays and lectures by Warren S. McCulloch and Walter Pitts , the inventors of the neural network (on paper) in 1943. The book includes that neural network founding paper itself, “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity” (1943), which provided the first mathematical blueprint for artificial neural networks and modern deep learning. It also includes a 1947 paper on how nervous circuits might recognize the same shape at any size or position. Twenty years after these astronomically important ideas were first formulated, this book helped repopularize the idea of neural networks and perceptrons in AI. This was the era pre-split, before neural networks were disdainfully prejudged (and underfunded) for nearly two decades.

name: Stanisław Lem Publishes The Cyberiad
desc: Karel Čapek gave us the word "robot" in R.U.R. , previously mentioned in this timeline. In 1965 Stanisław Lem published a new book of dire warnings (er, I mean fables). The book was Cyberiada and its heroes, Trurl and Klapaucius, are rival robot constructors who can build almost anything. In one story Trurl builds the Electronic Bard, a machine that writes poetry on command; asked for a love poem in the language of pure mathematics, it obliges, and its verse drives the kingdom's poets to despair. These fears have never been hard to imagine. What took sixty years was for fable to connect with theory, technology, data and compute to start turning into reality.

name: Anni Albers Publishes On Weaving
desc: Who is the most referenced historical artist to the code-based generation of today? It may very well be Anni Albers . To this author alone, several artists have mentioned her, including Emily Xie , Tyler Hobbs , Snowfro and Travess . Many likely have a copy of this book on their shelves. The former Bauhaus weaving workshop student and instructor had moved to the United States in 1933. On Weaving the book treats weaving as a structure of threads crossing at right angles, a grid of binary choices, over or under, from which patterns follow. Obviously "a grid of binary choices" offers a massive clue as to Albers's continued importance if you're reading this from an art and tech, contemporary perspective. In the book, Albers explained the loom's logic and traced weaving's history from ancient Peru ( Ancient Andean Textiles Weave Legacy of Identity ), whose textiles she collected, to industrial production. Her analysis of weaving as a system anticipates the view of textiles as a forerunner of computing, from the Jacquard loom onward.

name: Mary Allen Wilkes Takes a Computer Home
desc: Today, it's so common to have a computer in the home we barely notice them. They've become part of the furniture. While the personal computer revolution was still decades away (see the next two chapters), perhaps the first home computer appeared in 1965. Mary Allen Wilkes, a programmer on the LINC, the small laboratory computer designed at MIT's Lincoln Laboratory, wrote its operating system, LAP6. When the project moved to Washington University in St. Louis, she chose to keep working from her parents' home in Baltimore, where a LINC was installed in the living room. Wilkes is thus often described as the first person to use a personal computer at home. The LINC itself was extremely influential. Meant for one researcher at a time and operated at a console with a screen and keyboard, the LINC anticipated our desire for computers always nearby.

name: “Systemic Painting” Exhibition, The Guggenheim Museum
desc: This systems-based art exhibit would enable future digital generative practices. Curated by critic Lawrence Alloway , the exhibition coined the phrase “systemic painting” for systems-based work. Such work consisted of mostly abstract geometric compositions with repeated, organized patterns, rooted in minimalism. For Alloway, painting-as-a-system was when an artist created a collection of similar works based on simple rules. “The run of the image constitutes a system, with limits set up by the artist.” For systemic work, Alloway believed that “meaning is complete“ not after a single painting but only when viewing the entire collection as a whole. “The system is the means by which we approach the work of art.“ To analyze the system, “unity within variety" were also important. An example of the kind of system on display was the One Image, the recurring use of a single form. Examples included Kenneth Noland ’s chevrons (below) and Ad Reinhardt ’s crosses. 28 artists participated in the exhibition, including Agnes Martin (below), Ellsworth Kelly , Frank Stella and Jo Baer . The parallels are clear from this early exhibition of material generative art to today’s short and long form digital collections. “ Systemic Painting ” also profoundly influenced the aesthetics of artists beginning to create similar geometric compositions with computers.

name: CTG Pioneers Digital Generative Systems
desc: Computer Technique Group, a Tokyo-based student collective, was founded in 1966. They would pioneer the concept of the artist-as-system-creator and are one of the most important groups in generative art history (digital or material). This collective of art and engineering students, founded by Masao Kohmura and Haruki Tsuchiya , emphasized the role of the artistic expression in the group. The CTG manifesto explains how the group intended to function as not only a design office but also a think tank: “CTG is an active think tank that takes advantage of well developed electronic computer systems and makes them serve the needs of human beings. We, the post-war generation, have been exploring our place in machine society for all our born days. Living without machines is attractive in its own way in our dreadful age but it is regressive evolution back towards apes, and is different from the creative evolution we are aiming for. We will tame the computer’s appealing transcendental charm and restrain it from serving established power. This stance is the way to solve complicated problems in the machine society. We do not praise machine civilization, nor do we criticise it. By a strategic collaboration with artists, scientists and other creative people from a wide variety of backgrounds, we will deliberate carefully the relationships between human beings and machines, and how we should live in the computer age." Besides these lofty ambitions, CTG would go on to introduce the concept of the artist as system creator. These systems could produce unlimited complex forms and patterns rather than just individual works, an immensely influential concept now ubiquitous in today’s generative art. Image is copyrighted by The Artists and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: “9 Evenings: Theatre and Engineering” at the 69th Regiment Armory
desc: The event that legitimized the use of technology in art, Artist Robert Rauschenberg and engineer Billy Klüver ( Bell Labs ) organized 9 Evenings to promote artist-engineer collaboration. In just eighteen months, Bell Labs engineers went from experimenting with computer art and showcasing their results in a small gallery without much fanfare ( Howard Wise ) to this large-scale event at one of New York ’s most prestigious spaces. In fact, New York City’s 69th Regiment Armory was home to one of the most famous exhibition in North American history, the 1913 Armory Show, which first introduced modern art to America . It was the first large-scale collaboration between artists, engineers and scientists. 30 engineers and 10 artists staged a series of elaborate interdisciplinary performances. They realized work that would have been unachievable on their own. The artists used state-of-the-art technology such as computers, video cameras, and projectors to create their works. This marked a significant departure from traditional forms of art-making and opened up future possibilities for artists to experiment with technology. The show featured some of the most intrepid artists of the day including Deborah Hay , Lucinda Childs and John Cage . It also increased the awareness of technology’s use in art in the broader artist community. Besides the immense legacy of the show itself, 9 Evenings also directly led to Rauschenberg and Klüver forming Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT) . EAT, further promoting artist-engineer collaboration, would change the use of technology to make art irrevocably.

name: Maughan S. Mason’s Traveling Show of Analog Computer Generated Works
desc: Arranged by the Western Association of Art Museums, the show featured Mason’s analog computer work, much of it would later be included in Cybernetic Serendipity . The American Mason had a background in the military as well as computer science, working at IBM in Silicon Valley for decades. His contributions to computer art are less often noted today but a deeper dive into the mercurial artist’s work remains rewarding. Image is copyrighted by Maughan S. Mason and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Joseph Weizenbaum publishes ELIZA
desc: The early natural language processing (NLP) computer program ELIZA is published by Joseph Weizenbaum , a computer scientist and MIT professor. Named after the protagonist in George Bernard Shaw ’s Pygmalion, ELIZA is a forerunner of subsequent chatbots, using pattern matching rules to engage humans in conversation. -Sasha Stiles

name: Poemfields by Stan VanDerBeek
desc: Having studied with the poet M.C. Richards and composer John Cage at Black Mountain College , artist Stan VanDerBeek begins developing Poemfields, a series of eight computer-generated films that introduce his “image-based poetry language.” In collaboration with computer scientist Ken Knowlton at Bell Labs , VanDerBeek uses Knowlton’s BEFLIX and an IBM 7094 from 1966-1971. -Sasha Stiles Casey Reas also mentions Poemfields to Le Random as an important early generative film that played a role dematerializing art. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) where he discusses Knowlton, BEFLIX and the early days at Bell Labs. *Image credit: The Stan VanDerBeek Archive . Courtesy of the artist

name: “Information Theory and Esthetic Perception” by Abraham Moles
desc: First published in French in 1958 , and drawing from Claude Shannon’s Information Theory as well as George David Birkhoff , Moles aimed to use techniques of information theory to analyze art. In other words, he sought to view art as communication and analyze it like a science. He developed these theories independently from Max Bense despite both having the aim to of using scientific means to understand aesthetics. Philip Galanter argues that the work of Bense and Moles was instrumental in the early development of complexity science and aesthetics. Moles, for example explored statistical measures of musical order and disorder, valuing it from “banal” to “novel” in an early attempt to understand the relationship between complexity and aesthetics.
subjects: théorie de l'information et perception esthétique

name: Composition with Squares and Walk-through-Raster by Frieder Nake
desc: Nake won the first prize of the 1966 Computers and Automation contest with an untitled drawing of small squares, recorded by Compart as Zufällige Zeichenverteilung (1965). Nake then wrote about his other significant 1966 work, Walk-Through-Raster (plotter drawings). Underscoring the importance of mathematics in his work, Nake wrote about Walk-Through-Raster: “The secrets behind algorithmic art can really be fathomed only when we allow for mathematical descriptions.” Nake used the ALGOL 60 programming language and the Z64 Graphomat plotter.

name: Sol LeWitt Begins Producing “Serial” Work
desc: LeWitt’s Serials marked the beginning of his important rules-based, systems work that could produce many possible outcomes. Computer artists were experimenting at the same time with computer-algorithmically driven rules-based systems.

name: Untitled (one gallon of industrial high-gloss enamel, poured) by William Anastasi
desc: This piece stands as an important example of chance in art as well as an early conceptual and material generative art piece. Anastasi, the American Conceptual art pioneer, focused on relinquishing artistic control and submitting to chance operations. In Untitled, he poured a gallon of industrial paint down a wall and let gravity dictate the final form.
subjects: untitled (one gallon of industrial high-gloss enamel, poured)

name: “Primary Structures” Exhibition at The Jewish Museum Helps Introduce Minimalism
desc: The exhibition was the first in the United States to showcase the emerging Minimalism movement, presenting simplified geometric sculptures made with colorful, industrial materials. It was curated by Kynaston McShine who would go on to curate Information at MoMA in 1970 .

name: “Kunst-Licht-Kunst” Artificial Light Exhibition
desc: According to Art Historian Frank Popper , this exhibition was “one of the founding moments of technological art.” Featuring work from Man Ray , László Moholy-Nagy and others, the exhibition showcased the use of light in contemporary art and sculpture. It was an important step in the development of digital art. It was shown at Stedelijk van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, Holland.

name: Interference by Jean-Pierre Yvaral
desc: The work by Victor Vasarely ’s son, part of a series, was made of cord, steel and wood to create the illusion of pulsation and dynamism. The GRAV member Yvaral “created a link from his early optical research and his interest in science as a model for artistic creation with a subtle use of the computer for the programming of a pictorial surface,” according to Art Historian Frank Popper . The work is an important example of the link between New Tendencies , in particular GRAV.

name: "Behaviourist Art and the Cybernetic Vision” by Roy Ascott
desc: Artist Roy Ascott elucidated his detailed theory of cybernetic art in a two-part article for the journal Cybernetica, published in 1966 and 1967.
subjects: behaviourist art and the cybernetic vision

name: Experiments in Art and Technology Founded with “EAT News”
desc: Founded by engineers Billy Klüver and Fred Waldhauer and artists Robert Rauschenberg and Robert Whitman , following the success of their 9 Evenings show , the aim of Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT) was to promote collaboration between engineers and artists. The group would prove to be one of the most influential and important in computer art history. The first meeting was held in November 1966. EAT News, a newsletter featuring short articles, began the following year. The group formed after the successful 9 Evenings show earlier in the year.

name: “Herstellung von zeichnerischen Darstellungen, Tonfolgen und Texten mit elektronischen Rechenanlagen” (Production of graphic renderings, audio sequences, and texts by electronic computers) Exhibition
desc: This exhibition at the Deutsche Rechenzentrum (German Computing Center) in Darmstadt featured computer music, drawings and text. It helped to popularize computer art in Germany and beyond. It’s also important showing of several (~21) early Frieder Nake works. Released with the exhibition was “Programm-Information Pl-21” a booklet that was one of the first publications explicitly dedicated to computer art and included an essay by Nake on computer graphics.

name: Teletype Corporation develops Inktronic
desc: Printing 1,200 words per minute, this was one of the earliest inkjet printers, known as a teleprinter.

name: First Pattern Recognition Workshops Meet in Puerto Rico and Delft
desc: In October 1966, a pattern recognition committee of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) held the first Pattern Recognition Workshop in Dorado, Puerto Rico. A second met in Delft, the Netherlands , in August 1968. The workshops served researchers applying neural networks and statistical methods to pattern recognition, speech and computer vision, approaches that Nils Nilsson notes came to be called “nonsymbolic” to set them apart from symbol-processing (expert system) AI. Later, this "nonsymbolic" or learning approach would be called connectionism; finally, it would be called deep learning. The committee became the IEEE’s Technical Committee on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, which now sponsors the CVPR computer vision conference. Read about Luba Elliott 's curation of the CVPR 2026 Art Gallery in “Seeing Machines: Luba Elliott on the 2026 CVPR Art Gallery” .

name: Stanford Research Institute Builds Shakey the Robot
desc: Robots that can reason might be the stuff of sci-fi nightmares (and current realities). But in 1966, at their infancy, they seemed much more benign. Shakey the Robot, perhaps the first mobile robot to reason about its actions, looked like a photocopier on wheels and it moved blocks. If anything, it's a bit cute. Led by neural-network researcher Charles Rosen, a team at the Stanford Research Institute (SRI) spent six years building Shakey from 1966 to 1972. Rosen's team consisted of Nils Nilsson, Bertram Raphael and Peter Hart (who later led it), with Richard Duda, Richard Fikes and Helen Chan Wolf. Guided by a video camera and a remote mainframe, Shakey took instructions in ordinary English and pushed blocks between rooms. To plan its routes, Hart, Nilsson and Raphael devised the A* search algorithm, published in 1968 and still used to this day to steer characters in video games.

name: Hanne Darboven Begins Her Number Constructions
desc: German artist Hanne Darboven's works of manual systems and numeric thinking in art recall Vera Molnár 's machine imaginaire or Charles Csuri 's "After Artist" series, pre-computational work that is clearly cognizant of computation. Working in New York from 1966, Darboven began her Konstruktionen , drawings on graph paper built from systems of numbers. She soon based them on the calendar, adding the digits of each date to produce a sum she then wrote out by hand across page after page. The results, often filling hundreds of sheets, are records of time counted and written rather than pictures. They are the artifacts of rules and math rather than the divine hand. Darboven worked alongside Sol LeWitt and New York's conceptual art scene, solidifying the connection between rules and conceptualism.

name: The House of Dust by Alison Knowles
desc: Having collaborated with the likes of John Cage and Marcel Duchamp , Fluxus poet Alison Knowles teams up with composer James Tenney to write The House of Dust – one of the earliest computer-generated poems, dated 1966 to 1968 by ZKM. The text begins as a set of four lists written by Knowles, which are then generated into quatrains via a program written by Tenney using FORTRAN on an IBM computer. -Sasha Stiles Read Le Random’s article about Knowles’s House of Dust, “Generations of Verse .” Image: © Alison Knowles; photo © ZKM | Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe, photo: ONUK

name: E.A.T. Holds Its Press Launch at Rauschenberg’s Studio
desc: Following its first meeting in November 1966, EAT held its press launch at co-founder Robert Rauschenberg ’s Manhattan studio. The meeting was attended by a variety of artists and engineers (from IBM and Bell Labs ). EAT would go on to play an instrumental role in popularizing computer art and promoting technology and art, building upon their seminal 1966 exhibition, 9 Evenings .

name: Sol LeWitt Defines Conceptual Art in Print
desc: In his essay “Paragraphs on Conceptual Art,” LeWitt fixed the term in art-world usage, famously writing that “the idea becomes a machine that makes the art.” LeWitt continued: “I will refer to the kind of art in which I am involved as conceptual art. In conceptual art the idea of concept is the most important aspect of the work.”

name: Charles Csuri Enters the Computer Art Scene with Series of Important Works
desc: After a decade in painting and then years at The Ohio State University making analogue computer drawings, Charles Csuri finally got his hands on a digital computer for art making in 1967. His practice exploded onto the computer art scene that year with several key works. First was his piece with James Shaffer , Sine Curve Man , which was the Computers and Automation first prize winner for 1967. Csuri would also produce the seminal plotter drawings Random War and Aging Process in 1967. Random War would go on to be shown at Jasia Reichardt 's Cybernetic Serendipity the following year. Sine Curve Man began as a line drawing of a man. Csuri and Shaffer, of Ohio State’s mathematics department, reshaped it with a sine curve function on an IBM mainframe and drew the stages on a plotter, since they had no way yet to record it as animation. Csuri's experience reminds me of many people who already had a creative dam filling that was ready to burst once they got access to the right tooling. A contemporary example would be Ryan Murdock , who explained to me how his work with CLIP and GANs was already anticipated by his prior work. He just needed the CLIP part. Csuri, like Molnár around this same time, just needed access to digital computation.

name: Hummingbird by Charles Csuri
desc: One of the earliest computer animations, Csuri moved away from the geometric abstraction of his European computer art peers, introducing figuration to computer art. Csuri generated more than 14,000 frames in which the bird is exploded, scattered and put back together, outputting them to 16mm film. Csuri’s figurative work highlights the breadth of computer art’s capabilities, showing the world a computer could produce more than the abstract visualization of mathematical formulae. This piece is in the MoMA permanent collection and is one of the earliest computer-generated works to enter its collection. Image is copyrighted by Charles Csuri and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Untitled (Micro Innovation) by Georg Nees
desc: This work, from Nees’s series exploring the polygon from 1965-1968, investigates the relationship between “order and complexity” and "aesthetic measure.” These concepts were developed by Abraham Moles and Max Bense in Europe , drawing on George David Birkhoff’s aesthetic measure and on Claude Shannon’s information theory at Bell Labs . Image is copyrighted by Georg Nees and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Verifying star by Donald K. Robbins
desc: This piece by the pioneer computer artist Robbins celebrates the intricacy of geometric forms and their ability to capture nature’s inner beauty. Robbins describes the piece: “This five-pointed star is a three-pointed star, used to check out the incremental step on an incremental plotter, superimposed upon itself. The design has many straight lines at many differnt angles. It was produced on a large Gerber flatbed plotter.” Robbins would go on to be included at Cybernetic Serendipity the following year.

name: Matrix Multiplication Series 31 by Frieder Nake
desc: This colored plotter drawing features four squares with algorithmically assigned colors. An edition of this series is included in the Victoria and Albert Museum. Nake produced the series on a Telefunken TR 4 computer between 1967 and 1968. Image is copyrighted by Frieder Nake and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Computer Nude (Studies in Perception I) by Leon Harmon and Ken Knowlton
desc: Created by Harmon and Knowlton at Bell Labs , this computer generated photomural of a reclining nude, twelve feet long, was made entirely of abstract symbols. Consisting of small symbols standing for shades of grey rather than ASCII characters, Computer Nude is one of the most famous and recognizable of the early computer artworks and is an often-cited forerunner of ASCII art. Harmon and Knowlton had been introduced by Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT) . In the collection of the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, the piece “demonstrates the unique capacity of the viewer’s brain to interpret a composition of abstract symbols grouped to emulate areas of tonal value as a human figure.” The piece would be exhibited the following year at the legendary The machine, as seen at the end of the mechanical age . Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) . Image is copyrighted by The Artists and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Running Cola is Africa by Computer Technique Group (CTG)
desc: This iconic plotter drawing, exhibited at Cybernetic Serendipity , was created in 1967 and 1968 by CTG at the IBM Scientific Data Centre in Tokyo . The work is described in the Cybernetic Serendipity catalog as follows: “A computer algorithm converts a running man into a bottle of cola, which in turn is converted into the map of Africa.” Masao Kohmura , CTG co-founder, was credited with the concept. Image is copyrighted by The Artists and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: “The Science of Art” by Robert E. Mueller
desc: The book voices the growing sense amongst some artists that science was encroaching upon the art world. It represented the art community’s backlash against computer-generated art, lampooning the movement for “aesthetic ineptitude,” according to Grant Taylor .

name: “Research Center Art Technology and Society” Founded in Amsterdam by Robert Hartzema, Tjebbe van Tijen
desc: This early digital art group that would last until 1969 published research reports on issues such as enhanced collaboration between artists and scientists.
subjects: research center art technology and society

name: Gyorgy Kepes Establishes the “Center for Advanced Visual Studies” (CAVS) at MIT
desc: The Center was established at The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) by Kepes “to bring artists from around the world to collaborate with MIT’s community of scientists and engineers, [in order] to produce works using new directions in technological approach.” It was attempted to create a community of innovators, providing opportunities for artists such as Nam June Paik and Stan Vanderbeek. Over the course of 42 years, more than 200 artists would go through CAVS. This interdisciplinary center was MIT’s first foray into contemporary art and an important step in the development of MIT as a critical interlocutor between art and science.

name: Logo Language Developed
desc: Designed by Wally Feurzeig , Seymour Papert and Cynthia Solomon , Logo was a general purpose programming language that was hugely important to the development of computer art. It’s main innovation for computer graphics was the concept of “turtle graphics,” allowing a programmer to manipulate the movement of a robotic turtle sitting on the floor. After being further developed at MIT in the 1970s, Logo would play an instrumental role in the development of generative art again in the 1980s as the language was taught in public schools, influencing a new generation of creative coders and artists, such as Casey Reas .

name: Shun-ichi Amari Publishes Learning Rules for Neural Networks
desc: In 1967, Japanese engineer Shun-ichi Amari published “A Theory of Adaptive Pattern Classifiers” in IEEE Transactions on Electronic Computers . The paper described learning by nudging a machine’s weights after each example, the canonical method known as stochastic gradient descent. Jürgen Schmidhuber calls it probably the first paper to use the method for learning in multilayer neural networks. Amari trained a five-layer network to sort patterns that no single straight boundary could separate. In 1972 he published a network that learned to associate patterns by changing its connection weights. John Hopfield’s much more well known 1982 network rests on the same basic equations and is sometimes called the Amari-Hopfield network.

name: Stephen Todd Works on Early Computer Art
desc: This timeline is increasingly a source for firsthand accounts of generative art history. Todd shared some of his early computer work with us, stating: “I suddenly remembered a bit of algorithmic 'art' from earlier: 1967. Modern day version https://jsfiddle.net/sjpt/x7qn9wgb/156/ . I was working as a vac job for IBM at the Technical University of Denmark in Lyngby, writing a package for the Calcomp plotter . I was asked to prepare a drawing of a super-egg for Piet Hein who had recently popularized the super-egg in a design for a Swedish roundabout. The idea was that a superegg has less sharp ends for cars than those seen in an elliptical roundabout. I liked the idea, but not that it was not continuously differentiable at the points; so I came up with an alternative based on the principle of a driver turning the steering wheel in a regular sine wave. The resulting curve is related to Lissajous figures and hypoid curves, but different. With parameters taken outside the original elongated roundabout it gives nice patterns. The fiddle above is rather more interactive than the 1 day turnaround (if lucky) that I had on runs with the plotter.” Stephen Todd to Peter Bauman, February 9, 2024

name: Schotter by Georg Nees
desc: This iconic early computer-generated drawing features squares on a grid that become increasingly disordered from top to bottom, exploring what would become a central theme in computer generative art, the relationship between order and disorder.

name: “Cybernetic Serendipity” Defines a Movement
desc: Cybernetic Serendipity , Jasia Reichardt ’s landmark international exhibition at the Institute of Contemporary Arts , London , ran from 2 August to 20 October 1968 and was computer art’s first international exhibition. But it was also so much more than that. With cybernetic theory ( Cybernetics Is Born ) as an overarching theme, the exhibition probed the relationship between creativity and technology. It “aroused world-wide interest for computer art and especially for computer graphics,” according to Herbert Franke. It accomplished this by comprehensively showcasing the various movements’ pioneers. The show featured pioneers in a staggering variety of digital arts, including A. Michael Noll , Frieder Nake , Georg Nees , CTG and Charles Csuri (computer graphics), Nam June Paik (video art), Jean Tinguely (kinetic art), John Cage (generative music), Jeanne Beaman (generative choreography), John Whitney (computer film), Ken Knowlton (computer animation) and many others. Cybernetic Serendipity was forward looking, it “deal[t] with possibilities rather than achievements,” according to Reichardt. The genius of the exhibition is that several decades later the collective achievements of the artists at the exhibition are innumerable. The publication itself is even a prized possession today and a work of art. Reichardt said that “the most important single revelation of this exhibition” was that, due to the advent of computers, “people who would never have put pencil to paper, or brush to canvas, have started making images.” This is the legacy of Cybernetic Serendipity. Its promotion of art and technology inspired experimentation and collaboration in the arts that are still reverberating today. It established the computer as an integral force in the history of art, inspired numerous pioneers and introduced cybernetic art to a global audience. From Cybernetics Is Born : Cybernetics would play a vital role in both the birth of digital art and artificial intelligence, thus making it one of the single most important moments on the timeline. Max Bense and his role at the University of Stuttgart explains the connection to computer art, specifically. He taught the first European computer artists, Georg Nees and Frieder Nake, leaving an indelible marks on their thinking that last to this day, as youtube.com demonstrates. For artificial intelligence, cybernetics was an early attempt to unite machines and organic beings in a functional way, as it sought a theory of control, feedback and communication applicable to machines as well as animals. In the book Art in the Age of Machine Learning, author Sofian Audry argues that the concept of machine learning dates back to cybernetics. lerandom.art Listen to open.spotify.com ( transcript ) on Cybernetic Serendipity and Jasia Reichardt. spalterdigital.com Note: The show's famous catalogue appeared in July 1968 as a special issue of Studio International , edited by Reichardt, a month before the show opened.
subjects: art in the age of machine learning

name: “The machine, as seen at the end of the mechanical age” at MoMA
desc: The iconic exhibition inspired Software and facilitated art’s transition from the mechanical to the digital. Curated by collector and museum director, K.G. Pontus Hultén , the exhibition aimed to put the intersection of art and technology into historical perspective. Hultén wanted to examine the human-machine relationship with an extensive art historical overview. The detailed exhibition included over 200 pieces by more than 100 artists from the Renaissance to 1968. Artists ranged from Dürer and da Vinci to Tinguely and Tatlin. It traced the development of the myriad ways artists related to technology over time. From our mechanical past to the newly digitizing 1968, the exhibition questioned the consequences of these changes. “The Machine” also featured contemporary artists at the forefront of digital computing and art. Leon D. Harmon and Ken Knowlton of Bell Labs exhibited their celebrated early computer graphic, Studies in Perception I . Robert Rauschenberg , John Cage and Billy Klüver of Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT) exhibited nine works from a world-wide competition. The winner was Jean Dupuy ’s “Heart Beats Dust.” Art historian Frank Popper called the show "a significant early moment in the passage from the mechanical to the electronic age in art.” It examined humanity’s mechanical past, opening the door for future artists to ask the new, difficult questions facing humans and technology.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: “Generative Photography” at Bielefeld Kunsthaus
desc: Gottfried Jäger , Hein Gravenhorst , Kilian Breier and Pierre Cordier introduced the art world to the concept of generative photography with this eponymous exhibit at Bielefeld Kunsthaus. Rather than thinking about photography as a mirror of the real world, Jäger’s generative photography was non-representational. This abstract work showcased the creative, yet scientific, experimentation possible with the device. According to art critic Georg Bak : “Photomechanical transformations, chemigrams, luminograms and pinhole structures presented a non-representational, systematic-constructive photographic visual language.” While an important movement in its own right, generative photography also served as critical stepping stone in the digitization of art. Herbert Franke explains how the generative processes used by Gravenhorst and Jäger “are results of a generative photography created in programmed working stages. From here it is but a step to electronic automation and so to the computer.”

name: “Computer Graphic” Exhibition at Brno House of Arts
desc: Curated by Jiří Valoch , this was the first exhibition of computer art in Easter Europe . The exhibition featured works from pioneers A. Michael Noll , Charles Csuri , Leslie Mezei, Frieder Nake , Georg Nees and local Czech artist, Lubomír Sochor . Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: Aristid Lindenmayer Introduces the World to “L-Systems”
desc: The Hungarian theoretical biologist and botanist, Lindenmayer, developed Lindenmayer systems (or L-systems) to mathematically describe the growth processes of plant development. This algorithmic botany is still used today by artists such as Zancan and Johnathan McCabe in digital generative art to mimc the fractal patterns of trees and plants. In fact, Le Random’s collection has two excellent contemporary examples that highlight the algorithm: McCabe’s Evotree #1 (2023) and Zancan’s Lushtemples — Highlights of the Hike .

name: Douglas Engelbart Gives “The Mother of all Demos”
desc: This monumental demonstration showed how computers could “amplify human capabilities,” paving the way for modern user interface and experience, changing the way computers were used to make art forever. Engelbart’s presentation included demos of the mouse , word processing, the first graphical user interface (UGI), hypertext, video conferencing, real-time collaboration, and other modern computing concepts. He gave the demo at the Association for Computing Machinery / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (ACM/IEEE)—Computer Society’s Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco .
subjects: institute of electrical and electronics engineers (ieee)

name: "On the Path to Computer Art” by the Parallel Group
desc: The parallel group held the exhibition On the Path to Computer Art in conjunction with a joint conference of MIT and the Technical University, Berlin in the summer of 1968. The show exhibited the latest computer art of the day as well as “examples of their forerunners: mathematically and mechanically produced graphics.” According to Herbert Franke, “it was later shown in more than 150 towns and cities all over the world, also under the aegis of the Goethe-Institut.”
subjects: on the path to computer art

name: Leslie Mezei Develops SPARTA
desc: In an attempt to make graphic design on computers more accessible to those without programming experience, Mezei developed the early computer graphics language SPARTA in 1968. SPARTA, a Procedure Oriented Programming for the Manipulation Language of Arbitrary Line Drawings consisted of “ FORTRAN libraries of programs featuring graphic primitives and transformations like lines, polygons, rotation, and translation, and more sophisticated transformations, including a random number generator.”

name: First Publication of “Leonardo”
desc: Founded by kinetic artist and astronautical pioneer Frank Malina in Paris , the importance and relevance of Leonardo to this day cannot be overstated. It aimed “to serve as an international channel of communication among artists, with emphasis on the writings of artists who use science and developing technologies in their work.” Leonardo was published by Pergamon Press from 1968 to 1991 and has been published by the MIT Press since. It appears six times a year and continues today. For nearly 60 years it has played a an out-sized role in popularizing and promulgating insights and developments in the application of the arts on science and technology.

name: Centro de Estudios de Artes y Comunicación (CEAC), later CAyC, Established in Buenos Aires
desc: CAyC played an important role in the development of Systems art and Conceptual art in Latin America . It was led by Jorge Glusberg from its 1968 founding, as CEAC, until his death in 2012. CAyC was a space for artists to exhibit their work as well as “a multidisciplinary workshop to explore the relationship between art, science and social studies; it positioned itself as a space to generate a new wave of experimental art.” From the Bright Moments Buenos Aires Timeline Poster: Jorge Glusberg established the Centro de Arte y Comunicación (CAyC) in Buenos Aires. CAyC served as a multidisciplinary artist workshop, fostering an innovative space where artists converged to explore the intersection of art, science and communication. The concept of “systems” served as the central framework linking CAyC’s diverse endeavors.

name: Foundation of the Computer Arts Society
desc: Founded by Alan Sutcliffe , George Mallen and John Lansdown , the Society (1968-1985) was formed “to encourage the creative use of computers and to allow the exchange of information in this area.” For decades CAS has aimed to advance the understanding of digital and electronic media’s role in the arts. It was initially founded in ‘68 by Alan Sutcliffe, George Mallen and John Lansdown after advising and participating in Cybernetic Serendipity . The original version would run until 1985. It experienced a renaissance in between 2002 and 2004 and continues to this day (2024). Dedicated to fostering creative computer use, it preserves the rich history of computer-generated art and is now even part of the Victoria and Albert Museum’s collections. As of 2024, CAS continues to promote digital media in contemporary practice, hosts events, exhibitions and an annual Electronic Visualisation & the Arts (EVA) conference.

name: “Computer Art: Media Transformation through Electronics” by CTG
desc: This show by Computer Technique Group (CTG) was held at the Tokyo Gallery, Ginza Miyuki Avenue. The group exhibited Automatic Painting Machine No 1 for the first time, which helped to garner public attention in Japan and elsewhere for their work. Critic and Cybernetic Serendipity curator Jasia Reichardt “recognized that the images produced by CTG were not only different from those produced elsewhere, but were the “most imaginative,” according to Grant Taylor . CTG was seeking to transition the mechanical Lumino-Kinetic, participative art of the previous years, especially that of the Gutai group to the digital.
subjects: computer art: media transformation through electronics

name: Lillian Schwartz Begins Her Computer Art Career
desc: According to the biography on her website, “Schwartz began her computer art career as an offshoot of her merger of art and technology, which culminated in the selection of her kinetic sculpture, Proxima Centauri, by The Museum of Modern Art for its epoch-making 1968 Machine Exhibition .” She would soon after become an artist in residence at Bell Labs , working with Leon Harmon and Kenneth Knowlton.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Notable computer artworks
desc: Return to Square A, Computer Technique Group Return to Square B, Computer Technique Group Shot Kennedy No. 1, Computer Technique Group Christmas Wreath—Computer Style, Maughan S. Mason Intuitively Yours, Lloyd Sumner Self-Portrait, Lloyd Sumner spalterdigital.com

name: Plexus and The Snail by Kerry Strand and Larry Jenkins
desc: The Snail by Kerry Strand , and Symplexity by Kerry Strand and Larry Jenkins , were important early computer-generated drawings for their curvilinear forms. These more organic forms were in contrast to the mostly rectilinear compositions of the time. Grant Taylor explains: “The Snail and other curvilinear figures completed by technologists became precursors to the later 1980s computer art of William Latham and others who abstracted nature’s morphogenetic process and created strange biomorphic forms.” Image is copyrighted by The Artists and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Molnár’s Paris: First Computer Encounter: Bull-GE HQ
desc: Vera Molnár ’s machine imaginaire became a machine réelle in 1968, when she gained access to her first computer through her friend Pierre Barbaud , a French algorithmic composer. Barbaud invited Molnár to the Bull-GE headquarters in Gambetta, where she created the work 1 des premieres images d’après listing – BULL 1968. Molnár generated the piece by having the computer print out numbers corresponding to colors, which she then colored by hand. Molnár would not soon forget this experience, as she would ensure she had regular access to a computer later in the year.
subjects: 1 des premieres images d'après listing – bull 1968

name: Vera Molnár Begins her Computer Art Phase with the Interruptions Series
desc: Molnár’s earliest computer art phase began in 1968 with a short series of untitled plotter drawings and the open series Interruptions (1968–69). These early works consisted entirely of rectilinear forms of varying angles, randomly arranged by Molnár’s own algorithm. In her own words from an interview with Hans Ulrich Obrist she describes them: “They’re square grids, and in each frame there’s either a vertical or a horizontal line, or nothing. 45° and 135°. Four inclines, plus empty space. This you can’t do by hand. It’s the same thing – I still work like that with grids, it’s one of my subjects.” For Molnár it was both a learning experience and revelation: “I was not very good at programming but I finally understood how to do very simple things, this geometric way of working.” She would describe the beginning of her work with computers to Obrist as well: “The real, actual computer was in 1968. That I remember really well. In 1968 we thought that everything was possible and all you have to do is knock on the doors and the doors open. So, armed with this certainty, I went and knocked at the door of the Paris University computing centre, which was in Orsay, and I explained to the head of the centre that I wanted to try to make art with a computer. He gave me a look and I had the feeling that he was considering whether he should call for a nurse to sedate me or lock me up or something. Later, when I got to know this man, he told me: ‘I said yes to you because I thought of a famous quote by Voltaire, the one where he says: ‘I completely disagree with everything that you are saying but will defend until my death your right to do or say or write what you have in mind’’, and so he said yes. That was easily said, it was an honour for me, but I had no privileges whatsoever because it was for scientists and researchers: I was nothing in all that. Back then, it was very expensive, we had to rent computers by the minute, so I sort of shrunk in a corner, the last in line, but I was still there.” Image is copyrighted by Vera Molnár and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: “Beyond Modern Sculpture: The Effects of Science and Technology on the Sculpture of Our Time” by Jack Burnham
desc: The former Artforum editor played a key role in advancing the role of technology in art. His writings, including this book, also explain in great details the dematerialization of sculpture occuring, an important step in the advancement of digital art and electronic art. In the prescient book, Burnham outlines the historical transition from sculpture-as-object to sculpture-as-system, driven by technology. Sculpture-as-system included automata, kineticism, light and cybernetic. Burnham explores the historical roots of these movements, including the importance of New Tendencies and Cybernetics. According to Burnham, “change emanates not from things but from the way things are done.”

name: Georg Nees Completes His PhD Thesis (In German), “Generative Computergraphik”
desc: The pioneer’s doctoral thesis was instrumental in our continued association with computers and generative art. According to “What is Generative Art” : “That thesis was soon widely consulted by the small but growing community, harnessing the words generative and computer together in its readers’ minds.” One of the first book-length publications on computer art, this doctoral dissertation, completed with the guidance of Max Bense , was completed in 1968 and published in 1969.

name: Lee Harrison III Builds Scanimate
desc: The Scanimate was an analog computer animation system that succeeded Harrison’s earlier ANIMAC . From about 1969 until digital computer animation replaced it in the mid-1980s, the Scanimate would “produce a significant portion of the video-based animation seen on television in commercials, show titles, and other graphics.”

name: Stroud Cornock and Ernest Edmonds Meet in Leicester
desc: Leicester-based artists Stroud Cornock and Ernest Edmonds , working at Leicester School of Art and Leicester Technical College, recognize the potential of interactive computer-based art. The two begin working together and by 1970 the colleges merged to form Leicester Polytechnic . Leicester Polytechnic would for nearly a decade and a half become one of the most important centers of computer art in Britain and the world.

name: “The Art of Computer Programming” by Donald E. Knuth
desc: The first volume of a foundational seven-volume series of books seeks to “train the reader in various skills that go into the programmer’s craft.” Knuth continues publishing additional volumes to this day, as the series is still incomplete; the most recent is Volume 4B (2023). This consequential series helped to establish the theoretical ground on which programming was based.

name: Pénétrables by Jesús Rafael Soto
desc: The Venezuelan kinetic art pioneer sought to involve the viewer physically with his immense and immersive Pénétrables installations. These large works consisted of thousands of strands, hanging from above, encouraging viewers to physically interact with the work. These pieces are an important development from kinetic art to electronic art.

name: Sound Activated Mobile by Edward Ihnatowicz
desc: Sound Activated Mobile (SAM) was a pioneering cybernetic sculpture that responded to its surrounding audio environment. The pioneering work of kinetic sculpture was exhibited at Cybernetic Serendipity and serves as an important step in the development of electronic art.

name: “Bit International” Magazine Begins Publication
desc: This New Tendencies magazine published by Zagreb City Galleries would release nine editions from 1968-1972. The Zagreb group would go on to organize the iconic Tendencies 4 in 1969 . 1968 saw the release of “Bit No. 1: The Theory of Information and the New Aesthetics,” which closely examined the thoughts of Max Bense and Abraham Moles . “Bit No. 2: Computers and Visual Research” was also released in 1968 and featured the writings of A. Michael Noll , Herbert Franke, Hiroshi Kawano , Georg Nees , Frieder Nake and Leslie Mezei among others. The magazine serves a critical link between the New Tendencies movement and computer-generated art. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: Some More Beginnings at the Brooklyn Museum, New York
desc: From November 26, 1968, to January 5, 1969, the Brooklyn Museum hosted Some More Beginnings , an exhibition presented by Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.) . Shown in conjunction with MoMA ’s The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age . The previous year, E.A.T. announced a competition—aiming to spur collaboration between artists and engineers—with the best work being feature in MoMA’s The Machine. Nine works ended up being included, while the remaining 137 were shown at the Brooklyn Museum in Some More Beginnings. The nine works shown with The Machine include works by Jean Dupuy , Tsai Wen-Ying , Lucy Jackson Young , Hilary Harris , Lillian Schwartz , Robin Parkinson , Leon D. Harmon and John William Anthes . The work included cybernetic and interactive pieces that spoke, moved, and engaged viewers in new ways. The exhibition marked yet another demonstration of the widespread interest these interventions with emerging technologies elicited in the late 1960s.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Kleiner Sonnenuntergang (Small Sunset) by Dieter Roth
desc: This important example in the history of chance in art and material generative art was created with perishable, common materials that were meant to decay over time, such as paper and foodstuffs. The decomposition of the piece and the chance transformation it produced served as a substitute for the creative control of the artist’s hand.

name: Sol LeWitt Brings His Wall Drawings
desc: Begun in 1968 and continuing until his death in 2007, LeWitt’s seminal Wall Drawings were important examples of randomness in systems-based art. These instruction-based works of conceptual installation art also challenged the notions of authorship and permanence as LeWitt made the instructions for the drawings yet did not necessarily execute them himself.

name: Charles Csuri Carves a Computer-Defined Surface in Wood
desc: One of the earliest instances of a digitally modeled sculpture and something approaching 3D printing resulted from Charles Csuri testing a computer's outputs beyond the plotter and film. For Numeric Milling (1968) one of his collaborators at Ohio State wrote a tool for defining a mathematical surface, the form later known as the Ferguson patch. Csuri had that surface carved in wood on a milling machine in the university’s engineering department. Robert Mallary 's Quad III , shown at Cybernetic Serendipity , is another example from this time of computer-generated sculpture.

name: Wendy Carlos Releases Switched-On Bach
desc: A pioneering work in electronic music, Switched-On Bach consisted of Wendy Carlos, working with the producer Rachel Elkind, playing music by Johann Sebastian Bach on a Moog modular synthesizer, recording each line separately on multitrack tape. The album showed that an electronic instrument could perform familiar music with precision and character. It became one of the best-selling classical albums of its time and won three Grammy Awards in 1970. Carlos went on to score Stanley Kubrick's A Clockwork Orange (1971) and Tron (1982).

name: Richard Williams Develops Art1
desc: The myth of computer art (that this Timeline's chapter titles are guilty of propagating. Hey, myths are useful) is that it took artists until the 1970s to engage with computers. Of course, this began in the '60s, hello Bell Labs and 9 Evenings . It began with artists like Charles Csuri , Nam June Paik , Harold Cohen , Vera Molnár , the Bell Labs gang and others. Well, one more of those "others" is Frederick Hammersley, an art faculty member at the University of New Mexico in 1968. It just so happened that at that same time and place, Richard Williams invented Art1, one of the first programs written so painters and artists (so not computer scientists) could make art on a computer. In two years, Hammersley would go on to make 150-plus works with Art1 in a brilliant Bell-Labs-but-serendipitous collaboration between engineer and artist that echoed 9 Evenings and today's events like Rhizome's Seven on Seven. The electrical engineer Williams developed the computer art program Art1 with the encouragement of the art department chair and renowned kinetic artist Charles Mattox. They aimed to transform UNM into a hub of high-tech creativity and, on a broader scale, sought to bridge the cultural gap that separated the worlds of art and science. The late '60s was still a time brimming with optimism about the potential of blurring the lines between art and science. Narrator voice: "That optimism would not last the decade." But perhaps the project would have been lost to history if it were not for Hammersley and his strong interest in Art1. Patrick Frank’s book Sharing Code: Art1, Frederick Hammersley, and the Dawn of Computer Art draws attention to this fascinating early collaboration in computer art history.
subjects: sharing code: art1, frederick hammersley, and the computer

name: Quad III by Robert Mallary
desc: This computer-generated sculpture was first exhibited at the Whitney Museum and is now in the Tate collection; it was Quad I that was shown at Cybernetic Serendipity in London . It used the program TRAN2, developed by Mallary, the first program for computer-generated sculpture. With TRAN2 he generated 48 printed forms in sequence, the dimensions of which were used to cut plywood for the sculpture.

name: “TV as a Creative Medium”, at the Howard Wise Gallery
desc: This group exhibition, featuring artists such as Nam June Paik and Eric Siegel , saw TV as “the root of the cause of all these changes that [were] transforming our civilization.” This was an important exhibition in the development of video art, which was beginning to boom as video-recording technology was becoming cheaper and smaller, notably the Sony Portapak. The show is notable as one of the first gallery exhibitions given over entirely to television as an artistic medium.

name: “Kunst Und Computer” Exhibition at Vienna Sparkasse
desc: Vienna ’s first computer art exhibition was curated by Otto Beckmann and featured the works of artists such as Herbert Franke, Frieder Nake , Georg Nees and Kurd Alsleben .

name: “Art and Cybernetics” Exhibition by CAyC
desc: The Centro de Arte y Comunicación (CAyC) hold their first international exhibition, in August and September 1969, showing work by Japanese, British, American and Argentine artists. The exhibition showcased the work of artists that used “ideas, synthetic shapes or mathematical equations instead of paintings; lights and motors, and information instead of brushes,” according to the group director Jorge Glusberg .

name: Slant One by Auro Lecci
desc: The Italian artist and self-taught programmer, Lecci used Fortran and a pseudo-random number scheme to generate exact, linear forms inspired by Constructivism’s “machine aesthetic.” Image is copyrighted by Auro Lecci and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: “The Philosophy of Computer Art” by Haruki Tsuchiya
desc: Published in Computers and Automation , the brief article by Tsuchiya stresses the importance of process, randomness and system in computer art. It asks finally, “Can the computer art that is a hobby of engineers and automatically-made art become a new world of aesthetics?” Tsuchiya suggests that the “secrets of wonderful works” can be found in the “balance of system and randomness that computer art provides.”

name: “Tendencies 4: Computers and Visual Research” at Museum of Contemporary Art Zagreb
desc: Tendencies 4: Computers and Visual Research was a groundbreaking exhibition held at the Gallery of Contemporary Art, Zagreb , today the Museum of Contemporary Art, showcasing the convergence of art and digital technology. It featured the latest computer graphics and computer-programmed work of the time, featuring prominent artists such as Frieder Nake , Georg Nees and A. Michael Noll . The previous three Tencencies exhibitions earlier in the ’60s focused on op art, cybernetic art and lumino-kinetic sculpture, highlighting the importance of those movements in the genealogy of computer art and digital generative art. By Tendencies 4 in 1969, the focus had shifted away from the material and toward the digital, spurring the dematerialization of art. Tendencies 4 showcased computer-generated graphics, information theory and conceptual works. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: “Computerkunst - On the Eve of Tomorrow” Exhibition in Hanover
desc: Curated by Käthe Schröder at Galerie Kubus in Hannover, Germany , On the Eve of Tomorrow played an important role of popularizing computer art in Central Europe , as it was one of the largest such showcases in the region. The show featured work from artists such as Computer Technique Group (CTG), Georg Nees , Herbert Franke, A. Michael Noll and Leslie Mezei . Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .
subjects: computerkunst — on the eve of tomorrow

name: Notable Computer Artworks
desc: Herbert W. Franke , KAES series Manfred Mohr , P-18 (random walk), 1969–70 Robert Mallary , Computer Sculpture: Six Levels of Cybernetics spalterdigital.com
subjects: computer sculpture: six levels of cybernetics

name: “When Attitudes Become Form” at Kunsthalle, Bern
desc: This legendary process-based exhibition of Conceptual Art, Arte Povera and Process Art was curated by Harald Szeemann

name: “Event One” by Computer Arts Society
desc: The first exhibition of the newly formed Computer Arts Society , Event One took place at the Royal College of Art . It impacted the development of the “creative use of computers in the arts,” particularly in the UK. The exhibition featured works of architecture, dance, film, graphics, music, poetry and theater.

name: ARPANET Goes Live, Precursor to the Internet
desc: The Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (ARPANET), precursor to the modern Internet, went live in September 1969, with four host computers connected by year’s end. ARPANET’s development facilitated the exchange of information and ideas among scientists and researchers, creating a fertile environment for artistic experimentation in the coming decades.

name: International Psytech Art exhibition – “Electromagica ’69”
desc: The landmark exhibition and symposium held at the Sogetsu Hall in Tokyo featured Kinetic, Light, and Lumino-Kinetic works from Japan , Western Europe and North America . Its installations utilized the tools of mass media including lasers, UV, strobe lights, TVs and various other electronics. Computer Technique Group (CTG) exhibited their works Thermo Field (a thermal painting machine) and Plotting Field. For Plotting Field, the group used a CalComp plotter to produce iterations of their John F. Kennedy images. Besides CTG, several other prominent artists participated in the exhibition. Katsuhiro Yamaguchi showed his Image Modulator made from a TV and glass. Nicholas Schöffer exhibited Chrons 8, a two-meter high steel and light, mechanized sculpture. Finally, Minoru Yoshida of the Gutai group exhibited the cybernetic, mechanized sculpture, EP3. This exhibition further demonstrates the connection between Lumino-Kinetic Art and computer art, as well as the international nature of the movement.

name: CTG Participates in the Paris Biennale
desc: The Japanese Computer Technique Group (CTG) showed three plotted works along with an early computer animation, Computer Movie No. 1, “produced by filming their computer-generated images on an IBM 2250 CRT.”

name: Reticulárea by Gego (Gertrud Goldschmidt)
desc: Gego ’s best-known work, Reticulárea was exhibited at the Museo de Bellas Artes, Caracas. The work was a series of connected sculptures of net and wire-frame mesh that created an interactive environment occupying a large section of the museum’s floor, walls and ceiling. This exhibition was an important moment in the history of geometric abstraction in South America and the link between geometric, kinetic sculpture and digital art.

name: Hello by Allan Kaprow
desc: This interactive video happening utilized the Boston-area closed-circuit TV network with Kaprow as director. It explored human-digital connections and how technology was beginning to increasingly encroach upon such interactions, anticipating many of contemporary society’s issues. This work serves as an important early example of interactive video art.

name: “Cross Talk Intermedia” at the Yoyogi Gymnasium, Tokyo
desc: This exhibition was an attempt to promote a dialogue between American and Japanese artists experimenting with technology and “intermedia.” It featured several artists associated with Jikken Kobo movement. Artists involved include Jikken Kobo memebers Yuasa Jōji and Kuniharu Akiyama , composer John Cage , experimental filmmaker Toshio Matsumoto and Stan Vanderbeek. The exhibition highlights the growing international nature of the art and technology avant-garde movement. It also highlights the impact of Jikken Kobo on the movements of the time.

name: Square Tops by Wen-Ying Tsai
desc: The Chinese born Wen-Ying Tsai was a pioneer of cybernetic and kinetic sculpture. His 1969 works, Harmonic Sculpture and Square Tops exemplify his critical contributions to the development of electronic art from kinetic sculpture.

name: The Systems Group Founded
desc: Inspired by Constructivism, Jeffrey Steele , a former Op Art painter, founded the Systems group, which included artists such as John Ernest , Gillian Wise and Malcolm Hughes . Their work, which was anchored in postwar mathematics and cybernetics, investigated the increasing scale and complexity of systems, raising concerns about the visibility of underlying systems in the finished artwork. As technology improved, artists such as Steele and John Ernest adopted a materialist and generative art technique that celebrated chance and disturbed systems. The group’s goal was to investigate the productive capacities of systems other than humans, arguing for self-sufficient systems. Questions though developed about the potential alienation of systems from the artist, sparking arguments about the role of predefined and changing systems in artistic expression. In 1973, Malcolm Hughes would go on to found the Computer and Experimental Department at the University College London’s Slade School of Art , an important UK computer art hub. Artists such as Paul Brown , Stephen Bell , Stephen Scrivener and Dominic Boreham .

name: Sonakinatography I Movement #III for Multi-Media by Channa Horwitz
desc: Sonakinatography is the breakthrough series by Horwitz, meaning “sound,” “motion” and “notation.” On graph paper, she plotted the motion of eight entities over time with colors and numbers in 8x8 square grids. This work highlights the relationship between artists, technology and machines.

name: Computer Technique Group (CTG) Disbands
desc: At the end of 1969 the group decided to disband citing difficulties collaborating with each other. According to Grant Taylor , “ Haruki Tsuchiya said that the collaborative effort had not been as easy as expected and that ultimately artists and technologists are essentially different.” The end of the ’60s saw interest in technology and art peak before quieting down in the ’70s. The dissolution of CTG was indicative of this sentiment reversal. The group’s legacy remains immense, as CTG can be seen as the first modern digital generative artists for thinking of their work in terms of art-making systems. Grant Taylor explains their defining impact: “Most importantly, though, CTG was the first to envisage the artist as a constructor of a system—a system that would create large amounts of form rather than individual artworks.”

name: Leicester Polytechnic Is Formed
desc: Leicester Polytechnic is designated in April 1969, formed by the merger of Leicester School of Art and Leicester Technical College. Stroud Cornock and Ernest Edmonds become influential figures in the international computer art scene, emphasizing the intersection of art and technology. The school’s impact can still be felt today with its legacy alive through the Computer Arts Society where Edmonds is still active. Throughout the decade of the ’70s until the mid-80s, Leicester Polytechnic (eventually the HCIRU Research Group) would attract some of the brightest minds interested in the intersection of art and technology, including Stephen Scrivener and then Dominic Boreham .

name: Arte y Cibernética Held at Galería Bonino, Buenos Aires
desc: Held at Galería Bonino and organised by Jorge Glusberg , whose CAYC would prove instrumental in developing the computer art movement in South America during the 1970s.

name: The Split: Neural Networks Fall from Favor after Perceptrons
desc: Easily one of the most important and (in)famous moments in AI history, the moment when the field essentially was split in two. This division would last for decades and greatly impact the opposing side of learning almost irreparably. Into the 2000s, researchers in the symbolic camp would still cite (very mistakenly) Marvin Minsky for why neural nets would never work. Well this is the reason. By 2010, the learning side had all but won. By the second quarter of this century, deep learning, a direct descendant of Rosenblatt's perceptron, would be king. Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert ’s Perceptrons (1969) entrenched the two artificial intelligence traditions, by seemingly disproving the learning side and Rosenblatt's perceptron . Minsky and Papert backed symbolic AI's programs based on logical rules. Rosenblatt's learning tradition built networks that adjusted their connections from examples, whose limits the book set out in mathematical proofs. Those proofs were read as showing that neural networks had no future, and the Nobel Committee for Physics writes that the book “led to a hiatus funding-wise” for neural network research. Sociologist Mikel Olazaran traces that reading to symbolic AI’s rise and its control of resources and authority. When neural networks revived in the late 1980s, the official history was rewritten. Yes, it would take two decades before anyone, especially in the West, took neural nets seriously again.

name: Margaret Hamilton's Software Lands Apollo 11
desc: The most famous landing in human history was programmed by Margaret Hamilton, who led the team at MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory that wrote the on-board flight software for NASA 's Apollo missions. During the Apollo 11 landing on July 20, 1969, the guidance computer was overloaded with unneeded tasks and raised alarms. Hamilton's team's design, which ran the most important jobs first and dropped the rest, kept the landing on course. Hamilton even promoted and popularized the term “software engineering” to win the discipline the same standing as hardware. A photograph of her beside a stack of printed code as tall as she is has become an emblem of the work.

name: Trained Artists Intervene with Computers
desc: As the accessibility of computers improves, more trained artists begin directly intervening with the machines and code, such as Joan Truckenbrod and Colette Bangert . By the late 1960s, a highly established British painter in the London art scene, who had only recently represented Great Britain in the 1966 Venice Biennale , became interested in computers. He left London in 1968 to teach art in California , where he gained access to a CDC 3200 mainframe computer, becoming fascinated with artificial intelligence. By 1971 Harold Cohen had built a computer-controlled drawing machine, which he showed at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. In 1972, early drawings from this system were shown at LACMA in Three Behaviors for the Partitioning of Space and by 1973 he had dubbed the system AARON . This special decade thus saw the rise of AI in art from a trained painter. The ’70s also saw Chicago become the center of the generative art universe with Sonia Landy Sheridan at School of the Art Institute of Chicago founding Generative Systems . This experimental art and technology lab had access to the latest emerging devices, enabling them to explore their creative potential. Also in Chicago, Tom DeFanti at the University of Illinois Chicago developed GRASS at the legendary Electronic Visualization Lab that Larry Cuba used on Star Wars . For more context, we suggest watching or listening ( transcript ) to our Ch 5 Artist Discussion with Joan Truckenbrod and Hans Dehlinger , featuring special guest host Anika Meier .
subjects: school of the art institute of chicago
three behaviors for the partitioning of space

name: Information exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art
desc: This landmark Conceptual art exhibition reinforced the dematerialization of the art object. Kynaston McShine curated Information in consultation with art historian and critic Lucy Lippard . The show examined how culture had been altered by “communications systems such as television and film and by increased mobility.” Conceptual art defined the show. Artists employed language and rules to encourage participation. The works consisted of photographs, videos and ideas, representing “the sense of mobility and change that pervades their time.“ This anticipated the coming rise of digital mass media art. The show was “interested in ways of rapidly exchanging ideas, rather than embalming the idea in an 'object'" for visual pleasure, according to McShine. It was a crucial moment in the six year period (1966-1972) identified by Lucy Lippard as the dematerialization of the art object in her watershed book, Six Years: the Dematerialization of the Art Object from 1966 to 1972 . 150 artists from 15 countries participated, including Sol LeWitt , On Kawara , Joseph Beuys and Yoko Ono . The role of Information in the dematerialization of the art object was critical to the development of digital art. For McShine, the artwork wasn’t necessarily a physical object. It was "simply a method of distributing the visual information that interests the artist.”
subjects: six years: the dematerialization of the art object

name: Software at the Jewish Museum, New York
desc: Software - Information Technology: Its New Meaning for Art showcased programmed art’s potential as a creative tool. The experimental exhibition was curated by Jack Burnham . According to the catalogue, it aimed to “encourage [conceptual] artists to use the medium of electronic technology in challenging and unconventional ways.” The exhibition saw “software“ as a process that a machine or person could execute based on instructions from the artist. According to Burnham, the show provided “the means by which the public could personally respond to programmatic situations structured by artists.” The show was deeply inspired by cybernetics' interest in communication and the environment. Software presented art objects as communication devices in dialogue with a responsive audience. Participating artists included those at the forefront of technological and conceptual art: Sonia Sheridan, Allan Kaprow , Nam June Paik , Hans Haacke , and others. Nicholas Negroponte ’s Architecture Machine Group, which would go on to become the MIT Media Lab (with Negroponte as director), exhibited the installation, SEEK , a life-sensing computerized system that pioneered the use of machine learning. Following the strong momentum of the '60s, Software marked a high point in the use of technology in Conceptual art. That same summer, MoMA’s Information had already gathered dozens of conceptual artists, this time with no code involved and little mention of technology. Mainstream Conceptual art had shied away from the computer and code by 1970. Yet in 1970 at Software, Conceptual art and the computer were perhaps at their zenith. It also anticipated today’s digital, instruction-based art by several decades.

name: Computer Art Meets the Venice Biennale
desc: In a sign that computer art was gaining greater acceptance and recognition, some of the movement’s leading artists participated in the first computer art exhibition at the Venice Biennale . Participating computer artists included Herbert Franke, Frieder Nake , Georg Nees , Auro Lecci and the Japanese Computer Technique Group (CTG). The pioneers’ work was included alongside modern art masters Josef Albers and Max Bill . A parallel event also included Computer music and the work of John Cage , Earle Brown and Alan Sutcliffe .

name: Xerox PARC Founded
desc: Xerox’s Palot Alto Research Center (PARC) was founded by Dr. George Pake . The research center was composed of experts in science and information, “The Architects of Information.” They aimed to create “The Office of the Future.” Artists such as David Em in 1975 would go on to create their first digital images at PARC. The center would go on to contribute to the development of technologies such as the laser printer, Ethernet, the personal computer and GUI.

name: Gene Youngblood Publishes the Seminal Expanded Cinema
desc: Youngblood’s Expanded Cinema was an expansive survey of the use of computers and code to create film. The book was critical to the development of media and video art. According to Casey Reas in an interview with Le Random, the book was “an extraordinary primary document written at the moment and with direct contact and interviews with those [computer] artists.” The book in particular highlighted the contributions of John and James Whitney and Stan VanDerBeek .

name: 1970 Osaka World’s Fair Showcases Global Nature of Computer Art
desc: The Osaka Expo marked a pivotal turning point in post-war Japanese art history by marking an end to avant-garde movements and ushering in the era of new media art. Fujiko Nakaya created one of her iconic fog sculptures as part of the Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.) pavilion. She would go on to establish the Tokyo branch of E.A.T. in 1971. Billy Klüver was central to the design of The E.A.T. Pepsi-Cola Pavilion. He specifically sought to provide a participative environment that encouraged visitors to explore.
