The event marked what Grant Taylor describes as the beginning of the end of E.A.T.: “E.A.T. had suffered terribly at the hands of the Pepsi-Cola Company, which withdrew its support after Klüver and his colleagues had designed an intelligent environment for the company’s pavilion at the 1970 Osaka World’s Fair. This, according to [Douglas] Davis, cost EAT heavily in morale and public support. For the critics and artists, who opposed collaboration with profit-oriented firms from the start, the crisis proved their point.”

name: Women Pioneers Bring Naturalism to Computer Art
desc: The decade of the ’70s saw a group of Women pioneers, specifically Grace C. Hertlein , Joan Truckenbrod , Colette Bangert and Lillian Schwartz , infuse the computer art aesthetic with a more naturalist touch. This marked a transition away from the more rigid and precise symmetrical grids of the ’60s. Emblematic of this move were two foundational works in 1970: Grace C. Hertlein’s The Field and Colette and Charles Bangert’s Large Landscape: Ochre and Black. Image is copyrighted by Frieder Nake and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Early Computer Graphics Conferences Appear
desc: The spring of 1970 saw two of the first conferences dedicated to computer graphics. The first, Werkgroep voor Computers en Woord, Beeld en Geluid, took place in March in Delft and Amsterdam . The second, the International symposium Computer Graphics ‘70, took place in April at BruneI University, Uxbridge, England .
subjects: werkgroep voor computers en woord, beeld en geluid

name: Sonia Landy Sheridan Founds Generative Systems at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago
desc: Sheridan founded the Generative Systems program at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago that would continue for a decade. Often combining a variety of equipment in unusual ways, she was interested in exploring the creative possibilities of the latest technology. Like today’s generative art, Sheridan’s work was process and conceptual-focused. Sheridan wrote: "Generative Systems is not primarily equipment and machines, but an idea, an approach and a process that provides new dimensions to our continuing attempts to probe and express the emotional and intellectual lives of human beings.” The Generative Systems program had access to the newest industrial communication tools like Telecopiers, thermo-faxes, computers and more. Experimenters at heart, Sheridan and her students probed the possibilities of these technological systems in unusual ways to test their artistic limits. Sheridan and the hugely influential program demonstrated the creative possibilities of digital tools combined with generative processes.
subjects: school of the art institute of chicago

name: Generación Automática de Formas Plásticas Exhibition at the Centro de Cálculo of the University of Madrid
desc: This computer art exhibition, curated by Ernesto García Camarero featured the contributions of early pioneers of the movement including E. Robert Ashworth , Auro Lecci , Leslie Mezei, Petar Milojević , Frieder Nake , Georg Nees , A. Michael Noll , Zoran Radovic , and Rogers P. Saunders . It also included local artsits such as Manuel Barbadillo , Soledad Sevilla and José Luis Alexanco . Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: Martin Gardner Publishes John Conway’s Game of Life in Scientific American
desc: Originally played by hand with counters and published by Martin Gardner , Conway’s Life is the best-known two-dimensional cellular automaton. It served as a foundational concept and source of inspiration for many generative artists. Life is played on an infinite two-dimensional grid with a certain amount of occupied cells. Each generation determines whether each cell is alive or dead depending on the state of the cells that surround it. Each cell changes status each generation. Conway’s Life would have a profound affect on the field of computation and computer generated art, specifically through its influence on the use of cellular automata in complexity science. This enabled simulation modeling of an diverse range of phenomenon including insects, traffic, weather and astronomic bodies. Overall, Life has had a profound impact on generative art by inspiring artists to explore emergent behavior, pattern generation, and algorithmic systems.

name: Lewis Mumford’s The Pentagon Of Power: The Myth Of The Machine and Alvin Toffler’s Future Shock Take Pessimistic View on Technology
desc: These two books had a significant impact on views towards technology in the 1970s, challenging prevailing notions that technological progress was inherently positive and beneficial. The books encouraged a reevaluation of the relationship between humans and technology. The books marked a shift in the optimism that the art world felt in the ’60s about the future potential of art and technology. Indicative of the ’60s optimism were shows such as Cybernetic Serendipity and The Machine . With public sentiment turning against technology, the art world turned with it, and Conceptualism moved further away from the machine, as the show Information demonstrated.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Georg Nees, Computergrafik Computerplastik (Computer Graphics Computer Sculpture) Portfolio
desc: This portfolio of lithographs based on Nees’s plotted and sculptural work from the ’60s were based on the Information Aesthetics of Max Bense , whom Nees studied under at the University of Stuttgart . Image is copyrighted by The Artist and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: The Senster by Edward Ihnatowicz
desc: This cybernetic sculpture was an important example of the intersection of kinetic art and cybernetic systems.

name: City Painting by Grace C. Hertlein
desc: This work of about 1970 to 1972 by the woman computer art pioneer would go on to inspire contemporary artist Yazid , specifically his work Hashed Cities on fxhash. City Paining also demonstrates the move in the ’70s towards computer art’s interest in more formal compositions.

name: Journal Radical Software Begins Publication
desc: From 1970-1974 Radical Software , founded by Beryl Korot and Phyllis Gershuny with Ira Schneider as co-originator, was instrumental in the development and detailing of emerging trends in video, computer and media art. The periodical, itself heavily influenced by cybernetics, devoted itself to the burgeoning field of video art helped to give a voice to the new movement, while also embracing technology’s use in art at a time when that was become less popular.

name: Terry Winograd Builds SHRDLU at MIT
desc: The history of AI is a story of disillusionment. The reasons to get excited (and afraid) are easy enough to predict and see coming. The problem is time frame and so often theory and ideas had to wait (decades typically) for other fields to advance while their ideas were considered dead and disproven. History praises the true believers like Geoff Hinton who stuck with it through thick and thin. What about the field's apostates? Perhaps no figure in this story represents disillusionment and renunciation as precisely as Terry Winograd. His story overlaps with an early goal of the AI field: a machine that genuinely understood natural language the way people do. Why should humans spend so much time learning machine languages? Shouldn't they learn ours instead? Well, the issue is there are different ways of going about this task and two tracks had already settled by early 1970s, learning and rules. But since the incredibly damaging blow to the learning side of Minsky 's Perceptrons in the previous year , the rules side (symbolic, expert systems AI) was having a moment. Emblematic of that moment for expert systems was Winograd's SHRDLU. Between 1968 and 1970, Terry Winograd wrote SHRDLU at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory . A user typed English on a teletype, while the program could "reply" in a very limited way. It was a simple robot with only a hand and an eye that could move blocks, pyramids and a box shown on a display screen. But that was about it. It was an expert system after all. Every outcome and scenario and answer had to be anticipated and baked in. There was a lot of confusion. It asked which pyramid was meant when an order was unclear and even tried to account for its actions. Pressed on why it had stacked three blocks, it answered, “BECAUSE YOU ASKED ME TO.” The name you ask? It spells the second column of keys on a Linotype typesetting machine. Perhaps because of the clear and obvious limitation of expert systems , Winograd eventually abandoned the field entirely, rejecting it in a detailed and fundamental way. In a 1986 book with Fernando Flores, Understanding Computers and Cognition , Winograd and Flores argued that the task Winograd had spent decades on would be a failure even if it were to ever succeed. That's because, they argued, even fluent-seeming machines could never actually understand because they lacked embodiment and participation in life.

name: Lillian Schwartz and Ken Knowlton Make Pixillation
desc: A legendary piece that sits in MoMA , Pixillation is one of the most famous works of computer-generated film. The piece is by icons Lillian Schwartz and Ken Knowlton made at none other than Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey. Pixillation is a short film that alternates computer-generated mosaics made with Knowlton's EXPLOR language with hand-animated sequences, set to music by Gershon Kingsley on the Moog synthesizer. Schwartz colored the black-and-white computer output through the optical printer, giving the film a vivid, shifting palette. It was among the first films to combine computer animation and traditional techniques as art.

name: “Art et ordinateur” by Abraham Moles and Marie-Luce André
desc: Abraham Moles and Marie-Luce André publish the book “Art et ordinateur,” an important work in the field of computational aesthetics that synthesizes the work of Claude Shannon ’s theories into the work of cybernetics.

name: Howard Wise Gallery Closes
desc: The gallery, which had served as a, if not the, key supporter of technology and art-based practices, closed in 1971 after eleven years in operation. The gallery hosted the first exhibition of computer art in the United States and was critical to the development of the movement. Originally opened in Cleveland (1957-1961), the gallery run by the kinetic, light and video art lover, Howard Earl Wise, was instrumental in bridging the world of lumino-kinetic art to digital art.

name: Frieder Nake’s Publicly Announces End to Computer Art Practice
desc: With his article, “There Should Be No Computer Art,” Nake announced the end of his work with the medium of computers. The essay mirrored the growing pessimism surrounding technology and thus technology and art prevailing in the early ’70s. Ultimately, the essay advocates for the recognition and celebration of human artistic agency and the unique qualities that only human artists can bring to the creative process.
subjects: there should be no computer art

name: Herbert W. Franke Publishes Computer Graphics—Computer Art
desc: The tide was turning against computers and technology in art by 1971. Howard Wise had permanently closed . The same year one pioneer denounces the field and ends his practice in Frieder Nake , another doubles down, however, in Franke. A seminal text, Franke’s Computergraphik - Computerkunst (Computer Graphics—Computer Art) was the first comprehensive, first-hand account of computer art’s origins. The text covers the basics in the hardware, software, practice and history of the first decade of the movement. By highlighting the intersection of technology and art, the book played a pivotal role in shaping the discourse around generative art and establishing its significance as a distinct and innovative form of artistic practice. The book also helped maintain and spark additional interest in computers in art when they were rapidly becoming less fashionable. The veneer of optimism from the late ’60s and early ’70s had peaked. During, one of computer art’s first, dark periods, Franke was the light that held it together with this text.

name: Dan Sandin Creates the Sandin Image Processor
desc: Arriving at the University of Illinois at Chicago , Sandin quickly leaves his mark by developing the revolutionary Sandin IP (Image Processor). The Sandin IP would change thinking about video art as well as computational art as it was one of the earliest modular video synthesizers. The Sandin IP would be used to be make famous works of early video art including Phil Morton ’s Colorful Colorado and Spiral 5 PTL by Sandin, Tom DeFanti and Mimi Shevitz , which is in the collection of MoMA . In particular, Sandin would combine his IP with DeFanti’s GRASS to create a series of digital art masterpieces.

name: Jasia Reichardt’s Publishes The Computer in Art
desc: Reichardt’s follow up text to her landmark Cybernetic Serendipity show and catalog demonstrated her belief that computer art was a continuation of modernism’s transition to abstraction.

name: Franke: “The Program Is the Art”
desc: Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art explains the importance of programming in computer art. Taylor describes how Herbert W. Franke believed that, “it was not the ‘individual productions but the programs that are the real results of creative activity.’”

name: Art and Technology Exhibition at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
desc: Five years in the making and organized by Maurice Tuchman , Art and Technology was an attempt to involve industrial firms (and their machinery) in the production of art. Tuchman aimed “to ‘bring together the incredible resources and advanced technology of industry with the equally incredible imagination and talent of the best artists at work today.’” Tuchman aimed to pair artists with leading technological corporations such as IBM in a residence program for a twelve week period. This gave artists the opportunity to access facilities, research, technology and equipment that would otherwise be unavailable. The resulting artwork was exhibited at LACMA in 1971. Altogether, 76 artists participated including modern masters such as Andy Warhol , Ellsworth Kelly , Dan Flavin , Donald Judd , Victor Vasarely and Roy Lichtenstein . It also included computer and generative art pioneers such as Robert Mallary , Robert Rauschenberg , Eduardo Paolozzi , Hans Haacke and Otto Piene . Any ambitious attempt to pair art and corporations was going to experience blowback and Art and Technology certainly did. Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art explains: “ Max Kozloff in his Art Forum piece ‘Multimillion Dollar Art Boondoggle’ gave what [Jack] Burnham described as the ‘most vicious, inflammatory, and irrational attack ever written on the art and technology phenomenon.’ Kozloff depicted the artists involved in the ‘lavishly funded’ [Art and Technology] project held at the Los Angeles County Museum as ‘fledgling technocrats, acting out mad science fiction fantasies,’ while the ‘more sophisticated artists he envisaged as cynical opportunists.’” Despite changing political winds about the combination of technology and art, reluctance from the art world to embrace the corporatization of art and the enormous undertaking the program entailed, Art and Technology stands as a groundbreaking and visionary event that challenged traditional notions of practice, creativity and authorship.

name: Manfred Mohr’s First Solo Museum Exhibition of Computer-Generated Art
desc: Mohr’s show, Computer Graphics—Une Esthétique Programmée, was held at the ARC, Musée d’Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris , curated by Pierre Gaudibert . According to Margit Rosen , Mohr “made history with the solo exhibition.” Mohr describes the show himself: “I showed 20+ drawings, demonstrated some of the drawings on a large Benson high-resolution flatbed plotter (installed by the company), and hung a large white panel, a sort of guest book, asking what the visitors thought about art and the computer. This banner has become a survey of opinions of the time (on permanent loan at ZKM, Karlsruhe). Though I made hundreds of drawings at that time, the show and catalog emphasised the different algorithms that I wrote and not the multitude of drawings I made from each algorithm.” Image is copyrighted by The Artist and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.
subjects: arc (musée d'art moderne de la ville de paris)
musée d'art moderne de la ville de paris

name: James Seawright, Network III, 1971
desc: Between 1965 and 1971, the lumino-kinetic cybernetic sculptor Seawright created light and sound mechanical installations that were both emblematic of the techo-spirit of the time as well as deeply forward looking, anticipating interactive digital installations of two to three decades later. Network III, displayed at the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, consisted of floor sensors that when stood upon activated overhead lights producing patterns.

name: Key Tech Developments for Digital Generative Art
desc: 1. Intel develops the first commercially produced microprocessor, the Intel 4004. The first of many Intel CPUs. 2. A. Michael Noll develops scanned-display computer graphics Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .

name: Kenneth Martin, Chance and Order V, 1971-2
desc: Martin stands as an important figure in the material (non-digital) generative art movement, according to Philip Galanter . Beginning in 1949, he incorporated rules and chance into his material practice. His Chance and Order series began in 1971 and many pieces are held at the Tate . The abstract geometric compositions are determined by chance and rules.

name: Myron Krueger, Psychic Space
desc: Another lumino-kinetic interactive installation, Psychic Space consisted of a pressure-sensitive floor that activated a sound and visual program on the walls. This work was an important development in the journey to electronic art and continues the tradition of the New Tendencies art groups such as GRAV.

name: Tsai Wen-Ying, Umbrella
desc: Tsai Wen-Ying was important artist in the transition from cybernetic and lumino-kinetic to electronic art. Tsai began creating cybernetic sculptures composed of vibrating rods like Umbrella in 1966. The rotating rods would flash with light, creating illusions of a stationary object as well as chaotic dynamic energy.

name: Arteônica Exhibition by Waldemar Cordeiro
desc: This Sao Paulo exhibition by the Brazilian pioneer, Cordeiro, helped ignite computer art in the region with Brazil and Argentina serving as the cultural bases.

name: Graffiti Emerges as an Art Form
desc: Graffiti art has ancient roots but the modern form began in the '60s in the Northeastern United States . By the early '70s in New York , young people were writing their names and street numbers across the city. Particularly famous is the TAKI 183 tag. While not the first to appear (TAKI began around 1969), it was one of the first to gain widespread attention due to a 1971 New York Times article. Graffiti art plays an important role in the story of digital generative art. First, they share much of the same genealogy. Both have roots in the origins of digital art such as the increased focus on audience participation in the '50s and '60s. Kinetic artists in the '50s such as Yaacov Agam , Pol Bury and Jesús Rafael Soto began creating 3D, geometric and interactive sculptures. The ’60s saw New Tendencies , happenings and conceptualism push to bring art out of the realm of museums. They sought to bring art on to the streets and further involve the audience. Graffiti is a direct result of this growing impulse. Graffiti also continued these traditions. As a form of urban-scale environmental art, it espouses art’s social accessibility and increased interactivity. It was thus a step toward the digital art we know today. Finally, graffiti art has strong ties to web3 art culture. The similarities include: -a strong community ethos -pseudonymous artists -digital avatars -the artist as community leader -challenging the social order

name: Frank Rosenblatt Dies at 43
desc: Some people are programmed to think differently, the people whose ideas change the paradigm. The field of AI lost one of those and one of its best too soon in 1971 when Frank Rosenblatt died in a boating accident in Chesapeake Bay. It was the afternoon of July 11, 1971, his 43rd birthday. The story goes that Rosenblatt had taken some students who were inexperienced sailors out on his sailboat. When Rosenblatt accidentally fell in the water, he was unable to be rescued. As readers of this timeline know, the man is a bit of a hero, certainly a legend. He was the cybernetic lone wolf who was right all along, the unjustly accused . He was the inventor of the first working neural network. In 1958, at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, he described the Perceptron , an electronic device built on biological principles that could learn. He extended the approach in Principles of Neurodynamics . The man certainly had ideas. He was experimental and from 1966, in Cornell’s Section of Neurobiology and Behavior. There he tested whether learned behavior could pass from trained rats to untrained ones through injections of brain extract. Umm. He is so revered to this day, as the IEEE established an award named after him in 2004, the Frank Rosenblatt Award. It is awarded annually for "computational intelligence" and has since gone to another generation of legends, like Teuvo Kohonen , John Hopfield, Geoffrey Hinton and Paul Werbos .

name: Richard Fikes and Nils Nilsson Introduce STRIPS
desc: If you started from first principles, could you solve the world with only logic? Yeah probably not. Remember how before we said ( the split after Perceptrons ) that this period in AI history was a boom time for symbolic, rules-based AI (and a subsequent winter for cybernetic, learning, connectionist AI)? Well, here is another example of "experts" trying to get expert systems to work: STRIPS. Richard Fikes and Nils Nilsson of SRI presented STRIPS, the Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver, at the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in London in September 1971. Built for SRI’s robot research , it described the world in first-order logic and each action as an operator with a precondition, a delete list of facts that may stop being true and an add list of facts that become true. It then searched for a sequence of operators reaching the goal. Asked to gather three boxes in one place, it returned four steps: go, push, go, push. Unlike others from this period, STRIPS had lasting power. The Planning Domain Definition Language, a community standard since 1998, has STRIPS at its core.

name: Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis Publish a Theory of Learning From Examples
desc: After Minsky 's Perceptrons , terms like "neural network" had become akin to rude words in the "West," particularly for funding. They were more accepted, however, in places like U.S.S.R. and Japan . Those areas would contribute in fundamental ways to the connectionist tradition in the '70s, often only to have their work rediscovered (and reattributed) in the '80s and '90s as the West paid closer attention. Here is one such example of the U.S.S.R. keeping the learning torch lit in a time of otherwise darkness. In 1971 Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis of Moscow’s Institute of Control Sciences published in Theory of Probability and Its Applications the full proofs of a result they had announced in 1968. It set out when the frequencies observed in one sample converge to the true probabilities across a whole class of events at once, generalizing the law of large numbers. For learning, that tells when a rule chosen for making the fewest errors on training examples will also hold on new cases. Vapnik and Chervonenkis's proofs rested on a measure of a model class's capacity, now known as the VC dimension. Their theory became a popular way to analyze neural networks moving forward.

name: Charles Csuri Founds the Computer Graphics Research Group
desc: What this timeline (and history generally) teaches again and again is that nothing is the beginning. Everything has a predecessor and context. But some events participate in "beginning-ness" more than others we can say. And in many ways Charles Csuri 's Computer Graphics Research Group (CGRG) kicked off the field of computer graphics and animation as disciplines. Even other "beginnings" like Tom DeFanti and Dan Sandin in Chicago's EVL point back to this beginning. But of course this isn't quite the actual beginning . In 1969 Charles Csuri received a National Science Foundation grant to study the computer’s role in research and education in the visual arts. Not such an easy award for an artist to receive smack in the middle of the Space Race, Cold War and Vietnam War. But Csuri got it. In 1971 he proposed the CGRG at Ohio State, joining faculty and graduate students from art, industrial design, photography and cinema, computer science and mathematics. Starting on an IBM 1130 programmed in FORTRAN, the group worked on hidden-line and shading algorithms and on real-time animation languages. The program seeded two of the prominent real-time computer graphics languages of the next decade, including DeFanti’s GRASS and Manfred Knemeyer’s ANIMA. An internal NSF report would go on to attribute the greatest impact on computer animation in part to CGRG.

name: Lillian Schwartz and Ken Knowlton Make UFOs
desc: Following the seminal Pixillation (1970), in 1971 Lillian Schwartz and Ken Knowlton made UFOs at Bell Labs . It was another film of computer-generated shapes that raced and pulsed across the screen in saturated color, set to a score by Emmanuel Ghent. Like Pixillation, Schwartz again worked the computer output through color filters and an optical printer. The film's rapid alternation of frames was strong enough that viewers reported afterimages of colors that were not on the screen. With UFOs Schwartz pushed computer film toward perception itself, echoing later work by artists like Kurt Hentschlager . Schwartz went on to make more than thirty films at Bell Labs over the next two productive decades.

name: Dennis Ritchie Develops the C Language
desc: Devised by Ritchie at Bell Laps as a language for the budding Unix operating system, C was an upgrade over the B language and derived from the typeless BCPL. One of the most influential programming languages, C and its variations remain in wide use.

name: Harold Cohen’s early work exhibited at LACMA
desc: Cohen’s exhibition, Three Behaviors for the Partitioning of Space, at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art presented his early, pre- AARON computer drawings. This came after Cohen arrived at the University of California , San Diego as a visiting lecturer in 1968, becoming professor and department chairman in 1969, and learned programming from Jef Raskin .
subjects: three behaviors for the partitioning of space

name: Manfred Mohr Begins Exploring the Cube
desc: With Cubic Limit I (1972-1975), Mohr begins his hallowed work focusing on the cube. He created an alphabet of signs from the twelve lines of a cube. He then used programs to combine, rotate and generate these signs to create images. Noteworthy works include P-155 Cubic Limit (1974-76), which was exhibited at the 1986 SIGGRAPH exhibition, A Retrospective. Despite the similarity in content, style and subject to Sol LeWitt ’s exploration of the cube in the mid-70s, Mohr’s work never received close to the critical attention “on the grounds of its computational basis,” according to Grant Taylor .

name: Grenzgebiete der bildenden Kunst (“Frontiers of Fine Arts”) Exhibit at the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart
desc: This exhibition, according to Herbert W. Franke , was an example of “only a few events of purely artistically oriented institutions” displaying computer art at the time. This stands in contrast to “the best opportunities for presenting computer graphics” at the time: scientific conferences.

name: Atari Founded
desc: Crticial to the turn in human thinking that made a generation of artists love computers. The Atari would encourage millions to fall in love with digital devices, particularly with its 1977 release of the Atari 2600 . The Atari would also play a role in the emergence of the Demoscene as the earliest crackers used the console.

name: P-120-A Meta Language II by Manfred Mohr
desc: This work was heavily inspired by Max Bense ’s generative aesthetics and, by extension, Noam Chomsky’s Syntactic Structures and his work with generative linguistics. P-120-A Meta Language II, a dense grid of marks, explores the relationship between symbols and systems.

name: Important Early Publications Including Computer Art
desc: The following were three publications important to the development of computer art according to Herbert W. Franke : 1. La scienza e l’arte (ed. Ugo Volli ): contains the essay “Computer Art” by Ernesto Garcia Camarero highlighting the relationship between mathematics and shapes. 2. Open Research: highlights Dutch artists working with the computer as a tool at the time. 3. Computer Graphics (by Johann Willsberger ): covers a research team aiming to enhance artist-scientist collaboration.

name: Edward Lorenz Presents Paper on the Butterfly Effect
desc: A key text in the development of chaos theory and thus twentieth-century science, Lorenz “was the first to recognize what is now called chaotic behavior in the mathematical modeling of weather systems.” Chaos theory would play a critical role in the development of generative art according to academic Phil Galanter. Galanter stresses the role of systems in generative art and proposes a way to classify generative systems in terms of order and disorder based on chaos theory. Chaos theory and generative art are intertwined through the exploration of complex systems and the creation of dynamic, unpredictable patterns. Chaos theory studies the behavior of nonlinear systems, emphasizing sensitivity to initial conditions and the emergence of unpredictable outcomes. Generative art leverages algorithms and rule-based processes to generate artwork that evolves organically, often exhibiting complexity and self-similarity. By embracing chaos and randomness as creative forces, generative art can harness the principles of chaos theory to produce visually captivating and unique pieces.

name: Robert E. Mueller Pans Computer Art
desc: Writing in Art in America and one of the few times computer art is mentioned by a major mainstream art publication, Mueller describes visual outputs from computers as “exceedingly poor and uninspiring.” This sentiment reflects the growing skepticism of the times regarding technology and art.

name: Surface Substitution on 36 Plates by Jennifer Bartlett
desc: This important work in both math and chance in art demonstrates how algorithmic approaches to material art could produce visually interesting patterns based on numbers.

name: Shigeko Kubota’s Video Diaries
desc: The Fluxus artist’s work with video diaries began in 1972. Kubota’s experimental approach combined performance, technology, and personal narratives, creating visually striking and thought-provoking works. She explored themes of identity, feminism, and the relationship between nature and technology. Her influential video sculptures, installations, and performances paved the way for future generations of video artists, inspiring them to merge the personal with technology.

name: Atari Releases Pong
desc: A pioneer of electronic gaming, Nolan Bushnell commissioned Pong from the engineer Al Alcorn . Pong, one of the first successful video games of all time, introduced the world to interactive electronic entertainment. Beyond its technological impact, Pong also had artistic significance, blurring the lines between art and technology and showcasing the creative potential of digital media as a medium for artistic expression. Pong’s success demonstrated that video games could be more than just entertainment; they could be a form of interactive art, inspiring future generations of artists to explore the aesthetics, storytelling and interactivity within the realm of video games and media art.

name: Arteônica by Waldemar Cordeiro
desc: Computer art pioneer Waldemar Cordeiro advocated for the use of digital media in art the year following his Arteônica [art electronics] exhibition (1971) where he introduced his version of computer-aided design to the art world. Teaming up with physicist and engineer Giorgio Moscati , Cordeiro organized some of the earliest computer art shows in South America . From the Bright Moments Buenos Aires Timeline Poster: Computer art pioneer Waldemar Cordeiro advocated for the use of digital media in art the year following his Arteônica [art electronics] exhibition (1971), where he introduced his version of computer-aided design to the art world. His legacy extended through his daughter, Analivia Cordeiro, who embarked on pioneering research fusing dance and mathematics around the same time. Her creation, M 3x3 , became Brazil ’s first video art piece, debuting at the Edinburgh International Festival in 1973. It is also among the earliest video dance works globally.

name: Teuvo Kohonen, Kaoru Nakano and James Anderson Publish Associative Memory Networks
desc: Neural network research needed a win . It got that and began its long road to recovery after the Perceptrons book setback , especially in the West, with Associative Memory networks. In 1972 three researchers working separately published network models of associative memory: Teuvo Kohonen in Finland with a “correlation matrix memory,” Kaoru Nakano with the Associatron and James A. Anderson of Rockefeller University in New York with an “interactive memory.” Each stored many patterns across the same set of connections, so that a whole item could be recalled from an associated cue or from a fragment of itself. In other words, computers at the time stored memory like a filing cabinet. These stored memory as distributed, with every memory spread over all the connections. In the early 1980s Kohonen’s self-organizing map brought Finnish AI research to international attention when Hopfield's 1982 network built directly on this line. Breakthroughs in parallel and distributed computing in earnest would come a decade later but this was a critical step for connectionist, learning AI in an otherwise deep winter.

name: Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel Create Prolog
desc: Ah, the era of symbolic AI boom . It continues. In the fall of 1972, Philippe Roussel implemented the first Prolog in Marseille for Alain Colmerauer’s project to reason with a computer in French. The name, suggested by Roussel’s wife, abbreviates programmation en logique . A Prolog program was a set of facts and rules in logic. It ran by asking a question it answered by proof, backtracking when a line of reasoning fails. This was not too dissimilar to the English logic program STRIPS, by Richard Fikes and Nils Nilsson at Stanford Research Institute and mentioned previously in this timeline ( STRIPS ). The first large Prolog program, 610 clauses by Colmerauer, Robert Pasero and Henry Kanoui, answered questions about short French texts. Prolog was successful enough as Japan ’s 1982 Fifth Generation Computer Systems initiative took logic programming, and Prolog in particular, as its basis.

name: Hubert L. Dreyfus Publishes “What Computers Can't Do”
desc: Is the entire field of AI just fundamentally flawed, asking the wrong questions and making the assumptions from the very beginning? Today, as the power of these tools has flipped more to, "Uh oh, maybe we should actually be slowing this down," it seems harder to make this point. But in 1972, it fell on more receptive and convincible ears. Learning and neural nets were "disproven" and expert systems were showing their obvious limitations . The field was vulnerable, even at its very core. Enter philosopher Hubert L. Dreyfus and his book What Computers Can't Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason . Dreyfus is like today's Gary Marcus , someone with a long and consistent track record of AI skepticism, regardless of developments. He couldn't be dissuaded because his opposition came from somewhere deep and unmovable. Marcus (I mean Dreyfus) had begun his attack seven years prior in 1965's “Alchemy and Artificial Intelligence,” a paper for the RAND Corporation. His argument is familiar and persists to this day: That embodiment and experience are fundamental to intelligence. Drawing on Martin Heidegger and Maurice Merleau-Ponty, he argued that human intelligence depends on bodies, situations and tacit skills that cannot be written down as rules, so the symbolic programs of the day would stall. To be fair, they were correct in predicting the fall of expert systems . But they were less imaginative about the potential of other technologies to be more successful where expert systems failed (hello deep learning and its roots next decade ). So was this the end of AI? As you probably read an AI summary of this text instead of the real thing, obviously not. AI researchers largely dismissed Dreyfus. The guy didn't quit. He doubled down and revised the book as What Computers Still Can't Do in 1992. My takeaway from these critiques, which have persisted for decades, is to always be wary of saying what computers or machines can never do. Over time, they just might surprise you.

name: Edward Shortliffe and Colleagues Develop MYCIN at Stanford
desc: As mentioned, it's the early 1970s and expert systems are all the rage . Learning has fallen out of favor temporarily in the West . If you wanted AI funding at this time in places like the United States , it had better be symbolic AI. Work on the symbolic MYCIN began at Stanford in the spring of 1972. It was a collaboration of medical student Edward Shortliffe, computer scientist Bruce Buchanan and clinical pharmacologist Stanley Cohen that became Shortliffe’s 1974 dissertation. The expert system program advised physicians on antibiotics for bacterial blood infections and, later, meningitis. Its knowledge sat in if-then rules drawn from Cohen and infectious disease physician Stanton Axline, 200 at first and 450 later. MYCIN questioned the physician, reasoned backward from possible conclusions and could show which rule prompted each question. In a blinded 1979 test on ten meningitis cases, eight outside specialists rated it above all nine human prescribers. However, the system was never tested in an actual hospital setting on real people. Even symbolic AI had limited trust capital, especially when it came to people's health.

name: Cybernetic ARTRIP in Tokyo
desc: Held at the Sony Building in Tokyo , this notable Japanese computer art exhibit famously featured Shiro Takahashi ’s inflatable faces and hands that were computer controlled. It also featured international artists such as Ruth Leavitt and Miljenko Horvat . The exhibition also featured the work of pioneer Hiroshi Kawano .

name: Thomas DeFanti Develops Animation Language GRASS (Graphics Symbiosis System)
desc: GRASS (Graphics Symbiosis System) is simply put one of the most important advancements in computer graphics, well, ever, but especially of the 1970s. Combined with Dan Sandin 's Image Processor and others, it transformed the capabilities of computers. It gave them the ability to animate in real time on a screen, something dreamed of since the days of oscillographs. Completed as DeFanti’s doctoral work at Ohio State University, this landmark early computer animation language that was used by Larry Cuba to produce the graphics for the training sequence for the Rebel attack on the Death Star in Star Wars . Cuba would work on GRASS with DeFanti at the University of Illinois Chicago beginning in 1975. Copper Giloth worked on GRASS doing simulations of water sculptures for a friend experimentally. DeFanti wrote GRASS in Charles Csuri’s Computer Graphics Research Group , supported by Csuri’s 1971 National Science Foundation grant for real-time film animation. It ran on the group’s PDP-11/45 with a Vector General display.

name: Harold Cohen Pioneers AI Art with AARON
desc: AARON , the autonomous drawing machine Cohen named at Stanford in 1973, pioneered the use of AI to create art. With his seminal 1973 essay “Parallel to Perception: Some Notes on the Problem of Machine-Generated Art,” Harold Cohen articulated his efforts to develop “autonomous art-making behavior” that was inventive and could “conjure meaning.” Cohen differentiated this “autonomous art-making” from computer art, which he did not highly regard, claiming that “'computer art' can barely claim consideration as art at all.” Cohen’s collaboration with AARON as a human-machine collaboration lasted 40 years and demonstrated a machine’s ability to make creative choices. His ideas and concepts for these coming decades can be found in this paper. Image is copyrighted by The Artist and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: M 3x3 by Analívia Cordeiro
desc: The seminal work of Brazilian video and computer art pioneer, Analivia Cordeiro, M 3x3 is not only a work of generative choreography, it is also a work of video art. The piece syncs the movements of the cameras with the dancers who wear abstract geometric outfits in black and white. M 3x3 anticipates the merging of technology and dance while criticizing Brazil ’s military dictatorship at the time. It also serves as a continual commentary on the influence of technology and society. From the Bright Moments Buenos Aires Timeline Poster: Computer art pioneer Waldemar Cordeiro advocated for the use of digital media in art the year following his Arteônica [art electronics] exhibition (1971) , where he introduced his version of computer-aided design to the art world. His legacy extended through his daughter, Analivia Cordeiro, who embarked on pioneering research fusing dance and mathematics around the same time. Her creation, M 3x3, became Brazil’s first video art piece, debuting at the Edinburgh International Festival in 1973. It is also among the earliest video dance works globally.

name: Arte y Computadoras by CAYC
desc: Held in Buenos Aires , Argentina , in cooperation with the University of Minnesota Minneapolis, Arte y Computadoras (“Art and computers in Latin America ”) was part of CAYC’s exhibition at the International Conference on Computers in the Humanities (ICCH). The exhibition was closely related to CAYC’s 1971 exhibition, Arte y Cibernetica. It featured work by Waldemar Cordeiro and Jaume Maymó among other Latin American computer art pioneers. The ICCH would go on to hold talks in North America biennially until 1987.
subjects: international conference on computers in the humanities (icch)

name: France Hosts International Computer Art Events
desc: The first such event, Art et Ordinateur, held in Bordeaux was a seminar and exhibition that showcased the work of artists such as Manfred Mohr . The second was organized by SESA (Software et Engineering des Systemes d' Informatique et d' Automatique) which arranged the computer art show, Ordinateur et Creation Artistique.

name: The Computer Arts Society Organizes INTERACT: MACHINE: MAN: SOCIETY
desc: INTERACT: MACHINE: MAN: SOCIETY was an “eventibition” that took place over five days at Edinburgh University. It included papers, a conference and an exhibition of creative computer graphics, generative dance/choreography, cybernetics and poetry. The “eventibition” featured artists such as Manfred Mohr , CAYC, Alan Sutcliffe , Manuel Barbadillo and Greta Monach . The Computer Arts Society (CAS), founded in 1968 by Alan Sutcliffe, George Mallen and John Lansdown , has aimed to explore the role of digital and electronic media in the arts for decades. After a hiatus from 1985 to 2004, CAS experienced a renaissance, preserving computer-generated art history and becoming part of the Victoria and Albert Museum’s collections. In 2024, CAS actively promotes digital media through events, exhibitions, and the annual Electronic Visualisation & the Arts (EVA) conference.

name: Xerox PARC Develops Alto Personal Computer
desc: On the cutting edge, the Alto had a bitmapped screen and pioneered the graphics-based display, mouse, windows and icons that later systems inherited. It was never sold commercially and only 2,000 units were made, yet it was hugely influential particularly with upcoming personal computing breakthroughs like Apple ’s Macintosh and Microsoft ’s Windows. The Alto also signaled the growing accessibility of computers. Freed from the confines of government agencies and large corporations, computers were becoming accessible to artists directly. This enabled traditionally trained artists to begin explorations with computers, including Lillian Schwartz . Thus, the Alto would significantly impact the future of computer generated art and digital art as we know it by shaping its core design and facilitating its greater accessibility.

name: 1024 Colours by Gerhard Richter
desc: Inspired by hardware store paint color charts, this painting’s composition was determined by a randomly generated algorithm. This piece is part of a series started by Richter in the 1960s. They are related to the color collage work of Ellsworth Kelly , which Richter was unaware of at the time. Richter and Kelly’s algorithmic explorations of color and form stand as critical examples of material generative art’s importance and rich history.

name: Malcolm Hughes Establishes Experimental Department at the Slade
desc: Hugely important and later renamed the Experimental and Computing Department and lasting until 1981, the department introduced computer and video fine art to the Slade School of Fine Art at University College London , influenced by Slade staff member titans and students such as Harold Cohen , Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi . The Department marked a critical leap into the field of technology in by the art school. It was a rarity among traditional art schools, particularly in the UK. Independent Group figures including Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi had trained at the Slade, and Harold Cohen taught painting there from 1961 to 1968. William Coldstream , Slade Professor from 1950 to 1975, provided significant assistance for the Experimental and Computing Department, building on his experience at the General Post Office Film Unit in the 1930s. Harold Cohen, who was quite as a successful painter before turning to computer art, contributed to this technological revolution with early works that demonstrated an interest in systems and logical processes. Malcolm Hughes , co-founder of the Systems group in 1969 , played a crucial role in launching the new Slade department, which reflected Constructivism. Additional students from the department include artists such as Paul Brown , Stephen Bell , Stephen Scrivener and Dominic Boreham would study under Hughes at the Slade.

name: P-154-C by Manfred Mohr
desc: Work indicative of Mohr’s early to mid-70s work exploring and deconstructing the cube.

name: Motorola Begins Developing First Handheld Mobile Phone
desc: Motorola annonuced the development of the Dyna-Tac. It would not commercially available, however, until 1983. The development of mobile devices is seen by artist Casey Reas as an important pre-condition for NFTs.

name: IBM Produces First Portable Computer
desc: The IBM SCAMP Microcomputer was a prototype of one of the first portable computers, the IBM 5100 which would be announced in 1975. This stands a critical moment in the decade of the transition from mainframe to microcomputers, smaller, more portable computers that were becoming available to artists. Herbert W. Franke would write about the importance of the microcomputer in the ’70s: “But the emergence of microprocessors and microcomputers, which came as a surprise even to experts, and with it the general availability of “decentralized intelligence” has created an entirely new situation….Thus, the new situation provides the best conditions for activating artistic capabilities, but it also increases the chances of achieving better quality.”

name: International Computer Arts Festival at The Kitchen, New York
desc: This festival featured panels, films, graphics and music made or inspired by computers. It included the work from a particularly impressive set of computer video pioneers such as William Fetter , Lillian Schwartz , Stan Vanderbeek and John Whitney . It also included audio work by Fluxus artist, Alison Knowles .

name: Six Years: The Dematerialization of the Art Object from 1966 to 1972 by Lucy Lippard
desc: Lucy Lippard ’s book Six Years: The Dematerialization of the Art Object from 1966 to 1972 was a seminal publication that had a significant influence on contemporary generative art. Lippard’s book chronicled the emerging conceptual art movement, emphasizing the importance of ideas and processes over traditional art objects. Her focus on the dematerialization of art and the emphasis on concepts, systems and participation laid the foundation for generative art’s exploration of algorithmic and rule-based processes. In particular, the notion of a dematerialized art object has been critical to the contemporary understanding of art and its connection to the blockchain and NFTs. These instruments enable digital ownership. Lippard’s book also encouraged artists to embrace new technologies and computational methods, leading to the development of generative art practices that prioritize dynamic, interactive, and generative systems. Six Years served as a catalyst for redefining artistic practice and expanding the possibilities of art beyond materiality, inspiring generations of generative artists to experiment with digital technologies and dynamic processes.
subjects: six years: the dematerialization of the art object

name: Thomas DeFanti Founds Electronic Visualization Lab (EVL)
desc: Founded by Thomas DeFanti and Dan Sandin , the Electronic Visualization Lab (EVL) is still in existence today. EVL is a research lab at the University of Illinois at Chicago focused on computer science and advanced technologies. It specializes in collaborative visualization, virtual reality and data science. Over the years, they’ve created innovative technologies like the CAVE virtual reality system (90s) and SAGE graphics environment (2000s). They work on connecting scientists and engineers with tools to visualize complex data, allowing them to gain insights. EVL also collaborates globally and is supported by organizations like the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health and more.

name: The Lighthill Report Is Published
desc: This infamous report is blamed for essentially single-handedly beginning the first AI winter, especially in the UK. It's the best-known example of a direct link to funding drying up (the early robot FREDDY) due to outside skepticism. By this time in parts of the UK AI funding was growing and fast. But was it really worthwhile? Did any of this computer alchemy even work? There were levels of concern about AI from a very fundamental base at this time. In early 1973, Britain ’s Science Research Council published James Lighthill’s “Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey,” dated July 1972. The council had asked Lighthill, Cambridge’s Lucasian Professor of Applied Mathematics, for a personal review due to his outsider and supposedly unbiased status. He divided the field into advanced automation, computer-based studies of the central nervous system and robot building. His influential report backed the first two fields, but rejected general robotics. His reasons were issues of scale (sound familiar?) He blamed a failure to recognize the “combinatorial explosion” that swamps search as problems grow. In June 1973 he debated it on BBC television with AI proponents Donald Michie, John McCarthy and Richard Gregory. But the researchers lost the public's and funder's imaginations, as the report spread beyond the UK to places like DARPA, causing a world-wide AI winter ( the first AI winter ).

name: Inaugural SIGGRAPH Conference Held
desc: Occurring during the National Sciences Foundation Workshop on Computer Graphics in Boulder, Colorado, the inaugural SIGGRAPH (Special Interest Group on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques) conference, held in July 1974, marked a pivotal moment in the intersection of art and technology. Bob Schiffman and Jon Meads organized the event because they decided it had been too long since a dedicated computer graphics conference had been held. They then decided to piggy back on the larger NSF conference. The conference and its subsequent iterations would bring together researchers, artists, and industry professionals to showcase and discuss advancements in computer graphics and interactive techniques. SIGGRAPH provided a platform for the exchange of ideas, the presentation of groundbreaking computer-generated artworks and the establishment of a community focused on merging art and technology. The inaugural SIGGRAPH conference set the stage for future conferences and played a crucial role in shaping the history of art and technology, fostering collaboration, innovation, and the growth of computer-generated art.

name: Vera Molnár Begins her Iconic (Des)Ordres Series
desc: One of Molnár’s most recognizable series of works, (Des)Ordres consists of a grid of concentric squares with random distortions that highlight the distinction between order and chaos. According to the Digital Art Museum, “The title suggests a word play in French between two meanings: “désordres” (disorders) and “des ordres” (some orders), which implies that within the apparent dissarray one can find an underlying logic.” Image is copyrighted by the artist and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Art et Informatique by Maison de la Culture d’Angers
desc: The festival featured work by some of the leading computer graphics and photography artists of the time including: Vera Molnar, Hein Gravenhorst , Herbert W. Franke , Manfred Mohr , Gottfried Jager, Frieder Nake and Georg Nees .

name: The Bat-Sheva-Seminar on the Interaction of Art and Science
desc: Organized in Jerusalem by the computer artist Vladimir Bonačić , a member of Leonardo’s editorial advisory board, the seminar was attended by Jonathan Benthall , Herbert W. Franke , Frank Joseph Malina, Abraham A. Moles, A. Michael Noll and John Whitney . The aim of the twelve-day seminar, held 3 to 14 November 1974, was to promote lasting international cooperation in the field of computer art. Due to political events, only the first iteration was pursued. Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll ( transcript ) .
subjects: bat-sheva seminar on the interaction of art and science

name: Frieder Nake Publishes Ästhetik als Informationsverarbeitung (“Aesthetics as Information Processing”)
desc: According to Herbert W. Franke , this was “probably the most important book [on early computer art].” The book aimed to relate the Information Aesthetics of Max Bense and Abraham Moles to Computer graphics.

name: TV Buddha and TV Garden by Nam June Paik
desc: TV Buddha remains one of Paik’s signature works, a video sculpture consisting of a seated Buddha facing a television screen where it watches an image of itself. The work touches on themes of surveillance, East and West, past and present, religion and technology and the viewer’s role in an artwork. TV Buddha confronts the viewer with the juxtaposition of an ancient statue and its real-time image on a television screen, exploring the relationship between tradition and technology. TV Garden, another seminal video installation by Paik which was staged at the Guggenheim in 2000, consists of densely placed live plants with TV screens hidden throughout. The work merges technology and nature by surrounding viewers with a forest of televisions, contrasting the digital and physical realms. These immersive environments aimed to challenge traditional notions of art and introduced the concept of interactive and multi-sensory experiences. The groundbreaking installations not only showcased the creative potential of technology in art but also laid the foundation for the exploration of generative systems, interactivity and the fusion of digital and analog mediums that characterize digital generative art today.

name: Incomplete Open Cubes by Sol LeWitt
desc: In this seminal work, LeWitt demonstrates his mastery of seriality, exploring the 122 ways of making an incomplete cube. The work is meant to challenge the boundary between art and the outside world by framing elements from the surrounding space. LeWitt’s exploration of the cube garnered wide acclaim from the mainstream art world in contrast to the Manfred Mohr’s largely ignored exploration of the cube beginning a year earlier.

name: Jasia Reichardt Captures Key Theme of ‘70s Computer art: The Artist-Programmer
desc: According to Jasia Reichardt and Grant Taylor , the 1970s marked the era of the artist-programmer. The practitioners of computer art began shifting away from the engineers and scientists who began the movement a decade earlier. From the early ’70s it was being pushed forward according to Frank Dietrich in Taylor when “a growing breed of technological artists with hybrid capabilities started to appear.” Traditionally trained artists had access to computers for the first time as their access improved. The field was no longer dominated by those in control of very expensive and often secretive large machines. Further, Taylor writes how “Reichardt announced in 1974, ‘The bridges between art and science are finally only built by those who embody something of the two disciplines.’” The concept would permeate the computer art of the ’70s where artists saw themselves as modern-day Renaissance artists, combining scientific advancements and art, in the spirit of Leonardo da Vinci , the artist-engineer.

name: The Dinner Party by Judy Chicago
desc: A landmark work of feminist art made from 1974 to 1979, this installation consists of a large, triangular shaped banquet table set with symbolic place settings representing 39 historically significant women. The work challenges the preciousness and permanence of fine art while its mixed media and collaborative, conceptual nature mirror trends in digital art.

name: Noisefields by Steina and Woody Vasulka
desc: This audiovisual work of “video noise” was created by the electronic art pioneers Steina and Woody Vasulka who co-founded The Kitchen in 1971 where they helped non-technical artists incorporate technology into their practice. Noisefileds is the result of experimentation with modulators and video synthesizers in an attempt to build a visual vocabulary for their electronic images. This pioneering work explored the creative potential of analog video synthesis, manipulating electronic signals to generate abstract and dynamic visual compositions. Noisefields showcased the possibilities of real-time signal manipulation and the emergence of electronic aesthetics. The Vasulkas' experimentation with video and electronic systems laid the foundation for subsequent artists to explore generative processes, interactivity and the fusion of technology and art.

name: Videoplace by Myron Krueger
desc: Deemed “decades ahead of its time” by Casey Reas , Krueger developed Videoplace for nearly twenty years. This interactive computer system allowed users to engage with virtual environments through body movements and gestures. Built first with video alone, and with computer vision added over the following decade, Videoplace pioneered the concept of real-time interactive video art, blurring the line between the physical and digital worlds. Its influence on digital generative art lies in its exploration of user participation, interactivity and the creation of dynamic, responsive visual experiences.

name: Vera Molnár Develops “Molnart” Software
desc: Molnár developed “Molnart” with her husband François Molnár between the years 1974 and 1976. The software program enabled engagement in expérimentation picturale systématique (“systematic pictorial experimentation”). The program, written in FORTRAN , required a high capacity computer connected to a display screen and plotter. Molnart aimed to disrupt the monotony of regular, geometric patterns, achieving various “satisfactory…aesthetic states” by systematically modifying inputs step by step. Vera Molnár applies various techniques such as removing squares randomly, changing the probability of appearance for different-sized squares, introducing color and incorporating human-like irregularities. This approach was essentially what Molnár used to achieve (Dés)Ordres (1974) . The generated images could then be drawn on paper. Vera Molnár reflects on the aesthetic qualities of the computer-generated images compared to hand-drawn ones and explores the possibilities of combining different methods.

name: Science and Technology in the Arts: A Tour through the Realm of Science/Art by Stewart Kranz
desc: This comprehensive exploration of the intersection between science, technology and the arts provides a captivating journey into various disciplines, including visual arts, music, theater, film and literature, to reveal the profound influence of scientific advancements on artistic expression. Kranz’s work reads as a reflection of a decade (the ’60s) that both he and the artists he covers are responding to the vast social, technological and political developments. It covers topics such as digital art, artificial life, interactive installations and multimedia performances, showcasing the transformative power of science and technology in shaping contemporary artistic practices.

name: Muriel Cooper Founds the Visible Language Workshop
desc: Derived from a course taught by Cooper at MIT, “Messages and Means,” the Visible Language Workshop (VLW) took a multi-disciplinary approach to design. It specifically examined interactive design, photography, typesetting and platemaking. The VLW would prove to be highly influential to both Casey Reas and Zach Lieberman in their creations of Processing and openFrameworks respectively. “The VLW was well-connected to both the Center for Advanced Visual Studies and the Architecture Machine Group; and it was one of the original research groups of the Media Lab at its founding in 1985 .”

name: Marvin Minsky’s Frames and Roger Schank and Robert Abelson’s Scripts
desc: While Marvin Minsky 's story is so much more complex than the villain of neural networks, in the early 1970s, fresh from his Perceptrons mic drop on the entire field of neural networks, Minsky was still in the villainous symbolic AI phase. The odd thing about rejecting neural networks is that Minsky was still trying to model what brains did. Rather than modeling based on neuroscience, he made something up called frames. In a June 1974 MIT memo, “A Framework for Representing Knowledge,” Minsky proposed that a mind meeting a new situation, such as a child’s birthday party, selects a remembered structure called a frame and adapts its details to fit. A frame’s slots come filled with default assumptions that new information can displace. That I guess we can all mostly agree with. But how do they acquire that new information? Can they learn it through training or must it be hard-coded? Minsky went with hard coding. In 1975 Yale’s Roger Schank and Robert Abelson presented scripts as a specialization of frames: stereotyped action sequences for familiar events. SAM, a program by Chris Riesbeck, Richard Cullingford and Wendy Lehnert, used a restaurant script to fill in a short story’s unstated steps. Their 1977 book Scripts, Plans, Goals and Understanding expanded the theory. These theories were not entirely without use but they can be considered more cul de sacs than highways .

name: The First AI Winter
desc: First, with winters, it's important to note that they're more about funding than sentiment per se . Certainly capital and sentiment can go hand in hand. But just because AI capital mostly went away, no doubt damaging spirit, it in no way whatsoever permanently destroyed morale. Just to recap, from 1969 onwards , AI funding went nearly exclusively to its symbolic, expert system branch. The only issue is that after a few years, that camp's limitations became quite apparent. With apparently nowhere at all for the funds to go as symbolic enthusiasm waned, we enter the first AI winter proper. Now, AI does not completely disappear the rest of the decade as later moments ( MYCIN , frames and scripts ) will show, but things do get quieter for a bit. Hard to believe but even the US military with its unlimited budget and keen (KEEN) interest in smarter weapons stopped its funding. The Mansfield Amendment of November 1969 had limited Defense Department support to research of “direct and apparent” military use. But the real death knell was that pesky Lighthill Report . Its influence extended well beyond the UK as it prompted a Pentagon panel to review DARPA ’s own AI program. The result? DARPA moved money out of robotics, hurting Stanford Research Institute . DARPA also ended its five-year Speech Understanding Research program without the planned follow-on. But it's important to note that AI winters are best thought of as funding dry spells, slower periods, rather than full-fledged cataclysms of nothingness. (again, see the many future moments in this decade about AI). Plenty of evidence suggests that despite wintery conditions, grassroots efforts expanded during this time. The historian Thomas Haigh disputes talk of AI winters and notes that SIGART, the ACM’s AI interest group, grew from 1,241 members in 1973 to 3,500 by mid-1978. People might have cared even if dollars didn't at this time.

name: Brian Eno Releases Discreet Music
desc: Eno’s album Discreet Music employed techniques for randomness to compose generative music that resemble and build upon the work of artists such as John Cage , Terry Riley and Steve Reich . The album introduced the approach Eno would later call “generative music,” where musical compositions are created through rule-based processes rather than traditional composition methods. Eno utilized tape loops, delays, and ambient textures to create an evolving and infinitely variable sonic landscape. This approach challenged the notion of fixed, linear music, emphasizing the exploration of emergent and unpredictable outcomes in both music and visual art.

name: The 2nd International Conference on Computers and the Humanities (ICCH/2) at the University of Southern California
desc: Organized by Grace C. Hertlein , ICCH/2 was the largest computer art exhibition held in the United States at that point. It showcased computer made film, graphics and music. The show also marked a turning point in the use of the computer for art. According to Hertlein, “In earlier exhibitions, physicists, systems analysts and programmers dominated this field. Today’s computer artists are sculptors, painters and architects who use the computer primary as a designing aid.” The aesthetics of computer art were changing as well. Hertlein viewed earlier computer art exhibitions, including the most famous of them all, Cybernetic Serendipity , as “overly preoccupied with mathematics and line.”
subjects: international conference on computers in the humanities (icch)

name: Mandelbrot Coins the Term Fractal
desc: Benoit Mandelbrot coined the term fractal while working at IBM. Using computer generated images to illustrate his mathematically derived concepts, he was consolidating hundred of years of mathematical theory. Fractals, infinitely complex geometric patterns that exhibit self-similarity at various scales, include the Mandelbrot set, created with the iterative process where a specific pattern is repeated again and again. Mandelbrot’s groundbreaking work provided artists with a visual language to explore and create intricate, organic and visually captivating compositions. Fractals became a cornerstone of generative art, inspiring artists to use algorithms and iterative processes to generate complex and evolving imagery. The introduction of fractals revolutionized the aesthetic possibilities in digital art, fostering a deeper appreciation for the beauty of mathematical structures and the integration of science and art in the digital realm.

name: Computer Graphics by Melvin L. Prueitt
desc: Prueitt’s book showcases the PICTURE computer program that he developed at the Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory. The book consists of visual representations of numbers, particularly representations of surfaces in space, using the PICTURE algorithm.

name: Untitled Computer Assisted Drawing by Paul Brown
desc: Displayed at the Victoria and Albert Museum’s 2018 exhibition, Chance and Control: Art in the Age of Computers , Brown’s work is composed of black linear forms or “tiles” on a white background, showing how simple forms can combine to create dense patterns. Brown studied at London ’s Slade School of Fine Art, in the Experimental and Computing Department established by Malcolm Hughes .
subjects: chance and control: art in the age of computers

name: Altair 8800 Microcomputer
desc: First truly personal computers to sell in large numbers. It was available in 1975 for $397 as a kit and appeared on the January 1975 cover of Popular Electronics. This stands as another example of the microcomputer’s emergence in the ’70s that helped spur the second wave of computer art.

name: Hypertransformations by Vera Molnár
desc: One of Molnár’s most recognizable phases (1975-76), Hypertransformations “examines the effects of minor changes in parameters of the x- and y-axis to regular squares.” The works are similar to (Dés)Ordres except features only series of concentric squares instead of many on a grid. Some variations would be plotted and then painted over by Molnár, part of her attempt to add the human hand back into the work and explore the relationship between hand and machine.

name: Yoichiro Kawaguchi Develops the GROWTH Model
desc: One of this story’s greatest legends. Kawaguchi will go on to win the 2010 ACM SIGGRAPH Distinguished Artist Award for Lifetime Achievement. But his creative career began around this time in the late ’70s. In 1975 Kawaguchi, one of Japan ’s most revered generative artists and animators, began developing his famous GROWTH Model, a procedural algorithm that mimics organic growth and reproduction. Continuing to work with organic forms throughout his career, Kawaguchi showed his organic growth animations at SIGGRAPH from 1982. Kawaguchi’s GROWTH model— described as “a self-organizing approach to developing a formative algorithm of a complex life form”—in many ways pioneered artificial life and evolutionary art. His work comes nearly a decade before fellow Artificial Life pioneers William Latham and Karl Sims . Kawaguchi goes widely unrecognized as an artificial life pioneer despite this early work from the ’70s in the budding field.

name: James Baker and Fred Jelinek Bring Hidden Markov Models to Speech Recognition
desc: The 1970s is known as a " winter " for the learning tradition of AI in the West. But even brutal winters have the occasional bearable day. Learning research in these early days was still disjointed (and would be for decades). In speech recognition, Markov models and neural nets were first rivals, then partners. By around 2012 systems started using them both. But back in the 1970s, they were sub-rivals within the learning tradition. You must remember that "neural nets" were widely discredited still at this time, largely thanks to Marvin Minsky's Perceptrons . But what are these things? A Markov model is a simple rule that what comes next depends only on what came just before. The odds are taken from counting real examples. But the catch is they can’t see far back and don't understand anything. Neural nets are the smarty pants that can understand. They learn their own patterns from data, so they can find much richer relationships and use much longer context. Hidden Markov models taught machines from piles of recordings to predict what most likely came next. Jelinek’s IBM team carried that approach into statistical translation and next-word prediction. Today’s large language models still do the same basic job of predicting the next word from probabilities learned from data, only over far longer stretches of text, to put it lightly. The disjointed nature of AI research in these days meant this breakthrough came from researchers in three places and took years. First, James Baker at Carnegie Mellon described DRAGON, a speech recognizer built on “a probabilistic function of a Markov process.” Then, in 1976 Fred Jelinek of IBM Research published statistical methods for recognizing continuous speech. Both built on theory from Leonard Baum and colleagues at the Institute for Defense Analyses. Yes, military funding always seems just around the corner from AI research. In this further blow to our poor neural nets, Markov models would remain the learning field’s preferred method until the early 1990s. Minsky, you devil.

name: Joan Truckenbrod Makes Coded Algorithmic Drawings
desc: Friend of the Le Random Podcast, Joan Truckenbrod began her FORTRAN series Coded Algorithmic Drawings as an artist teaching at Northern Illinois University. This work is indicative of the decade's deliberate turn away from hard-edged abstraction toward more natural computer-made work. This was possible because of the growing interest in computers of artists like Truckenbrod and Grace Hertlein , as well as an improving technical environment, especially in plotters. It's also indicative because it takes place in Chicago, probably art and tech's epicenter for the 1970s with EVL , Sonia Sheridan's Generative Systems and Truckenbrod. Truckenbrod wrote FORTRAN programs on a university mainframe to model invisible natural phenomena, like the way light reflects off a surface. The artist then plotted the results. She wrote the code by hand on punched cards, one of a small number of artists programming directly in the 1970s. Truckenbrod later taught at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, where she helped build its art and technology program. Her drawings today are held by the Victoria and Albert Museum. Listen to our conversation with Truckenbrod .

name: Ruth Leavitt Publishes Groundbreaking Book, Artist and Computer
desc: Leavitt’s book explores the relationship between artist and computer in depth. She sent a list of questions to dozens of contemporary computer artists. The responses she then compiled into a book. “Some of the authors address the questions in their articles; some do not. Many of the papers are purely statements about the artist’s work. Just as the artists' artwork differs, so do their papers.” The book stands as a treasure trove of information on artistic practice with computers by some of the time’s most distinguished artists. Leavitt includes artists such as Vera Molnár , Lillian Schwartz , John Whitney and Hiroshi Kawano .

name: Vera Molnár First Solo Exhibition Transformations
desc: Held at the gallery of the Polytechnic of Central London , Molnár’s Transformations is a series of 21 drawings plotted in black ink on white paper on a Benson plotter. Each image depicts a 5x5 grid of closely drawn concentric squares. The first image in the series is perfectly uniform, with crisply drawn concentric squares orderly presented in a perfect grid. Disorder is introduced to each subsequent iteration. Finally, image 21 resembles a scribbled mess with a barely recognizable grid. The entire series is now held in the Tate collection.

name: Grace Hertlein Begins Editing Computer Graphics and Art
desc: Hertlein’s Computer Graphics and Art played a crucial role in the development of generative art history. The journal provided a platform for artists, researchers and technologists to showcase and exchange ideas about computer-generated art. It documented the evolving landscape of generative art, featuring articles, interviews and examples of innovative artworks. The journal served as a catalyst for the growth of generative art by fostering a community and facilitating the dissemination of knowledge and techniques. It thereby helped establish generative art as a recognized field, influencing subsequent generations of artists and contributing to the expansion and exploration of generative practices in the art world.

name: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak Develop the Apple I and Found Apple
desc: Apple Computer Company was founded on 1 April 1976 by Steve Jobs , Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne , with the goals of making computers more user-friendly for a mass market. The company’s first product was the Apple I, which they built in Jobs’s garage, selling the device for $666.66 without a monitor or keyboard. They produced 200 units which did not even sell out after 9-10 months. The Apple I was the predecessor to the iconic Apple II which would be released the following year. This moment marks an important step in the computers’ increasing accessibility, including with artists, that would only be amplified with Apple’s more successful release of the Apple II in the following year.

name: The VHS Recorder Brings Digital Media to the Home
desc: This seemingly benign event marks the beginning of what I argue is one of the most significant shifts in the history of human thinking: our love affair with digital devices. These devices, made for the home, ushered in an era marked by a new relationship with digital devices and computers. VHS (Video Home System) allowed for the playing and recording of analog video on cassettes invented by the Japanese company. The technology set off the maturation of mass media, enabling digital media to enter people’s homes on a mass scale for the first time. As these devices entered homes, society’s perception of computers significantly altered, as an inscrutable, blackbox, previously associated with war became as close to use as family and friends. VHS machines would be followed by similarly tectonic events that continue this progression of mass media entering the home, including the 1977 release and widespread success of the Apple II , igniting the personal computer era. This was instantly followed by the introduction of the video game console the same year with the Atari 2600 . In 1976 Shugart Associates introduced the 5.25-inch floppy disk drive and diskette. This would become the vital storage device for computers in general as well as computer art and digital art in the 1980s. Finally, the same year would see the introduction of the LaserDisc , the first commercially successful optical storage device, which would also store digital art such as Lynn Hershmann Leeson’s Lorna .

name: Bertram Raphael Publishes The Thinking Computer
desc: Bertram Raphael’s book was one of the first to explain to ordinary readers how AI actually worked, written by someone who helped build Shakey (remember him?), the first robot that could plan its own actions. The skills it covers, searching for answers, storing knowledge, understanding English and planning steps, are still the core jobs of today’s AI. But not the process of today because Raphael’s book described symbolic, rules-based AI and not the learning kind. Raphael was a computer scientist at the Stanford Research Institute when he published The Thinking Computer: Mind Inside Matter .
