Written for general readers, it explained how programs of the time searched for solutions, represented knowledge, understood simple English and planned the actions of robots, with examples from SRI and other laboratories. Raphael also wrote SIR, a 1964 program at MIT that answered questions by storing facts as relations between words. Raphael with this book, SIR and Shakey was the epitome of symbolic AI, nearing its peak in the 1970s.

name: Joseph Weizenbaum Publishes Computer Power and Human Reason
desc: Weizenbaum was the legendary creator of the ELIZA chatbot, which to this day remains relevant to the discussion around trusting relationships with AI and ascribing personhood to AIs. Weizenbaum saw people fall into this trap in the 1960s of trusting a simple chatbot as if it understood them. This book demonstrates his warning that some jobs, like therapy and judging, should never go to machines, which sounds eerily familiar to contemporary debates with (hundreds of?) millions of people confiding in ChatGPT and Claude. Since ELIZA, Weizenbaum was disturbed to see people confide in his chatbot as if it actually understood them, with some psychiatrists at the time even proposing it for therapy. The book sought to lay out why precisely we shouldn't be trusting these machines. It distinguished deciding, which computers can be programmed to do, from choosing, which requires judgment. Weizenbaum saw where this was all headed and used his deciding-vs-choosing position to argue against giving machines certain jobs (cough, cough in the future), whatever they become capable of. It made Weizenbaum one of the first critics of AI from within computer science. He's still celebrated as such today by artists like Eva and Franco Mattes.

name: Kenneth M. Sayre Publishes Cybernetics and the Philosophy of Mind
desc: Can machines be conscious? Can AI? Can AI ever have something like a mind? Our friends, perhaps the heroes of the AI myth, the cyberneticists, have long been asking these questions. Kenneth M. Sayre, a philosopher at the University of Notre Dame, published Cybernetics and the Philosophy of Mind , proposing that mental states can be explained through cybernetics: information and feedback, the concepts of Claude Shannon's information theory and Norbert Wiener's cybernetics , without either reducing mind to mechanism or placing it outside nature. In other words, Sayre argued that thinking is a kind of information processing that any self-correcting system could do, be it man or machine. His foundational ideas still sit under today’s question of AI and machine consciousness.

name: Stephen Grossberg Introduces Adaptive Resonance Theory
desc: All the way back in 1976 in a brutally fiendish AI learning winter , Stephen Grossberg asked a question still mostly unsolved today: how a machine can keep learning without forgetting what it already knows. Models like ChatGPT stop learning once training ends, and teaching them new things can even damage old skills. Grossberg's solution was feedback and his theory was adaptive resonance theory (ART), which he introduced in two 1976 papers in Biological Cybernetics . ART understood the power of feedback: a learned top-down expectation is matched against each bottom-up input. ART's memory changed only when the two agreed closely enough or when something completely new appeared. In Grossberg and Gail Carpenter’s words from 2003, “ART matching leads either to a resonant state, which persists long enough to permit learning, or to a parallel memory search.” Carpenter and Grossberg later built ART networks such as ART 1 but the system never became mainstream. While Grossberg and later Carpenter were not necessarily solving these problems, they were at least working on the right ones. It was hard to say that about most AI research of this time of symbolic AI's heyday.

name: Harold Cohen Exhibits AARON at the Stedelijk Museum
desc: Now referred to as his “turtle,” AARON was showcased in a one-person show at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam across 1977 and 1978. At the exhibition the turtle would roam around drawing while viewers could see finished pieces on display such as the Amsterdam Suite, prints from which are now in the Victoria and Albert Museum. AARON was only capable of drawing in black and white at this time. Cohen would hand paint AARON drawings later in the 1980s. This exhibition also serves as an exception to the general disregard shown to computer art by the mainstream art world in this decade.

name: ICCH Held at the University of Waterloo in Canada
desc: This mostly academic conference was also held in conjunction with relevant computer graphics conferences of the time. It also featured work on computer choreography by the architect and computer artist John Lansdown , titled, “Computer Choreography and Video.”
subjects: international conference on computers in the humanities (icch)

name: Atari 2600 Released
desc: The Atari 2600 helped humanity transition from fearing computers a decade prior to loving them. It was also critical to the advancement of digital devices in our homes and the early Demoscene.

name: L’ordinateur et les arts visuels by François Molnar
desc: This book on computers and the visual arts published by Centre Pompidou and the University of Paris brings together academic texts from the field. One of the major texts is by Vera Molnár ’s husband, François. He attempts to bridge science and art in his published paper researching computational aesthetics.

name: P-196-A and P-197-A by Manfred Mohr
desc: Mohr produced this series of computer-generated drawings from 1977, within the Cubic Limit II phase. The series consisted of images of deconstructed single cubes. Dissected, the cubes were not symmetrical. This concept of broken symmetry has roots in the work of Renaissance artist, Leonardo da Vinci , who was hugely influential in this decade as the embodiment of the artist-scientist. Lillian Schwartz a decade later would explore this topic more explicity in her Mona/Leo , which bisects the face of the Mona Lisa and combines it with the visage of da Vinci. Image is copyrighted by The Artist and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

name: Computergraphik by Lothar Limbeck
desc: This master’s thesis, Computergrafik, Ein Lehr- und Lernbuch (“Computer graphics, a text and learning book”), was a survey of computer graphics. It also published in detail SNE (COMP) ART, one of the first art machines based on parameters. The code was significant as SNE ART became a way to enhance generative art’s accessibility. It was used to teach the field (using FORTRAN ). Nearly 40 years later in 2013, Dietrich M. Scheringer would bring SNE ART to Processing , based on the original FORTRAN code.

name: Apple Introduces Apple II
desc: One of the first mass-produced “microcomputers,” the Apple II helped begin the personal computer crazy in the late 1970s, revolutionizing computing and computer art forms. It would also help kick of the Demoscene as one of the first devices to attract cracker crews. With its accessible hardware and user-friendly interface, the Apple II democratized computing and provided artists with a powerful tool for creating generative artworks. The computer’s graphics and sound capabilities, along with the availability of programming languages like BASIC , enabled artists to experiment with algorithms and create interactive visual and audio experiences. The Apple II represented an exponential jump in computer popularity and accessibility as between 1977 and 1984, over 2 million units sold. The Apple II’s popularity and widespread adoption also fostered a growing community of artists exploring generative art.

name: Alan Kay and Adele Goldberg of PARC Publish "Personal Dynamic Media”
desc: This paper conceived of the laptop and tablet computers decades before their existence. It outlines the goals and developments of Kay and Goldberg’s “dream” to create a portable computer the size of a “notebook,” which they called the Dynabook. Mock-ups of the Dynabook were decades ahead of their time. It looked more like a tablet than today’s “notebook” computers. The device was designed for artists in particular, as its sketch pad like design facilitated hand drawing and painting. It also theoretically included software for the creation of animation and music. It wasn’t until after a decade of early attempts in the 1980s that Apple would produce the PowerBook in 1991 and IBM the ThinkPad in 1992 that the vision of the Dynabook even started to be fulfilled. It was not until 2010 that Apple would introduce the iPad

name: “3-D Computer Animation” by Charles Csuri
desc: This book chapter by one of the founders of computer art would have a significant impact on the development of 3D computer graphics in the coming decades. The work “emphasizes the ideas and concepts that give 3-D computer animation its special character and quality.” Csuri “describes the technique of using a refresh buffer to display pictures in computer graphics.” This and other work exemplifies SIGGRAPH ’s description of Csuri: “His research and artistic vision led to advances in software that created new artistic tools for 3D computer graphics, computer animation, gaming and 3d printing – all in advance of their broad commercial applications.”

name: PostScript Language Developed
desc: PostScript, which would go on to influence the Processing language created by Casey Reas and Ben Fry 25 years later, was developed by Dr John Warnock at PARC, Xerox’s research arm. The PostScript language was built to “to communicate complex graphic printing instructions to digital laser printers.” Warnock attempted to develop PostScript, then known as Interpress at PARC but was turned down. He then, along with Charles M. ‘Chuck’ Geschke, founded the company Adobe to rival Interpress, developing PostScript at Adobe as a robust, geometric procedural language that was more than just software to control printers. They released PostScript finally in 1984 .

name: The Third Mind by Beat Writer William Burroughs
desc: The Third Mind is published by Beat writer William Burroughs and the artist/poet/inventor Brion Gysin . This collection of experimental cut-up writings and essays investigates the technique popularized by Burroughs, inspired in part by the interpolation of diverse sources and voices in T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land, and explored earlier in the 1966 short film “ The Cut Ups, ” by Burroughs and director Antony Balch . Burroughs believed cutting up and rearranging fragments of language was a way to unlock the true meaning of a text, and said, “When you cut into the present the future leaks out.” -Sasha Stiles

name: Alvy Ray Smith Develops PAINT
desc: From Smith’s 1978 Technical Memo No. 7 at the New York Institute of Technology’s Computer Graphics Lab: “Paint is a menu-driven computer program for handpainting two-dimensional images in full color. It is a highly interactive software package with which a human artist may employ the power of a digital computer to compose paintings which are entirely of [their] own creation.” Paint would go on to serve as a prototype for subsequent graphic design software. As one of the earliest software tools for digital painting, it revolutionized the artistic process by providing artists with a digital canvas and a range of tools for creating and manipulating images. Paint allowed artists to explore new possibilities for expression, enabling them to experiment with color, texture and composition in ways that were not previously achievable. Paint’s user-friendly interface and intuitive controls democratized digital art creation, opening the doors for artists to embrace the potential of digital tools and techniques in generative art.

name: Arbitrary Fragments by Barbara Latham
desc: This pioneering work of video art saw Latham commenting on the inherently fragmented nature of video. The work features extensively manipulated and processed visuals showcasing this fragmentation. Latham explores the blending perceptions of herself and her creations, highlighting the interconnected nature of video, storytelling and identity formation, where fact and fiction intertwine to shape one’s identity. Latham’s creation is a video persona that is something distinct from her true self. The piece anticipates the growing tension between video art and identity, which contemporary artists like Maya Man explore .

name: Arts et Informatique organized by the Swedish Cultural Centre in Paris
desc: Part two of three successive exhibitions by the Swedish Cultural Center that accompanied seminars in Paris between 1977 and 1979. The exhibitions were: L’ordinateur et les arts visuels (1977), Arts et Informatique (1978), and Artiste et Ordinateur (1979). They showcased Swedish artists in particular, including according to Herbert W. Franke , Holger Bäckström , Bo Ljungberg , Sven Höglund , Bror Wikström and Torsten Ridell .

name: Art of the Space Era – Museum of Art, Huntsville, Alabama
desc: Held at the Huntsville Museum of Art in the United States , this two part exhibition curated by Thomas A. Bowles & Carolyn Wood featured work by Vera Molnár (variations), Ben Laposky , Kenneth Knowlton, Lillian Schwartz and Edward Zajec .

name: Art and the Computer at the Worcester Art Museum and Computer Generated Art Exhibit at Old Dominion University
desc: These events held in the United States were “some of the most important computer graphics exhibitions of the last years,” according to Herbert W. Franke in Computer Graphics, Computer Art (1985) .

name: Algorithmic Aesthetics: Computer Models for Criticism and Design in the Arts by George Stiny and James Gips
desc: Suggesting an algorithmic approach to aesthetics and criticism, George Stiny and James Gips continue the tradition of Max Bense and François Morellet . They write: “What we do attempt in this study is to suggest, in very broad strokes, what an algorithm for criticizing or designing works of art might look like. In the process, we attempt to show how various approaches to art might be modeled using this structure and we investigate some traditional issues in aesthetics in terms of this structure.”

name: Computer Art Grows
desc: According to Grant Taylor , In When the Machine Made Art , “By 1978, there were 30 times more computer art practitioners than a decade earlier.” One decade after its humble beginnings, computer art was growing. Computers and programming increased in accessibility as well as technical training conducted at an increasing number of universities with computer art-related classes.

name: Energized Artscience at the Chicago Museum of Science and Industry
desc: Curated by pioneer, Sonia Landy Sheridan who also wrote the show catalog, this exhibition at the Museum of Science and Industry does not have much existing information about it. Anymore would be greatly appreciated.

name: The Vasulka’s: Steina: Machine Vision; Woody: Description at the Albright-Knox Art Gallery
desc: Curated by Linda Cathcart , this exhibition featured the work of artists and partners, Steina and Woody Vasulka , pioneers of video art. Along with Nam June Paik and Bruce Nauman , the Vasulkas were some of the first artists to use video as the primary focus of their practice. The exhibition featured their video installation work as well as their experimental photography.

name: Computer Graphics World begins publication
desc: Still in print today, Computer Graphics World (CGW) was started by Joel Orr after originally existing as a Newsletter.

name: Thomas DeFanti, Jamie Fenton and Nola Donato Develop Zgrass
desc: An extension of Defanti’s GRASS , ZGRASS was used for generating 3D imagery and developed to be used on smaller, personal computers and gaming devices. In an effort to better control images and make electronic visualization easier, Thomas DeFanti developed ZGRASS with Jamie Fenton and Nola Donato for the Bally Home Library Computer. Fenton is herself a legendary artist, computer and video game programmer. Fenton is widely credited for creating an early instance of glitch art, the legendary Digital TV Dinner (1978) that came out of EVL in Chicago. Fenton is less known, but this researcher believes, for making perhaps some of the first video game art, as Digital TV Dinner was made by distressing video game equipment. Fenton was also known for programming in essentially Assembly Language and programmed Macromedia Director , an important tool for creatives in the coming decades. She is a powerhouse of a legend, who is painfully under-recognized, especially for her contributions to art. But, back to ZGRASS. It would go on to be used as a programming language for artists and educators in the 1980s. For example, pioneering animation artist Larry Cuba completed his film Calculated Movements on ZGRASS. Victor Acevedo would use it for his experiments in the mid ’80s he told Peter Bauman via a call 11 July 2023. Copper Giloth was the first artist to work with ZGRASS.

name: “Space Invaders,” “Asteroids” and “Pac Man” Released
desc: Sparking the first video game craze, the release of Space Invaders was followed by Asteroids (1979) and Pac-Man (1980). The released helped to popularize the arcade, which would have an enormous impact on not only digital aesthetics (to this day) but also how a generation of young artists would grow up viewing machines, digital art and computers. Gone were the years of the 1960s (less than 20 years prior) when computers were enigmatic with strong associations with the military, war, the powerful and questionable ethics. Very few people had ever seen one let alone knew how to interact one. In the course of eighteen years, the relationship between machine and human had changed profoundly. Children from Japan to the United States began growing up with computers in their homes. They began to interact with them and spend hours forming an intimate bond with the machine, having a profound impact on the history of any digital art.

name: LaserDisc Introduced
desc: The first commercially successful optical storage device, the LaserDisc played an important in bringing digital media and changing the public’s mind about computers. The LaserDisc would go on house iconic works of digital art such as as Lynn Hershman Leeson’s Lorna (1979-84).

name: Digital TV Dinner by Jamie Fenton and Raul Zaritsky
desc: This may be one of the most under-appreciated works in media art history. It's one of the first instances of video game art, normally dated to the '90s by institutions like Rhizome. Yet, here in 1978, Jamie Fenton and Raul Zaritsky were distressing video game consoles to make art. So let's rightly place it in that bucket of art history, a bucket growing in importance by the day, by the way. Then, it's also widely recognized and cited as one of the first glitch videos; it was shown again in Chicago New Media 1973–1992 in 2018, noted as a work of glitch art not as a work of video game art. So we're talking about one of the practically pre-historical works of video game art, by an absolute legend in Fenton, as well as its cemented place in glitch art history. That makes this piece and Fenton pretty important I'd say. Fenton and Zaritsky made the three-minute video Digital TV Dinner for the legendary EVL 's (oft mentioned in this timeline) Electronic Visualization Event 3 in Chicago. How are we pretty sure about Fenton's place as one of the earliest video game artists ever? Because she was the lead programmer on the Bally Astrocade home game console, which she used for this work. They made its images by ejecting the game cartridge from the running machine and striking the console, which broke the picture into bursts of color and pattern. They recorded the results on video with Dick Ainsworth making the music. A second version of the famed piece aired on WTTW Chicago in 1979.

name: C++ Developed by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Laboratories
desc: One of the most popular programming languages of the 1990s and still widely used today, C++ began in 1979 with Bjarne Stroustrup ’s arrival at the “1127 Computing Science Research Center of AT&T Bell Laboratories.” After five years, the first C++ language reference manual was internally published in 1984 and commercially released in 1985.

name: The First ARS ELECTRONICA Festival Takes Place in Linz, Austria
desc: “With electronics, a progressive element has entered our technical world, whose influence is not limited to industry and research, but intervenes in all areas of life. This has set in motion a development that opens up astonishing and fantastic aspects, but in other respects also arouses criticism and scepticism.” So begins Herbert W. Franke ’s opening text, introducing Ars Electronica . The first edition of the now iconic event, co-founded by Hannes Leopoldseder , Hubert Bognermayr , Herbert W. Franke and Ulrich Rützel , in new media art which continues to this day, annually. Its base is now the Ars Electronica Center (AEC), a museum complex in Linz . While now a new media art institution, its beginnings in 1979 were more humble. Back then, the event was only every two years and was a part of the larger International Bruckner Festival, a Linz music festival. There was also no Prix Ars Electronica until 1987 when the now prestigious award was first handed out.

name: Dance by Lucinda Childs
desc: By the legendary generative choreographer Lucinda Childs , this piece would be exhibited for the first time in 2009 at the Whitney Museum. Dance included choreography by Childs, musical composition by Philip Glass and visuals by Sol LeWitt . It was commissioned by the Brooklyn Academy of Music.

name: Frank J Malina Publishes Visual Art, Mathematics, and Computers
desc: This book contained Malina’s papers he published in the journal Leonardo . Herbert W. Franke called Malina a “patron of art technology” in 1985, four years after Malina’s death in 1981.

name: Informatrix by Edward Zajec
desc: This book by Zajec was published in 1979 from work he developed between 1970 and 1978. Informatrix was also a series of works by Zajec that he worked on over the course of nearly thirty years between 1970 and 1996. This innovative and interactive book was not only a presentation of Zajec’s works but also served as a teaching device. As one progressed through the book, layers were added to images like a flip book.

name: Douglas Hofstadter’s Publishes Book Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid
desc: This book exploring the latest trends in math, logic and computer language, would greatly influence artist Roman Verostko .

name: Jim Blinn Simulates Voyager Probe for NASA’s JPL
desc: Jim Blinn ’s simulation of the Voyager Probe’s flyby of Jupiter for NASA ’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) would have a significant impact on the development of digital art history. Blinn’s groundbreaking work utilized computer graphics techniques to visualize complex astronomical data, creating a realistic and immersive experience for scientists and the public. This pioneering use of computer graphics for scientific visualization reimagined digital art as it was known and demonstrated the potential of technology in communicating scientific concepts. David Em , JPL’s artist in residence since 1977, was introduced to Blinn’s work there, and the classically trained painter matured in his computer art style, developing works from the same year such as Transjovian Pipeline and Nora. Em would even name works after Blinn, including the piece Dr. Jim, Number 1. Blinn’s work paved the way for future collaborations between artists and scientists, shaping the field of digital art history and advancing the use of computer-generated imagery in various disciplines.

name: Cybernetic Symbiosis, Berkeley: Lawrence Hall of Science
desc: Organized by artist and California State University, Chico Computer Science professor, Grace C. Hertlein , this exhibition “feature[d] a definitive display of varied international invitational computer art.” According to the catalogue , the exhibition’s “artists represent[ed] the most important computer artists in the world today,” according to the exhibition announcement. It lasted for six months from March to August 1979.

name: Larry Cuba, Two Space
desc: Larry Cuba was a computer animation pioneer of the generation that directly followed John Whitney Sr. In 1975 Whitney invited Cuba to be the programmer on Arabesque . Earlier in the 1970s Cuba worked with Thomas DeFanti on GRASS . He also worked with George Lucas on Star Wars , providing the animation for the Death Star attack training sequence. A 4k version of the original Two Space can be viewed here . The film was completed with Defanti’s GRASS and according to the artwork description it: “systematically explores symmetries used by Islamic artists to create abstract temple decorations. The two dimensional patterns, like the tile patterns of Islamic temples, are generated by performing a set of symmetry operations (translations, rotations, and reflections) upon a basic figure or tile.”

name: Lorna, Lynn Hershman Leeson
desc: The artist describes Lorna, made from 1979 to 1984, as the first artwork to use laserdisc technology , and as an early interactive video art disc. Exploiting the interactive capabilities of the medium, the artist enables users to explore and intervene in the world of an agoraphobic woman named Lorna.” The work highlights the continued importance of interactivity in digital art with roots to cybernetics. Lorna stands as an important example of early digital mass media art, consisting of artists releasing work on digital media that could be distributed easily around the world. According to Casey Reas , the rise of digital mass media is one of the pre-conditions for NFTs. Maya Man mentioned the impact of Leeson on her work to Le Random.

name: A Decade of Contrasts
desc: Contrasts were everywhere in the eighties. The decade would see us going from mainframes to PCs, computer art at its peak to it’s death, communities formed yet artists were more disparate than ever, we went from fearing machines to…fearing them slightly less. But millions—vastly more than possible before—were growing to love them. Humanity’s relationship with machines transformed over the course of the decade, as mass media entered homes with PCs, VHS and video games. While derided by some at the time as toys, these early mass media devices propelled entire genres, including computer, digital and video art. The early practitioners saw something that few others did. By calling them toys, critics at the time were infantilizing their use but really they were unable to glimpse the same—more accurate—future as the pioneers of this decade. Le Random was fortunate enough to speak to many of them. For more context, we suggest watching or listening ( transcript ) to our Ch 6 Artist Discussion with Mark Wilson ⁠, ⁠ Copper Giloth ⁠, ⁠ Dan Sandin ⁠, ⁠ David Em ⁠, ⁠ William Latham ⁠, ⁠ Stephen Todd ⁠, ⁠ Darcy Gerbarg ⁠ + ⁠ Geoff Davis ⁠⁠⁠. Additionally, in this piece on Le Random Editorials, Operator speaks with Rebecca Allen, one of the most significant voices from the decade. Community formation was also an important aspect of the decade. Curated by Darcy Gerbarg and later Copper Giloth , the annual SIGGRAPH computer art show became instrumental in establishing a community of artists in the decade. The shows demonstrated the importance of in-person events for digital communities. The formation of the demoscene in Europe was another important community of the decade. Finally, software and network advancements also reshaped the decade, as HyperCard and Director transformed multimedia, while Tim Berners-Lee had a radically impactful technological invention in store for us at the end of the decade with the World Wide Web .

name: Vera Molnár Joins François at the Sorbonne
desc: Vera Molnár was heavily involved with Sorbonne University throughout the 1980s. In 1980, she and Franćois established the Centre de Recherche Expérimentale et Informatique des Arts Visuels (CREIAV) . From 1985 to 1990, she taught fine art, aesthetics and art history at the Sorbonne’s Department of Plastic Arts and Art Sciences. This period was also fruitful for her practice, as it included some of her most well-known projects, such as Lettres à ma mère (1981-1990). Molnár stopped using plotters in 1991 and switched to prints. 1980 was a big year for Vera, as it also marked the publishing of her first artist’s book Un pourcent de désordre (One per cent disorder) by Wedgepress & Cheese in Bjärred (Sweden).
subjects: centre de recherche expérimentale et informatique des arts visuels (creiav)
sorbonne department of plastic arts and art sciences

name: Spiral 5 PTL by Dan Sandin, Tom DeFanti and Mimi Shevitz
desc: This early computer graphics art video by Dan Sandin , Tom DeFanti and Mimi Shevitz uses the image processor as a musical instrument, generating variations on a spiral motif synchronized with an eclectic audio track. Created in 1980 and 1981 by combining Tom DeFanti’s GRASS system and the Sandin Image Processor , this innovative piece was among the first video art works included in the Museum of Modern Art’s collection. The work thus stands as an important achievement in not only early computer animation but in digital art and more broadly the intersection of technology and visual art.

name: Traditionally Trained Artist, Mark Wilson, Buys Microcomputer to Make Art
desc: A representational beginning to the decade, which would be responsible for the explosion of “digital art” due to the emerging prevalence of computers and digital devices becoming smaller and entering homes. Besides the micro effect on artists, on a macro level, the impact of these devices cannot be overstated. Devices such as the VHS machine, the Apple II and the Atari 2600 would revolutionize the personal relationship between humanity and digital devices. Wilson, a pioneer of digital art, began his career as a traditionally trained artist. In 1980, he purchased a microcomputer, taught himself programming and started producing plotter drawings. His work today is featured in the collection at the V&A. This marks an important example in the development of generative art that would symbolize the 1980s: the increased accessibility of computers.

name: Divisibility I by Manfred Mohr
desc: Divisibility I is a series that Mohr began in 1980 and would last until 1984. Again, Mohr returns to the cube as his main point of departure and inspiration. The series consists of various cubes that have been divided, cut and rearranged.

name: Art In/Art Out at the Ukrainian Institute of Modern Art, Chicago
desc: Art In/Art Out: ComputerAided Graphics was a “group show examining recent computer graphics as art, a recent area of serious artistic inquiry,” according to a Museum retrospective. According to a 1980 edition of Creative Computing Magazine: “The exhibition has been coordinated and organized by William J. Kolomyjec , computer artist, Lansing, Michigan.” The state of the art of the medium of computer graphics will be illustrated and the works of seventeen established computer graphic artists of national and international origin will be on display.” The show featured the work of Colette Bangert among those “seventeen established computer graphic artists.”

name: Video Art: The Electronic Man at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago
desc: This exhibit stands out as a key moment in the transition from video art to video game art. Copper Giloth bridged the gap between the rapidly rising popularity of video games and video art. Her piece, From Video Games to Video Art was an interactive installation that used Thomas DeFanti’s ZGRASS . Giloth herself explains: “Using a joystick and buttons the user to could create a simple image and then using that image and its 7 simple symmetries create more complex drawings. Additional software and hardware designed by T. DeFanti and D. Harris . 10 plotter drawings were included in the exhibition. Hardware: Datamax Zgrass UV-1 machine with a custom interface.”
subjects: from video games to video art

name: David Topper and John H. Holloway, “Interrelationships between the Visual Arts, Science and Technology: A Bibliography”
desc: This work was a thorough “​​bibliography of texts dealing either explicitly or implicitly with interrelationships between the visual arts, science and technology,” according to the article’s abstract . The piece played an important role in synthesizing, compiling and documenting the role that technology has played in art in order to showcase the illustrious history.

name: Digital Harmony: On the Complementarity of Music and Visual Art by John Whitney
desc: In the book, Whitney wrote of the future of art and society: “The future of Society: the way we communicate, learn and entertain ourselves lay in making pictures that move, images created by cameras and computers and displayed on a computer screen.”

name: Vol Libre – Loren Carpenter of Boeing
desc: The first film to use fractals to generate graphics, this little-known animated short was decades ahead of its time and presaged the now ubiquitous usage of fractals in computer graphics and film. The animation was produced at Boeing , where Carpenter was employed. He created it to simulate backgrounds for images of experimental plane designs. This marks another innovation in computer graphics history from Boeing, dating back to the 1960s and William Fetter .

name: First “Symposium on Small Computers in the Arts” Held in Philadelphia
desc: Held from 20 to 22 November 1981 and sponsored by the Philadelphia Area Computer Society, the University of Pennsylvania and the IEEE, the symposium would become an annual event and an important gathering of American computer artists in the 1980s. Roughly 150 “enthusiasts” attended with the goals of “increas[ing] the participants’ awareness of the uses of small computers in the arts and to provide a forum for information exchange in this area,” according to a report from that year in the Computer Music Journal . Christopher Morgan , editor-in-chief of Byte, gave the keynote address in 1981.
subjects: institute of electrical and electronics engineers (ieee)
symposium on small computers in the arts

name: Persepol by David Em
desc: David Em transitioned from traditional painting to computer-generated art in the late ’70s. Experimenting with electronic manipulations of TV images, Em collaborated with computer graphics pioneers at Xerox Palo Alto Research Center (PARC). His pivotal moment came at NASA ’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), where, as an artist-in-residence, he adapted scientist James Blinn’s visualization software to craft his own unique computer art style. Em’s creations, influenced by the deep space environment, earned him the first-ever artist’s monograph on digital art. Renowned author Ray Bradbury praised Em for wielding technology as a tool, not a threat, marking a transformative period in the evolution of generative art.

name: Plan K International Festival voor Elektronische Muziek, Video en Computer Art in Brussels.
desc: Arranged by Peter Beyls , this was one of the earliest electronic music festivals. The festival had its second edition in 1981 after debuting the previous year. It would be a full decade later, in the late ’80s and early ’90s, that electronic music festivals as we know them began appearing. The festival featured experimental computer animation in addition to music. The musicians involved included John Appleton , Morton Subotnick , Donald Buchla , John Chowning , Jean-Claude Risset and others.

name: SIGGRAPH 1981 Computer Culture Art Show
desc: As part of the larger computer graphics conference, SIGGRAPH hosted the Computer Culture Art Show ’81 in Dallas , Texas , USA. Curated by Darcy Gerbarg , the show was incredibly varied, featuring “many forms, including sculpture, painting, printmaking, drawing, ceramics, photography and filmmaking.” Yet, “the common ground upon which these artists stand, the thread which ties this show together, is the shared utilization of high technology,” said Gerbarg. Gerbarg exhibited artwork at the exhibition as well, including May I, a patterned work on ceramic tile. The show featured artists such as Edward Zajec , Colette and Charles Bangert, Nelson Max , Stan Vanderbeek, Copper Giloth , Rebecca Allen , Lillian Schwartz , Ken Knowlton , David Em , Ruth Leavitt , Joan Truckenbrod and Jim Blinn .

name: Carla’s Island by Nelson Max
desc: This four-minute animation by Max pioneered the use of realistic, simulated water. It also featured weather effects. This work of realistic fluid simulation was instrumental in the development of computer-generated images for films, animation and art.

name: Yoichiro Kawaguchi Designates His Work “Digital Art”
desc: One of the foremost computer artists of the time, Yoichiro Kawaguchi collaborated with the developers of the LINKS computer, which he also used to produce much of his work. His interest in organic, alien-like 3D forms was achieved algorithmically, mostly using a technology he called metaballs. An example of his randomly constructed, recursive algorithmic art is Tendril, also from 1981. In the book Digital Image, he refers to his work as digital art in one of the first instances of the term’s use. Another thing he has in common with Harold Cohen , yet for which Kawaguchi is significantly less credited, is the pioneering of AI art. His GROWTH model, which he began working on in the late ’70s is some of the first instances of evolutionary concepts in art. Further, his work more closely aligns with today’s machine learning—and AI art—than Cohen’s Expert System, logic based AI. 1981 also saw the beginning of his famous Growth Model going public as he would release a seminal paper 1982 on his findings. This paper would see him rise to international prominence.

name: Digital Image Published by アスキー
desc: Herbery W. Franke highlighted this survey of computer graphic activities in Japan , noting in 1985 that “the activities of Japanese artists seem to be particularly interesting.” This book is where the term “digital art” appears for possibly the first terms, used by Japanese artist, Yoichiro Kawaguchi . In 2024, Kawaguchi will speak at the Herbert W. Franke Foundation’s Generative Art Summit in Berlin .

name: IBM Introduces Their First PC (5150)
desc: With Intel’s 8088, a 16-bit processor with an 8-bit external bus, the 5150 had a significant impact on the PC market, particularly on the enterprise side, which makes it less the focus of this story.

name: Nordisk MobilTelefoni, The First Fully Automatic Cellular Phone System
desc: Based on analog, first-generation technology (1G), this network was developed by Swedish Electrical engineer and inventor, Östen Mäkitalo . It served the countries of Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark . The rise of mobile phone technology plays an important role in the development of NFTs and digital art. It allows for the present-day ubiquity of powerful computers and screens in our pockets, enabling us to view, purchase and even create art.

name: Computer Culture 81, Ontario College of Art
desc: Organized by CIRCA (Centre International de Recherche, de Création et d’Animation) which aimed to “better understand the impacts and cultural implications of computers and to create a center for the production of new methods of artistic creation.” The event consisted of speakers, workshops and an art fair. It would operate yearly until at least 1983.

name: High Technology Art: A Congressional Exhibition, Library of Congress, Washington, D.C.
desc: This show was ​​exhibited at the Library of Congress in Washington D.C . in April before “travel[ing] from Washington to the Electro Arts Gallery in San Francisco , where Ray Lauzzana directed the installation.” This show formed the basis of Darcy Gerbarg ’s exhibition at the 1981 SIGGRAPH conference.
subjects: high technology art: a congressional exhibition

name: MTV Goes Live
desc: Music Television (MTV), the first 24-hour television station based on music videos, was launched on 1 August 1981, a seminal day in the history of digital creativity and storytelling. MTV’s popularization of music videos fostered a culture of dynamic, short-form visual expression. This cultural shift towards innovative visuals and rapid editing techniques would influence all digital expression, including digital generative art. By popularizing unconventional visual aesthetics and embracing experimental techniques, MTV helped shaped the digital aesthetic of the ’80s and sparked a mindset receptive to the video as an art form.

name: Bill Viola, Hatsu-Yume (First Dream)
desc: This work by Viola , a pioneer of video art, now stands in the collection of MoMA . Viola himself wrote of the work: “[It] fuses a personal observation of Japanese culture with a metaphysical contemplation of life, death and nature, achieved through a symbolic exploration of video’s relation to light and reflection.”

name: Art and Technology: Chicago Video at MoMA
desc: This exhibition at MoMA highlighted pioneering collaborations between artists and technology in the 1970s. By showcasing innovative computer-generated video works, it helped establish video art. It highlighted the evolving relationship between art and emerging technologies, providing a platform for experimentation and creative exploration. Artists including Copper Giloth , Dan Sandin , Tom DeFanti and Jane Veeder showed algorithmic imagery and interactive work. The exhibition’s fusion of art and technology catalyzed a mindset that later artists embraced, leading to the exploration of code-based, evolving artworks characteristic of the digital generative art movement.

name: Paul Werbos Proposes Backpropagation to Train Neural Networks
desc: In a major advancement in AI and Machine Learning research, Paul Werbos proposed using backpropagation to train neural networks at the “System Modeling and Optimization” conference in New York . The method was initially introduced by Seppo Linnainmaa in 1970 for automatic differentiation in complex systems. Werbos’s adaptation of this algorithm marked a significant advancement in neural network training, enabling the efficient adjustment of network weights by propagating errors backward through the layers. Jürgen Schmidhuber describes it as “essentially an efficient way of implementing Leibniz’s chain rule for deep networks.” Backprop's roots go back further, though, to control theory: Henry J. Kelley published a precursor in 1960 for computing optimal flight paths, followed by Arthur E. Bryson and Stuart Dreyfus. Werbos’s own 1974 thesis included a preliminary discussion of applying it to neural networks. This breakthrough became foundational to modern deep learning, influencing the development of widely used AI frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch.

name: The Commodore 64 Released
desc: The Commodore 64, also known as the C64, was an 8-bit device that helped popularize the personal computer. It democratized home computing, bringing affordable and accessible technology to artists as well as hackers. With its impressive graphics and sound capabilities, it catalyzed the growth of the video game industry and software development. Like the Amiga and Apple ’s devices, the Commodore 64 helped alter humanity’s relationship with machines and computers. Bringing them from military, government and corporate control to one’s home demystified machines that only a decade earlier were associated, particularly in the art world, with the military and a severely unpopular Vietnam War fought by the United States , the leader in computing technology. Little-known pockets of illegal software crackers would also use the C64 (and other 8-bit devices) throughout the decade of the ’80s (and beyond!), helping to spawn the Demoscene. So-called “cracktos” were crackers that removed the software’s copy protection and added personalized cracked intros. Hugely influential for its role in democratizing computing and invigorating the creation of computing, the Commodore 64 remains one of the most iconic computers ever built.

name: Pitfall! by David Crane
desc: A huge hit, Pitfall! was one of the Atari 2600 ’s signature games and one of 1982’s most popular. It was also a work of generative art, as it used an algorithmically generated world.

name: Roman Verostko Debuts The Magic Hand of Chance Series
desc: The Magic Hand of Chance Series (1982–85) was the legendary “Algorist’s” first foray into software work. It was inspired by the chance work of Dadaist Hans Arp. Verostko wrote of the series: “My first effort with coded procedures attempted to use the operating system of the computer as the form generator. This would be a form of ‘computer automatism,’ miming the work of certain late Dada and early surrealist works.I had in mind especially how artists like Hans Arp had experimented with dropping torn shapes of paper on the floor to achieve a composition with ‘chance’” arrangements.”
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: V-yramid by Nam June Paik
desc: Consisting of forty televisions, V-yramid was one of Paik’s largest video installations. It was made on behalf of the artist’s retrospective at the Whitney. Like much of Paik’s work, the piece focuses on duality: contemporary vs. traditional, technology vs. handcraft, high vs. low culture.

name: Ernest Edmonds Founds HCIRU Research Group
desc: Edmonds founded the Human Computer Interface Research Unit (HCIRU) at Leicester Polytechnic. The group helped Leicester Polytechnic become a significant center for computer art and Human-Computer Interaction research, attracting artists and researchers, including Stephen Scrivener and Dominic Boreham .

name: Computer Rendering of Stochastic Models by Alain Fournier, Don Fussell, Loren Carpenter
desc: This famous paper in the history of computer graphics outlines the breakthrough that was fractal rendering, which is still hugely important to this day. This seminal work explores the simulation of randomness in visual representation, leading to the creation of realistic natural phenomena such as clouds and landscapes. The paper laid the groundwork for rendering complex, organic structures through algorithmic techniques based on Mandelbrot’s fractals. By integrating stochastic processes into graphics, the paper revolutionized visual effects and paved the way for today’s sophisticated CGI techniques, deeply impacting film, gaming, design and, of course, digital generative art.

name: The First Touchpad Introduced
desc: The Apollo Domain computer featured what’s believed to be the first touchpad. It was placed to the right of the keyboard.

name: Montana by Jane Veeder
desc: This two-dimensional video by pioneering video artist Jane Veeder was developed with ZGRASS with a custom-made language she derived from arcade and video games. This work was an important example of proto-demoscene and early video-game art, on top of being groundbreaking in its own regard. Veeder dearly regarded ZGRASS, the early graphics system, saying that it provided "real-time animation and real-time sound synthesis accessed by a custom language optimized for interactive artmaking, all wrapped up together like a hot little sports car.”

name: Artists/Computers/Art at the Canada House Gallery, London
desc: This exhibition toured around four locations in 1982: London , Paris , Milton Keynes, England and Belfast, Northern Ireland. Please share if you have more information.

name: L’Art et l’ordinateur in Paris
desc: Organized in Paris by CISI (Compagnie Inter-nationale de Service en Informatique), this event was a seminar and notable computer art exhibition for this period. If it involved computer art and took place in Paris, then the grande dame, Vera Molnár was involved. She wrote a Kandinsky-inspired reflection on computers in art for the exhibition .
subjects: cisi (compagnie internationale de service en informatique)

name: Nam June Paik at Whitney Museum of American Art
desc: This Nam June Paik retrospective exhibition at the Whitney Museum celebrated the contributions of the pioneering video artist while also showcasing his latest work, V-yrimads. According to a 1982 review in the New York Times : “The largest show ever devoted to a single video artist, according to the museum, the exhibition comprises more than 60 works that go back to the beginnings of the Paik career.”

name: The Computer Image by Donald Greenberg, Aaron Marcus, Allan H. Schmidt, and Vernon Gorter
desc: The Computer Image was an important book in the burgeoning field of computer graphics, exploring its diverse applications. The book showcases how computers generate and manipulate images and how these have impacted various industries, such as art, design and engineering. It was around this time. It discusses algorithms, hardware and software tools, elucidating their role in creating visual representations. The text focuses on practical use cases, highlighting real-world examples and potential innovations.

name: Bill Reeves Early Advancement in Particle Systems
desc: Most computer graphics up to this point were hard-edged and linear with crisp RGB colors. It was difficult to produce images that appeared truly organic or naturally realistic. Bill Reeves , then at Lucasfilm and later at Pixar , was an early contributor to the solution of this problem by introducing particle systems in a foundational paper published in 1983, “Particle Systems: A Technique for Modeling a Class of Fuzzy Objects,” presented at SIGGRAPH ’83. This is an entirely generative process, as Wayne E. Carlson explains in his book, Computer Graphics and Computer Animation: A Retrospective Overview: “Each particle in the system is born (or generated), undergoes some dynamic changes, and dies. Particles in the system are generated semi-randomly within the bounds of some initial object. This space is termed the generation shape of the fuzzy object. Each of the particle’s attributes is given an initial value that may be fixed or may be determined by a stochastic process.” The power of a particle system is that these “graphical primitives” can be used to create nearly anything from simple points and lines to complex organic and inorganic systems (grass, fire, etc.). Particle systems were famously used in the 1982 film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan for the famous “ genesis effect .” [Carlson, 562]
subjects: star trek ii: the wrath of khan

name: Cryptographer David Chaum First Proposes Blockchain-Like Protocol
desc: David Lee Chaum, an American pioneering cryptographer, released his dissertation, “Computer Systems Established, Maintained, and Trusted by Mutually Suspicious Groups.” This paper is considered the first known proposal for a blockchain protocol. It even included the code to implement the system. Throughout the '80s, Chaum would pioneer privacy and digital currencies. His idea of “blind signatures” allowed a user to create an untraceable digital payment. While Chaum’s work laid the groundwork for anonymous transactions, his proposed systems still relied on a centralized authority, raising concerns about privacy and control. Satoshi Nakamoto would go on to solve these issues. Nakamoto’s innovation was the consensus mechanism called Proof of Work, which enabled a network of computers to validate transactions without the need for a central authority. This decentralized approach addressed the issues of control and trust present in Chaum’s earlier work.

name: Growth by Yoichiro Kawaguchi
desc: After working on his GROWTH algorithm for several years at this point, Kawaguchi exhibits his first artistic expression from the algorithm with Growth. This truly groundbreaking piece by Kawaguchi, who developed the animation using a supercomputer in Osaka , Japan , is some of the earliest evolutionary and artificial life art. Thus, it is some of the first proto-AI art, as we know AI art today. This piece explains more about the computing power that the brilliant Kawaguchi took full advantage of: “Kawaguchi worked with Professor Koichi Omura at the University of Osaka when his lab developed LINKS-1, a computer graphic system for realistic renderings. The machine was unprecedented for its processing power and, unlike supercomputers at the time, consisted of 34–62 regular-size processors connected in a networked system for faster calculations and the easy removal of deficient parts. From summer 1982 to spring 1983—an extraordinarily short duration process—Omura and Kawaguchi used LINKS to develop Growth: Mysterious Galaxy, a complex, 5-minute-long animation sequence that stunned the computer art community at ACM SIGGRAPH that year, including Pixar ’s then-president Ed Catmull , who noted the piece’s unique sharpness and image quality.”

name: SIGGRAPH’s Exhibition of Computer Art
desc: The third iteration of a computer art exhibition at the annual SIGGRAPH conference’s Exhibition of Computer Art was its most successful yet, traveling to “over 30 locations throughout the U.S., Canada , France , Italy , and Japan ” well into 1984. Forty years on, the show was a progressive highlight for women in generative art, as the show’s committee and jury were overwhelmingly women. The exhibition also highlighted the breadth of computer-based practices at the time. A SIGGRAPH overview of the show states that the “artist’s work should transcend technique, realize the full potential of the chosen medium, and reflect a consistency in their overall body of work.”

name: The Computer/The Artist exhibitions at the Long Beach Museum of Art
desc: This exhibition in Long Beach, California , sought to present “computer-generated video, installation and static artworks. It featured the work of artists such as Tom DeFanti , David Em , Darcy Gerbarg and Steina and Woody Vasulka .

name: “Portrait of the Artist As a Young Computer” by Grace Glueck
desc: As Grant Taylor points out, the title of this essay by art critic Grace Glueck in the New York Times is both a nod to James Joyce “as well as a parallel to the first article that pushed computerized art into the realm of popular culture: John R. Pierce ’s 1965 Playboy article entitled ‘ Portrait of the Machine As a Young Artist .’” Taylor continues by quoting Glueck’s opening: “‘Given what we’ve seen of it to date, it’s small wonder that when we hear the term “computer art” our attention begins to wander. By now we’ve developed an understandable resistance to the boring optical shenanigans that result when computers are programmed to make drawings by technicians who lack the imagination of artists.’” The article’s broad panning of computer-programmed work provides a necessary temperature check on the state of technology and art. While computers themselves were finally becoming the beloved devices we know them as today, the art produced by them was still considered in a far less positive light.
subjects: portrait of the artist as a young computer
portrait of the machine as a young artist

name: Harold Cohen’s Arnolfini Series
desc: This series of plotter drawings created by Cohen’s AARON were exhibited at the Arnolfini Gallery in Bristol, England . Ink on paper, the series were each 57 x 76 cm. It ran from August 1 to September 9, 1983. The series has since been loaned to Tate Modern and is owned by the Spalter Digital Collection.

name: Water Tower, Verviers, Belgium by Bernd and Hilla Becher
desc: German photographers Bernd and Hilla Becher have been instrumental in carrying on the twentieth-century Bauhaus tradition of the geometric aesthetic. Over the course of several decades, the couple photographed European and North American water towers. Their updated portrayal of the Bauhaus aesthetic was both a celebration of the rigidity of form but also commented on the idealistic promise of the Bauhaus with scenes of dilapidation. They developed the “Becher School” style, emphasizing objective, serial imagery, which anticipates the long-form generative art collections of today.

name: Apple’s Lisa: Early Personal Computer with GUI
desc: Developed by Apple , the Lisa was one of the first commercial personal computers with a GUI (Graphical User Interface). Lisa was short for “Local Integrated Software Architecture” as well as the name of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs ’s daughter. Lisa holds crucial importance in the history of computer graphics as one of the first personal computers to feature a graphical user interface (GUI) and a mouse. It introduced intuitive visual elements like icons, windows and menus, setting the foundation for modern user interactions with computers. While commercially unsuccessful due in large part to its high price tag, the Lisa’s GUI concept profoundly influenced subsequent Apple products, notably the Macintosh. Its user-centric design revolutionized computer interaction by making it more accessible and user-friendly.

name: Jaron Lanier’s Moondust
desc: This generative music game for the Commodore 64 was one of the first video games produced with the intention of being a work of art. It was created by Jaron Lanier , the American computer scientist and artist who is active to this day. Moondust serves as another example of the rise of video games, propelling digital and generative art. It again highlights how generative music has impacted computer graphics, often preceding it, as at Bell Labs with Max Matthews—which preceded generative imagery by several years—and David Cope ’s EMI work with primitive neural networks.

name: Proto-Demoscene: Cracktros Appear
desc: Rise of the demoscene The demoscene began out of the software cracking community that developed in Europe around this time when legal protections were more nebulous. Legal protection for software arrived later in much of Europe, the United Kingdom legislating in 1985 and the European Community harmonizing in 1991. Legislation in Europe was enacted in the late '80s and throughout the ’90s. In the US, however, legislation was enacted in 1980, meaning that the demoscene and cracker/hacker scene would be more prevalent in Europe, where greater liberties could be taken with software (and those liberties became the expectation). As video games and the personal computer began to emerge in the late ’70s and early ’80s, crackers would remove the software copy protection from computer games on the Atari and Commodore 64 . It became a challenge in the early ’80s for young video game enthusiasts to remove these copy protections to the point where a community began to form. The first to crack a new game would win prestige within the cracker community. Eventually, crackers took it a step further by changing the software of the game itself and adding their own personal intro to their copy, which they would share and distribute amongst friends at parties. While cracked screens began appearing as early as the Apple II , it wasn’t until the early ’80s that the practice became more mainstream. By the late ’80s and early ’90s, this practice of cracking and its community would evolve: “from people cracking games to writing graphic/sound demonstrations that showed off the computer they had just learned to program. Sure, cracking games was still popular, but some people decided that learning about the machine and using it as a tool for creativity was cooler” than cracking one dime-store game after another." -Demoscene activist Jim “Trixter” Leonard. This quote highlights the connection between the demoscene and digital generative art, as the demoscene carried on the tradition, since around this period in the early ’80s, of creativity in computer coding and creative expressions with software.

name: Computer/Culture 83 at La Chartreuse de Villeneuve in Avignon, France
desc: Computer/Culture 83 was organized by C.I.R.C.A (Centre International de Recherche, de Création et d’Animation) at La Chartreuse de Villeneuve in Avignon, France . According to the catalog , the exhibition was “composed of a multiplicity of events both complementary and dissimilar which allow the public to discover these new technologies from [their] own point of interest.” More than just an exhibition, the event featured conferences, a software festival, demos and workshops. In fact, it was even more than just a single exhibition, as the event showed the works from SIGGRAPH ‘83, Photo/Electric Art Show and Exposition: “Ceci N’est Pas un….”

name: Alyce Kaprow, Fazes
desc: Kaprow, part of MIT’s Architecture Machine Group, created Fazes, a work of generative photography displayed at SIGGRAPH ‘83.

name: Major Publications of 1983
desc: 1983 featured a wealth of important articles and publications related to art and technology, as highlighted by Copper Giloth and Lynn Pocock-Williams , including: 1. Jean Baudrillard , Simulations 2. Hal Foster , ed: “ The Anti-Aesthetic : Essays on Postmodern Culture” 3. Lucinda Furlong : “Notes toward a History of Image-Processed Video” 4. Myron Krueger : Artificial Reality 5. Robert Scott Root-Bernstein : “On Paradigms and Revolutions in Science and Art: The Challenge of Interpretation,” Art Journal (1984). 6. Gene Youngblood : “Computer Art as a Way of Life.”
subjects: computer art as a way of life
notes toward a history of image-processed video

name: Jim Blinn receives the first (1983) ACM SIGGRAPH CG Achievement Award
desc: Jim Blinn was the first person to receive SIGGRAPH’s Computer Graphics Achievement Award , “given [each year] to an individual for outstanding achievement in computer graphics and interactive techniques.” Blinn was a NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) mainstay who would greatly impact the world of computer graphics, influencing those who also came through JPL, including David Em , Alvy Ray Smith and Pat Cole . Blinn was particularly known for his NASA simulations of the Voyager spacecraft in 1979.
subjects: acm siggraph computer graphics achievement award

name: AARON – Harold Cohen exhibitions at major museums around the world, including Britain’s Tate Gallery in 1983
desc: As mentioned as a key “under the radar” event in generative art history by Casey Reas in an interview with Le Random , the exhibition of Harold Cohen ’s AARON at major institutions around the world was sadly an outlier in terms of computer-generated art’s institutional acceptance. Reas continues: “We always talk about the fact that institutions have never supported generative art. And I think that they haven’t at all, in a really awful way, but there are exceptions. Harold Cohen had AARON making drawings at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art ( SFMOMA ) and the Tate Gallery in London . Those are really big events that we should promote more. Harold was an extraordinary pioneer in the field.” Cohen’s SFMOMA show was in 1979, and 1983 is when AARON appeared at Britain ’s Tate Gallery, a critical moment of exposure to the legacy art world that was all too rare in computer-generated art’s history.

name: Electra Exhibition Curated by Frank Popper and Marie-Odile Briot
desc: Electra (1983) was an exhibition curated by Frank Popper and Marie-Odile Briot at the Musée d’Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris from 1983 until 1984. The full name of the exhibition was Electra. L’électricité et l’électronique dans l’art au XXe siècle [Electricity and Electronics in the Art of the XXth Century]. The initial exhibition would feature two works from Herbert W. Franke , including Butterfly and Mikado, which both focused on color combinations. Sonia Sheridan from Generative Systems and Roy Ascott would also produce work for the show. In her typical preponderance to incorporate the new, Sheridan’s work was the first to use the Paintbox system, according to Geoff Davis at MicroArts . Vera Molnár’s work was also referenced by the exhibition catalogue ; her participation in a Parisian Computer art event in the 1980s is far from shocking.
subjects: musée d'art moderne de la ville de paris

name: The Policeman’s Beard is Half-Constructed Published
desc: Billed as “the first book ever written by a computer,” this experimental text comprised of computer prose and poetry is rooted in a program that writes without prompting, developed by William Chamberlain with Thomas Etter ; illustrations by Joan Hall . -Sasha Stiles

name: Divisibility II + III (1984-1986)
desc: A continuation for Manfred Mohr from his Divisibility I (1980), in which he incorporates more complex forms of growth and distortion in his on-going experimentation with the cube.

name: Art and the Computer by Melvin Prueitt
desc: Artist Melvin Prueitt’s well-received publication explained how computers were being used at the time to create art. It also included a variety of computer-generated work. According to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art , the book “reflected a newfound optimism in computer art.” [Taylor, 160] Taylor continues about Prueitt’s work: “The book follows many of the computer graphic publications of the period, which outline the different techniques and their application in science, business, and entertainment. Although Prueitt’s publication was concerned mostly with art, scientists and technologists produced much of the work, and the publication had a tendency to view the imagery through scientific paradigms and metaphors.” [Taylor, 160]

name: Neuromancer by William Gibson
desc: William Gibson ’s classic novel reimagined the sci-fi genre. Optimistic visions of the future with their jetpacks and flying cars were replaced with a darker alternative, helping to popularize the cyberpunk aesthetic and its associations with the ’80s and ultimately the digital aesthetic. Dystopian societies dominated by mega-corporations and drugs served as the backdrop for hacker anti-heroes to resist. In addition to impacting the aesthetics of the 1980s that persist to this day, the book also captured the spirit of the anti-establishment hacker culture, which has been instrumental in forming crypto-art, separate from generative art.

name: Order Out of Chaos: Man’s New Dialogue with Nature by Ilya Prigogine and Isabelle Stengers
desc: Order Out of Chaos: Man’s New Dialogue with Nature by Ilya Prigogine and Isabelle Stengers first published in French in 1979, is a groundbreaking book that explores the concept of chaos theory and its relevance to various scientific disciplines. Prigogine, a Nobel laureate in chemistry, and Stengers, a philosopher, probe how chaos theory revolutionizes our understanding of complex systems and the natural world. In the context of digital generative art, this book helped to popularize the field of complexity and mythologize the role of the scientist, according to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art . the idea that seemingly random and chaotic processes can lead to the emergence of order and beauty. Digital artists have long drawn inspiration from chaos theory to create artworks that reflect the balance of order and chaos in the world. Chaos theory, in particular, encouraged artists to experiment with algorithms and computational methods to generate patterns found in nature.
subjects: order out of chaos: man's new dialogue with nature

name: “Art After Modernism: Rethinking Representation”, edited by Brian Wallis
desc: This seminal book, comprised of twenty-five essays, explores the evolving landscape of contemporary art in the post-modern era, marking a critical shift in art discourse by examining the rejection of modernist principles and the emergence of new artistic paradigms. The essays collected here discuss how artists began to embrace a more pluralistic approach, drawing from diverse traditions and mediums and challenging traditional hierarchies and categories. The book highlights elements of the postmodern framework that were here to stay, especially looking at work through a diverse set of lenses in careful context and the production of work through various media. This book is particularly significant for the development of digital art because it helped establish the intellectual framework for understanding art in the digital age. It laid the groundwork for appreciating digital art’s departure from traditional forms, highlighting the importance of interactivity, non-linearity and the fusion of art and technology, which reflect its roots in lumino-kinetic art and op art.

name: The Postmodern Condition by Jean-François Lyotard Criticizes the Computer (in Art)
desc: Another important postmodern text, published in French in 1979, this one was harshly critical of computers and particularly their use in art. The book argued that computers and society’s adaptation to them would have long-term negative consequences. Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art explains how Lyotard bleakly argued that the computerization of society would “reduce society to an efficient system, founded on the best possible input/output calculation.”

name: Chromas by Edward Zajec
desc: This series of works by Edward Zajec would continue until 1987. Art historian Frank Popper explains the significance of Chromas, which Zajec references on his website : “Edward Zajec sees his work not only in the narrow perspective of exploring the computer as an image generator, but also in the wider context of the expanded communication possibilities deriving from the interaction of art and technology. His ideas and techniques are concerned with the fluid articulation of colour and form in time. The focus is not on the choreography of forms in motion (animation), but rather on those transitional states where dimensions interpenetrate, motifs dissolve into patterns and the geometric blends with the organic. Zajec aims beyond even this in trying to formulate some codes for a hypothetical language of light and sound (Orphics). In a work called Chromas, crossed rays dissolve into one of several possible derivatives while modulating from a siena/cobalt to an ultramarine/green tonality. The actual unfolding of the images is based on the rhythms and sounds of a composition for piano by the contemporary Italian composer Giampaolo Coral . Chromas is an attempt to develop and manipulate an aural theme in terms of colour and form. Thus the formative principle behind this development is not shape animation but thematic transformation. -Frank Popper

name: German Cracking Service: Slamball
desc: One of the earliest German cracker groups, based in Dortmund, the German Cracking Service was among the groups whose crack intros anticipated the demoscene, especially on the C64. Legendary members of the group included 1103/JEDI and Snoopy . Their earliest catalogued intro, carrying the iconic three stripes, dates to 1984. You can still view their 1984 cracktro in a similar style, now introducing the game Slamball. The group’s activity was disrupted in the mid-1980s, though releases under the GCS name continued into 1988. Talented programmers, many members went on to have successful careers in early video games and software. These are some of the earliest whispers of the Demonscene.

name: Major Publications of 1984
desc: Copper Giloth and Lynn Pocock-Williams miraculously tracked the major publications for the decade and they are listed here: 1. Stan Augarten , Bit by Bit: An Illustrated History of Computers 2. Herbert W. Franke , ComputergrafikGalerie; Bilder nach Programm: Kunst im elektronischen Zeitalter. 3. Hiroshi Inose and John Peirce, Information Technology and Civilization ( Japan ) 4. Judy E. Sachter , “The Basic Concepts of Three-Dimensional Computer Graphics for Artists.” 5. Lee Silverman , “Inside the Loop: Computer Graphics within the Technological Highway.” 7. Thomas Defanti, “The Mass Impact of Videogame Technology.”
subjects: bilder nach programm: kunst im elektronischen zeitalter
bit by bit: an illustrated history of computers
the mass impact of videogame technology

name: Apple’s Macintosh Introduction Commercial
desc: Directed by Ridley Scott , this iconic commercial premiered during the Super Bowl, showcasing Apple ’s Macintosh computer release. Its significance lies in its revolutionary approach to advertising, blending cinematic storytelling with technology. The ad presents a dystopian narrative inspired by George Orwell ’s 1984, where a totalitarian regime is disrupted by a rebellious heroine wielding a sledgehammer. This commercial introduced the world to the concept of personal computing as a tool for liberation and creativity, emphasizing the Macintosh’s potential to empower individuals. In the context of digital generative art history, this commercial highlights the transformative power of computers, foreshadowing their role as the dominant creative tools of artists and designers around the world. The commercial also plays on the bad reputation that computers had due to their association with war and the military. This skepticism had remained around computers since as far back as the 1950s. These powerful, society-changing (and ending) machines that had been kept away from the general public for decades were finally becoming available as a commercially viable mass-market product. The world would genuinely never be the same.

name: Robert Abel and Associates Produce the First Computer-Generated Commercial, Brilliance
desc: Abel did early film work with John Whitney Sr. and Saul Bass for Alfred Hitchcock ’s Vertigo. This famous ad, “Brilliance,” was produced in 1984 and premiered a year after the Macintosh commercial, during Super Bowl XIX in January 1985. This thirty-second ad for, of all things, the Canned Food Information Council featured a risqué robot based on motion capture. It was an important example of raster graphics developed with software.

name: Cubicomp Picture Maker
desc: From 1984 to 1988, Cubicomp specialized in computer-aided design (CAD) software and played a pivotal role in the development of 3D computer graphics on the personal computer. Cubicomp’s PictureMaker and ModelMaker software was instrumental in revolutionizing how artists and designers created and visualized complex 3D models. Additionally, Picture Maker was some of the earliest PC-based 3D animation software and was used by artists such as Victor Acevedo . He used the Cubicomp to create works including Wired Couple Series (1989-1990), 6.26.27.86 (1989-1991) and Tell Me the Truth (1989-1990), which entered the Victoria and Albert Museum in 2008 as part of the Patric Prince gift, the museum dating the print it holds to 1991. Acevedo spoke to Peter Bauman (Monk Antony) about Cubicomp, saying: “After my early experiments with algorithmic computer graphics in 1983 and 1984, in early 1985, I moved to the Cubicomp system because I could interactively and visually build polyhedral models, combine them with digitized photographs and animate image sequences. I wanted to expand on the type of hybrid geometrical imagery that I had developed with traditional analog media in the years 1977–1984.”

name: PostScript Released
desc: Founded by John Warnock and Charles Geschke , Adobe Systems in 1984 unveiled PostScript, a groundbreaking page description language and computer graphics technology that played a pivotal role in the history of digital art and graphic design, used by artists such as Mark Wilson . PostScript empowered artists, designers, and publishers to create high-quality, scalable graphics and text for both print and digital media. This innovation helped popularize digital typography and graphic design, as it provided a standardized language for describing page layouts and graphics, ensuring consistency across different output devices. The release of PostScript impacted the graphic arts industry by simplifying the printing process and enabling the creation of complex, vector-based artwork, as demonstrated, again, by Mark Wilson. It pushed us toward the desktop publishing revolution, which would give rise to ever more accessible and sophisticated design tools.

name: Cook, Porter and Carpenter Introduce Distributed Ray Tracing
desc: A critical technique in computer graphics, the distributed ray tracing algorithm, was developed by Loren Carptenter, Robert Cook and Thomas Porter for Lucasfilm and described in detail in this paper . Carpenter famously also developed fractal techniques for motion graphics in 1982. Distributed ray tracing allowed for motion blur effects. Ray tracing enables the rendering of advanced lighting phenomena such as “shadows, reflections, and refracted light, phenomena that are difficult or impossible with other techniques.” However, there were limitations that Carpenter and his team solved, as outlined in the paper : “By distributing the directions of the rays according to the analytic function they sample, ray tracing can incorporate fuzzy phenomena. This provides correct and easy solutions to some previously unsolved or partially solved problems, including motion blur, depth of field, penumbras, translucency, and fuzzy reflections.”

name: Commodore Launches the Amiga
desc: One of the most well-known and beloved PCs of all time, the Amiga’s introduction marked a significant leap in personal computing capabilities, particularly in graphics and multimedia performance. More critical to this story, it was instrumental in altering humanity’s relationship with machines. At the time, PCs like the Amiga were often derided as toys for “nerds,” yet now these early adopters appear visionary, seeing the potential of these humanity-shaping machines. The device itself was equipped with advanced graphics and sound chips, enabling artists and designers to explore new creative interventions, as it quickly gained a devoted following among digital creatives. The Amiga’s goal was to compete with Apple ’s Macintosh and the IBM PC but with better sound and graphics. The Amiga, at $1,295 and cheaper than the Macintosh, was the only one of its competitors at the time that could run multiple programs at once. Additionally, according to this history : “One of the key features of the Amiga was its custom graphics and sound chipset, which allowed it to display graphics and play sound that was far superior to what was possible on other personal computers. This made the Amiga a popular choice for artists and musicians, who used it to create animations, music, and other multimedia content.” The Amiga’s capacity to handle sophisticated graphics and animations was foundational for the development of digital art and animation. It became a favored platform for pioneering digital artists, showcasing its potential at the intersection of technology and art. This platform’s influence on the emerging demoscene and computer art communities was profound, fostering experimentation with generative visuals and interactive experiences. The launch of the Commodore Amiga in 1985 catalyzed the evolution of digital generative art by providing accessible, powerful tools for artists, contributing significantly to the medium’s growth and diversification in the years to come.

name: Calculated Movements by Larry Cuba
desc: In this masterpiece of computer animation, Calculated Movements , Larry Cuba demonstrates his painstaking method of computer animation, creating elaborately choreographed scenes using basic elements that are repeated and arranged in a hierarchical fashion. As each level builds on the one before it, Gene Youngblood wrote that “if there is a Bach of abstract animation it is Larry Cuba,” creating aesthetically stunning compositions with intricate mathematical structures and cascading designs. Inspired by abstract animation pioneers such as Viking Eggeling and Oskar Fischinger , Cuba created Calculated Movements at his Santa Cruz studio with a Datamax UV-1 personal computer and Tom DeFanti ’s ZGRASS graphics language.
