Cuba could now work with solid areas and volumes, breaking away from the conventional dot-based rendering thanks to this raster-graphics system.

name: Mark Wilson Publishes Drawing with Computers
desc: In what may be the first creative coding book for artists, Mark Wilson published the seminal Drawing with Computers . The book served as manual for anyone to pick up and learn about making art with computers. In the mid-80s when the book was released, there was intrigue and enthusiasm for art by algorithms but it was difficult to learn. Wilson’s book filled this gap and would prove influential to artist and educator Travess Smalley, who spoke to Wilson about the book and much more in his profile on Le Random Editorials . Also read this piece by Wilson himself on Le Random Editorials, where he reflects on his practice in his own words.

name: Mark Wilson, Skew J17
desc: This plotter drawing (22 x 38 inches (56 x 96 cm.), pigmented ink on paper) in Wilson’s unconventional yet recognizable style stands as one of the artist’s signature outputs. Wilson was known throughout the decade for producing wall-size plotter painting outputs over eight feet long (30x100 inches).

name: Herbert W. Franke Reissues Computer Graphics, Computer Art
desc: Originally published in 1971, this updated edition of the book reaffirmed its enduring relevance by including nearly fifteen more years of history. Franke’s work has been instrumental in introducing computer-generated art to a broader audience, and the re-release solidified his position as a pioneering figure in the field. The book highlights the history, methods and theoretical foundations of computer art as a movement, as only Franke could. Thus, the reissue not only served as a historical record of the early days of computer art but also underscored the ongoing evolution of the practice.

name: Perlin Noise Invented
desc: First developed in 1983 and formally described in 1995, Ken Perlin ’s groundbreaking invention of Perlin Noise marked a watershed moment in the history of computer graphics and digital generative art that reverberates to this very day (just check out the latest release on fxhash ). Perlin, a computer scientist and computer graphics pioneer, created this algorithm to generate naturalistic textures for Disney ’s animated film " Tron .” Perlin Noise quickly became a foundational tool in computer graphics, offering a method for simulating intricate, organic patterns such as clouds, fire, and terrain. Its ability to create complex, visually appealing randomness with controllable characteristics transformed the artistic and technical possibilities of digital art and animation. Perlin noise played a vital role in shaping the aesthetic of digital landscapes, making it an essential tool for artists, game developers and filmmakers. Artist Emily Xie added this to the author, Peter Bauman , about Perlin: “Ken Perlin develops Perlin Noise, a gradient noise function that generates natural-appearing randomness. It was a huge stepping stone for graphical computing, allowing simulation of the natural world with realistic surfaces, patterns and textures. Perlin noise has been integral to generative art and is considered a foundational technique of the space.”

name: MIT Media Lab Opened by Nicholas Negroponte and Jerome Wiesner
desc: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Media Lab opened its doors under the visionary leadership of Nicholas Negroponte and Jerome Wiesner . This event marked a significant turning point in the history of digital innovation, research, and generative art. The MIT Media Lab became a crucible of interdisciplinary collaboration, bringing together artists, engineers, designers, and scientists. Under Negroponte’s guidance, it fostered a creative environment where groundbreaking technologies and digital artistry could flourish. The lab’s pioneering work in fields such as computer graphics, virtual reality, and human-computer interaction influenced the development of digital art by providing access to cutting-edge tools and expertise. It served as a breeding ground for generative artists and researchers who explored the creative possibilities of emerging technologies. Nicholas Negroponte’s vision and the MIT Media Lab’s collaborative spirit have left an indelible mark on the digital art landscape. Their contributions have inspired generations of innovators and artists, shaping the ever-evolving intersection of technology and creativity.

name: Emerging Expressions at the Bronx Museum of the Arts, New York
desc: The exhibition showcased over one hundred works by artists such as Richard Ziegler , Nancy Burson and Manfred Mohr . Mohr was mentioned in a June 14, 1985, New York Times review of the exhibition, which he shared on his website : “Several of the participants have appeared in New York galleries and one, Manfred Mohr, is noteworthy for being the most automated, since he owned his own computer and has his paintings painted by a plotter.”
subjects: the bronx museum of the arts

name: Duality and Co-Existence Exhibition, London
desc: Computer art pioneer Ernest Edmonds shows a generative work publicly for the first time. He writes of the exhibition : “I did not show such a work publicly until 1985, but in many ways, that showing was the culmination of much of the work of the 1970s. “Fragments” was the generative work shown at Exhibiting Space” in London .

name: Shoe-Field by Sonya Rapopport
desc: Shoe-Field (1982–89), an interactive artwork begun with a performance in a Berkeley computer store, offered a unique exploration of personal feelings about footwear. Participants responded to shoe-related questions, resulting in a unique “shoe-psyche charge” represented by five plot patterns. The interactive aspect extended to choosing shoes from a chart, which influenced a podiatric Rorschach plot. Shoe-Field’s significance stands as a further example of experimentation combining technology and interactive personal expression, allowing participants to investigate the impact of individual choices on their perceived shoe psyche. The artwork exemplifies how creative expression and technology can combine in ways that are novel yet clearly carry on the lineage of the history of art and technology.

name: Vizgame by Jane Veeder
desc: One of the earliest examples of artwork as a videogame, VIZGAME ran on a Datamax UV-1 Graphics System. The program enables the “player” to create their own real-time animations using the controls and joysticks.

name: Important publications of 1985
desc: Again, we reference Copper Giloth and Lynn Pocock-Williams ’s invaluable work: 1. Roy Ascott , “Concerning Nets and Spurs” 2. Katherine Dieckmann , “Electra Myths: Video, Modernism, Postmodernism” 3. Frank Dietrich , “Visual Intelligence: The First Decade of Computer Art (1965-1975)” 4. Lucinda Furlong , “Tracking Video Art: 'Image Processing' as a Genre” 5. Copper Giloth and Jane Veeder , “ The Paint Problem “ 6. Joan L. Kirsch , “When Will Computer Art Be Taken Seriously?“ 7. Barbara London , “Video: A Selected Chronology, 1963-1983“ 8. Joachim Schmid , “The Electronic Photographer is Coming" 9. Visual Computer begins publication
subjects: tracking video art: 'image processing' as a genre
when will computer art be taken seriously?

name: SIGGRAPH 85
desc: The end of the early years of SIGGRAPH , the ‘85 show was once again led by women. According to this history : “In 1985, in San Francisco , Louise (Etra) Ledeen chaired the SIGGRAPH Art Show. Rachel E. Carpenter was the Art Show Administrator and Joanne Culver once again was the Traveling Arts Show Chair. The art show jury consisted of: Kathy Rae Huffman ; Robin King ; Margot Lovejoy ; Beau Takahara and Woody Vasulka .” The Traveling Art Show in 1985 would make it to Tokyo with Hakuhodo, Inc. Loren Carpenter received the ACM SIGGRAPH CG Achievement Award.
subjects: acm siggraph computer graphics achievement award

name: Boids by Craig Reynolds
desc: Computer scientist Craig Reynolds introduced the groundbreaking Boids algorithm, a significant milestone in the history of digital generative art and artificial life simulations. Inspired by the mesmerizing patterns of bird flocking and fish schooling, Reynolds' Boids simulated the collective behavior of autonomous agents. It allowed these virtual creatures, or “boids,” to navigate their digital world by following a few simple rules: separation, alignment and cohesion. These rules gave rise to intricate and lifelike group dynamics in computer-generated animations and simulations. Reynolds' work not only fascinated computer scientists and animators but also inspired a generation of artists, including Casey Reas, who mentioned this development to Le Random . Boids became a powerful metaphor for exploring the emergent complexity that arises from the interactions of simple entities. Boids remains a symbol of the fruitful crossroads between technology, nature and artistic expression.

name: Langton’s Ant
desc: Langton’s ant was a cellular automaton created by Christopher Langton . Operating on a two-dimensional grid, this simple algorithmic system features an “ant” that follows a set of rules. Surprisingly, it produces emergent, complex, and beautiful patterns, blurring the line between randomness and determinism. This phenomenon laid the groundwork for a new era of generative art, inspiring artists and programmers to explore the aesthetic potential of algorithms based on organic life. Langton’s Ant demonstrated that, with basic rules and repetition, intricate, visually captivating patterns could emerge organically. Artist Casey Reas mentioned this development to Le Random as an example of an important moment to include on the Timeline.

name: The Beauty of Fractals by Heinz-Otto Peitgen and Peter Richter
desc: This book explores the emerging world of fractals, the mathematical objects with intricate, self-replicating patterns coined by Benoit Mandelbrot but popularized in computer graphics by Loren Carpenter . Peitgen and Richter’s work played a pivotal role in introducing fractals to an even wider audience, emphasizing their aesthetic and artistic potential. The book’s vivid illustrations and accessible explanations captured the imagination of readers, bridging the gap between mathematics and art. It inspired a generation of artists, scientists and programmers to explore fractals as a creative medium.

name: “Evolving aesthetic criteria for computer generated art: A Delphi Study” by Richard Lucas
desc: This Ohio State University MA thesis, submitted by Richard Lucas , explored the aesthetics of computer art through a survey. Respondents to the survey included some of the field’s most respected voices, including Charles Csuri , Frank Dietrich , Hiroshi Kawano , Lillian Schwartz , Gene Youngblood and Frider Nake. The general findings were that traditional aesthetic criteria were largely deemed adequate for computer art evaluation.

name: 1986 Venice Biennale: Art and Science
desc: The 1986 Biennale’s theme, Art and Science, was a topic largely ignored by major institutions for the past decade. The event marked what Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art described as a renewed “interest in technoscience paradigms” of the time. It did but only to a point. The event may have been indicative of a growing acceptance of science and technology in the arts after video games and personal computers helped dull techno-science fears of prior decades. Yet this resurgence in interest at the Biennale largely covered work in the firs thalf of the twentieth century as opposed to focusing on the most contemporary applications of science and art, such as the work of Craig Reynolds or Loren Carpenter . Jasia Reichardt , beloved curator of Cybernetic Serendipity , covered “this special event with its unexpected juxtapositions of ideas and objects.” She continued, saying : “The Art and Science exhibition was the major event of the Biennale. It covered Alchemy, Space, Biology, Technology and Informatics, Wunderkammer (Cabinet of Curiosities), Colour, and Science in the Service of Art.”

name: Ernest Edmonds Establishes LUTCHI Research Centre
desc: Edmonds moved from Leicester Polytechnic to Loughborough, establishing the Loughborough University of Technology Computer Human Interaction (LUTCHI) Research Centre. This would serve as his new base to continue exploring the intersection of art and technology. He would be joined by Stephen Scrivener , who made LUTCHI a pivotal research center investigating the amalgamation of computers, art and technology. The center had a particular focus on Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), becoming a thriving hub for artists and researchers, including luminaries like Stephen Bell . Notably, it played a crucial role in fostering the transition of individuals, such as Sean Clark , from computer scientists to artists. Clark and Edmonds continue to be active in the Computer Arts Society to this day. LUTCHI’s legacy can be felt decades later.

name: Ken Knowlton Asks “Why It Isn’t Art Yet?”
desc: In the SIGGRAPH 1986 Art Show Catalogue , Ken Knowlton wrote an essay that captured the frustration within computer art that legitimacy had continued to elude the community, according to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art . Taylor describes the article as Knowlton asking a question yet the article is actually an explanation, Knowlton telling us, “Why It Isn’t Art Yet.” There is no question mark at the end of the title. Knowlton felt that, despite more than twenty years making the art himself and considering himself a computer artist: “We are not yet beyond the gee-whiz stage of cuteness, of stunts, and of novelty for its own sake. In order for the artist to get into serious art, he/she must have a more nearly complete command of the tools, including the understanding and ability to build, redefine and/or augment them.” He concludes the essay by saying: “At this point, it does not make much sense to me to be trying to produce better computer art. The more appropriate challenge is to create better environments for the development of art-making tools.” This call for better tooling would take time to be answered but would be steadily developed over the next fifteen years, culminating in Processing .

name: The Blind Watchmaker by Richard Dawkins
desc: This groundbreaking book, The Blind Watchmaker, by Richard Dawkins ignited a paradigm shift in the discourse surrounding evolution and biology in art. According to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art , this book’s importance cannot be overstated: “One of the most important shifts for computer art was the work of the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins.” Taylor explains that this is because of Dawkins’s use of simulated artificial organisms called “biomorphs” that Dawkins created “seeking to illustrate how complexity could be generated by simple rules.”

name: Woman of War, Lady of the Wild Things by Liliane Lijn
desc: Woman of War (1986) and Lady of the Wild Things (1983) by Liliane Lijn stand as striking testaments to the intersection of art, feminism, performance and computers during this era. Lijn’s computer-controlled, kinetic sculptures made from steel and lasers confront societal norms and gender roles in all fields. Not what comes to mind for many when they think of “computer art,” Lijn’s sculptures feature the dynamism of light, kineticism and symbolism. The pieces challenge viewers to contemplate the complexities of womanhood and the wild, untamed spirit within, hinting that technology could serve as an empowering agent.

name: Modélisation d’un visage by Rebecca Allen
desc: Rebecca Allen ’s Modélisation d’un visage represents the artist’s continued work with computer-generated imagery of the human form and its movement. This work, which translates to “Modeling a Face” in English, encapsulates the essence of early digital art experimentation with 3D modeling techniques that were cutting-edge at the time. Modélisation d’un visage besides being a technical achievement, also explores the complexities within real and digital representation, provoking contemplation about identity and perception. More about Allen: Pioneer of generative motion Inspired by the aesthetics of motion, Rebecca Allen’s decades-long career spans innovations in video, performance and installation art. Her work also examines themes such as gender, identity and technology’s impact on humanity. Educated at both RISD and MIT, Allen feels comfortable in an artist studio as well as a research lab. Her scientific research informs her artistic practice, where she explores topics such as human motion simulation and artificial life algorithms. Allen understood, early in her career, the power of the computer as an artistic tool. In Swimmer (1981), she created one of the first examples of computer animation capturing human motion. In 1986, she collaborated with Kraftwerk on the revolutionary music video for “Musique Non-Stop.” It was one of the earliest examples of rendered 3D graphics in a music video. "My artistic goal was to define a digital aesthetic, and my research aim was to get the face to move, to express and to talk.” Her interactive installation, Bush Soul (#1) in 1997 incorporated Allen’s research into artificial life and virtual environments. She created a generative space where participants could role-play as avatars in a virtual world. Allen’s artistic vision and technical mastery led her to collaborate with other artists, including Nam June Paik , Peter Gabriel and John Paul Jones (Led Zeppelin). Her work is also in the permanent collections at the Centre Pompidou , the Whitney Museum of American Art and MoMA . Allen recognized the impact of technology on human behavior, seeking generative techniques for art creation that explored this dynamic. She not only had the brilliance to invent new technologies, but she also had the creative vision to incorporate them into her artistic practice.

name: Art ware: Kunst und Elektronik at Messe AG and Siemens AG, Hannover, Germany
desc: Premiering in 1986, this exhibition of mostly German electronic artists would continue annually until 1990.

name: The Computer as an Art Tool at Hurlbutt Gallery at the Greenwich Public Library, Connecticut
desc: This small exhibition in Connecticut, where Mark Wilson is based, featured many of the prominent computer artists of the 1980s. The show defied was a relative rarity in that it showed work in North America in a fine art setting as opposed to being attached to technological and scientific conferences. The show demonstrated that art made by computers was still continuing to gain acceptance. According to this review in the New York Times , while there was excitement for the event, many viewers found the results underwhelming, especially given the sophisticated tools involved. The exhibition featured works by various artists and mediums, including the early experiments by the legendary Darcy Gerbarg in computer-generated abstract art. Mark Wilson and Manfred Mohr ’s highly detailed computer-generated pieces came closest to fulfilling the expectations of the general public. Margot Lovejoy incorporated computer-derived images into three-dimensional constructions, addressing societal changes. The exhibition also included computer-generated motion in videos set to music. Lillian Schwartz ’s steel mobile, programmed to move uniquely for years, was exhibited and particularly appreciated at the event, according to the New York Times review. Visitors could interact with painting programs on Apple computers in a back room, offering a glimpse into the future of computer art.
subjects: the computer as an art tool

name: Bilder Images Digital, Computer Artists in Germany, Galerie Der Kuenstler, Munich
desc: This exhibition in Munich highlighted the contributions of Germans in computer art’s history, including the work of Georg Nees and Manfred Mohr . The exhibition catalogue had contributions from the luminaries of the past twenty years of computer art, including writings by Max Bense , Herbert W. Franke , Frieder Nake and Georg Nees.

name: Additional important publications of 1986
desc: Additional important publications as curated by Copper Giloth and Lynn Pocock-Williams : 1. Rene Berger and Lloyd Eby , eds., Art and Technology . 2. Nancy Burson , Richard Carling , and David Kramlich , Composites: ComputerGenerated Portraits. 3. Isaac Victor Kerlow and Judson Rosebush , Computer Graphics for Designers and Artists.
subjects: computer graphics for designers and artists

name: Pixar purchased from Lucasfilm by Steve Jobs
desc: In 1986, Steve Jobs , the visionary co-founder of Apple , made a historic move by purchasing Lucasfilm’s computer graphics division and incorporating it as Pixar . This acquisition, which initially seemed like an unconventional venture, would go on to reshape the computer graphics industry. Pixar, at the time, was a small computer graphics division of Lucasfilm, experimenting with computer-generated imagery. Under Jobs’s leadership, Pixar would evolve into an animation powerhouse, revolutionizing not only computer-generated images but filmmaking itself. In 1995, they released Toy Story , the world’s first feature-length computer-animated film, setting a new standard for animated storytelling using computers, a trend that to this day has not been reversed.

name: Suzete Venturelli Founds the Computational Art Research Laboratory, MediaLab/UnB
desc: Professor Venturelli founded the computational art research laboratory at the MediaLab/UnB to bring together a diverse community of students and researchers passionate about the intersection of art and technology. This visionary institution continues to cultivate inventive projects spanning animation, computational art, AR, HCI and more. MediaLab/UnB fosters a dynamic synergy between art and technology while addressing the socio-artistic and political issues of contemporary society.

name: Mona-Leo by Lillian Schwartz
desc: Lillian Schwartz ’s Mona-Leo was the artist’s attempt to use computers to analyze portraits of both Leonardo da Vinci and the Mona Lisa . According to Schwartz , “With Unix-based machines, she proved indisputably that Leonardo used himself as the final model for the Mona Lisa.” More about Schwartz: Pioneer of computer-generated film Schwartz’s vision to innovate with the latest tools led to a career of genre-shattering experimentation. She had “an intense interest in new materials,” which would remain throughout her career. Mirroring computer art’s own genealogy, she worked in lumino-kinetic, “light box” sculptures before turning to computers. Her kinetic work brought her in contact with the E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology ) group. This led to Schwartz’s “Proxima Centauri” being selected by MoMA for its epochal “ The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age ” ( New York ) in 1968. She then joined Bell Labs as its first female artist, working on her own and with the likes of Ken Knowlton . Here, she would create some of the lab’s most important early work with computers. At Bell Labs, she experimented with computer-generated film, combining traditional techniques with the latest digital methods. Her films were at once modernist and based on abstract geometric forms, yet they generated a vast array of advanced computer imagery. Schwartz’s pioneering use of various physical and digital media pushed the limitations of technology to embrace the unexpected. Her career showed how, in her own words, "computers can be made to accommodate the entire breadth of artistic thought.” The work was featured in Frank Popper ’s Art of the Electronic Age.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: HyperCard Released
desc: In 1987, Apple Inc. introduced the revolutionary HyperCard software, forever altering personal computing. Created by Bill Atkinson , HyperCard was a groundbreaking hypermedia system that enabled users to create interactive “stacks” of digital cards containing text, graphics and multimedia elements, akin to today’s hypertext and precursor to the World Wide Web . According to Casey Reas , this software was significant for the development of generative art. As he told Le Random , “HyperCard software was really essential. A lot of poets and a lot of artists were making Hypercard stacks in this multimedia environment to make generative work with.” HyperCard’s intuitive “stack” structure, combined with a user-friendly interface, empowered individuals, educators and artists to craft interactive content without extensive programming knowledge. It was a pioneering tool for multimedia authoring, paving the way for interactive presentations, educational materials and early digital art, all before the emergence of the World Wide Web in a few short years. HyperCard also influenced the early web’s aesthetics. According to Thomas Dreher , “ Pei-Yuan Wei was inspired by HyperCard when he developed the browser "Viola WWW,” one of the earliest web browsers in the early-90s.

name: Director 1.0 Released
desc: MacroMind Director 1.0 made its debut, forever transforming multimedia content creation. Developed by MacroMind, this pioneering software, later passing to Macromedia and then Adobe , allowed designers to craft interactive multimedia presentations and animations with remarkable ease relative to previous software. A standout artist in the use of Director is LIA, who began coding with it in 1995 and in the ’90s was at the forefront of this powerful language. She described in a conversation with Le Random: “I got a copy of the program. I got the handbook, and I basically copied the Macromedia Director Handbook by hand twice until I understood what a function was. It was called a handler, and the language was lingo, and it still is or was, actually. It was one of the most powerful programs ever out there. Macromedia Director. It allowed people really quickly do some animations by dragging and dropping without knowing how to code, and then you could enter the next level by actually writing code.” According to Casey Reas , this software was significant for the development of generative because, lerandom.art : “When I was cutting my teeth in this world, everything was being made with Macromedia Director. It preceded Flash as the medium that people were making work in. A timeline that I could get really excited about would be the tools that generative artists use and how that evolved over time. This time period was also the CD-ROM era. There were a number of extraordinary, experimental releases on CD-ROM made with Director, for example by LIA, which is also skipped over a lot.” LIA made her seminal 1999 net.art work Re-move with Macromedia Director. What exactly made Director so successful? It can be partly explained by its revolutionary “score” metaphor, which simplified complex multimedia sequencing, enabling users to orchestrate audio, video and graphics with much greater ease than ever before. This innovation spurred the creation of interactive CD-ROMs, kiosks, and early web content. As multimedia rapidly evolved, Director remained at the forefront, allowing creators to push digital storytelling forward. Its influence extended beyond creative coding and digital generative art to include educational software, immersive video games and filmmaking.

name: CompuServe Introduces the GIF
desc: CompuServe introduced the Graphics Interchange Format, commonly known as the GIF, in 1987, which forever changed how we share and communicate through images on the internet. Developed by Steve Wilhite , the GIF was initially designed to efficiently store and transmit color images for CompuServe’s file downloading areas. Its innovative compression algorithm allowed for compact files that could be easily shared. This ease of sharing gained the attention of early Internet platforms. With the emergence of the Internet, the GIF quickly gained popularity due to its versatility and support for animations. It would play an instrumental role in the development of humor and meme culture online, a direct antecedent to net and eventually “crypto and NFT” art. The GIF’s looping graphics became a hallmark of early web culture and, two decades later, early NFT culture.

name: SIGGRAPH Art Show in 1987 Attracts 23,000
desc: The break-out success of the 1987 show cemented the SIGGRAPH Art Show as “a major site for the exhibition of computer art and a place for the artist to gain new insight into current technical achievements in computer graphics,” according to Grand Taylor in When the Machine Made Art . This new interest in digital art was sparked by the increasing popularity of the personal computer. As argued in the last chapter, a major shift in human thinking occurred in the late ’70s as digital media first began entering people’s homes, beginning in earnest with the VHS player and Apple II .

name: Digital Visions by Cynthia Goodman
desc: Cynthia Goodman ’s groundbreaking exhibition, Digital Visions , marked a watershed moment in the acceptance of computer-generated art. The touring exhibition, which opened at the Everson Museum of Art in Syracuse, featured a plethora of artworks that explored the intersection of technology and creativity. Goodman’s observation that fine artists were embracing computers with great enthusiasm signaled a departure from previous years' disinterest and outright hostility. This renewed optimism in the 1980s reflected a growing acceptance of digital art, in contrast to a more pessimistic ’70s. This led to additional research and innovation in the field, including at IBM by William Latham who started this same year.

name: “The Expanding Medium: The Future of Computer Art” by Herbert W. Franke
desc: Originally published in Leonardo , the essay exhibited an optimistic tone, particularly “on perspective and interdisciplinary practice.” This optimism echoed the reversal of sentiment in human-computer interaction. Since the late 1970s, an on-going sense of optimism, fueled by the growing popularity of PCs and video games, had developed regarding digital technology.
subjects: the expanding medium: the future of computer art

name: Photoshop Developed
desc: Thomas and John Knoll began their journey to revolutionize digital image editing with the development of Photoshop. Originally conceived as a way to showcase grayscale images on a monochrome display, this software would go on to redefine the creative possibilities of visual art and photography. Adobe licensed the software two years later, in 1989, and subsequent versions of Photoshop continued to innovate. The introduction of features such as layers, filters and an easy-to-use interface changed the way professionals and beginners approached image editing. Photoshop democratized image manipulation by enabling anyone with a computer to become a digital artist or photo editor. This is in stark contrast to the additional levels of difficulty previously required in terms of specialized coding knowledge, which could take years or decades to master. Since its inception, Photoshop has become an essential tool across diverse industries, from graphic design and advertising to photography and web design. Its name has become synonymous with image editing, and its impact on visual culture is immeasurable.

name: Artificial Life Founded
desc: Organized by Christopher Langton of the ant program, this workshop, which became a book, served as the foundation for the study of artificial life.
subjects: artificial life: the proceedings of an interdisciplinary workshop on the synthesis and simulation of living systems

name: William Latham Begins Collaborations with Stephen Todd
desc: As an artist and research fellow at the IBM UK Scientific Centre, William Latham would first meet Stephen Todd , beginning a life-long collaboration that continues to this day. Their collaboration had foundations in artificial life and would profoundly impact evolutionary art, in many ways the basis for AI art as we know it today. While at IBM with Todd, they developed Mutator and FormGrow on IBM state of the art mainframe computers. Latham and Todd began working on the evolutionary art system Mutator at IBM in 1987. Lance Putnam and Peter Todd joined the Mutator work much later, on Mutator VR from 2016. Their work displayed “strange organic, often serpentine, forms, produced using [an] “alternative evolutionary software system” (developed with Stephen Todd and team), which William uses to pick and breed 3D forms freed from the limits of the human imagination.” According to Latham’s biography, “William’s work is focussed on using evolutionary processes to create art centered on the idea of 'Artist as Gardener,' an idea which originated from his time as Henry Moore Scholar at the Royal College of Art in the early eighties where he created his FormSynth drawings and etchings which were to become a blueprint for his later Mutator work.” The advancement of evolutionary art has had a profound and lasting impact on the generative art of today, as it helped spur the concept of generative art with changeable characteristics, particularly those that could evolve over time. This has specifically impacted AI art. The evolutionary work of Latham and Todd can be considered proto-machine learning art, as the evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning. Prior to 1987, Latham developed his well-known Form Synth algorithm (1979-1986). Latham would continue at IBM until 1993. In particular, the work of Latham and Todd has influenced contemporary work in artificial life, including by Ciphrd and Sage Jenson .

name: Red Ridge by Karen Guzak
desc: A lithograph print, arts.wa.gov of computer-generated abstract expressionism possesses a unique energy. Inspired by her mother’s weaving, textiles and beaded tapestries, the work is not made with code; rather, Guzak drew on a digitizing tablet to create the eleven plates used for each of the twelve prints. She used IBIS, a color-graphics illustration system.

name: “Computers and Art,” Syracuse: Everson Museum of Art.
desc: Organized by Cynthia Goodman , this group exhibition was shown across the east coast of the United States . Billed as “the first major museum group show on computer art in the U.S.,” the exhibit showcased works from artists including Manfred Mohr , Lillian Schwartz and Mark Wilson .

name: The Interactive Image at the University of Illinois at Chicago
desc: Held by the Electronic Visualization Lab (EVL) at the University of Illinois at Chicago , the show lasted in installments from 1987 until 1989. A SIGGRAPH 2017 paper looked back at this event and highlighted the importance of the show in retrospect.

name: The Second Emerging Expression Biennial: The Artist and Computer at the Bronx Museum of the Arts, New York
desc: Curated by Luis R. Cancel , the entire catalog for this exhibition can mercifully be found online in its entirety. The exhibition, according to the catalog, sought “to capture the extent to which computers are being utilized as creative tools by visual artists.” The exhibition featured the work of artists such as David Em , Mark Wilson , Manfred Mohr , Margot Lovejoy ,
subjects: the bronx museum of the arts
the second emerging expression biennial: the artist and computer

name: Other Major Publications of 1987
desc: Publications by the singular Copper Giloth and Lynn Pocock-Williams : 1. Hal Foster , ed., Discussions in Contemporary Culture: Number One. 2. Catherine Richards , “Virtual Worlds, Digital Images.”
subjects: discussions in contemporary culture: number one

name: Adobe Illustrator Developed
desc: Developed in 1986 but first shipped in 1987, Adobe Illustrator emerged as a groundbreaking vector graphics software, revolutionizing the design industry. Developed by Adobe Systems for the Apple Macintoush, Illustrator provided designers with a powerful toolset for creating scalable and precise, visually compelling illustrations. Its intuitive interface and robust features quickly made it an essential piece of software for graphic designers, allowing for the creation of logos, icons and intricate artwork. Illustrator is the companion product to Photoshop that focuses on areas of typesetting and logography in design. The program was a step forward in graphic design from software such as MacDraw and was the commercialization of Adobe’s PostScript.

name: Apple Introduces the Mac II
desc: With the introduction of the Mac II, Apple ushered in a new era of computing with the first 32-bit Mac. This desktop computer boasted groundbreaking features such as color graphics, expansion slots and enhanced processing power, making it the first Mac with color capabilities. The Mac II became a powerhouse for creative professionals, offering unprecedented capabilities for graphic design, desktop publishing and multimedia production. For instance, with the right graphics card, the Mac II could handle up to 16.7 million colors . Its modular design and color capabilities transformed the Macintosh into a versatile platform, solidifying Apple’s impact on the PC market. The machine was still quite expensive, selling at $3,898 for the most basic model, roughly $10,556 in 2023.

name: Scanners Become Available for PCs
desc: A transformative development occurred in the realm of personal computing with the availability of scanners for PCs. This technological advancement enabled users to digitize physical images and documents, bridging the gap between the analog and digital worlds. The newfound ability to convert photographs, artwork, and printed material into digital formats revolutionized content creation, graphic design, and document management. The integration of scanners into personal computing marked a significant step toward the digitization of visual information, paving the way for diverse applications across industries and contributing to the democratization of image digitization.

name: Demoscene Splinters into PC and Home Computer
desc: This year represents the beginning of the split in the demoscene community that would coalesce over the next several years, as some practitioners moved to the PC while others stayed on home computers such as the Commodore 64 , Amiga and Atari ST. Those who chose the PC mostly used the operating system MS-DOS. According to Dreher [Dreher 162], by 1992, the PC demoscene had become independent from the Amiga demoscene.

name: Celestino Soddu, Medieval Towns Generative Variations
desc: Based on the paintings of Simone Martini and other Italian masters, the Italian professor and architect’s project consisted of “typical Italian Medieval Towns” algorithmically and serially generated. The designs were part of Soddu’s longstanding fascination with the “ideal city” and his belief that computers and generativity could augment human creativity.

name: Geometric Love by Masaki Fujihata
desc: This important work in the history of Japanese computer graphics was highlighted by Frank Popper in his seminal text, Art of the Electronic Age.

name: Roman Verostko with Seminal Article “Epigenetic Painting”
desc: Verostko’s paper is said to have “identified biological analogues to autonomous form generating procedures. His ‘epigenetic art’ includes a limited edition of George Boole ’s ‘Derivation of the laws illustrated with his own ‘personal expert system,’” known as Hodos. Presented at FISEA in 1988 and published in Leonardo in 1990, the paper anticipated prompt-based AI in many ways, outlining a new era in art-making systems. Artists use program feedback to iteratively develop software, akin to refining compilers. The evolving software becomes a distinct art form, comparable to genetic code. Verostko envisions hybridization, coding art ideas from different creators, resulting in unique combinations like “Kandinsky-Mussorgsky” with audio and visual drivers. Anticipating future advancements, he sees artists easily constructing personal expert systems, fostering generational growth in improvisational works. In this uncanny process, software takes on a life of its own, requiring artists to humanize it—providing form and structure to align with artistic and life quality.
subjects: first international symposium on electronic art (fisea)

name: First International Symposium on Electronic Art (FISEA) Held in Utrecht
desc: 1988 saw the inception of the ISEA conference, initiated by Theo Hesper and Wim van der Plas in 1986, which materialized as the “FIRST International Symposium on Electronic Art ” (FISEA) in 1988. Conceived to establish a network exploring the intersection of art and science, the inaugural symposium unfolded in Utrecht, with satellite activities in Groningen and The Hague. ISEA from this point forward became a crucial platform for digital artists. Subsequent events spanned global locations, including Sydney, Minneapolis and Helsinki. Over time, ISEA evolved into a nomadic event, a distinctive feature shaping its history. The name was coined at FISEA in 1988 and the Inter-Society founded in 1990, laying the foundation for an enduring international platform fostering interdisciplinary discourse and the advancement of electronic art. The symposium’s impact on the development of the digital art from the late ’80s onwards is little-known but huge. Is fusion of academic discourse with creative showcases, facilitated interdisciplinary collaboration and showcased cutting-edge electronic art and technological innovations on a global scale for over three decades.
subjects: first international symposium on electronic art (fisea)

name: F. Kenton Musgrave, Blessed State
desc: The algorithmic work was an important development in the rendering of fractal terrains that played a role in computer game landscapes appearing more realistic.

name: Visual Music by Yaacov Agam
desc: Highlighted by Frank Popper in his seminal text, Art of the Electronic Age, Agam’s Visual Music Orchestration is one of the Israeli sculptor and experimental abstract kinetic artist’s most known works. Agam is known for his use of audience participation, light and sound, anticipating today’s digital art.

name: Nam June Paik Builds Media Tower for Seoul Olympics
desc: Marking a critical moment in new media art in Asia , Korean-American Nam June Paik was commissioned to build a monumental media tower for the 1988 Seoul Olympics. Paik incorporated 1,003 TV screens into his design for the work titled The More, the Better (Dadaikseon in Korean).

name: Computers and Art at the IBM Gallery of Science and Art, New York
desc: Organized by Cynthia Goodman , this exhibition was also shown in Ohio , Syracuse and Miami . It was written of the show that it was the “first major museum group show on computer art in the U.S. Its seven-week run was said to have attracted 100,000 visitors.
subjects: ibm gallery of art and science

name: “Digital Photography: Captured Images, Volatile Memory, and New Montage,” San Francisco: SF Camerawork.
desc: The exhibition was one of the first to combine the terms “digital photography.” The exhibition showed “works by Paul Berger , MANUAL, George Legrady and Esther Parada [that] didn’t look like conventional photographic imagery at all, but rather resembled photomontages, often containing typographical elements and visible pixilation.” This early digital photography exhibition looks at how digital tools have transformed the photographic medium. The show presented the opportunity for dialogue on the changing nature of digital image creation, storage and composition.

name: Other Major 1988 Publications
desc: Publications for the year, as always curated by Copper Giloth and Lynn Pocock-Williams : 1. Timothy Binkley , “Camera Fantasia.” 2. Christopher Burnett , “ Computers and Art in the Age of the World Picture.” 3. Timothy Druckrey , “User Friendly?” 4. David Ross, The Art of David Em : 100 Computer Paintings. 5. Wim Van Der Plas, ed., Electronic Art
subjects: computers and art in the age of the world picture
the art of david em: 100 computer paintings

name: FAX Machines Mass Marketed
desc: This moment serves as an additional example of digital machines entering people’s homes and altering the human-machine relationship and sentiment. In a watershed moment for digital mass media, FAX machines became widely available, altering the communication landscape. This technology breakthrough gave enterprises and individuals alike the power of fast document transmission. The FAX machine was a precursor to the instant document transfer we have now, altering how we shared ideas and interacted. As FAX machines spread, they cross geographical gaps, speeding up information flow. The machine and its wide-spread availability thus represent a watershed moment in the democratization of communication tools, signaling an era in which document transmission transcends physical constraints, opening up new avenues for global connectedness and collaboration.

name: MPEG Established
desc: Dr. Hiroshi Yasuda and Dr. Leonardo Chiariglione founded MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group), which would go on to develop the MPEG standard, which is still largely in use to this day.

name: Vent Noir II by Jean-Pierre Hébert
desc: These plotter drawings, which are among Hébert’s most well-known works, were created using extremely precise and closely drawn lines. These pieces took several days to plan and were inspired by Bauhaus and Benoit Mandelbrot ’s fractal papers. In other words, Hébert took Bauhaus concepts and applied the self-similarity of fractals to these works.

name: GR8: First demo released by Future Crew on a PC
desc: The legendary Finnish Demoscene group released their first PC demo, GR8, an EGA sinus-scrolling demo. Sinus-scrolling is a text effect where text scrolls across a screen in the form of a wave, moving up and down while scrolling. The group, up to this point, had released its demos on the Commodore 64 .

name: Tim Berners-Lee Invents the World Wide Web
desc: One of the key moments in mass-media art but also in human history, Berners-Lee’s invention revolutionized the digital landscape as the visionary computer scientist conceived of the concept of the World Wide Web (WWW). The invention was also critical to the eventual development of NFTs. Working at CERN , he proposed a decentralized system to share and retrieve information, laying the foundation for the Internet we know today. By the end of 1990 he had built the first browser, server and web page, ushering in a new era of global communication. Berners-Lee’s invention broke down technological barriers, democratizing access to information. The rise of mass-media technology and art were critical steps in enabling NFTs. Thus, this can be seen as a critical step in the development of digital art, such as net art. Also, more broadly speaking, it’s a major step towards the global, collaborative and instantly shareable art environment we enjoy today.

name: SIGGRAPH ‘89
desc: The SIGGRAPH ‘89 conference marked a watershed point in computer art history. A significant panel session evolved among the convergence of creative minds, provocatively titled “Computer Art—An Oxymoron?” This debate, dubbed “Views from the Mainstream,” probed into the heart of artists' discontent and, according to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art , was the first major attempt to critically study computer art. As the SIGGRAPH '89 debates progressed, philosophically divergent viewpoints emerged, providing the framework for a series of major journal publications. This historic event not only addressed the changing world of computer art, but it also sparked a critical perspective that would define the debate surrounding this dynamic junction of technology and creativity. The investigation also stands in contrast to contemporary belief that criticism in computer art has little precedence. The art show itself featured work from Ana Ursyn, Mark Wilson , Jean-Pierre Hebert, Hans Dehlinger , Brian Reffin Smith , Colette Bangert , Charles Bangert and Manfred Mohr .
subjects: computer art—an oxymoron? views from the mainstream

name: The Death of “Computer Art”
desc: Several instances around this time period signaled the end of “Computer Art” and the rise of “Digital” or New Media Art, as argued originally by Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art . The first instance was the art critic David Carrier , writing in Leonardo , rejecting computer art and casting a contemplative shadow on the movement by declaring, “it is genuinely unclear to me whether any art using computers is truly significant.” This was a watershed moment in our story, as computer art now grappled with an existential crisis. Perhaps feeling the pressure of decades of lack of recognition, the remark alluded to the skepticism surrounding technology’s transformative power in art, ushering in an era of critical examination. Carrier would also not be the only one to give up on computer art over the years. The remark signals the crisis evident in a movement where it was a point of pride and distinction to make computer graphics from code. But as this was increasingly becoming possible with the use of design software, “computer art” as a unified movement was called into question. This year can be, in some ways, thought of as the end of “computer art,” as it had been known since the 1960s. Taylor explains in further detail: “The term ‘computer art’ had a fundamental problem which arose when there was a complex intertwining of traditional analog, electronic, and digital technologies, and when the artist had no desire to proclaim the medium as central to the work. In fact, artist Judson Rosebush proclaimed in 1989 that ‘computer art has become a meaningless term.’ That same year, Brian Reffin Smith proclaimed this to his readers: ‘Let us make an art that does not need the computer to justify it.’ Richard Wright in the 1989 SIGGRAPH Computer Art show catalogue also asks, “Does ‘Computer Art’ Still Exist?”

name: “Beyond Computer Art” by Brian Reffin Smith
desc: In an honest but heartbreaking article, Brian Reffin Smith ’s philippic against computer art presented a devastating case against the entire movement that Smith helped pioneer. The text criticizes the state of computer art, arguing that it is often outdated, commercially driven and lacking true artistic significance. Smith points out that much of what is labeled as “computer art” is actually graphic design created for non-artistic purposes. The text highlights a disconnect between the computer art world and traditional art institutions, with galleries and critics often dismissing it. The author acknowledges some improvement in computer art but contends that it remains isolated from contemporary art problems and lacks genuine innovation. Calling for a more honest evaluation of computer art, the text also demands a focus on teaching the importance of ideas over technical aspects, and a shift towards creating computer art that challenges conventions and incorporates critical discourse. Smith encourages artists to explore the interactive capabilities of computers and produce work that transcends the need for technological justification. The conclusion emphasizes the need for courage and innovative ideas to truly advance computer art beyond its current limitations.

name: Kid Pix Empowers Young Creativity
desc: Digital creativity witnessed a revolution with the invention of Kid Pix. Developed by Craig Hickman and published by Broderbund Software in 1991, Kid Pix marked a paradigm shift in computer software designed for children. lerandom.art : “Kid Pix is a drawing program written for children. It was made as a direct response to MacPaint (1984). And it includes a lot of generative drawing tools. You can drag your mouse across the screen and things drip down or you drag your mouse across the screen and all of these concentric circles emerge from that point.” lerandom.art “I think the huge disappointment in Mac Paint, it’s an extraordinary piece of software but all it, is that it emulates existing tools. This is the airbrush tool. This is the Eraser tool. This is the Pen tool. Kid Pix branches out from there and makes drawing tools that are unique, and that can only be made with code. It really encouraged a generation of children to play with drawing in software.”

name: Roman Verostko, Carnival, Pathway Series
desc: Carnival, an exquisite work from Verostko’s Pathway Series, represents a five-decade exploration of unseen worlds. Verostko pioneers the convergence of software form-generators and fine-arts practice, rooted in the legacy of early twentieth-century abstraction. He creates visual worlds by combining computational precision with artistic contemplation using BASIC and DM/PL, Houston Instrument’s Digital Microprocessor Plotting Language. A “fine art form generator,” as Verostko referred to his algorithms, serves as a biological genotype in his methodology, encoding the information for form generation. Verostko’s works, created with a multipen plotter, reveal a meticulous dance of thousands of lines, with each pen change and occasional brush stroke orchestrated by software. As Verostko’s art transcends intentional representation, titles are arbitrary, reminiscent of labeling flowers. Instead, he intends for each piece to unfold as a unique journey into uncharted territories. These visual manifestations honor the dynamic processes that underpin their creation, inviting viewers to savor the mystery of coded procedures that result in unexpected grace and beauty.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: Magiciens de la Terre at the Centre Georges Pompidou
desc: This important Centre Georges Pompidou exhibition highlighted global inequalities within the contemporary art world, with curator Jean-Hubert Martin featuring half the work of Western and half non-Western artists. The show highlights in our story mass-media art’s rise throughout the 1980s as well as the increasingly globalized and interconnected nature of art, which would only be accelerated in future decades as the Internet popularized.

name: Sans lever la plume by Jean-Pierre Hébert
desc: The artist’s first solo show was held at the Galerie Alphonse Chave and featured Hébert’s plotted work. At this time, Hébert was working independently. It was later in 1989 that he would discover SIGGRAPH and its community. He submitted work to participate in the 1989 SIGGRAPH show and went on to appear in the next seventeen in a row.

name: Postmodern Currents: Art and Artists in the Age of Electronic Media by Margot Lovejoy
desc: In Postmodern Currents: Art and Artists in the Age of Electronic Media, Margot Lovejoy explores how art has changed with the rise of electronic media. Lovejoy takes a straightforward approach to dissecting the impact of technology on artistic expression in the postmodern era. The book studies how artists navigate traditional forms in the face of emerging technologies. Lovejoy’s work serves as a foundational text in the genealogy of electronic art.

name: The Mac Portable
desc: Apple launched the Macintosh (Mac) Portable, ushering in a new era of portable computing. Weighing around 16 pounds, this ground-breaking device became the first battery-powered Macintosh, providing users with previously unheard-of mobility. The Mac Portable catered to professionals on the go, with a crisp active matrix display, a built-in trackball and the power of a desktop Mac. Despite its weight, this early attempt at a portable Mac was a major advancement in mobile computing technology. The Mac Portable paved the way for Apple’s portable product line to evolve, paving the way for the more compact and lightweight laptops that would follow, as well as the iPhone and iPad.

name: TCC Release Classic Megademo on Commodore Amiga
desc: The subgroup of Red Sector Inc., TCC, released this classic of the demoscene, winning first in the Tristar Part 1989 and voted 1st in the Cracher Journal 16.

name: The Legible City by Jeffrey Shaw
desc: The Legible City, a game-changing interactive art installation, made its debut in Nagoya, Japan . The hardware and software were meticulously crafted by a dedicated team after being conceptualized by Jeffrey Shaw and Dirk Groeneveld . Cyclists rode stationary bikes through a virtual city made of computer-generated letters, which replaced actual architecture. The handlebars and pedals gave users control, fusing physical and virtual effort. The Manhattan version added color-coded fictional narratives for exploration. Legible City, which was shown at Artec '89 in Nagoya, SIGGRAPH '89 in Boston and Ars Electronica '89 in Linz , and later at MultiMediale 2 in Karlsruhe in 1991, remains a landmark in digital generative art, combining physical engagement with immersive, text-based cityscapes.

name: Jenny Holzer at the Guggenheim in New York
desc: Digital art was slowly becoming more mainstream as some of the biggest names in contemporary art experimented with the mechanical. One example was the neo-conceptualist Jenny Holzer . Her 1989 to 1990 exhibition at the Guggenheim was a site-specific LED installation that spiraled up the parapet of the museum’s Frank Lloyd Wright-designed rotunda.

name: Image World at the Whitney Museum of American Art
desc: This influential exhibition, which is accompanied by essays by Marvin Heiferman , Lisa Phillips and John G. Hanhardt , captures the essence of the “Image World.” The exhibition’s diverse perspectives offer a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic relationship between art and media at a pivotal moment in cultural history, from Heiferman’s examination of media omnipresence to Phillips' exploration of art within evolving media landscapes and Hanhardt’s investigation into the role of film and video in the television era.
subjects: image world: art and media culture

name: Important Publications of 1989
desc: Copper Giloth and Lynn Pocock-Williams miraculously tracked the major publications for the decade and they are listed here: 1. Edward Barrett , The Society of Text: Hypertext, Hypermedia, and the Social Construction of Information. 2. Andrew S. Glassner , 3D Computer Graphics: A User’s Guide for Artists and Designers. 3. John Lansdown and Rae A. Earshaw, eds., Computers in Art, Design, and Animation. 5. Martha Rosler , “Image Simulations, Computer Manipulations: Some Considerations.” 6. Leonardo begins publication of F.A.S.T. Electronic Bulletin Board.
subjects: 3d computer graphics: a user's guide for artists and designers
computers in art, design, and animation
image simulations, computer manipulations: some considerations

name: Intel introduces the 80860 microprocessor chip-equivalent power of a Cray 1 supercomputer
desc: The introduction of Intel’s 80860 microprocessor marked a paradigm shift in processing power, with capabilities comparable to the formidable Cray 1 supercomputer. This microprocessor represented a significant advancement in computational efficiency and performance. The integration of Cray-level power into a single chip changed the computing landscape, opening up new possibilities for a wide range of applications, including in the visual arts.

name: Paul Brown’s 1990 essay “Beyond Art”
desc: Paul Brown ’s 1990 essay “Beyond Art”, published in 21C, envisions the impact of information technology on the art world. It anticipates collaboration between artists and emerging technologies like supercomputing and artificial intelligence. Brown also speculates on a direct link between the brain and computers, emphasizing artists' role in shaping this interaction. The essay also calls for computer art to usher in a new era of democratization in art, offering an optimistic contrast to much of the pessimism surrounding computer art to close out the decade.

name: World Wide Web Tooling Complete
desc: “The 1990s witnessed a technological development of unprecedented speed for the digital medium—the so-called ‘digital revolution.’” -Christiane Paul in Digital Art (2003) The eminent Paul attributes this revolution to two factors: 1. Hardware and software improvements and affordability 2. The birth of the Internet Many of these hardware and software developments occurred in our previous chapter on the ’80s. These include the release affordable PCs like Apple ’s Macintosh and the Commodore 64 as well as software like Macromedia Director . [For more context, we suggest youtube.com or open.spotify.com ( transcript ) to our Ch 7 Artist Discussion with Auriea Harvey ⁠, ⁠ Joshua Davis ⁠, ⁠LIA⁠, ⁠ Scott Draves ⁠ and ⁠ Vuk Ćosić ⁠⁠.] But the Internet, or this early public version called the World Wide Web, was a ’90s phenomena as Paul said. We begin the decade slightly out of order at the end of 1990 instead of the beginning. We make this choice to emphasize the looming paradigm shift that is the Internet. It would come to dominate the rest of the decade and that, of course, was only the beginning. For art itself and our story, the Internet not only brought us net.art, which we discuss at length in this chapter beginning in the middle part of the decade, but it also enabled the continued rise of mass-media art. This is the idea that art could be produced in infinite quantities and distributed globally in an instant. The rise of mass-media art can be seen as a theme throughout this decade, where artists, enabled by the Internet, could share their work globally in an instant. The ramifications that would have on art and the art world would be immense. The Internet has changed so much in our lives, it’s easy to forget how much it has also changed art. By the end of the first year of the decade, Christmas 1990, Berners-Lee, with Robert Cailliau and Nicola Pellow , had created all of the tools required for a functional Web, including HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP), HyperText Markup Language (HTML), the first Web browser (WorldWideWeb), the first HTTP server software, the first web server ( info.cern.ch ), and the first Web pages that described the project itself. The project would be compiled in its entirety and debuted just a few days later in January, 1991. Just as our decade begins, a foundational shift in human history occurs.

name: Panspermia by Karl Sims
desc: This standout generative film by the icon Sims depicted an artificial world and remains an example of an early animation born from artificial evolution. Sims’s work with artificial life can also be thought of as a continuation in the development of AI art. It inspired the work later in this decade of Scott Draves , a machine-learning art pioneer, and many others. This evolutionary work of Sims can be considered proto-machine learning art. According to Sims: “This botanical form of life, reproducing itself from planet to planet through space, is in many ways analogous to other self replicating systems including organisms, entire species, or even ideas.” These evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning. As for Panspermia itself, Sims created the piece using original software, in which he created a virtual universe teeming with 3D organic plant structures. Employing chaos, complexity and self-replication, the animation mirrors the biological world, suggesting life’s interstellar distribution through spores. Dynamic simulations and particle systems animated these digital life forms, displaying Sims’s self-propagating systems. Panspermia not only showcases the potential of artificial evolution in computer graphics but also prompts contemplation about life’s interconnectedness and propagation on a planetary scale. Thomas Dreher describes it as such in History of Computer Art: “ Karl Sims presents in the short film “Panspermia” an artificial world of biological forms as an autonomous cosmos with recurring parallels to the evolution of geology and fauna on earth” [Dreher 180]. This major work by the legendary Sims continues to influence the work of generative artists today (ciphrd) but had a profound impact on the decade of the ’90s and the rise of artificial intelligence art.

name: Scream Tracker 2 released by Future Crew
desc: The final major trend we begin this chapter with is the rise of the demoscene. Cracking, which refers to the removal of a game’s copyright and duplication mechanisms, was a practice that began shortly after video games existed in the late ‘70 and early ’80s. What began with Crackers and Cracktros (programming, pirating and video game hobbyists who programmed introductions to cracked video games in groups) in the ’80s eventually branched off into the demoscene by the late ’80s. This split is believed to be the result of an interest in programming and creativity in the demoscene over piracy and questionably legal activities. Once certain groups such as Future Crew began producing more and more advanced mega-demos, which were strings of intros linked together, the demoscene began to more clearly distinguish itself. It wasn’t until the 1990s that the demoscene truly took off, however. To characterize the demoscene as entirely breaking from its cracker roots would be inaccurate, yet two groups, as we know of them today, did form. Crackers continue to focus on piracy to this day, which demosceners became much more interested in the technical skill of creative programming. The demoscene’s relevance to algorithmic art should be abundantly clear with this following quote from Jim “Trixter” Leonard a few years later in 1994: “Around this time, a gradual shift occurred, from people cracking games to writing graphic/sound demonstrations that showed off the computer they had just learned to program. Sure, cracking games was still popular, but some people decided that learning about the machine and using it as a tool for creativity was cooler” than cracking one dime-store game after another.”

name: February: initial public release of Adobe Photoshop
desc: In Feb 1990, Adobe Photoshop, the ground-breaking image editing program, was made public. It changed the digital art world by providing strong tools for graphic design and photo manipulation. Creatives loved its potential, allowing for complex editing and visual storytelling. Photoshop has become a design studio staple and an indispensable tool for artists worldwide, affecting how visual information is generated and altered. The software’s constant progress has left an unmistakable effect on generative art, allowing creators to realize their visionary projects with unparalleled accuracy and originality.

name: Fleshy Growth, Yoichiro Kawaguchi
desc: A monumentally important figure, Kawaguchi is a pioneer of computer 3D graphics and of procedural artificial-life work. Heralded in Frank Popper ’s Art of the Electronic Age, this example of the legendary growth algorithm by Kawaguchi stands out in the algorithm’s evolution. According to Popper, “The light, aided by the sophisticated technology of ray tracing recalls the art of Japanese lacquer or porcelain.” [Popper 88] The same year, Kawaguchi spoke to SIGGRRAPH, saying: “My pieces are being carried out on a paradigm that ‘growth model is created by the recursive structure of the self-organization, thus being the fruit of complexed form of evolutional cells.’” Kawaguchi’s growth models, first presented at SIGGRAPH in 1982, are a procedural precursor to later artificial-life and AI art rather than machine learning themselves.

name: The Evolution of Form by William Latham
desc: Mentioned in Frank Popper ’s Art of the Electronic Age, Latham’s work showcased his Mutator algorithm, combining chance mutations with creative choices to produce ever-evolving 3D forms of enormous complexity. The work is actually a collaboration with Latham’s long-time collaborator Stephen Todd . Latham and Todd began working on the revolutionary generative art system, Mutator Evolutionary Art, together with a team at IBM beginning in 1987. Besides Latham and Todd, the team included Lance Putnam and Peter Todd . Their work displayed “strange organic, often serpentine, forms, produced using [an] “alternative evolutionary software system” (developed with Stephen Todd and team), which William uses to pick and breed 3D forms freed from the limits of the human imagination.” Latham and Todd collaborated on Mutator and FormGrow between 1987 and 1993 so this piece marks a middle-point in their time creating together. This evolutionary work of Latham and Todd can be considered proto-machine learning art, as the evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning. There is even an image of Latham working on this very piece.

name: Emerging Forms 3 by Hillary Kapan
desc: Mentioned in Frank Popper ’s Art of the Electronic Age and shown at the Artifices exhibition, and dated 1989 by the SIGGRAPH archive, this interactive animated work was produced from “a program generating changing forms from a scattered field of pixels,” according to Popper [89].

name: Rise of ArtFutura
desc: As we begin the 1990s, a major trend, besides the rise of the Internet and the transition from “computer” to “digital” art, was a fascination with virtual reality. Focusing on virtual reality, the first ArtFutura, a now annual festival of digital culture, was held at Mercat de les Flors in Barcelona, marking a significant milestone in the realm of art and technology. The event showcased a one-hour projection and a 30-minute performance titled Mugra, a collaboration between Rebecca Allen and La Fura dels Baus. It was a very early attempt at virtual reality and art. A memorable moment was Eric Gullichsen ’s presentation of a virtual reality helmet during the press conference, allowing journalists to experience real-time 3D environments. The event even included an early 3D animation from the little-known Pixar animation studio.

name: Computers and the Creative Process at the University of Oregon Museum of Art
desc: This exhibition actually traveled around North America to ten locations, from Oregon to Michigan and Texas to Canada . It would travel for two years until January 5, 1992. 31 artists were involved, including Professor Donna Cox . Ken O’Connell curated a previous iteration of this exhibition that traveled between 1985 and 1986.
subjects: university of oregon museum of art

name: Publications
desc: Like the light going off after the chronicling of the Greek historian Herodotus around the 5th c. BCE, when the ancient world lost much of its color. So we have the final entry from Copper Giloth and Lynn Pocock-Williams ’s epic chronicling of their own of publication, exhibition and technology history of generative art since 1945 from which this Timeline has extensively utilized. 1990 marks the final years covered by Giloth and Pocock-Williams. Here are the final publications of note mentioned: Terry Gips , “Critical Questions for Computer Artists of the 1990's.” Renee LeWinter and Cynthia Baron , “Artistic Challenge.” Fred Ritchin , In Our Own Image: The Coming Revolution in Photography. Dorothy Spencer , “Computer Art-An Oxymoron? Views from the Mainstream.”
subjects: a selected chronology of computer art: exhibitions, publications, and technology
computer art—an oxymoron? views from the mainstream
critical questions for computer artists of the 1990s
in our own image: the coming revolution in photography

name: Jürgen Schmidhuber Proposes “Artificial Curiosity”
desc: This pioneering idea in machine learning during the supposed “AI winter” was a proposal of a generative adversarial network (GAN), which would not be formally realized until 2014. This was an example of an important development in the creative application of neural networks, demonstrating how far-reaching the ideas of the past decade-plus extend. The framework involved two competing neural networks: a generator (controller) that creates outputs and a predictor (world model) that anticipates the consequences of these outputs. The networks engage in a minimax game, where the generator aims to maximize the predictor’s error, while the predictor minimizes it. This early concept laid the groundwork for future developments in generative models, including the now widely used Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).

name: Music and Connectionism, edited by Peter M. Todd and D. Gareth Loy
desc: This book stands as a survey of the field of the creative application of neural networks to create music. The work expounds the early work of David Cope from 1981 and Todd’s own earlier ideas. This includes Todd’s influential work, “A Connectionist Approach to Algorithmic Composition,” (1989) in which he describes some of the earliest creative application of the ability to “generalize” from data rather than follow programmed rules. Todd explains how a: “fundamental shift allows the development of new algorithmic composition methods that rely on learning the structure of existing musical examples and generalizing from these learned structures to compose new pieces. These methods contrast greatly with the majority of older schemes that simply follow a previously assembled set of compositional rules.” The book’s research introduced parallel distributed processing (PDP) to the field of music composition, which allowed for the generation of new musical pieces based on learned structures from existing examples. As Todd explained, this approach marked a significant shift from rule-based methods to a more dynamic, self-learning system.
subjects: a connectionist approach to algorithmic composition

name: World Wide Web goes public
desc: January 1991 the first Web servers outside CERN itself were switched on. On August 6, 1991, Berners-Lee posted a short summary of the World Wide Web project on the alt.hypertext newsgroup. This date also marked the debut of the Web as a publicly available service on the Internet. While CERN would not place the Web software in the public domain until 30 April 1993, this event twenty months earlier ushered in a new era of information accessibility. Tim Berners-Lee ’s idea unleashed a rush of digital inventiveness, as within just a few years of even this launch, artists would be making the first net art. This would of course impact programmatic art, as much of the later part of the decade was spent creating the early tooling (e.g., ACU , DBN ) for visual creatives and not computer scientists. As previously mentioned, the Web propelled the rise of mass-media art, but it also represented the democratization of online spaces, which would fuel generative art by allowing creators all over the globe to share their thoughts, cooperate across borders and alter the bounds of artistic expression in the digital age.

name: Java Language Project Initiated at Sun Microsystems
desc: In the early ’90s, Sun Microsystems began the development of the Java programming language, a watershed moment in the history of creative coding as it would be the basis for the upcoming Processing in ten years. This versatile and platform-independent language intended for network computing would transform much more than digital generative art, however. The project, led by James Gosling and Mike Sheridan , aimed to develop a language that could run on a variety of devices, ranging from small embedded systems to large-scale business servers. Java would subsequently revolutionize web development with its “Write Once, Run Anywhere” attitude, cementing its place as a cornerstone of modern software development.

name: Symposium: Art & Algorithm - Mind & Machine, 1991 (organized by Verostko)
desc: Roman Verostko , noted for his pioneering work such as The Magic Hand of Chance (1982), organized the Art & Algorithm Symposium at the Minneapolis College of Art and Design in 1991 (February 23-24). This was key proto-Algorist event, named “Mind & Machine,” celebrating the intersection of art and computational techniques. With a name juxtaposing words like “mind” and “machine” in early 1991, along with the work of evolutionary art pioneers like Sims and Latham at the time, this can be seen as proto-artificial intelligence art event. The conference included an audio-visual exhibition titled “Images of the Unseen From the Worlds of Art & Science,” which showcased works by 23 artists and scientists from six nations. Among them are pioneers such as Vera Molnár (Algorithmic drawing, 1990), Donna Cox , Char Davies , Samia Halaby , Hans Dehlinger , Mark Wilson , Jean Pierre Hebert, Yoichiro Kawaguchi and William Latham .
subjects: images of the unseen from the worlds of art & science
minneapolis college of art and design

name: Keith Tyson begins working on ArtMachine
desc: Keith Tyson revolutionized the art world with ArtMachine in 1991, which he would work on for the next ten years. Born from the mind of the artist, then in his early twenties, this semi-computerized algorithm scanned the world’s information sources, generating unique “iterations”—artistic directives that Tyson translated into tangible creations. In other words, the system generated proposed artworks for Tyson to make. The ridiculousness of its plans was matched by their literal implementation, ranging from an artwork made of 366 painted breadboards to a “scubasculpture” kept on the bottom of the ocean for sixteen years. Tyson left the creative choices up to ArtMachine in one of the most important examples of material generative art since Cohen’s AARON , particularly from a mainstream, Turner Prize-winning contemporary artist.

name: Les Artistes et la lumiere, exhibition held in Rheims
desc: Included by Frank Popper in Art of the Electronic Age as an important exhibition in the development of electronic art [Popper 14], this exposition focused on works inspired by neon lighting. Held at the Centre National Art and Technologie (CNAT), Les Artistes et la Lumiere (Artists and Light) in Reims, France , this worldwide exposition featured the bright creations of 18 artists from around the world. From neon to lasers, holograms to LEDs, the exhibition celebrated the relationship between light and artistic expression. Aiming to spark interest in light-based art, a key predecessor of digital art, artists included Liliane Lijn , Bill Bell and Pierre-Alain Hubert .

name: Trojan Room Coffee Pot Camera Set Up at Cambridge
desc: The humble coffee pot sparked a technological revolution when computer scientists at the University of Cambridge invented the world’s first webcam. Quentin Stafford-Fraser and Paul Jardetzky built the internal XCoffee camera system in 1991 to monitor the elusive coffee levels in the Trojan Room, their lab’s main computer room. Daniel Gordon and Martyn Johnson later rebuilt it with a new frame grabber and put the images on the World Wide Web on 22 November 1993, making it the first webcam. From the commonplace coffee pot, an era of video chats and live webcasts emerged, forever altering human-machine communication and interaction.

name: Sociotecture, Joan Truckenbrod
desc: One of four similar works in a series, this piece was included by Frank Popper in Art of the Electronic Age. Joan Truckenbrod ’s Sociotecture series, initiated in 1991, explored the unseen dimensions of the human experience. Informed by the mythology of Native American beliefs in animating spirits, Truckenbrod’s algorithmic images embody these invisible forces. The series gradually evolves, mixing mathematical symbols within a natural ecology of leaves and flower petals.
