The project was inspired by emotional echoes of Gertrude Stein , John Cage ’s avant-garde methods and Pierre Boulez and George Benjamin ’s compositions. Truckenbrod herself wrote of the work: “To create my early algorithmic images I created my own personal geometry that embodied these animating spirits. Coding was a vehicle for giving form to algebraic formulas that scientifically describes invisible forces such as how light waves reflect off of irregular surfaces.” Listen to this author’s ( Peter Bauman ) Le Random’s talk with Truckenbrod here. ( transcript )

name: Cercle Syncopé, Gillian Wise
desc: A member of Jeffrey Steele ’s Systems Group (1969) and a former member of the British Constructivists, Wise was a prominent example of a systems artist, like Vera Molnar, moving from systematic thinking to programmed art with computers. This work was made by creating color computerized images with symmetrical forms and is featured in Frank Popper ’s Art of the Electronic Age. Wise continued working with material forms throughout her career as well.

name: The Virtual Museum by Jeffrey Shaw
desc: The Virtual Museum by Jeffrey Shaw emerged in Frankfurt , Germany , as a pioneering exploration of virtual reality. With hardware by Huib Nelissen and software by Gideon May , this three-dimensional computer-generated museum marked a conceptual shift in exhibiting immaterial artistic creations. Viewers engaged in interactive journeys, controlling their movement through a circular, rotating platform with a large video projection monitor. The Virtual Museum featured five rooms, deemphasizing differences between real and virtual spaces that are now commonplace but were much more radical in 1991. In this sense, like many of these early-90s VR displays, it can be seen as a proto-Metaverse. Exhibited globally, it left a undeniable mark on the evolving landscape of virtual art, contributing to exhibitions in Frankfurt, Paris , Nagoya, Linz , Munich, Madrid, Los Angeles , Hannover, San José, Madrid, Valladolid, Reykjavik, Hengelo, Shanghai , Zagreb , Karlsruhe, and beyond.

name: Fleischmann, Monika/Strauss, Wolfgang: Home of the Brain, virtual reality installation, 1989-1990
desc: Made between 1989 and 1990, the work by Monika Fleischmann and Wolfgang Strauss is described by the artists as the first artistic virtual reality installation. Participants, equipped with VPL Datagloves, could enter and explore the spaces of images by moving their feet, hands and head in Proto-Metaverse, immerse VR environment popular at the time. The following year, the project would go on to receive the Golden Nica at the Prix Ars Electronica in 1992.

name: Cruz-Neira, Sandin and DeFanti Begin Developing “CAVE”
desc: Carolina Cruz-Neira , Daniel J. Sandin and Thomas A. DeFanti, with Robert V. Kenyon and John C. Hart , pioneered the development of the “CAVE” (Cave Automatic Virtual Environment) in the Electronic Visualization Laboratory at the University of Illinois in Chicago beginning in 1991. They would continue development until 1993. This surround-screen, surround-sound, projection-based virtual reality (VR) system transformed immersive experiences. The CAVE featured 3D computer graphics projected into a 10'x10'x9' cube, with display screens surrounding the viewer. Users were able to explore the virtual world without wearing helmets thanks to lightweight stereo glasses and a wand-like device. Designed for scientific visualization, the CAVE enabled collaborative exploration and discussions among users, making it a transformative tool for scientific discovery.

name: Primordial Dance by Karl Sims
desc: Karl Sims unveiled this important work in the development of artificial life-based art, Primordial Dance, an experimental one-minute and 35-second code-based animation exploring abstract textures and colors. Sims worked with the computer to generate images and movements that exceeded their individual capabilities through an interactive process known as “artificial evolution.” Sims explains how his “artificial evolution” is essentially a slightly more manual GAN process. There is a clear connection between the AI of today and Sims’s work, as he explains his process himself: “The computer generates and displays a collection of experimental abstract images. The artist chooses the most aesthetically interesting images, and those survive and are “bred” to produce a new collection of images. The equations, or artificial genes, of the survivors are copied, mutated, and mated by the computer to generate new offspring pictures.” Thus, this evolutionary work of Sims can be considered proto-GAN art. Artists in the upcoming decades would continue to automate the process until now these tasks are done “under the hood” and instantly. But this is a hugely important step in the development of AI-art-as-we-know-it-today.

name: Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta Describe a Cryptographically Secured Chain of Blocks
desc: A key moment in the development of blockchain technology and, thus, NFTs, Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta described a cryptographically secure chain of blocks, presented at CRYPTO ’90 and published in 1991. This moment, along with David Chaum ’s 1982 dissertation, essentially introduced the concept of blockchain technology. The research would lay the groundwork for what would eventually become blockchain technology. Haber and Stornetta developed a novel method for timestamping digital documents using a cryptographic hash function. This novel approach resulted in an immutable chain of blocks that maintained the integrity and chronological order of digital records. These ideas have obviously become foundational to any blockchain-based activity, including NFTs.

name: JPEG Standard Created
desc: Similar to the MPEG standard released the same year, the JPEG 1 standard (ISO/IEC 10918) was developed in 1992 as part of an effort to reduce the standard image file size, a process that began in 1986. Though this standard is sometimes referred to as a single specification, it is really made up of four independent components and a combination of coding modes. It’s still in use to this day after a 1994 update.

name: Merkle Trees Added to Blockchain
desc: Stuart Haber , W. Scott Stornetta and Dave Bayer introduced Merkle trees, for which Ralph Merkle filed a patent in 1979, granted in 1982, to blockchain technology. This development increased their efficiency and allowed more than one document to be stored in each block.

name: MPEG 1 standard introduced
desc: The Moving Picture Experts Group (MPEG) approved the MPEG-1 standard in November 1992, published as ISO/IEC 11172 in 1993, marking a pivotal moment in the history of digital audio and video compression that various groups had been working on for several years. This comprehensive standard, organized into five parts, addressed the growing need for efficient encoding and decoding of multimedia content. MPEG aimed to create a reference standard to overcome technological barriers and ensure the success of digital audio and video.

name: Leicester Polytechnic officially Becomes De Montfort University
desc: As Leicester Polytechnic evolved into De Montfort University, its legacy as the epicenter for British (if not the world) computer art in the ’70s and ’80s remains. With luminaries such as Ernest Edmonds , Stephen Scrivener and Dominic Boreham at HCIRU leaving an indelible mark.

name: Breeding Forms on the Infinite Plane by William Latham
desc: Breeding Forms on the Infinite Plane, an exemplary work of Latham’s evolutionary art, creates biomorphic prints that resemble insect and crustacean forms. Latham collaborated with Stephen Todd to create intricate 3D shapes and textures using an artificial embryology system called Form Grow and an evolution-based search algorithm known as Mutator . This pioneering work, arguably the first computer-mediated evolutionary art, according to Philip Galanter , helped rejuvenate code-based art, sparking a new era of artistic experimentation. Mutator and FormGrow were developed by the pair at IBM on their state of the art mainframes beginning in 1987. The collaboration would only last for one more year in 1993. The work is actually a collaboration with Latham’s long-time collaborator Stephen Todd. Latham and Todd began working on the revolutionary generative art system, Mutator Evolutionary Art, together with a team at IBM beginning in 1987. Besides Latham and Todd, the team included Lance Putnam and Peter Todd . Their work displayed “strange organic, often serpentine, forms, produced using [an] “alternative evolutionary software system” (developed with Stephen Todd and team), which William uses to pick and breed 3D forms freed from the limits of the human imagination.” Latham and Todd collaborated on Mutator and FormGrow between 1987 and 1993 so this piece marks a middle-point in their time creating together. This evolutionary work of Latham and Todd can be considered proto-machine learning art, as the evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning.
subjects: breeding forms on the infinite plane

name: Mutations by William Latham
desc: William Latham ’s Mutations (1991-92) depicts a surreal journey of real-time evolutionary art, showcasing intricate breeding and growth processes through animated forms engaged in complex interactions. This significant work represents a watershed moment in the development of artificial life in the realm of art, providing viewers with a glimpse into a dynamic and evolving world now achievable due to the digital. Latham’s work showcased his Mutator algorithm, combining chance mutations with creative choices to produce ever-evolving 3D forms of enormous complexity. The work is actually a collaboration with Latham’s long-time collaborator Stephen Todd . Latham and Todd began working on the revolutionary generative art system, Mutator Evolutionary Art, together with a team at IBM beginning in 1987. Besides Latham and Todd, the team included Lance Putnam and Peter Todd . Their work displayed “strange organic, often serpentine, forms, produced using [an] “alternative evolutionary software system” (developed with Stephen Todd and team), which William uses to pick and breed 3D forms freed from the limits of the human imagination.” Latham and Todd collaborated on Mutator and FormGrow between 1987 and 1993 so this piece marks a middle-point in their time creating together. This evolutionary work of Latham and Todd can be considered proto-machine learning art, as the evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning.

name: Scott Draves developed the Fractal Flame algorithm
desc: Described by Arthur I. Miller in Colliding Worlds as an early piece of open-source graphics software, Fractal Flames made Scott Draves one of software art’s most prominent names. The algorithm, a notable addition to the Iterated Function System (IFS) class of fractal algorithms, was, according to Draves, “art out of math.” The work would go on to gain recognition the following year, receiving it honorary mention for the Prix Ars Electronica . The algorithm typified the belief that enabling other community members and artists was important. This became increasingly relevant during the early ’90s when the web was still in its infancy. The algorithm went viral in mid ’90s as it was used by others artists without needing to credit Draves at all. It was used in an IBM Super Bowl commercial as well as the cover of popular books and albums, including the work of Stephen King and Paul Simon .

name: Angels by Nicole Stenger
desc: Between 1989 and 1992, Stenger worked on Angels, the first immersive movie and an important early VR work. She developed the project at MIT and the University of Washington with an Advanced Visualizer. Users could interact in the space with a VPL Dataglove. This work further demonstrates the popularity of VR as we began the early ’90s. Further, this and similar works can be seen as an emerging “Proto-Metaverse” with direct genealogy to today’s concepts.

name: First Assembly Party in Finland
desc: The winning PC demo of the inaugural Assembly Party, Unreal, marked a significant milestone in the demoscene community. Created by Future Crew, the piece highlighted the creators' innovative talents, as Unreal not only won the Assembly Party, but also laid the groundwork for Future Crew’s evolution into Futuremark, a well-known developer of PC benchmark tests such as 3D Mark and PCMark. Furthermore, key members of the Finnish game developer Remedy emerged from the Future Crew team, demonstrating the demoscene’s interconnectedness to the gaming industry, particularly in the Nordic region. Results from these early demoscene competitions can still be found online and some of the works can still be played on emulators.

name: Legend I, Yoshiyuki Abe
desc: Legend I is the first piece in Yoshiyuki Abe ’s renowned series, which ran until 2001 and was featured at ISEA94. Abe’s digital creations use a variation of the ray tracing algorithm to display intricate features of hyperbolic paraboloid surfaces in Cartesian coordinates. This innovative approach to “un-normalized” shading results in complex visual compositions. Abe’s extensive knowledge of digital art and technology has cemented his reputation as a leading figure in Japan ’s algorithmic and electronic art scenes. Abe’s generative process investigates the use of quadratic parameters to define lighting, surface attributes and colors that appear metallic and gel-like in Legend, evoking the contemporary work of Cyril Diagne.

name: On Justifying the Hypothetical Nature of Art and the Non-Identicality within the Object World by Peter Weibel
desc: On Justifying the Hypothetical Nature of Art and the Non-Identicality within the Object World at Gallery Tanja Grunert, Cologne, presented an interactive computer installation that immersed visitors into a dark triangular space illuminated only by a large screen, serving as a portal to virtual worlds. By stepping on colored spots on the floor, visitors navigated between real and virtual environments, influencing the appearance and behavior of the digital landscapes. This interactive digital installation challenged perceptions of reality and anticipated the immersive digital work of artists today like Refik Anadol .
subjects: on justifying the hypothetical nature of art and the non-identicality within the object world

name: Placeholder by Brenda Laurel and Rachel Strickland
desc: Another work of Virtual Reality in the early ’90s, Placeholder, a VR initiative by Interval Research Corporation and The Banff Centre for The Performing Arts, was created by Brenda Laurel and Rachel Strickland . The work pioneered multi-person narrative action in virtual environments. Additionally, the publication “Placeholder: Landscape and Narrative In Virtual Environments,” authored by Brenda Laurel, Rachel Strickland and Rob Tow , offers insights into the project’s objectives and achievements. For a visual journey through the project, see Rachel Strickland’s documentary video on Placeholder.
subjects: placeholder: landscape and narrative in virtual environments

name: Fuse by Scott Draves
desc: This moment stands as one of the earliest predecessors of the big-data, machine-learning AI art of today, as opposed to the symbolic AI art of Harold Cohen . “One of the earliest machine learning image2image algorithm[s],” according to Draves himself, Fuse stands as a critical step in the development of AI art. Scott Draves developed the Fuse algorithm, drawing inspiration from the Dissociated Press and Cut-Up technique. The process worked by slicing and rearranging images into new compositions, predating Efros and Leung’s texture synthesis (1999) and Robert Silvers ’s Photomosaics (1995). Released as open source in 1993, Fuse became influential in digital art. Draves' self-portrait, composed of fragmented images, exemplified its creative potential and is one of the earliest examples machine-learning art as we know it. Draves’s work was inspired by the artificial life work of Karl Sims and also can be traced back to the work of William Latham .

name: “Computer Art” No More
desc: According to Art Historian Frank Popper , by 1993, the term “computer art” had evolved from a distinct category to simply one of many electronic art forms. Grant Taylor ’s observations in When the Machine Made Art highlight this shift, citing the emergence of the New York Digital Salon in 1993 as a watershed moment in the transition from “computer” to “digital” art. As discussed, in the previous chapter, the term began falling out of favor in late 1980s. The term was in retreat by 1993, though it remained in institutional use: the New York Digital Salon’s own 1993 founding statement described the venture as a venue for the exhibition of computer art.

name: A-Volve by Christa Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau
desc: A-Volve (1993–94) was an interactive-evolutionary art environment that stands as an important step in the development of AI art. For the piece, visitors could draw virtual organisms using a sensor pencil, which then came to life in a water-filled glass pool. These three-dimensional creatures reacted to human behavior, evolving and interacting with each other and the visitors. This participatory-evolutionary-immersive art display anticipates the work of Karl Sims ’s Galapagos in 1997. The algorithmic evolution achieved by Sommerer and Mignonneau also anticipate machine learning and GAN art. The process for the piece worked as follows : “If two strong creatures meet, they can create an offspring and a new creature can be born. It carries the genetic code of its parents. Mutation and cross-over provides a nature-like reproduction mechanism, that follows the genetic rules of Mendel.“ This evolutionary process is a much more simplified version of the complex learning machines are capable of today. But this early work is a direct predecessor. Artists in the upcoming decades would continue to automate the process until now these tasks are done “under the hood” and instantly. But this is a hugely important step in the development of AI-art-as-we-know-it-today. Beyond its significance to the development of AI art, the installation blurred the lines between real and unreal, exploring popular themes of generative art at the time: concepts of artificial life and evolution, while adding Sommerer and Mignonneau’s distinct individuality. A-Volve continued the artists' exploration of natural interfaces and complex interactivity, challenging perceptions of reality and creating a dynamic ecosystem where visitors become integral participants in the evolution of artificial life. This would continue into the next decade as well with Life Writer (2006).

name: Second Reality Demo Released by Future Crew at Assembly 93
desc: At Assembly 93 in July 1993, Future Crew debuted Second Reality, a significant demo showcasing cutting-edge 2D and 3D computer graphics rendering. It captivated audiences for 16 minutes and 19 seconds with its synchronized visuals and Skaven and Purple Motion ’s techno soundtrack. The demo, which was released to the public in October 1993, became legendary, being hailed as one of the best creations of the early 1990s PC demo scene. Its innovative techniques, such as real-time mesh deformation and ray tracing, cemented its place as a generative art landmark, inspiring countless remixes and leaving an indelible imprint on digital creativity incorporating generativity.

name: Just This Once by Scott French
desc: Just This Once is a computer-generative romance novel authored by a Macintosh IIcx computer named “Hal” in collaboration with programmer Scott French . The radical reinterpretation of the novel and authorship challenged literary norms. French, investing $40,000 and 8 years, developed an AI program to mimic Valley of the Dolls novelist Jacqueline Susann ’s writing style. Hal’s output, after significant editing, produced the novel’s plot and style. Eventually, legal disputes with Susann’s estate over copyright were settled, leading to its publication by Carol Publishing Group. Despite mixed reviews, it sparked discussions in legal circles on copyright law’s applicability to computer-generated creative works that anticipate and mirror those questions raised today by AI. Just This Once remains a testament to the intersection of technology and literature, blurring the lines of authorship.

name: Virtual Reality: An Emerging Medium, held at the Guggenheim Museum
desc: The early ’90s fascination with virtual reality continued with an exhibition at none other than the Guggenheim. The Guggenheim Museum’s Virtual Reality: An Emerging Medium was an Intel Digital Education & Arts Program event. Curators were initially uncertain of the shows reception but the exhibition became a sensation, selling out daily and capturing global media attention. Reflecting on art history, it emphasized VR’s profound impact, similar to Renaissance linear perspective. Notable works include Jenny Holzer ’s interactive World I and World II, which challenges communication assumptions, and Thomas Dolby ’s Virtual String Quartet, which provides dynamic soundscapes. This event highlighted the intense fascination with VR technology in the early ’90s despite being several decades early in terms of a commercially viable product.

name: Genetic Images by Karl Sims
desc: Genetic Images, a groundbreaking media installation conceived by Karl Sims in 1993, explored the concept of interactive evolution within virtual environments. As with his work Panspermia (1990), Genetic Images can also be thought of as proto-AI art. It inspired the work later in this decade of Scott Draves , a machine-learning art pioneer. Displayed on an arc of screens, this installation allowed visitors to actively participate in the evolution of abstract images. By standing on sensors and selecting aesthetically pleasing images, viewers determined which visuals would survive and reproduce, guiding the course of artificial evolution. It was thus an important example of public interactive art as well in the spirit of GRAV. Exhibited at renowned venues like the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris and Ars Electronica in Linz , Austria , Genetic Images sparked discussions about the intersection of art and technology while challenging traditional notions of creativity and design in some of the mainstream art world’s most prestigious institutions. That is beside the impact it had on the “evolution” of AI art.

name: do it Concept and Catalogue Released
desc: All about instruction-based generative art, do it began in 1993 as a conversation and a book of instructions from twelve artists, from which the exhibitions grew. Initiated by Hans Ulrich Obrist in conversation with artists Christian Boltanski and Bertrand Lavier , do it explores the interpretive role of the viewer in generative art, transcending traditional notions of static displays. Each venue hosted unique interpretations, blurring lines between art and daily life. Do it championed audience involvement, fostering dynamic, ever-changing experiences. Unlike conventional exhibitions, it prioritized human interaction over physical artifacts, inviting diverse renditions that engaged with site specificity.

name: AI Infinity by John Maeda
desc: “I recall being surprised by how the computer could do so much at the beckon of a few lines of code.” -John Maeda This profound work marks Maeda’s return to computer programming using the PostScript language after a long hiatus. Inspired by his typography teacher’s questions about Maeda’s ultimate motivation in life, Maeda crafted this piece. He made it for the NeXT computer, with the piece itself featuring an infinite loop, symbolizing the endless potential of digital creation. This concept would appear in future books, such as How To Speak Machine (2019). Maeda halted the drawing at the 10,000th loop stroke. This work not only represents a pivotal moment in Maeda’s career but also reflects his journey from aspiring classical typographer to digital pioneer. AI Infinity holds deep personal significance, illustrating the convergence of his artistic and technological passions.

name: Information Landscapes by Muriel Cooper
desc: Muriel Cooper ’s Information Landscapes Project, made with David Small and six others, featured in MoMA ’s collection and unveiled at a 1994 TED talk, represented a pinnacle in her illustrious career . Information Landscapes defied traditional graphic design paradigms, exemplifying over four decades of research and experimentation. Cooper, a pioneering figure at MIT, reshaped design education with her visionary approach, founding the Visible Language Workshop in the Bauhaus tradition and designing the iconic MIT Press Logo. Her projects, such as Typography in Space and Personalized Galaxies of Information, celebrated multidimensionality and encouraged viewers to engage actively and explore nonlinearly. Cooper legacy continued beyond her time, which unfortunately passed shortly after this talk, as John Maeda was the direct descendant of Cooper’s traditions at the VLW. He would found the Aesthetics and Computation Group at the MIT Media Lab , where students Ben Fry and Casey Reas developed Processing .

name: Evolved Virtual Creatures by Karl Sims
desc: This is an early example of art built on artificial neural networks, although the networks were evolved by genetic algorithms rather than trained on data. The work stands as one of the most significant links from the rule-based AI of Cohen to “Modern AI art,” relying on the evaluation of trained data. The work showcased the evolution of virtual block creatures through simulated Darwinian processes. These creatures were tested on their abilities to perform tasks such as swimming, jumping, and competing. The most successful ones had their virtual genes copied, combined,and mutated to create a new generation. This iterative process led to the emergence of increasingly adept creatures. The project was a continuation and further demonstration of the potential of evolutionary algorithms in artificial life, demonstrating how virtual entities could evolve complex behaviors over successive generations. Sims' work remains influential in the fields of computer graphics and artificial life along with pioneers Yoichioro Kawaguchi, William Latham and Christa Sommerer .

name: First do it Exhibition Takes Place
desc: This open exhibition premiered in 1994 at the Ritter Kunsthalle in Klagenfurt after its conceptual roots were laid the previous year. Begun by Hans Ulrich Obrist with Christian Boltanski and Bertrand Lavier , the first do it featured instruction-based work by artists such as Mike Kelley , Alison Knowles , Rirkrit Tiravanija , Jean-Jacques Rullier and Bertrand Lavier. The exhibitions were meant to encourage audience participation and interaction.

name: The world’s first smartphone
desc: The IBM Simon Personal Communicator, a handheld mobile device with a touchscreen is often hailed as the first true smartphone, making its debut in the United States . Distributed by BellSouth Cellular Corp., it sold 50,000 units between August 1994 and February 1995. Combining PDA features with mobile capabilities, the Simon offered functionalities such as faxing, emailing and cellular paging. Despite its innovative design, it faced challenges due to a short battery life and the rise of sleeker flip phones. The Simon’s legacy lies in pioneering the integration of communication and computing, setting the stage for the future of mobile technology. One of Casey Reas ’s pre conditions for NFTs is supercomputers in our pockets with high res screens. Like many things that impact our lives so much today, it began in the mid-90s.

name: Nettime Forms and net.art Begins
desc: In the spring of 1995, Nettime , a mailing list and platform that was instrumental in the formation of net.art, formed. The list gathered the earliest net.art practitioners and was where the term took hold. It consisted of JODI ’s Joan Heemskerk and Dirk Paesmans , Geert Lovink , Heath Bunting , Vuk Ćosić and Alexei Shoulgin. Organized by Geert Lovink and Pit Schultz , Nettime as a group met in June at the Venice Biennale , laying the foundation for what was to come. By fall, nettime-l had taken root, fostering the exchange of ideas and discourse and some of the earliest net.art. Ćosić explained to the author ( Peter Bauman ) how in his view JODI were the first net.art practitioners: “On the nettime list itself we didn’t post net.art pieces that could be displayed or collected but we spoke about it and gave it life. I personally adored the JODI posts that were consistently pushing the idea of net.art as a liberating force. They were the first in many regards.”

name: Roman Verostko and Jean-Pierre Hébert
desc: Roman Verostko and Jean-Pierre Hébert founded “The Algorists ,” along with Charles Csuri , Manfred Mohr , Mark Wilson and Ken Musgrave, to form a group based on the mutual adoration of the art that could be produced by algorithms. These were not artists new to the field but were a collection of artists who had dedicated decades, entire careers or lifetimes to the craft. Their work utilized algorithms for both form and social commentary but it was Hébert’s manifesto where he defined the term “algorist,” referring to artists who used algorithmic processes. Beyond plotted work, their influence extends to textiles, games, biological interfaces and experiments with evolutionary forms. It’s no surprise that artists formed around this time as the mid-1990s were marked by the widespread use of computers. In these conditions algorithmic art was flourishing, influencing a wide range of creative disciplines. Hebert and Verostko stand as two of the more under-appreciated pioneers of digital expression yet their legacy continues to this day through this special group.

name: The Slade Centre for Electronic Media in Fine Art (SCEMFA) Opens
desc: The Slade Centre for Electronic Media in Fine Art (SCEMFA) was opened. The history of the department extends back to 1973 when Malcolm Hughes founded the Experimental Department at the Slade. Thus, the legacy of Hughes’s groundbreaking department continues to this very day. The Centre’s goal was to unite artists and researchers at the Slade School of Fine Art. It became a hub for exploring digital materials, fostering research into Electronic Media and Fine Art. Over the years, SCEMFA has played a vital role in shaping national and international dialogues on digital art, hosting events like Collision and Spontaneous Reaction.
subjects: slade centre for electronic media in fine art (scemfa)

name: jodi.org by JODI
desc: In the early days of the public web, JODI emerged as pioneers of net art with their enigmatic website, begun around 1993, archived at wwwwwwwww.jodi.org . Their webpages, visually jarring and avant garde, challenged traditional site design norms. Navigation relied on cursor movements, with links hidden within repeated images. Some images led to new visual landscapes, blurring the lines between art and exploration. wwwwwwwww.jodi.org/ epitomized the experimental spirit of net art, offering a glimpse into the limitless possibilities of digital expression on the web. JODI’s work underscored the transformative power of the Internet as an art distribution mechanism, fitting into the long history of mass media art. Fellow net.art pioneer Vuk Ćosić explained to the author ( Peter Bauman ) how in his view JODI were the first net.art practitioners: “On the nettime list itself we didn’t post net.art pieces that could be displayed or collected but we spoke about it and gave it life. I personally adored the JODI posts that were consistently pushing the idea of net.art as a liberating force. They were the first in many regards.” wwwwwwwww.jodi.org/ is not only socially critical but also self-reflexive work, commenting on the early Web while using the Internet itself as a canvas. The Internet gave artists the ability to self-publish their work to a global audience for the first time in human history. JODI’s early net art is a powerful demonstration of how the Internet would soon impact every art practice.

name: unendlich, fast… by Holger Friese
desc: Another example of early net art, Holger Friese ’s Unendlich, fast... was a bold departure from the early internet landscape, which emphasized clarity and navigability. In contrast to the expected plethora of pages and links, Friese presented a single, enigmatic webpage. Visitors were greeted by a sea of vibrant blue, with only scroll bars for navigation. This minimalist space challenged conventions, encouraging interactivity, questions and exploration. It was an invitation to touch the art, using a webpage to play with point of view and perspective. At the center of the page to the right is a static image resembling stars in a vast cosmos. However, there are no clickable links or pathways to other destinations. Friese’s rejection of conventional navigation systems encourages visitors to embrace the unknown and seek meaning beyond traditional structures. The work encapsulates Friese’s rejection of imposed order, inviting users to navigate the infinite within the confines of a single, captivating space.

name: Electronic Superhighway: Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii by Nam June Paik
desc: Nam June Paik ’s Electronic Superhighway : Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii captured the United States ’ shift into the information age in the mid-90s with the uncertainty and optimism that entailed. Paik’s work combined neon lights and video screens, illustrating the interconnectedness fostered by the rising Internet. Beyond its celebration of global communication, the piece prompts contemplation of technology’s encroaching cultural impact. The work’s scale evokes feelings of information overload, despite the still relativelyt small size of the mid-90s Internet. This work stands as one of Paik’s most well known, standing as a rare example of media art that garnered widespread attention, capturing the zeitgeist of society’s mid-90s relationship with a history-changing technology.

name: David Bowie and Ty Roberts Develop The Verbasizer
desc: The Verbasizer is developed by David Bowie and Ty Roberts as a way to automate and speed up Bowie’s long-standing technique of cutting up fragments of text and rearranging them at random to create song lyrics. -Sasha Stiles

name: Google is born
desc: Larry Page and Sergey Brin met at Stanford in 1995 and formed their partnership the following year, when they built the search engine they called BackRub, running on Stanford’s servers. It laid the groundwork for what would become Google . By creating a powerful search engine algorithm, Page and Brin hoped to efficiently organize the vast amount of data on the internet. Their approach prioritized relevant search results, giving users a more intuitive and efficient way to find information. The birth of Google was a watershed moment in the digital age, where the rise of big data was only in its infancy. Google’s early entry into big data positioned it to become one of the world’s most valuable companies nearly thirty years later.

name: Osmose by Char Davies
desc: Another early work of virtual reality and interactive art that anticipated virtual worlds, Char Davies ’s Osmose transported participants into a perception distorting realm. Participants could navigate various landscapes, from serene forests to subterranean realms, using a head-mounted display and abreath and balance-based motion tracking. Unlike traditional VR, Osmose used semi-representational, translucent visuals along with spatially multi-dimensional soundscapes to achieve a contemplative space. It invited participants to engage the body’s most basic functions—breathing and balance. The work explored how the digital affected our consciousness, anticipating the work of contemporary artists such as Lauren Lee McCarthy .

name: Puppet Motel by Laurie Anderson
desc: This “really significant work” in the rise of digital mass media art according to Casey Reas , Puppet Motel is an enigmatic CD-ROM by Laurie Anderson , designed with Hsin-Chien Huang and released on Voyager. With a blend of multimedia elements, including spoken word, video, music and computer graphics, Anderson crafts an immersive game-like experience that explores themes such as technology’s impact on time memory and human connection. Set within a series of interconnected scenes, the art-game invites participant-players to navigate through haunting environments, from monolithic rooms to surreal landscapes, each filled with snippets of art and conversation. Anderson’s distinctive voice echoes throughout, guiding players through the multimedia labyrinth. Back in 1995, Puppet Motel was posing poignant questions about the digital age, juxtaposing abstract spaces with tangible objects to evoke a sense of disconnection and longing for human connection. It’s Despite its complexity and darkness, the game maintains a playful spirit, inviting players to explore its depths and uncover its layers of meaning. Puppet Motel stands as a testament to Anderson’s approach to interactive art with the most cutting-edge technology of the time, the clunky CD-ROM, challenging players to confront the realities of existence in a continually digitizing world.

name: Legend of the net.art coinage
desc: There is a legend that has persisted— for decades —that net.art was first coined by Vuk Ćosić from a garbled email. I spoke to to Ćosić about the claim, who debunked the legend but not for the first time: “First coinage: there is this legend that I received an e.mail with garbled text. False. That story itself is one of the better pieces of net.art, done by Alexei Shoulgin. It was widely repeated and for me it works as our take at the words such as Impressionism and Cubism that came from outside or Dada that came from inside but is foggy. The expression net.art was invented by Pit Schultz during our debates about online specific art, and we all liked it because .art was just like a file extension. Like .pdf or .doc.”

name: Macromedia Flash 1.0 Released
desc: December 19, 1996 marked the initial release of Macromedia Flash, a technology that paved the way rich graphics on the maturing web and for contemporary generative-web-based practices, pioneered by artists such as Joshua Davis , Yugo Nakamura , Brendan Dawes and James Paterson . Flash, now a ubiquitous name in the annals of the web’s history, traces its roots back to a serendipitous meeting between Jonathan Gay and Charlie Jackson at a local Macintosh Users Group. Their 1993 brainchild, FutureWave Software, initially set its sights on pen computing. With the fading trend, they pivoted towards the burgeoning World Wide Web . The culmination of their efforts was FutureSplash, a pioneering web animation tool released in May 1996. FutureSplash Animator empowered designers to craft animations with increased ease, while the accompanying FutureSplash Viewer allowed for playback on browsers. When FutureSplash caught the attention of Netscape and Microsoft , its trajectory shifted dramatically. Netscape featured it as an extension, while Microsoft integrated it into MSN.com , catapulting FutureSplash into the public’s attention. Recognizing its potential, Macromedia acquired FutureWave in December 1996, rebranding it as Macromedia Flash.

name: My boyfriend came back from the war Olia Lialina
desc: Another important example in the rise of Mass Media art, a Casey Reas precondition for NFTs, and net art, My boyfriend came back from the war by Olia Lialina is one of the most recognizable net art works. Russian artist Olia Lialina crafted My Boyfriend, a browser-based net-art piece consists of a nonlinear narrative using nested frames and grainy GIF images. The work’s interactive hypertext storytelling unfolds as users click hyperlinks, splitting the frame into smaller frames and revealing fragments of a couple’s reunion after a nameless military conflict. Lialina’s innovative use of frames within frames creates a mosaic-like experience, reminiscent of early silent movies. Lialina’s work, self-described as a “netfilm,” merges cinematic narrative techniques with HTML code, merging web and cinema. My Boyfriend stands as a significant example of art distributed solely through the Internet, showcasing Lialina’s mastery of spatial and temporal montage.
subjects: my boyfriend came back from the war

name: Rhizome Begins
desc: Rhizome begins: “Rhizome is the home of born-digital art and culture since 1996.” That 1996 start occurred when Mark Tribe founded Rhizome, initially as an email list that attracted some of the earliest artists exploring online mediums. Since its inception, Rhizome has been instrumental in shaping the trajectory of art intersecting with the internet and networked technologies. From its humble beginnings, Rhizome has evolved into a thriving non-profit organization affiliated with the New Museum . Today, its robust programs encompass a wide range of initiatives aimed at supporting and preserving artistic practices that engage with technology. It remains an important repository for early net art, especially.

name: Sun Microsystems Release Java 1.0
desc: Despite initiating the project in June 1991, on January 23, 1996, JavaSoft, the newly formed operating company of Sun Microsystems, released Java 1.0, marking a significant milestone in the history of software development. Java 1.0 introduced the “write-once-run-everywhere” capability, enabling developers and artists to create platform-independent applications and algorithms. With components like the Java Applet Viewer and class libraries included, Java 1.0 quickly gained traction in the software and internet communities. Its widespread adoption by companies like IBM and Netscape solidified its position as the de facto standard for networked applications, shaping the future of software development as well as creative expression with code. The release of Java is particularly important to digital generative art’s history as the Processing creative coding language used the Java language.

name: John Maeda joins the MIT Media Lab
desc: John Maeda ’s arrival at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1996 marked a pivotal moment in the intersection of technology, design and art. As the founder of the Aesthetics + Computation Group (ACG), an evolution of Visible Language Workshop, Maeda continued the exploration of how computation could enhance graphic design, initiated by Muriel Cooper in 1975. Under Maeda’s leadership, the ACG scrutinized the possibilities of code as a medium for expression, laying the groundwork for the development of innovative tools like Processing . Collaborators Ben Fry and Casey Reas , inspired by Maeda’s vision, began crafting Processing in 2001 as a simplified environment for coding, bridging the gap between programming and design. This endeavor continues to greatly impact the broader culture today, as the Processing Foundation and Lauren Lee McCarthy would go on to develop p5.js .

name: Traffic, CAPC Musée d’Art Contemporain, Bordeaux
desc: With Traffic at Bordeaux’s CAPC Contemporary Museum, Nicolas Bourriaud introduced his concept of 'relational aesthetics,' art that serves as “a vehicle for creating encounters between the artist and the viewers, the latter of which is ideally involved as an active participant.” The exhibition matters for this timeline because it stands as an example of the digital’s concerns manifested in the mainstream art world. These concerns include interactivity, the removing distinctions between art and everyday life and an inclusive definition of what art can entail.

name: The Crossing by Bill Viola
desc: The Crossing by Bill Viola showcases his pioneering use of video technologies since the 1970s. Viola’s early experiments with portable recording devices evolved into immersive installations, featuring multi-channel displays that envelop viewers in meticulously crafted visuals, often set within darkened environments.

name: Form Art by Alexei Shulgin
desc: Alexei Shulgin ’s Form Art is c3.hu of net art that explores the HTML language’s potential as a medium for artistic expression. Shulgin uses playful manipulation and repetition of basic HTML elements to create visually dynamic and ever-changing compositions that were meant to be interpreted as challenges to traditional notions of art in the rising idea of the digital age that was taking hold in the mid-90s. Society was coming to terms on a mass level that we could no longer afford to fear or slow digitization. Art began reflecting this slow coming to terms and that included net art in general. Form Art received an honorary mention at the 1997 Ars Electronica .

name: Documenta Done by the net art pioneer Vuk Ćosić
desc: Documenta Done by the net art pioneer Vuk Ćosić subverts institutional control over net art’s circulation, epitomizing the artist’s role as a digital pirate. Born from the controversial decision to sell the documenta X website as a CD-ROM, Ćosić's work of art was an interpreted at the time as an act of artistic piracy. The work involved copying, republishing and circulating the site, framing it as a major international art theft. Serving both as critique and archival intervention, Documenta Done underscores the challenges institutions face in preserving digital culture’s social memory. Despite its provocative origins, the project has evolved into a vital artifact of the net.art period, continuing to provoke discourse on the intersection of art, technology, and institutional power.

name: Galapagos by Karl Sims
desc: Karl Sims continued to pioneer evolutionary art with his work Galápagos, blending audience interaction with computational evolution. Viewers could influence the survival and reproduction of virtual organisms by selecting preferred forms via step sensor pads. Sims' approach combined genetics, neural networks and physics simulations to create lifelike animations based on Darwinian evolution. Sims’s use of of plant-like abstract imagery and virtual creatures demonstrated how algorithmic art could contribute to the fields of artificial and evolutionary life and their impact on emergent systems. This work was first displayed at the ICC in Tokyo from 1997 to 2000. Sims like Primordial Dance earlier in the decade is using evolutionary principles to recreate what is essentially a slightly more manual GAN process. In Galapagos, Sims increases the complexity of Dance by including audience participation and including an immersive environment. There is a clear connection between the AI of today and Sims’s work, as he explains his process in this piece himself: “Twelve computers simulate the growth and behaviors of a population of abstract animated forms and display them on twelve screens arranged in an arc. The viewers participate in this exhibit by selecting which organisms they find most aesthetically interesting and standing on step sensors in front of those displays. The selected organisms survive, mate, mutate and reproduce.” This evolutionary work of Sims can be considered proto-AI art. Artists in the upcoming decades would continue to automate the process until now these tasks are done “under the hood” and instantly. But this is a hugely important step in the development of AI-art-as-we-know-it-today. To further display how instrumental this work has been in the development of contemporaneous AI-art, in 1999, Scott Draves ’s legendary early AI-art was inspired by the immersive, gallery-bound approach of Sims’s Galapagos.

name: NTT InterCommunication Center Opens in Tokyo
desc: This cultural facility in Tokyo , dedicated to exploring the intersections of art, science, and technology, has been instrumental in creating a platform for generative art in Japan . Since opening, it has held exhibitions and a variety of programs while publishing a journal to expose the public to new media art. Karl Sims exhibited work here from 1997-2000 and Golan Levin and Zach Lieberman exhibited their interactive work here in 2007.

name: My Private Album by Feng Mengbo
desc: Feng Mengbo ’s My Private Album was a pioneering work of interactive CD-ROM art, examining the combination of digital storytelling and interactivity. The work provides viewers with a dynamic look at how families change and evolve over time, questioning the concept of our family as static. Feng’s work deviates from conventional linear narratives, allowing audiences to interact choose their own path also integrating the complex nature of memory. Feng captures the essence of human resilience and hope in his art, which transcends aestheticism through intimate reflections on the ordinary lives of people. Carefully and humbly put together, My Private Album elevates the commonplace to the extraordinary, offering a moving audiovisual record that is available to everyone. It’s a standout of mid-90s interactive CD-ROM art.

name: World Skin by Maurice Benayoun
desc: This immersive art project used the CAVE, developed by Carolina Cruz-Neira , Daniel J. Sandin and Thomas A. DeFanti at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, University of Illinois at Chicago . The CAVE is a room-sized, surround-screen, projection-based virtual reality environment. The year prior in 1996, At the Ars Electronica Center in Austria , EVL set up the first CAVE that was open to the public and showcased several virtual reality artworks. World Skin, by Maurice Benayoun with the composer Jean-Baptiste Barrière , made an immersive space for participants to embark on a haunting “photo safari” through landscapes of warfare. Awarded the Golden Nica Prize for Interactive Art in 1998, the installation confronted viewers with a compilation of visceral images from battle zones, inviting them to intervene by capturing fragments of this grim reality with cameras. Each photographed moment was replaced by a black silhouette, symbolizing the extinguishing of a piece of the world. Through this poignant exploration, World Skin grappled with the significance of media images in shaping our perception of global conflicts, highlighting the paradox of how images simultaneously reveal and neutralize the rawness of human suffering. The work underscores the importance of concept and digital art that spoke to contemporary societal issues beyond simply celebrating technology.

name: Cities on the move: Contemporary Asian Art at the turn of the 21st c., Vienna
desc: Cities on the Move : Contemporary Asian Art at the Turn of the 21st Century” in Vienna , Austria , was the first presentation of a traveling exhibition curated by Hans Ulrich Obrist and Hou Hanru . Emerging against the backdrop of East Asia ’s rapid urbanization, the exhibition went beyond traditional art displays, incorporating visual art, architecture and film to depict the cultural ramifications of the region’s urban development. With over 150 contributors, it took place in a variety of global venues, including MoMA PS1 in New York and the Hayward Gallery in London . But the first iteration took place in Vienna.

name: Processos criativos com os meios eletrônicos: poéticas digitais
desc: This book taught a generation of Brazilian creative coders in the mid-to-late ’90s. The book investigated the technical mechanisms behind electronic image creation. The book also championed the unique qualities and potential of electronic media that it argued was becoming increasingly relevant for expressing creativity in the digital age.
subjects: processos criativos com os meios eletrônicos: poéticas digitais

name: Inaugural International Generative Art Conference at Politecnico di Milano University
desc: For the purposes of this Timeline , this event stands as tremendously more important than perhaps it should on first glance, as it marks the transition to the usage of the term of “generative art” as we understand and use it today. Previously, the movement was much more frequently called computer or algorithmic art. This is conference is an important step in the transition to and popularization of the term “generative art.” Milan hosted said inaugural Generative Art conference, spearheaded by Celestino Soddu with Enrica Colabella . The event, which continues to this day, convened architects, mathematicians, poets and artists, uniting diverse disciplines under the banner of generative design. With discussions ranging from universal visual grammar to digital art, the conference aimed to spark enthusiasm for the generative process as understood in a more general way. This broader understanding of the generative is what makes the conference important. Soddu explains in the proceedings introduction : “The Generative Art is a way to think and to design. Following this approach we can find, united by the same enthusiasm, architects and mathematicians, poets and musicians, physicists and semiothics, philosophers and painters, engineers and designers.” Soddu and collaborators envision an annual gathering to further explore this interdisciplinary frontier. The conference proceedings, published with unique covers, mark a milestone in the evolution of generative art, affirming its status as a vibrant field of creative inquiry.

name: Yellowtail by Golan Levin
desc: This now legendary piece of software was begun by Levin at the Interval Research Corporation in 1998 and completed at MIT in 1999 and 2000. He would go on to show this piece to John Maeda , which would convince Maeda to let Levin join MIT’s Aesthetics and Computation Group (ACG) the following year. Once there, Yellowtail , which was conceived before Maeda even created DBN , “was first implemented using the EasyDraw DirectDraw framework by Scott Snibbe ; then the ACU C++ graphics framework by the MIT ACG, and then in the Processing Java framework by Ben Fry and Casey Reas .” The work, beyond getting Levin in MIT, also was one of the first to be tested in the legendary development of Processing at MIT in the mid-to-late-’90s. This work’s place in art history is secured. Levin spoke to this author, Peter Bauman , about his work in the 1990s saying : “My work from the late-90s was a reaction to the making culture that assumed that multimedia was constructed from preloaded assets like sprites and background images. I was like, ‘No, the computer is a dynamic medium that can generate things on the fly.’” The piece itself is an interactive software work that transforms user gestures into dynamic, abstract animations. Strokes made by the user are looped continuously, allowing control over both the shape and movement quality of lines. Each line has its unique cycle, creating a fluid, responsive animation, resembling organic textures.

name: _readme – own, be owned, or remain invisible by Heath Bunting
desc: This pioneering work of net.art transforms a newspaper article about Heath Bunting , the artist, into a hyperlinked guide, where each word links to a corresponding website. Initially leading to dead ends in 1998, the project highlighted the commercialization of online visibility, as banal words led to purchased domain sites. Through this hypertext exploration, Bunting explored how Internet perception structures ownership conditions, exposing the ruins of the grand narrative as the foundation of the new economy. This project anticipated the blockchain and NFT’s contemporary exploration of ownership.

name: SHREDDER by Mark Napier
desc: A classic of net. art, SHREDDER was a challenge to traditional print metaphors, embracing the web’s digita, data-based nature. potatoland.org transforms web pages into digital confetti, scattering markup, text, and images across the screen in a form of digital Abstract Expressionism. SHREDDER even gained the attention of the NY Times, showcasing how net.art was beginning to go mainstream at the end of the decade.

name: MPEG-4 standard announced
desc: An important step in the rise of Mass Media Art, an important pre-condition for NFTs, according to Casey Reas , in October 1998, the MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) announced the MPEG-4 standard, ISO/IEC 14496, following the success of MPEG-1 and MPEG-2. This global effort involved hundreds of researchers and engineers, resulting in approval of an International Standard by early 1999. Importantly, the fully backward compatible MPEG-4 Version 2 extensions followed, extending capabilities for digital television, interactive graphics and multimedia applications for the early web. Critical to the rise of Madd Media Art, the standard facilitated the integration of production, distribution and content access. It thus laid the foundation for interactive video, CD-ROMs and digital television and their use in creative expression. Further extensions continued into the upcoming decades, ensuring ongoing advancements in multimedia technology.

name: Joshua Davis releases ps0.praystation.v0
desc: Flash creative coder pioneer Joshua Davis released ps0.praystation.v0, his website for exhibiting experimental design and art using code, specifically Flash. The site also served as an important community resource for open source code. As a place for artists to both exhibit and learn, praystation.com was critical in the development of the intersection of the Internet, digital art and Mass Media art.

name: ACU Program Begins
desc: According to Tom White , ACU, a key predecessor of Processing formed in 1998. Before Processing, MIT’s Aesthetics and Computation Group (ACG) was already innovating, with the ACU toolkit, a C++ and OpenGL-based precursor that underpinned screen-based projects within the Aesthetics and Computation Group from 1999 to 2002. Preceding iterations like acWorlds and acJava paved the path, while echoes of earlier projects, such as Bob Sabiston ’s “BadWindows” in the vlw era, reverberated through its development. ACU, in particular, provided a foundational structure for interactive graphics research, fueling endeavors in dynamic typography, visual programming systems, audio-visual environments and information visualization. ACU was thus a key pre-Processeing MIT ACG development.

name: Frankensteinian Methods for Evolutionary Music Composition by Peter Todd and Gregory Werner
desc: This book chapter, “Frankensteinian Methods for Evolutionary Music Composition,” by Peter Todd and Gregory Werner looks at co-evolutionary techniques in music composition. The pair aimed to create intelligent algorithmic music composition systems, inspired by the story of Frankenstein . The duo explains in their own words: ”[Our] approach involves separate populations of critic agents and composer agents, striving to establish a consistent aesthetic within a simulated culture. However, while their method yielded a coherent aesthetic, it often diverged from human sensibilities.” In other words, they created a novel, cybernetic-feedback loop method for refining musical compositions that combined rules, learning and evolution, published in Musical Networks ( MIT Press , 1999).
subjects: frankensteinian methods for evolutionary music composition

name: John Maeda publishes Design By Numbers
desc: In surely one of generative art’s most legendary moments, John Maeda published Design By Numbers, with the aim of simplifying programming for artists and designers at the MIT Media Lab ’s Aesthetics and Computation Group. Its minimalist interface and intuitive design enabled users to experiment with computational creativity, inspiring a new generation of digital artists and toolmakers to further fine tune and expand. The system’s simplified distribution and user-friendly syntax enabled workshops and courses at MIT and elsewhere. Benjamin Fry built DBN 2 and 3 and Casey Reas the courseware, gathering invaluable feedback, laying the groundwork for future improvements, eventually evolving into Processing . Golan Levin, an ACG student around this time, spoke to me about DBN : “Processing grew out of Design by Numbers (DBN), which Zach’s current graduate student, Lingdong Huang, who was also my former student, just got working online . You can actually now play with DBN in the browser. This was announced only in October 2023. Now you can actually see projects that Casey Reas, Ben Fry and I made some twenty-odd years ago. DBN was John Maeda’s concept. And it allowed you to do interactive, computational and generative form on a canvas that had very specific limitations. And John is like the ultimate Bauhaus guy in terms of really liking simplicity and stark limitations. With DBN, you were limited to grayscale; you were limited to a canvas that was 100 x 100 pixels. It was kind of like a no-fun zone because you couldn’t make stuff that’s full of sexy colors. That’s because it was specifically a pedagogical tool. ‍‍Casey and Ben were like, “Yeah, this is great but we actually want to make art bigger than 100 pixels.” And John was like, “Well, that’s your business. If you want to make things that are colorful, artsy, big and whatever, go ahead.” Casey and Ben wanted to make an actually useful tool and not just a conceptual learning environment. They started working on it close to the time that I was graduating so I didn’t have a lot of direct involvement in it. But Yellowtail , for example, has been a demo in Processing since 2000. They looked to me to provide examples like that sometimes. I was probably one of the very first people to teach with it, other than Casey and Ben themselves.”

name: Electric Sheep by Scott Draves
desc: Described as a “collective intelligence,” this early example of machine learning in art was inspired by the evolutionary art work of Karl Sims . Scott Draves ’s software art Electric Sheep is a distributed screen-saver-as-art and pivotal advancement in AI, artificial life and fractal art that originated from the Fractal Flame algorithm. Electric Sheep leveraged a distributed system with a client/server architecture, transforming computer screensavers into dynamic, networked canvases for fractal animations. Each “sheep” in the system consisted of 128 frames and a genetic code defined by 160 floating-point numbers. An early AI-driven art project, Electric Sheep enlisted 450,000 participants globally, pioneering machine learning art and AI. The Flame algorithm mirrors contemporary neural networks' vector floating point approach. The collaborative rendering system allows computers worldwide to contribute, guided by human votes for the fittest animations. Each computer follows Draves' Flame algorithm to create a segment of the collective artwork. Open source and constantly evolving with contributions, Electric Sheep showcases family trees and resemblance through electricsheep.org . Draves serves as head Shepherd, overseeing this dynamic, participatory project in AI-driven art.

name: SOD by JODI
desc: The renowned net art duo JODI ’s release of SOD represented a blend of their net.art roots, video game art and the video game cracking culture that led to the demoscene. The work is a warped, scrambled version of “Wolfenstein3D” (1992), a game chosen for “its ‘abandonware’ status,” as the game was seven years old in 1999, according to Phillipa Stalker . A participator from the time was quoted as saying, “Every ‘wall’ of the maze is rendered in black and white geometric patterns, while the main enemy in the game appears as two inverted triangles.” Despite this graphical reduction and intentional obfuscation, gameplay remarkably remains intact. JODI invites viewers to become active participators in a world of their own creation, making SOD not only a unique digital expression capturing the late ’90s gaming and internet culture, but also a journey into JODI’s surreal vision of the world.

name: Re-move by LIA
desc: Another important example of net.art and the rise of Mass Media art that was popularizing around the end of the decade, LIA’s Re-move (1999–2003) explores generative-audiovisual compositions that combine organic forms “with the rawness of fin-de-siècle Viennese abstraction.” These works were originally created in Macromedia Director and played in the browser through the Shockwave plugin, released “on the internet to be accessible by everyone,” the artist told author Peter Bauman . They were also later released on CD-ROM. The work has since been restored for the Net Art Anthology . Each composition in Re-move achieves a delicate balance between the artist’s formal choices, user interaction, chance and algorithmic processes. These elements emphasizes the computer’s role as a dynamic medium rather than a static device. By balancing responsiveness, randomness and repetition, the time-based abstractions maintain legibility amidst their intricate complexity. Casey Reas mentions the Macromedia Director work of LIA, released on CD-ROM, as important experimental work of this time.

name: skinonskinonskin by Auriea Harvey and Michaël Samyn
desc: This pioneering work of Flash art and net.art by Auriea Harvey and Michaël Samyn , skinonskinonskin, was a collection of the pair’s digital love letters. Initially shared privately, the two turned the letters into interactive web pages—which included Flash animations, audio, text and images. They were later made available to paid subscribers as online artwork. The project typifies the decade-long rise of mass-media art, looking at the intersection of artistic collaboration and romantic connection in the digital age. Harvey and Samyn’s shared practice, Entropy8Zuper!, merged their individual artistry, blurring the lines between their personal and professional lives. skinonskinonskin challenged traditional notions of the cold digital and how humans displayed intimacy, anticipating the Internet’s impact on romantic relationships and dating apps in the twenty-first century. The piece invited viewers to feel a touch that transcended physical space, symbolizing a profound connection through the internet’s newly laid wires.

name: Term Web 2.0 Coined by Darcy DiNucci
desc: Firmly in what many believe is the Web3 era, this nomenclature was first developed over twenty years prior. Darcy DiNucci coined the term “Web 2.0” in her article “Fragmented Future” for Print magazine. The designation was meant to underscore the Web fragmenting across devices as a transport layer. Web 2.0 includes early social networking platforms, forums, wikis and multimedia sharing sites such as Joshua Davis ’s praystation.v0. Tim O’Reilly and Dale Dougherty popularized the term even further in 2004 when they hosted a Web 2.0 conference.

name: Raging Bull and Deep ASCII by Vuk Cosic
desc: Based on custom software he developed in 1996 and released in 1998, according to DAM, Ćosić’s Raging Bull and Deep ASCII were some of the first ASCII films, as all the visuals are reduced to green ASCII characters. Deep ASCII was first and with a running time of fifty-five minutes recreates the pornographic film with ASCII characters. Knowing this was likely a first, the work stands as punk nod to Ćosić’s net.art roots. The works also may have influenced the aesthetics for the Matrix and many other “hacker” portraying films of the time and their use animated binary code in green with a black background. The work asks questions about what is lost when we send messages within a digital context.

name: Yugo Nakamura Launches yugop.com
desc: The Flash 4 savant Nakamura originally launched yugop.com in 1999. The Flash-based site demonstrated a masterful blend of simplicity and interactivity that would influence the trajectory of art and design on the web. MoMA even used Nakamura’s design firm for the bespoke page for the Paola Antonelli curated, Design and the Elastic Mind website. moma.org : “Paola Antonelli, the exhibition curator, had gone through around twenty links from three firms when we showed her Yugo Nakamura ’s personal site, yugop.com . The simple white page that greeted us was immediately invaded by dark, two-dimensional cascading balls. We watched for a few minutes, mesmerized by the simple physics of bouncing. Paola decided to go with Yugo’s firm, tha.jp , on the spot.” He was one of the contributing authors of New Masters of Flash (friends of ED, 2000).

name: Enter Y2K
desc: The decade of the 2000s began with the optimism of the dot-com era and the promise of the Internet’s potential. While markets were cooling on the initial profitability of Internet companies, the realization of the full power of the Internet was only being realized by the developed populations that were benefiting from them. This interest in the Internet sparked a renewed interest in digital art, especially as it pertained to net art and software art. For more context, we suggest [watching or listening ( transcript ) to our Ch 8 Artist Discussion with Christiane Paul ⁠, ⁠ Casey Reas ⁠, ⁠ Christa Sommerer ⁠ and ⁠ Golan Levin ⁠.] This optimism was exemplified by exhibitions at the Whitney, such as BitStreams and Data Dynamics . Bitforms Gallery opened its doors in 2001, celebrating artists engaging with new technologies and media art. This optimistic trend was solidified and forever memorialized by the seminal 2003 publication of Christiane Paul’s Digital Art . Paul explained further in a conversation with me : “We have seen these waves [of optimism] before. Like 2000 [2001] was a big one, when at that moment the Whitney did BitStreams and Data Dynamics and suddenly all of the institutions were commissioning net art. And then it all collapsed. I’m not saying that will happen. I think this is a more sustained engagement but there are also always ups and downs.” This optimism, combined with the emergence of Processing in 2001 and computer-generated art, experienced not its first nor its last renaissance. Or perhaps, as Paul also noticed, the baton changed from one digital generative art movement ( Algorists ) to another (Process-ists).

name: “New Masters of Flash” published by friends of ED
desc: While Flash was a tool bred from the 1990s, it still continued to be extensively used throughout this decade. Just a few short years after Macromedia released Flash 1.0, New Masters of Flash, a friends of ED anthology in which a dozen practitioners including Yugo Nakamura , Joshua Davis and Brendan Dawes each contributed a chapter, changed the course of digital design through tutorials, design essays and author interviews. The book provided step-by-step instructions for creating innovative interfaces and effects in Flash 5. It served as a showcase and practical guide for aspiring designers, with a CD-ROM containing animated tutorials and completed projects. With its global perspective and pioneering approach, New Masters of Flash is still considered a seminal work in interactive interface design. The book is in the category of Pre- Processing coded art textbooks and includes Mark Wilson ’s famed Drawing with Computers (1985).
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: FILE Festival Showcases Regional Digital Art
desc: Founded in 2000 by Ricardo Barreto and Paula Perissinotto to exhibit the diversity of media art in the region, South America ’s largest art and technology festival has operated annually since 2000. This free festival provides a platform for artists to present their work and receive awards while allowing audience members to immerse themselves in the latest developments in digital art.

name: Ray Kurzweil’s Cybernetic Poet
desc: Ray Kurzweil’s Cybernetic Poet first written in the mid-1980s, creates language models of the works of various human authors and uses language analysis and mathematical modeling to generate original poems “inspired” by these authors. -Sasha Stiles

name: Casey Reas and Ben Fry Initiate Processing Project
desc: Perhaps important enough for the name of the entire decade, Processing is that important to the development of generative art. It will have to suffice to have heavily inspired the decade’s title, which, to be fair, does include other tooling breakthroughs such as Zach Lieberman ’s openFrameworks . Created by Casey Reas and Ben Fry at MIT’s ACG under John Maeda , Processing changed generative art irrevocably. It educated and inspired a new generation of artist-coders, expanding generative art’s talent pool exponentially. Artist and digital researcher Karsten Schmidt recently shared with the author Peter Bauman (Monk Antony) about the importance of Processing as an open-source tool. As such, it adhered to decades of anti-commercial, open-sharing and communal learning sentiment from the computation community, with ideals dating back to the humanist thought of Ivan Illich . Prior to this, educational institutions and artists had to pay for the latest version of commercial software, such as Macromedia ’s Director . Processing gave artists not only greater control of their work but was also free to use and was continuously updated by the community, relying on the incredibly dedicated work of Project Leads Ben Fry and Casey Reas as well as dozens of other contributors and alumni that have made it all possible and deserve tremendous credit. Golan Levin spoke to me about Processing as a response to the commercially available tools at the time: “Processing in its full-flowered implementation was a reaction to the limits of Flash and Director in terms of the assumptions that they made about artist tooling. What Ben and Casey knew was that the computer was capable of vastly more than Adobe would lead you to believe in terms of the flexibility and malleability of dynamic digital form. ‍‍‍They showed that you could actually control the individual vertices of a polygon. You don’t just have to be stuck with ellipses and rectangles. That’s why Ben and Casey made that a first-order feature in Processing. As for the moment itself, the site www.proce55ing.net went live on October 20, 2001 with some sparse examples and the following description : “Proce55ing is an environment for programming images, movement, and interaction. It is a sketchbook for developing ideas, a tool for creating prototypes, and a context for learning the fundamentals of computer programming. The Pr0cess1ng environment is in its early stages and will continue to develop.Pr()ce55ing is written in Java and enables the creation of Java Applications and Applets within a carefully designed set of constraints. It uses a 2D/3D Java rendering API that is a cross between postscript-style imaging in 2D and 3D rendering with OpenGL.” Processing continues to be an essential tool for many creative coders, artists and students. Beyond being an invaluable tool across classrooms worldwide teaching creative coding to the newest generation of artists and designers, Processing offers a way for illustrious artists with careers measured in the decades to continue their practice. Frieder Nake , the icon, one of the earliest computer and digital artists, spoke to me about Processing in 2024, saying: “I have for the last 15 years—maybe more—used Processing. Now, Casey Reas, one of the two founders, it’s so fantastic that he himself is an artist. Ben Fry, his friend, the two did it at MIT. They were still students when they did this. So the fact that here an artist, who was an artist before he was using computers, designed together with his friend, that programming language, that’s a historic fact that the world should really become aware of. And to use Processing is really simple. Ever since, I’ve never taught anything else to my students. Processing, it is so powerful because it’s based on Java. But you don’t have to know Java.”

name: BitStreams at the Whitney Museum, New York
desc: “Nothing since the invention of photography has had a greater impact on artistic practice than the emergence of digital technologies,” begins the Whitney Museum’s description of BitStreams , a startling admission from a major art museum. As the Internet reinvigorated interest in technology and art, BitStreams was tied together through a common use of software. This exhibition would profoundly impact recent graduate Zach Lieberman , who in 2005 would go on to release openFrameworks , software similar to Processing but C++ based. Lieberman shared with me about the impact of this exhibition on his practice : “For me, personally, the BitStreams exhibition at the Whitney in 2001 was especially meaningful. I was a student when I went to the Whitney Museum and I saw Jason Salavon ’s artwork; I heard Yasunao Tone ’s “ Solo for Wounded CD .” I was a student and I put on these headphones. Here’s this artist making glitch music, basically breaking CDs and I was thinking, “Woah, what is this? It’s wild.”

name: Data Dynamics at the Whitney
desc: Curated by Christiane Paul and indicative of the early millennium enthusiasm for digital art—as the Internet sucked more and more of the cultural air— New York ’s Whitney Museum hosted two major digital themed exhibitions in 2001 with Data Dynamics (March 2001) and BitStreams . lerandom.art : “Overall, I would say I’m always a little bit skeptical because we have seen these waves before. For instance, 2000 was a big one when, at that moment, the Whitney did BitStreams and Data Dynamics and suddenly all of the institutions were commissioning net art.” The exhibition itself was inspired by the recent enthusiasm for net.art and showcased Internet-based art, addressing the challenge of visually representing the fluidity of data and information. The exhibition featured installations in the museum and online, anticipating our contemporary digitized art market by nearly twenty years. The online experience also provided diverse navigational experiences through visual and textual data in a net.art-inspired interactive experience. Works by Marek Walczak , Martin Wattenberg , Mark Napier , Maciej Wisniewski , Beth Stryker , Sawad Brooks and Adrianne Wortzel explored various data dynamics, from mapping language and stories to traffic in physical and virtual spaces.

name: Inaugural Exhibition at bitforms: Casey Reas’s first commercial gallery showing
desc: This show is the first for the newly opened gallery, bitforms, which would help to reintroduce the fine art world to technology and art at the turn of the millennium. Founded by Steve Sacks , bitforms opened its doors in 2001 with Inaugural Exhibition. The new Chelsea gallery aimed to “celebrate the nexus of art and technology,” serving as "a forum to display digital and digitally inspired art.” The opening of bitforms in 2001, combined with the release of Processing by Casey Reas and Ben Fry to reinvigorate code-based art. Inaugural Exhibition featured Casey Reas along with Golan Levin , Dorothy Krause and four others. Reas’s displayed work, Path series, would go on to become Tissue, exhibited as software the following year at bitforms and in 2021 as Phototaxis on Art Blocks . Path and Tissue can even be seen as primitive-AI work. Reas himself explains in Medium: “Late in my time studying Media Arts and Sciences as a graduate student at MIT, I found my way into an Artificial Intelligence class taught by Rodney Brooks . In that class, I was introduced to the book Vehicles written by the neuroanatomist Valentino Braitenberg . The ideas in this short but profound book were the origin for the Path and Tissue prints that I created 2001–03. Braitenberg’s “vehicles” are minimal, simulated bodies that have behaviors similar to living organisms.
