Through writing code, I interpreted these organisms as software machines for drawing.” Beyond the Reas and Levin show, a year later, Manfred Mohr would open the first of his several solo shows at bitforms. It featured works spanning the first three decades of the digital generative art pioneer’s career. Bitforms continues to showcase the depth and breadth of contemporary, digitally inspired art. It has exhibited pieces spanning from the hand-woven linen textiles of Beryl Korot to works utilizing quantum computing by Refik Anadol . In the 22 years since Inaugural Exhibition, bitforms has provided a critical space for the intersection of art and technology to flourish. It has continued a decades-long tradition to which New York has contributed so much.

name: Alphabet Synthesis Machine by Golan Levin
desc: The culmination of several years of collaboration between Golan Levin , Jonathan Feinberg , and Cassidy Curtis , Alphabet Synthesis Machine was an online interactive artwork commissioned by PBS and Art21.org. The platform enabled users to design and evolve potential writing systems for fictional civilizations. Users could create abstract alphabets with the software, which could be downloaded as TrueType fonts and added to a comprehensive archive of user-generated content. The project explored the edges of familiarity and chaos, as well as language and gesture. Levin spoke to me about the project and its impact on his future work , including the asemic writing in his Art Blocks Curated release, Cytographia : “I’ve had an interest for a long time in nonsense alphabet systems. There’s a talk I gave at Resonate Festival 2013, where I introduce why asemic writing is interesting to me. In 2001, I did a project that was actually the culmination of several years of research with Cassidy Curtis and Jonathan Feinberg called the Alphabet Synthesis Machine, which allowed you to use a genetic algorithm to synthesize your own nonsense writing system. The great Italian artist designer Bruno Munari also had a wonderful script of an uncontacted civilization and plenty of people have done similar work as well.”

name: Transmediale 2001: DIY (do it yourself!)
desc: Transmediale, the Berlin festival-conference, was emblematic of the excitement globally for software and net-based art at the turn of the new millennium, as in 2001 it introduced an artistic software award. According to the event’s jury pastwebsites.transmediale.de , “To our knowledge, this is the first award given and solely dedicated to software art.” SIGGRAPH or Ars Electronica might have something to say about that claim, however. The shortlisted works included pieces by Golan Levin and net.art pioneer Netochka Nezvanova .

name: Genomic Cartography: Chromosome 18, Ben Fry
desc: Part of MoMA ’s permanent collection and from Fry‘s time at the MIT Media Lab ’s Aesthetics and Computation Group, Chromosome 18 was part of genomic cartography and an example of Fry’s expert use and interest in data visualization.

name: Agent Ruby by Lynn Hershman Leeson
desc: An important example in the development of AI art by Lesson, Agent Ruby (1998–2002), commissioned by SFMOMA , grew out of the expanded cinema experience from Leeson’s film Teknolust. This interactive, multiuser artwork features Ruby—a web agent with a female persona based within a website mimicking the lab of the film’s characters, Rosetta Stone and Agent Ruby. Users to this day can engage with Ruby , who responds to inquiries with varying expressions and moods that adapt based on her interactions and web traffic. Continually learning, Ruby searches the internet to augment her knowledge, evolving her responses and capabilities over time. The work stands as a clear predecessor to today’s LLM AI chat bots. Agent Ruby makes clear the relationship between art and the development of AI.

name: teamLab Formed
desc: Toshiyuki Inoko founded the digital art collective teamLab in 2001 with four friends, bringing together approximately 400 'ultratechnologists' with backgrounds across art, mathematics and technology. teamLab, headquartered in Tokyo and with branches in Singapore and Shanghai , from the beginning aimed to transform how people interact with their surroundings through digital art. To this day, they create immersive installations that combine the physical and digital worlds, redefining our perceptions of space. The group is known for investigating sensory experiences with viewer interaction, creating one-of-a-kind environments in which participants can transcend reality. The group’s immersive installations recall the work from the previous decade of CAVE from EVL (Electronic Visualization Lab). Toshiyuki spoke to Artnet about the collective’s first project in 2001: “The first work for teamLab was in 2001. It was a collaboration artwork with a musician. While the musician was singing, people watching the live show could put a comment on the internet. We took these comments and displayed them inside the space, so the comments were floating all around. It was projected on the wall, and the comments eventually created the shape of a tree, kind of like an immersive space, with all of the comments floating.”

name: Doug Eck Advances Neural Network Creative Expression
desc: These early creative expressions with neural networks continued decades of previous research covered in the Timeline by Peter M. Todd, J. P. Lewis, Jürgen Schmidhuber and others. A key figure in the foundation of modern AI art, Doug Eck created four “Blues Improvisations” in the essay “Composing Music with LSTM Recurrent Networks - Blues Improvisation.” In this unassuming but fascinating paper, Eck, a former postdoc of Schmidhuber, explored using “Long Short-Term Memory” [LSTM] recurrent neural networks for music composition. The project focused on creating blues improvisations, training the network with a 12-bar jazz bebop blues structure. The LSTM learned to generate coherent melodies and harmonize with fixed chords, showcasing its ability to capture long-term musical structure. Often the first experiments with new technologies and system appear in music or text with their pre-set rules. Christopher Strachey and Max Mathew working with the earliest computers in text (1952) and sound (1957) respectively both pre-date Michael Noll’s first visual experimentation. As it is with neural network art, where artistic experimentation with music preceded the visual.
subjects: composing music with lstm recurrent networks

name: Golan Levin and Casey Reas, The Art of Code at Bitforms, New York
desc: This exhibition featured Casey Reas ’s Tissue, a continuation of Path from the year prior, which today is known as Phototaxis and can be found on Art Blocks . Levin exhibited his interactive work Meshy (1998). The Art of Code at Bitforms, New York , spotlighted the early software works of Casey Reas and Golan Levin . Reas presented Tissue, an early foray into digital, generative systems with boundless outcomes, later evolving into Phototaxis on Art Blocks , exemplifying the algorithm’s long-form potential. Tissue, incorporating Braitenberg’s “vehicles” can be seen as primitive AI art. Levin’s Meshy offered an immersive drawing space where user interactions shaped a responsive, animated mesh, evolving with each new line drawn, showcasing the fluidity between artist, audience and digital medium. The Art of Code was the gallery’s second show, following the Inaugural Exhibition of November 2001, and its first two-person exhibition. bitforms, founded by Steve Sacks to bridge art and technological innovation, became a beacon for code-based art, notably after the release of Processing , invigorating the genre. Over the years, Bitforms has nurtured the art-tech nexus, displaying a spectrum from Beryl Korot’s textiles to Refik Anadol ’s quantum computing art.

name: The first Processing Forum
desc: Generative art witnessed a significant community milestone with the launch of the Processing Forum, an online platform named Discourse . Announced on the Processing site in August 2002, it was where Casey Reas , Ben Fry and other early contributors began an explorative dialogue that would shape the future of this medium. A collaborative space, the forum fostered an environment of mutual support and creativity, propelling the exploration and knowledge-sharing of Processing. It has thus been critical to the nurturing of one of the most significant developments in generative art, especially since the turn of the millennium. The forum underwent several evolutions, transitioning from “alpha” 2005 to “1.0” in 2010 and beyond, each phase marking an expansion in the community and its contributions to the field. Today, the forum still exists as a place to share and elicit information about Processing.

name: Re:MARK by Golan Levin & Zach Lieberman
desc: A commission of the Ars Electronica Museum of the Future, Re:MARK, by Tmema ( Golan Levin and Zachary Lieberman) with production support from the Ars Electronica Futurelab, was an interactive installation that visualized speech as whimsical animated text and shapes. Utilizing voice analysis, motion sensing and real-time animation, the installation cast the spoken words and sounds of participants as shadows, creating a playful, reactive and interactive environment. The exhibition created a shadow world of cartoon language that became a stage for participants. This immersive and participatory experience showcased the lighter side of software art and its ability to amaze.

name: isometricblocks, Ben Fry
desc: Emanating from his tenure at the MIT Media Lab ’s Aesthetics + Computation Group (ACG), Ben Fry ’s isometricblocks (2002–2004) is a seminal work that marries generative art with genetic data visualization. The work showcases Fry’s brilliant software-based data visualization. Utilizing the nascent versions of Processing , this project offers a comparative visual analysis of genomes, transforming complex genetic information into an accessible and visually striking format. Developed during Fry’s doctoral research, isometricblocks integrates various analytical methods into a unified visual narrative, enhancing our comprehension of genetic differences. By making intricate genetic structures more perceptible, isometricblocks serves as a quintessential example of how art and science can intersect, using algorithmic artistry to cast light on complex scientific data now recognized and preserved within MoMA ’s permanent collection.

name: Super Mario Clouds by Cory Arcangel
desc: In a masterpiece of video game art, Cory Arcangel deconstructs a familiar cultural artifact, reducing the iconic Super Mario Brothers game to its ethereal background only. By hacking into the game’s original 1985 cartridge, Arcangel eliminated all elements except for the clouds, transforming a bustling digital landscape filled with danger and user interaction into a minimalist meditation. As a classically trained musician, the piece reflects Arcangel’s deep engagement with his tools—here, the computer and game console—mirroring his belief in fully mastering technology to craft art. Further, the work challenges the viewer to find meaning in reduction but also lack of control. A user is in full control of a video game, yet Arcangel invites us to relinquish this need. The piece also encourages an examination of our rapid technological churn and reminds us that a physical, endlessly generative sky exists as well. The piece is a mocking cry to touch grass or maybe air. It rightly positions Arcangel’s practice in rarified air at the intersection of nostalgia, technical skill and conceptual rigor.

name: Velvet Strike modifies Counter Strike
desc: In another classic work of video game history, Velvet-Strike, by Anne-Marie Schleiner , Joan Leandre and Brody Condon , merged activism with video-game art as it was a protest against the newly launched Bush-era war on terrorism. The game “Counter-Strike,” renowned for its portrayal of terrorism and counterterrorism, was clearly intentional, as players fired spray paint graffiti rather than bullets as a tool to inscribe peace messages and anti-war art onto the game’s walls. This served as a direct challenge to the game’s inherent violence and competitive ethos, while questioning the labels (terrorists or soldiers) of the combatants. The project juxtaposes the playful, often escapist nature of gaming with stark political commentary, prompting players to reflect on real-world violence, the ethics of entertainment and their role in societal violence. Encouraging contributions from the global gaming community, Velvet Strike transformed digital spaces into canvases for not only activism but also self-reflection, underlining how interactive media can be harnessed for critical discourse.

name: Waiting Room by Mark Napier
desc: Waiting Room by Mark Napier is an innovative exploration of digital space and collaborative art, engaging 50 online users in a shared creative experience that bridges the realms of net.art and proto-AI art. This networked, interactive artwork serves as a midpoint between net.art and the nascent AI art movement, transforming participants' actions into integral components of a dynamic, evolving canvas. In Waiting Room, users' interactions—clicks, movements, and decisions—catalyze shifts in the artwork’s mood, color, and form, creating an ever-changing visual narrative. Each participant’s input introduces new shapes or shadows, suggesting architecture or dissolving light and encapsulating a sense of anticipation akin to that in physical waiting rooms. Through this collaborative digital environment, Waiting Room emerges as a living artwork, reflecting a collective artistic will and illustrating the potential for shared creativity from human-machine interaction.

name: Derivative launches TouchDesigner
desc: TouchDesigner, introduced by Derivative, marked a transformative advancement in interactive, real-time multimedia programming for visual artists. Launched by founders Greg Hermanovic , Rob Bairos , and Jarrett Smith , this innovative platform was born from the Houdini 4.1 source code, aimed at revolutionizing live visual performances. As a comprehensive real-time visual tool, TouchDesigner catered to the interest in interactive and dynamic digital artistry that started in earnest a decade prior, at the beginning of the 1990s, with events like artFutura as well as the work of early interactive pioneers such as Karl Sims . This was pioneered in the ’70s at EVL in Chicago with CAVE. TouchDesigner offered creators the ability to author, perform, and interact with visuals in unprecedented ways. With its first generation running from 2002, TouchDesigner established itself as an essential medium for artists to meld creativity with cutting-edge technology, fostering a new wave of digital expression.

name: Christian Bök Publishes “The Piecemeal Bard is Deconstructed”
desc: Writing in response to RACTER’s The Policeman’s Beard is Half-Constructed, Christian Bök publishes the essay “ The Piecemeal Bard is Deconstructed: Notes Toward a Poential Robopoetics, ” in Object 10: Cyberpoetics (edited by Kenneth Goldsmith ). In it, Bök suggests that “We are probably the first generation of poets who can reasonably expect to write literature for a machinic audience of artificially intellectual peers… If we want to commit an act of poetic innovation in an era of formal exhaustion, we may have to consider this heretofore unimagined, but nevertheless prohibited, option: writing poetry for inhuman readers, who do not yet exist, because such aliens, clones, or robots have not yet evolved to read it.” -Sasha Stiles

name: Machado and Cardoso’s NEvAr system
desc: Machado and Cardoso’s NEvAr system is an artistic tool that leverages concepts from evolutionary art. It is thus a continuation of decades of evolutionary and genetic algorithm art, which shares machine learning roots with today’s AI art. Developed by Penousal Machado and Amílcar Cardoso at the University of Coimbra, the NEvAr (Neuro Evolutionary Art) system harnesses evolutionary algorithms to automate aesthetic decision-making. Users engage with NEvAr by evaluating and selecting images, which then undergo evolutionary processes to enhance their appeal based on the users' preferences. This system utilizes a fitness function that incorporates complexity measures, aligning with Philip Galanter ’s exploration of evolutionary art’s potential to overcome the “fitness bottleneck” in creative processes. NEvAr’s capacity to generate visually compelling artwork with limited human intervention underscores how evolutionary artists were pushing for—or creating their own—tools that today resemble more automated processes like GANs and generative AI. Like many evolutionary art and early AI work, NEvAr was inspired by the work of Karl Sims as well as Richard Dawkins . Yet its roots extend to Yoichiro Kawaguchi from Japan .

name: Substrate, Jared Tarbell
desc: Made with Processing , this 2003 masterpiece by Tarbell highlights one of the powers of generative art and computation: the ability to convey complexity from simplicity. A single growth rule based on perpendicular growth, from just a single line, manufactures intricate, urban-esque compositions. The simplicity of the rule in Tarbell’s Substrate helped to amplify the power of the new tool to creatives and still stands as a source of inspiration for artists. 2010s generative artist inconvergent wrote: “One of the first pieces of generative art I ever saw and took notice of was Tarbell’s Substrate. It’s a genius algorithm in all it’s simplicity.” In Jason Bailey ’s ( Artnome ) seminal text, “ Why Love Generative Art? ” he wrote of Tarbell and Substrate: “For me, Tarbell’s work is the perfect generative art. It is the poster child for the duality of chaos and control, and has an intense level of visual complexity that slowly emerges from simplicity, making it feel more like it grew out of the soil than coming from algorithms.”

name: Samorost by Amanita Design
desc: This Flash art video game, known for its artistic emphasis, was created by Amanita Design, a Czech indie game studio. The studio was founded by Jakub Dvorsky, in 2003, when it introduced the gaming world to Samorost, an adventure that distinctively blended surreal landscapes, whimsical humor and a handcrafted aesthetic. The hero of the story is a gnome. This title marked Amanita Design’s commitment to creating rich, audiovisual gaming experiences, setting a precedent for their future works. Samorost, with its unique art style and engaging gameplay, established Amanita Design as a key player in the indie game development sphere but also showcased the potential for games to transcend traditional entertainment, becoming immersive, artistic experiences.

name: Digital Art by Christiane Paul
desc: This seminal book gave legitimacy to a field that was receiving renewed interest due to the success and rise of the Internet and net art. In Digital Art, Christiane Paul chronicles the transformative role of digital technology in art, focusing on technology as a medium itself from the early ’90s onwards, including net art and virtual reality. By beginning its “survey” of the evolution of digital art in the early-’90s, the text distinguishes between digital technology as a tool for traditional art-making (e.g., plotter work) and as a medium for pioneering new artistic forms (e.g., net.art and Flash ). Paul discusses pivotal artists and works while inspecting critical themes like interactivity, artificial intelligence and social activism, alongside issues concerning the preservation, presentation and ownership of digital art. Paul spoke to this author ( Peter Bauman ) about Digital Art two decades later for a piece on Le Random Editorials . Beyond her watershed book, Paul’s impact was vital in sustaining institutional interest throughout the decade once it began to wane. Paul singularly legitimized an emerging field, while chronicling and contextualizing its history.

name: Galanter Defines Generative Art
desc: In his seminal text from over twenty years ago, Galanter asks and answers, “What is Generative Art?” in the must-read essay for anyone interested in generative art: “What is Generative Art? Complexity Theory as a Context for Art Theory.” This is the essay that nearly everyone cites when defining generative art. This author’s own definition is highly influenced by Galanter. Galanter spoke to this author ( Peter Bauman ) about his enduring definition two decades later for a piece on Le Random Editorials . Here is Galanter’s iconic definition in full: “Generative art refers to any art practice where the artist uses a system, such as a set of natural language rules, a computer program, a machine, or other procedural invention, which is set into motion with some degree of autonomy contributing to or resulting in a completed work of art.” In other words, it is: Art using autonomous systems . The essay goes on to explore generative art through the lens of complexity scienceGalanter explains how generative art integrates principles from complexity theory, showing that systems range from highly ordered to highly disordered, with generative art often embodying a mixture of both. By situating generative art within this framework, he offers a broad historical perspective—much as this Timeline aims to—revealing that generative processes have been intrinsic to art-making throughout history, from ancient geometric patterns to contemporary digital and algorithmic methods. This comprehensive view not only clarifies the definition of generative art but also highlights its pervasive influence across diverse artistic domains. The view was also highly influential on this author, as this first moment on our Timeline attests to.

name: Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM) in Japan
desc: Defined by the pursuit of new artistic expression that incorporates technology and media, the Center continues to play an important role in showcasing, cultivating and supporting the generative art community in Japan .
subjects: yamaguchi center for arts and media (ycam)

name: Imaginary・Numbers by Keiko Kimoto
desc: This award-winning installation generates an infinite series of abstract images based on mathematical formulas and random elements. Exploring the relationship between the viewer’s psychological response and machine-generated imagery, the work highlights the potency of artistic expression through computational processes. The Japanese artist developed her elaborate two-dimensional works while conducting academic research at ERATO of JST ( Japan Science and Technology Agency). Kimoto thought deeply about the interaction of the systems and results in her work, writing: “I believe that art is not intended to be a gateway to understanding the artist’s system, but a method of activating the viewers’ psychological-motion systems (memory and physical sensation). These should be triggered by looking at the artwork. When viewers can realise their own feelings and memories, the artwork is truly completed.” As such, I included Kimoto as a Resultist in my article, “Demystifying Generative Art.”

name: Facebook launches at Harvard
desc: On 4 February 2004 Mark Zuckerberg launched thefacebook.com, open at first only to Harvard e-mail addresses, marking a turning point in humanity’s relationship with communities and popularizing online identities and interactions in a way that mainstreamed what before was looked on as niche. In many ways it was the culmination of the computer nerd transforming into the most popular kid on campus, reflecting our newfound embrace of the digital and the networked. Needless to say, the moment was a pivotal development in the evolution of social media, a term so pervasive it would practically come to define the time period of the proceeding decade. The platform, initially created for college students to connect and share information, quickly expanded beyond the academic setting, making countless millions comfortable with a life—at least a social one—online.

name: Pitch and Volume by Anna Ursyn
desc: Exhibited at SIGGRAPH 2004’s Synaesthesia, Pitch and Volume by Anna Ursyn , scrutinizes the intricate relationship between the digital and natural orders, exploring how both domains manifest structured patterns that can be perceived and analyzed. Ursyn articulates her process of merging these patterns in her art, employing techniques that range from initial sketches to complex computer programming. Her work reflects on how urban environments and big datasets resonate with natural rhythms and structures, influencing her artistic expression and teaching in computer art and graphics. Through this blend, Ursyn emphasizes the symbiotic interaction between human technological impacts and the inherent order of the natural world, enriching our understanding and engagement with both. Other artists to exhibit include Roman Verostko , Casey Reas and Hans Dehlinger .

name: Pac-Manhattan
desc: This IRL Pac-Man Pac-Manhattan was an innovative work of urban-performance art that transformed the streets of New York City into a live-action videogame, replicating the classic 1980's arcade game Pac-Man. The project recalled the work of GRAV and other performance artists who encouraged—rather, required—audience participation. Developed within NYU’s Interactive Telecommunications graduate program under Frank Lantz , the artwork experimented with the dynamics of gaming by bringing digital play into the physical realm of Manhattan ’s Washington Square Park area. Players dressed as Pac-Man and the ghosts navigated the city’s grid, with Pac-Man attempting to collect all virtual “dots” along the streets, while the ghosts tried to tag him. Each street player was paired by mobile phone with a controller in a Wi-Fi-equipped control room who moved their icon on a shared map, and the game state was broadcast over the internet. It can also be seen as an early attempt at an immersive, virtual reality performance piece on a large scale.

name: {Software} Structures by Casey Reas, Jared Tarbell, Robert Hodgin and William Ngan
desc: This online commission for the Whitney Museum’s Artport was created by Casey Reas as a way to explain generative art’s ability to visualize the same simple instructions in many different ways depending on the execution of the artist’s algorithm. The technique is rooted in the instruction-based wall drawings of Sol LeWitt . {Software} Structures by Casey Reas, alongside collaborators Jared Tarbell , Robert Hodgin , and William Ngan , investigated the relationship between algorithmic rigor and artistic fluidity. Inspired by Sol LeWitt’s conceptual methodologies, Reas reimagined the creation of art, making programming as immediate and fluid as drawing. By spending initial days crafting core technical code, he then engaged with this foundation intuitively for months, akin to modifying a sketch, thus allowing for dynamic and iterative creation without the constraints of the original algorithms. This process culminated in artworks that, rather than being direct outputs of code, emerged from processes of pre-planned structures and real-time artistic intervention. This approach not only echoed LeWitt’s wall drawings, which separate the conception of art from its execution by involving external actors, but also implemented these concepts through software, where the 'actors' were replaced by dynamic, interactive systems. These software structures, therefore, did not merely replicate physical artworks digitally but transformed them.

name: DiNA chatbot by Lynn Hershman Leeson
desc: With the release of Leeson’s video chatbot, DiNA, the artist expanded upon Agent Ruby (1998–2002), her text-based chatbot exhibited at SFMOMA . DiNA, much like today’s Siri or Alexa, could be conversed with. Users could speak to DiNA through a microphone, to which she responded on a projected video screen in front. The piece also anticipates the work of contemporary AI artists like Huemin who have developed interactive AI devices like the Bright Moments Dream Machine.

name: Margot Lovejoy Publishes Digital Currents: Art in the Electronic Age
desc: Similar To Christiane Paul ’s Digital Art , Lovejoy’s book offers an insightful look into the transformative role of digital technologies in contemporary art. Unlike Paul—whose Digital Art began in the 1990s—Lovejoy meticulously traced the evolution of electronic media in artistic expression, from early forays into video and computer art to the expansive realm of internet-based projects. Through detailed discussions of key artists and their groundbreaking works, Lovejoy not only chronicles artistic innovations but also examines the profound impact of these technologies on the artist’s role as a social communicator. This comprehensive study, richly illustrated and thoroughly researched, addresses a critical void by providing a nuanced understanding of how art, technology and society mix within a historical perspective.
subjects: digital currents: art in the electronic age

name: Matthew Cook proved that CA Rule 110 is capable of universal computation
desc: Matthew Cook ’s proof, developed while assisting Stephen Wolfram on A New Kind of Science and published in Complex Systems in 2004, resolved a conjecture Wolfram had posited in the 1980s. Cook proved that Rule 110, a seemingly simple one-dimensional cellular automaton, is capable of universal computation. This significant achievement confirmed that Rule 110 could simulate a Turing machine, thus performing any computation that a Turing machine is capable of. Cook’s proof not only validated Wolfram’s hypothesis but also underscored the profound computational possibilities inherent in cellular automata, enhancing their standing in computational theory and the study of complex systems. This all in turn led to the continued usage and interest in the creation of visual forms.

name: Cinema Redux, Brendan Dawes
desc: Part of MoMA ’s permanent collection, Dawes’s Cinema Redux transformed the experience of a film into a singular visual artifact. This innovative concept distills an entire movie into one image, where each row corresponds to one minute of the film, with each of the 60 frames representing a second. This technique effectively creates a “visual fingerprint” of a film, capturing its essence in a composite image. Acquired by the MoMA in 2008, Cinema Redux was a work on Processing by Dawes. Dawes recalls the impact of the piece and the relevance of Processing to its success: “Then in 2007 I got an email from The Museum of Modern Art asking if they could feature Cinema Redux in their new exhibition called Design and the Elastic Mind . I still remember starring at that email in absolute disbelief — after all I only managed to get a grade C in art at high school. This was ridiculous. In 2008 myself and my wife travelled to New York for the opening and saw Cinema Redux printed thirty feet high, proudly sat alongside other beautiful work. MoMA would then go to acquire the work for the permanent collection, featuring in three more MoMA exhibitions as well as other exhibitions around the world including Big Bang Data . All this made possible because of freely messing about in this wonderful thing called Processing.”

name: Reas Begins Process Series (2004-2010)
desc: In his seminal series Process, documented comprehensively in the book Process Compendium 2004-2010, Casey Reas explores the intricate phenomenon of emergence through his unique artistic system. This system is built on the foundational elements of Forms, Behaviors and Elements, allowing Reas to generate an endless variety of visual compositions with his chosen visual grammar. Each element in this system—referred to as a simple machine—combines form with dynamic behaviors within a defined processual environment. For example, Process 4 populates a surface with simple machines, circles moving in straight lines at consistent speeds. As these elements overlap, lines are drawn between them, visually capturing their interaction. This kinetic drawing machine, devoid of a predetermined end, evolves visually through discrete steps where each element adapts based on its behavior, thus continuously creating new forms. Over seven years, Reas refined this system, producing a rich tapestry of forms that draw from diverse influences, including the history of mathematics and the concepts of artificial life. The Process Compendium captures this evolution through a collection of fifteen prints from Process 4 to Process 18, offering insights into the static and dynamic variations of these processes and the emergent visual phenomena they produce.

name: Twenty-Six Visions of Hildegarde by Roman Verostko
desc: Twenty-Six Visions of Hildegarde by Roman Verostko the pioneering Algorist who was deeply influenced by early twentieth-century abstractionists, was created for the SIGGRAPH 2004 Synaesthesia exhibition. This collection comprises pen-and-ink drawings enhanced with gold leaf, each measuring 25 by 33 inches. In this series, Verostko continues to explore the interface between digital procedures and artistic expression, using algorithms akin to his painting methods. These artworks are meticulously drawn using a pen plotter controlled by algorithms developed through Verostko’s Hodos program, manifesting complexity through code and encapsulating his lifelong engagement with algorithmic art.

name: Eden by Jon McCormack
desc: Eden is an interactive, self-generating, artificial ecosystem installation active from 2004–2012. McCormack created artificial creatures that inhabited a virtual world governed by minimal physics, seeking survival through adaptation and learning. These beings exhibited complex behaviors such as foraging, communication and hibernation in response to seasonal changes and human presence. Projected onto floating screens, the creatures interacted within a translucent, immersive space, blurring distinctions between reality and simulation. Audience interaction influences the ecosystem, as the presence of viewers sustains the creatures' food supply. Over time, a symbiotic relationship between audience and artwork emerges, shaping the evolution of the virtual ecosystem and highlighting the interconnectedness of art, technology and human engagement. The system was mentioned by Phil Galanter as a prime example of generative artificial life.

name: Zach Lieberman releases OpenFrameworks v0.01
desc: With a decade titled the “Tooling Era,” tools clearly played a critical role in this decade’s impact on the history of generative thinking and art. Along with Processing , that was developed at MIT’s ACG by Casey Reas and Ben Fry under John Maeda , openFrameworks was developed a few years later by Zach Lieberman , who had spent much of his early career collaborating with former Parsons professor Golan Levin . Levin also studied at ACG under Maeda. On August 3, 2005, Zach Lieberman released OpenFrameworks v0.01; Theodore Watson and Arturo Castro joined afterwards. To this day, the release of openFrameworks represents a significant move to bolster the creative coding community. It’s an open-source C++ toolkit designed to streamline the creative process. The comprehensive framework integrates several widely used libraries, facilitating tasks in graphics, audio, video and computer vision across multiple platforms, including Windows, OSX, Linux, iOS and Android. The language aims at making coding more accessible and fostering a collaborative and extensible development environment focused on inclusion. Like Processing, the software is open source, ensuring an open ecosystem of learning and sharing, which is foundational to the history of computing outside of military laboratories.

name: Arduino Developed
desc: Arduino was developed in Ivrea, Italy , following Hernando Barragán ’s Wiring project, supervised by Casey Reas and Massimo Banzi in 2003. Two years later, a team of five, including Banzi, David Cuartielles , Tom Igoe , David Mellis and Gianluca Martino , forked Wiring at the Interaction Design Institute Ivrea (IDII) to create Arduino. Named after a local bar in Ivrea, Arduino began by creating low-cost microcontroller boards that revolutionized the DIY electronics world by making technology accessible to novices. The open-source hardware and software allowed users to easily create and share projects, setting off a process of democratization of engineering, which has inspired a global community of makers, leading to innovations in various fields. Critically, the Arduino Programming Language was inspired by Processing , as Reas supervised Barragán’s Wiring.

name: Soft Cinema by Lev Manovich
desc: As included in Casey Reas ’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA , Manovich’s Soft Cinema is an innovative exploration into the dynamics of digital cinema. This project emerged from Manovich’s collaborations with Andreas Kratky and notable contributors across various fields, including music by DJ Spooky and Scanner. Soft Cinema utilizes algorithms to edit media dynamically, creating an ever-changing narrative from a database of video clips. The software, written in Lingo, sorts clips based on both content and formal attributes such as color and movement, allowing the creation of varied cinematic sequences. This approach exemplifies a shift towards a database-driven narrative, which Manovich has termed 'Soft(ware) Cinema,' reflecting a new era where software and human inputs merge to generate unique cinematic experiences. This project highlights a pivotal moment in the evolution of digital and software media, offering a profound insight into the possibilities of algorithmic creativity beyond static imagery.

name: Monster Movie by Takeshi Murata
desc: In the collection of SFMOMA and included in Casey Reas ’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA , Takeshi Murata ’s sub-four-minute digital video, Monster Movie was a revolutionary work in digital video art. It transformed a snippet from the 1981 B movie Caveman into a dynamic, disintegrating spectacle of digital forms. To achieve this, Murata applied datamoshing—a technique where he manipulates video compression—to dissolve and mutate traditional film imagery into a fluid mosaic of color and shape. This piece, characterized by its aggressive audio track and ceaseless visual transformation, critiques and manipulates the digital medium itself. Murata’s work exemplified a shift from static cinematic narratives to dynamic digital realms, challenging viewers' perceptions of continuity and identity in our digitizing times. Through Monster Movie, Murata both reflects and distorts the visual music and abstraction traditions in film, illustrating the transformative potential of digital tools while commenting on the ephemeral nature of digital identity.

name: Part Object Part Sculpture, Columbus, Ohio
desc: At Columbus, Ohio ’s Wexner Center for the Arts, Part Object Part Sculpture, organized by curator Helen Molesworth , presented a compelling rethinking of post-World War II sculpture that highlighted the work of Duchamp’s Conceptualism in the art historical canon. By making room for Duchamp and Conceptualism, Molesworth also ties in the history of generative art with Duchamp as a common ancestor of electronic sculpture, randomness in art, the material-generative, minimalism, cybernetic (feedback loops in art) and more. Focusing on the tactile and artisanal aspects of Marcel Duchamp ’s later works, the show reevaluated the notion of the “Duchampian” beyond the ready-made, emphasizing the handcrafted, erotic and absurd elements. Molesworth positioned artists like Louise Bourgeois , Yayoi Kusama , and Eva Hesse not as peripheral figures but as central to a new narrative that highlighted materiality, memory and form over institutional critique.

name: Seven Easy Pieces by Marina Abramović at the Guggenheim
desc: In November 2005, Marina Abramović presented Seven Easy Pieces at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York . This exhibition featured seven consecutive nights of performance, reenacting legendary works by pioneering performance artists alongside one of Abramović’s own pieces. Each night, from 5 pm to 12 am, she explored various themes, from physical limits to intimate connections with the audience. The performances included Bruce Nauman ’s Body Pressure, Vito Acconci ’s Seedbed and Joseph Beuys ' How to Explain Pictures to a Dead Hare, showcasing a range from provocative intimacy to physical endurance and pain. This work from Abramović carries on the tradition of Fluxus artists and can be seen as performative generative art.
subjects: how to explain pictures to a dead hare

name: Marius Watz Begins generator.x Project
desc: In an important early attempt at digital preservation, Marius Watz began his generator.x project documenting generative art in collaboration with Atle Barcley , director of Atelier Nord. This curatorial platform researches the use of generative strategies and software processes across digital art, architecture and design. It championed and supported this new generation of creatives who use code as a medium for artistic expression that was increasing after the introduction of the tools of the decade, including Processing and openFrameworks . The project kicked off with Generator.x 1.0: Art from Code, which featured a conference and a touring exhibition starting in Oslo in September 2005, culminating in December 2007. The initiative reflects a commitment to exploring the frontiers of digital creativity through generative methodologies.

name: Atom by Christopher Bauder and Robert Henke
desc: This large-scale audio-visual experience by Christopher Bauder and Robert Henke used algorithmic choreography to transform a room into a dynamic, immersive environment. The work references and continues the legacy of kinetic sound and light installations that date back to Duchamp, László Moholy-Nagy and the various New Tendencies groups. These were critical predecessors to digital art, which Frank Popper highlights extensively in his book Art of the Electronic Age. For this work, an ensemble of white, self-illuminated balloons, suspended like the atoms of a complex molecule, floats throughout the space. These helium-filled balloons are connected to a computer-controlled system that adjusts their height and internal illumination through dimmable, super-bright LEDs, turning each sphere into a pixel within a three-dimensional matrix. The installation is accompanied by a four-channel sound system that emits deep, evolving noises synchronized with the rhythmic movement and changing patterns of light.

name: Twitter Founded
desc: Launched in the summer of 2006, just two years after the initial release of Facebook ’s rising popularity, 2006 served as a critical year in the development of the social media-dominated period that would follow and in which we still largely live nearly twenty years later. Just look at where we are promoting the release of this chapter. It’s Twitter . As for the history itself, in March 2006, Jack Dorsey , alongside co-founders Noah Glass , Biz Stone and Evan Williams , conceptualized Twitter as a text-based communication platform during a brainstorming session at Odeo, a struggling podcast company. Originally named “twttr” after a trend of dropping vowels to secure domain names, Twitter was birthed from the necessity to pivot Odeo’s business following Apple ’s entry into podcasting. The first tweet, “just setting up my twttr,” was sent by Dorsey on March 21, 2006. This marked the inception of Twitter, setting the stage for its massive future global impact on Web2 and Web3, as well as for artists, collectors and community members to share, collaborate and communicate in a global village.

name: Christa Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau’s Life Writer
desc: Christa Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau ’s Life Writer, an excellent example of mid-2000s cybernetic—or feedback loop-based art—that was artificial life in nature. It was exhibited for the first time in 2006 at the Museum of Contemporary Art Cleveland ( MOCA ). It continues to be exhibited in museums around the world as of 2024. The work carries on the tradition of Duchamp from the early-twentieth century, cybernetics in the mid-twentieth century and evolutionary art of the later-twentieth century. It thus connects these movements as well to contemporary AI art that’s based on feedback loops, evolutionary algorithms and self-learning. Sommerer and Mignonneau’s interactive installation Life Writer visually merged the nostalgic charm of a vintage typewriter with advanced artificial life technology. Debuting as a poignant fusion of analog and digital realms, the artwork transforms the simple act of typing into a generative process of life creation. When users type, the characters are projected onto paper, morphing into dynamic, black-and-white creatures upon hitting the carriage return. These creatures, governed by genetic algorithms derived from the duo’s earlier work, Life Spacies, exhibit behaviors influenced by the textual “genetic code” input by the user. In this digital ecosystem, the artificial life forms must consume text to survive, growing and reproducing as they interact with newly typed characters. Users can manipulate these creatures using the typewriter’s scroll, adding a tactile dimension to the digital interaction. Life Writer not only revisits the history of text processing but also invites users to ponder the creation of life and interaction within an emergent system.

name: Academy by R. Luke DuBois
desc: As included in Casey Reas ’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA as a standout example of computer film, specifically digital video, Academy compresses seventy years of film history into the length of a seventy-six-minute film. Presented at the 2007 Sundance Film Festival, the piece takes the first seventy-five years of Oscar-winning Best Picture films from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and condenses each into a single minute per film, displayed in chronological order. DuBois uses frame-averaging and time-lapse phonography to distill each film’s essence, allowing viewers to observe the evolution of cinematic techniques and themes over decades. Academy challenges our perceptions of film history and canon by asking questions about the implications of the digital on film, expressed through digital media itself.
subjects: academy of motion picture arts and sciences

name: Deep Time of the Media: Toward an Archaeology of Hearing and Seeing by Technical Means by Siegfried Zielinski
desc: This book, first published in German in 2002 and a great influence on this very timeline, looks at sciences, technology and the arts from a deeply intellectually rigorous perspective, where Zielinski incorporates both historiography and philosophy to explore media’s archaeological depth. For this Timeline’s influence, it begins at the title, where “Deep Time” suggests an exploration of the long history and evolution of media and technology, going far beyond just recent developments. This Timeline begins 70,000 years ago, in part influenced by the ideas of Zielinski. In his book, like this Timeline, Zielinski examines the way media technologies have evolved over centuries, from ancient forms of communication like cave paintings and hieroglyphs to modern digital devices. He emphasizes that media isn’t just about what’s current but also about understanding its historical roots and how it has shaped human culture. His Deep Time of the Media: Toward an Archaeology of Hearing and Seeing by Technical Means examines the intricate relationship between technology and human perception through historical depth. The book investigates how media technologies have shaped our understanding and interaction with the world, tracing a lineage from ancient philosophies to contemporary media practices. Zielinski challenges progressive narratives of technological evolution, promoting a view of media history that recognizes the heterogeneity and complexity of past technologies as fundamentally influential in today’s digital culture. This archaeological approach not only highlights forgotten or overlooked aspects of media history but also reflects on how these might inform present and future engagements with media technologies. Zielinski emphasizes the concept of “deep time,” borrowed from geology, to illustrate the profound, layered history of media technologies, challenging the notion that newer technologies are simply improved versions of the old. The work encourages a profound rethinking of how media is integrated into the fabric of societal development and cultural expression, advocating for an approach that values the heterogeneity and complexity of past technologies as fundamental to understanding our contemporary media landscape.

name: Google Buys YouTube
desc: YouTube was created by three former PayPal employees and bought by Google , announced 9 October and completed 13 November 2006, for $1.65 billion in what some have described as “ the best tech deal ever. ” The move signifies for the sake of this timeline, both the peak of Web2’s dominance and the ever-continuing rise of mass-media art. This precondition for NFTs, according to Casey Reas , began in earnest with the appearance of digital media devices in the home, like early video and music players (e.g., VHS and tape players) in the late ’70s and early ’80s. The purchase of YouTube by Google signified another giant step in mass media art’s decades-long development.

name: 16 Études sur les origines de Blum by Vera Molnár
desc: The grande dame herself, Vera Molnár , ventured into the literary domain with an unlikely commissioned tribute to James Joyce ’s Ulysses. Commissioned in 2006 by Leo Kanders in Zurich , Molnár’s tribute involved sixteen studies that resonated with the intricate layering of language seen in Ulysses, reflecting Joyce’s knack for infusing words with dense, enigmatic qualities. The work demonstrates Molnár’s continued activity into the new millennium.
subjects: 16 études sur les origines de blum

name: 20th Century Computer Art at Tama Art University Museum, Tokyo
desc: The rise of educational tooling for artists in the first half of the decade, as we have covered, such as Processing and openFrameworks served the main purpose of making it easier for artists to create works using software. This increased accessibility—also due to the maturing Internet—led to increased interest, artistic output and, ultimately, academic and institutional importance, as demonstrated by this exhibition at a museum associated with a university. The show closely examined and reevaluated the history of computer art and is especially important in celebrating the contribution of many Japanese artists as well as indicating a rising level of interest in the country and the region. 20th Century Computer Art: Beginnings and Developments. The Work and Thought of Pioneers and Contemporary Practitioners of Algorithmic Art at Tama Art University Museum in Tokyo , Japan , displayed over 250 works combining historic and contemporary computer art mostly from Japan. Contributing Japanese artists included Hiroshi Kawano , Elichi Izuhara, Koji Kusabuka , Chihaya Shimomura , Akihiro Kubota , Computer Technique Group, Masao Kohmura , Yoshiyuki Abe and Atsuhiko Iwakoshi . International contributors were Georg Nees , Herbert W. Franke , Frieder Nake , Eugen Roth , Wolfgang Kiwus , A. Michael Noll , Harold Cohen , Manfred Mohr , Edward Zajec , Roman Verostko , Vera Molnar, Erwin Steller , Hervé Huitric , Monique Nahas and Manuel Barbadillo .
subjects: 20th century computer art: beginnings and developments

name: Daito MANABE launches Rhizomatiks
desc: Rhizomatiks , a pioneering collective, emerged in 2006 and was renamed Abstract Engine in 2020, incorporated technology and artistry to focus on experimental projects that blended R&D with artistic expression. The group, comprising artists, designers and engineers, explores how humans and technology co-exist, by leading projects from development to execution, continuously delivering avant-garde creations through interdisciplinary collaborations. It was founded by Daito Manabe , whose work ranges into a variety of fields, taking a new approach to everyday materials and phenomena. However, his end goal is not simply rich, high-definition realism but recombining these familiar elemental building blocks. His practice is informed by careful observation to discover and elucidate the essential potentialities inherent to the human body, data, programming, computers and other phenomena, thus probing how the analog and digital, real and virtual worlds collide.

name: Rondo by Anna Ursyn
desc: This work of digital generative art remains fascinating—a work so contemporary yet rooted in Fortran , a programming language dating to the 1950s. The work encapsulates Ursyn’s exploration of the intersections between natural order and human technological constructs. Through her methodical creative process, she sketches and then uses computer programs to transform these ideas into iconic images of animals and other objects, portraying them within dynamic, abstract landscapes. Ursyn explains : “I create programs in Fortran, then I add photographic content using scanners and digital cameras. To attain the composition, I use repetition of lines, shapes, and forms, select color combinations, transform light intensity, apply grid patterns and moire effects, and distort and manipulate images by scaling, rotating, slanting, and changing perspective.” Her work combines elements from both the physical and digital realms, utilizing techniques such as photolithography, digital manipulation, and traditional painting to enrich the textures and depth of her compositions. Ursyn’s art serves as a bridge between the scientific understanding of data and the aesthetic appreciation of visual arts, challenging observers to perceive the world through a blend of nature’s randomness and human-designed order through a scientific and artistic lens.

name: Steve Jobs Announces the iPhone
desc: On January 9, 2007, Steve Jobs changed the world by announcing the iPhone. The touchscreen device combined the previously wildly popular iPod with a camera, web browsing and other Apple native “apps.” Prior to this, phones were largely utilitarian devices that mostly served as communication devices. Overnight, Jobs replaced this useful-but-not-extraordinary hardware with a supercomputer. The effect that this had—not only on creativity but on our relationship with machines and the digital—is profound practically beyond hyperbole. As mentioned many times in this Timeline, Casey Reas mentioned several pre-conditions for NFTs in human history, including the dematerialization of the art object beginning in the 1960s and the rise of mass media art—coupled with our changing relationship with the machine and mechanical devices, as this author argues—in the 1970s and ’80s that paved the way for the NFT and digital art’s potential mass adoption. The next key step, according to Reas, is the sudden ubiquitous computer power afforded to billions of people on the planet in the form of a computer in their pocket. A gigantic leap in this development is the announcement of the first iPhone. Another theme of this Timeline is the challenges of accessibility of computers, dating back to Vera Molnar needing to sneak into Parisian mainframe premises to access one. Again, overnight, that issue, on a conceptual level, disappeared. The pathway to billions having access to a computer became apparent. It would take time to realize but the effects on human creativity and expression are still only being reached on a superficial level.

name: Tumblr Launched
desc: Launched on 1 March 2007, Tumblr , founded by David Karp with lead developer Marco Arment , served as a critical place for the presentation and distribution of digital art from the mid- to late-2000s. The microblogging site served a similar function two decades ago to sites like Instagram and Twitter today. Tumblr serves as an important step in the pre-conditions for NFTs, as well as it combined with the emergence of smartphones, the iPhone having been announced two months earlier and released that June, to transform how digital media was consumed and shared. With the same iPhones but simply the more popular Instagram emerging as the distribution method of choice, we are still living with the smartphone-social-media-fication of digital art that largely began these first two months of 2007.

name: Allison Parrish Launches Everyword
desc: Allison Parrish launches @everyword , a Twitter poetry bot tasked with tweeting “every word in the English language, in alphabetical order, one word at a time, every thirty minutes.” The bot completed its mission in June 2014. -Sasha Stiles

name: Casey Reas and Ben Fry Publish Processing Textbook
desc: In order to lay out “our vision for how Processing could be used in a university classroom,” Casey Reas and Ben Fry published the Processing textbook, Processing: a programming handbook for visual designers and artists. The textbook served as an essential guide to introduce computer programming to those within the visual arts community. This book leveraged six years of software development and educational insights gained from Reas’s teaching at UCLA and Fry’s time at the MIT Media Lab and Carnegie Mellon . Designed for individuals with minimal coding experience, the book guides those who are keen on exploring interactive and visual software creation. Through tutorials, professional project interviews and extension sections, the book thoroughly discusses the integration of software with arts like photography, drawing, animation and more. This and other texts, such as the earliest one by Ira Greenberg , helped with the practicalities of teaching Processing once it was already initiated.

name: Cory Arcangel Begins His Photoshop Gradients
desc: Cory Arcangel ’s Photoshop Gradient and Smudge Tool Demonstration would go on to become some of the most well known software-based work of the decade. Arcangel continues his work exploring gradients to this day (2024) and the work has been acquired by the Whitney Museum and the Smithsonian American Art Museum. Arcangel became known a few years prior for his work creating videos from old video games, “applying archaeology to historical computer technology of the 1980s,” according to Thaddaeus Ropac, his gallery.
subjects: photoshop gradient and smudge tool demonstration

name: Wack! Art and the Feminist Revolution, Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles
desc: Organized by MOCA Curator Connie Butler , this was the first major museum exhibition to comprehensively examine the global impact and legacy of feminist art from 1965 to 1980. This pivotal era, marked by intense feminist activism and creativity, is explored through a diverse array of media including painting, sculpture, photography, film, video and performance. The exhibition features works from approximately 120 artists across 21 countries, highlighting the intercontinental connections and themes that emerged from feminist art practice during this period. The exhibition included important digital, generative and participatory works by women artists such as Lynn Hershman Leeson , Yoko Ono and Yvonne Rainer respectively.
subjects: wack! art and the feminist revolution

name: All Streets by Ben Fry
desc: Perhaps Fry’s most well-known work and a standout work of data visualization, All Streets is a compelling visual representation of every road in the lower 48 states of the United States , totaling over 26 million individual road segments. The work demonstrates the power of code to convey detail and texture with line that is also based on reality. Created initially as example code for a student in 2006, this project vividly illustrates the nation’s infrastructure without the use of traditional geographic features such as state outlines. The roads themselves form an emergent map, highlighting population densities and natural barriers like mountains. The work appeared as an example in Fry’s 2007 book Visualizing Data. The work, based on data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s TIGER/Line files, achieves visualization through Processing , which Fry co-created with Casey Reas .

name: RMB City by Cao Fei
desc: In the most well-known proto-Metaverse work, conceived by artist Cao Fei in the virtual world of Second Life, RMB City was a vibrant exploration of urban and cultural evolution within a fictional online Chinese metropolis. Opening to the public in 2009 and active until 2011, this digital playground melded symbols of Chinese reality with futuristic visions, featuring floating architecture and surreal landscapes. The online, open space was available to the public via avatar to explore. While the work was active, through her avatar, China Tracy, Cao Fei curated events, exhibitions, and installations that attracted a global audience. The project was both a social experiment and an artistic commentary, reflecting on China’s rapid urban transformation and the blurring lines between virtual spaces and real-world dynamics while anticipating major upcoming trends in immersive environments like the metaverse. The work has been exhibited at MoMA ’s PS1.

name: VVEBCAM by Petra Cortright
desc: The important work of software-badsed art was recorded on webcam by Post-Internet artist Petra Cortright is in the collection of MoMA , where it was part of the 2020 gallery of the collection, “Search Engines.” This seminal digital artwork explores the interface of self-presentation and digital manipulation. Departing from traditional video art and selfie-culture, Cortright presents herself impassively before a webcam, interacting with floating clip art that occasionally obscures her face. Originally crafted for YouTube , VVEBCAM subverts viewer expectations cultivated by the platform’s search and comment functions. By embedding keywords related to erotic or controversial content, Cortright manipulated viewer engagement, turning an artistic video into a critique of online voyeurism and the unexpected disruptions of digital culture.

name: “Evolution and Collective Intelligence of the Electric Sheep” by Scott Draves
desc: This article, released in the book The Art of Artificial Evolution, showcases Draves’s innovative use of distributed computing via a screensaver that animates and evolves fractal art, the Electric Sheep that Draves began in 1999. These sheep are created and evolved through a genetic algorithm influenced by the preferences of thousands of users across a network of 40,000 computers. Users can vote on, modify, and even design sheep, integrating human creativity with artificial evolution. This ongoing project, inspired by the SETI@Home distributed screensaver, melds technology with participatory art, offering a dynamic exploration of aesthetics through collective user engagement and sophisticated algorithmic processes. The work also anticipates much of the neural-network based AI art of today and was based on the ideas of Karl Sims . The system reached its peak in this decade with 450,000 participants.
subjects: evolution and collective intelligence of the electric sheep

name: Satoshi Nakamoto publishes Bitcoin Whitepaper
desc: Satoshi Nakamoto ’s bitcoin.org is important to the story of digital art as it was the first conceptualization of a decentralized blockchain. Decentralization was long part of the net.art global ethos, along with an anti-authority mindset, lerandom.art , specifically Bitcoin. He elaborates, “In retrospect, people think of net.art as websites and HTML but it was more diffuse than that. Websites are the things that can easily survive after the fact, but it was all kinds of performances, events, software or tools that people could work with. Net.art was just an element in a broader form of digital experimentation and digital creativity that was happening and that broader ethos was very much about decentralization, anti-authoritarianism, bottom-up approaches and anti-surveillance. Then I started seeing with Bitcoin, especially at that early time, a very cypherpunk, anti-authoritarian project. It was easy to connect with that for me. I definitely saw this in that same vein.” But it also had an enormous impact on digital art, as quickly artists would begin exploring the intersection of blockchains and art. McCoy himself released some of the earliest proto-NFTs on NameCoin, Bitcoin fork, in 2014. This list also extend to Rhea Myers early Bitcoin art experiments, and Sarah Meyohas ’s Bitchcoin from 2015. As for the landmark paper itself, “Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System” introduced the concept of Bitcoin and the mechanics of a decentralized digital currency to the world in the midst of the worst financial crisis since arguably the Great Depression. The paper proposed a long-sought solution to the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network, which timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof-of-work. This forms a record that is computationally impractical to change, creating a robust ledger without the need for a trusted third party. Nakamoto’s introduction of Bitcoin fundamentally challenged traditional notions of currency and financial systems in an era of uncertainty.

name: Bitcoin Genesis Block
desc: The Bitcoin genesis block executed by Satoshi Nakamoto demonstrated the workability of Bitcoin as more than just a concept. As explained above, Bitcoin would go on to play a crucial role in the evolution of digital art by aligning with the net.art ethos of decentralization and anti-authoritarianism. This ethos resonated with digital artists who saw Bitcoin’s potential for anti-surveillance, bottom-up creative expression. Kevin McCoy , linking these philosophies, was among the artists exploring blockchain’s application in digital art, leading to early forms of NFTs and innovative projects like Bitchcoin . Nakamoto’s paper not only proposed a solution to digital currency’s double-spending problem but also challenged the traditional financial systems during a global crisis, embedding blockchain as a tool for artistic and financial disruption.

name: ImageNet Launches
desc: Conceived by Fei-Fei Li at Princeton University, ImageNet launched in 2009 as a pivotal image database aimed at enhancing machine learning capabilities in image recognition. Spanning 3.2 million annotated images at launch and over 14 million today, it established a new benchmark through the annual ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC), accelerating the adoption of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). This tool for advancing computer vision played a significant role in the development of AI, GANs and AI art, making it one of the most impactful moments of the decade. ImageNet stands as perhaps the decade’s most meaningful contribution to the development of AI and AI art that would explode in the following decade.
subjects: imagenet large scale visual recognition challenge (ilsvrc)

name: First ART && CODE Conference Organized by Golan Levin
desc: Organized by Golan Levin to promote software-arts education, the conference took place from March 7-9, 2009, at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh , focusing on “programming environments for artists, young people, and the rest of us.” It attracted 234 attendees from 7 countries and 23 U.S. states, ranging in age from 11 to 75. Participants included middle-school teachers, computer science professors, European C++ hackers and students from various educational backgrounds. It featured 26 workshops across 11 different arts-programming languages and lectures by fifteen innovators revolutionizing software-arts education. This gathering highlighted the expansive interest and diverse applications of coding in creative and educational contexts. Levin spoke to me about the importance of the conference : “I also helped organize conferences like Art && Code, where I was bringing people together to have conversations about what it means to make open-source software tools for the arts. In 2009 I ran the very first Art && Code and it’s ongoing to this day . The conference brought together the people who were creating programming environments for artists. Zach was there, Casey was there and Ben was there. Luke DuBois was there from Max/MSP/Jitter. Dan Shiffman was there. It was an interesting group of folks working on all sorts of different tools. This was one of the first times I was able to organize something that leveraged my resources and ability to bring people together to have conversations to advance the state of the art in open-source software toolkits for the arts.”

name: scoreLight by Alvaro Cassinelli, Masatoshi Ishikawa, Yusaku Kuribara and Daito Manabe
desc: The innovative work from Japan explored the intersection of visual art and sound by transforming doodles and three-dimensional objects into musical sequences. The instrument, which operates without cameras or projectors, employs a laser to trace contours much like a stylus reads a vinyl record, but with visual forms generating the sound. Users can influence pitch by altering the inclination of lines or rotating the drawing, while tempo varies with contour length. This method reflects the continued evolution of interactive art, reminiscent of earlier explorations like the reactive installations of Myron Krueger in the 1970s. scoreLight extends these concepts into the auditory realm, merging sculptural visuals and sound in a fluid, interactive experience.

name: MuirMcNeil founded
desc: Founded by Paul McNeil and Hamish Muir , MuirMcNeil uses software to explore parametric design systems in typography and graphic design. Their work can be seen as generative typography or generative design. The pair have spoken to Eye Magazine about a lack of acceptance from peers of their algorithmic-derived methodology, echoing a lot of early criticism of computer art, with their work referred to “as something that anybody could do—as if there’s no real quality to it.”

name: “A Philosophy of Computer Art” by Dominic Lopes
desc: This book critically examines the unique characteristics of computer art, setting a new theoretical foundation for understanding its place in the art world. Lopes challenges traditional art concepts like meaning, form and expression, positing that computer art requires a shift in focus towards interactivity and user engagement. His analysis underscores the distinct roles of the computer artist and the user, which diverge significantly from those of conventional artists and viewers, reflecting ideas that extend to cybernetics and the information theory of Abraham Moles and Norbert Weiner.

name: Desire of Codes, Seiko Mikami
desc: Seiko Mikami ’s interactive installation Desire of Codes premiered at the Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM), critically merging human sensory perceptions with digital surveillance technology to reflect on the pervasive encoding in an information-oriented society. The installation featured wall-mounted sculptures made of human skin-like silicone engraved with barcodes, which moved in response to audience movement, visualizing the intimate and often unseen interactions between human behavior and digital tracking systems. Enhanced with a matrix of sensors, mini light spots, and surveillance cameras, the artwork dynamically mapped visitor movements, illustrating the blurriness between organic human identities and digital data profiles. This exhibition not only underscored Mikami’s long-standing themes around the integration of technology with human corporeal form but also served as a poignant commentary on privacy, desire and control in a digital age, positioning her as a pivotal figure in contemporary media art. The work anticipates the body-surveillance work of contemporaneous digital artists such as Operator .
subjects: yamaguchi center for arts and media (ycam)

name: Enter the Turbo-Charged 2010s
desc: Epoch AI separates AI history into three eras based on compute trends. Epoch dates the start of the Deep Learning Era to somewhere between 2010 and 2012. This year thus marks a hugely significant turning point in AI, as the decade in some ways resembles the 1990s of the Internet and the 1960s’ transition from the analog to the digital, featuring several key AI developments, including the breakthrough of Convolutional Neural Networks and the invention of Diffusion models , GANs and DeepDream . For more context, we suggest [watching or listening ( transcript ) to our Ch 9 Artist Discussion with Tyler Hobbs , Helena Sarin , Rhea Myers and Gene Kogan .] In several areas beyond AI this decade takes the themes from our previous chapter(s) and expands upon them with renewed vigor, due to a decade of robust technological growth. As introduced many times previously, AI and blockchain-based art have finally become more prominent parts of this story in a decade marked by ubiquitous social media, renewed institutional interest and a continued boom in tooling developments. While NFTs would not gain popularity until the following decade—and chapter—their introduction and impact begin here. We follow their evolution in detail throughout the decade, examining the themes and developments that continue to shape our story today. This is also a decade broadly defined by growth and a historically low interest rate environment. Following the previous decade’s twin American-led wars and Global Financial Crisis (GFC) in 2008–2009, the 2010s marked a resetting of the geopolitical-financial order that had settled post-Cold War. For our story, the technology sector experienced the boom in the 2010s it had failed to realize in the previous decade following the dot-com bust, wars and GFC. In the GFC’s aftermath, interest rates remained at historically low levels at 0.25% for half the decade. The Nasdaq index increased over 300% from 2010 to 2019 and the Nasdaq 100 increased nearly 400%, led by growth in the rapidly rising tech giants of Apple , Google , Facebook , Amazon and Netflix. This technological leap partly explains—and is a result of—corresponding tech developments and compute power increases in the decade. These developments unlocked our ambitions for AI, which had laid dormant as theory until the tech caught up. What this growth in tech signified—and further spurred—was humanity’s broader adoption of technology across the globe, as computing and network speeds that were unthinkable just a few years ago became possible due to the global proliferation of smartphones. Our pendulum-esque relationship with technology shifted once more—with the latest nadir coming in the '70s, marked mostly by fear—to now blind acquiescence. Smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, VR headsets and a growing number of delightful consumer tech devices meant that the rise of mass media and tech devices in our homes—which this author has mentioned dozens of times in previous chapters—skyrocketed this decade. Not only were tech devices found in our homes, beginning in earnest in the 1980s in the developed world, they were now constantly on our person. They were in our pockets, on our wrists, in our bags and even on our face. They were now part of us, a trend that does not appear to be slowing, which artists like Lauren Lee McCarthy , Sougwen Chung and Tyler Hobbs are responding to in this decade. Humanity’s relationship with technology was different. This Timeline is the story—going very far back—of how that happened and an examination of our dynamic relationship with technology throughout history. This chapter is the story of how that relationship turned a corner.

name: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge
desc: This competition would play an out-sized role in this story, as the little-known event was responsible for the decade’s most important machine vision breakthrough in 2012, when deep convolutional neural networks, a technique first built in the 1980s, won the competition outright. ImageNet was also responsible for Neural Style Transfers in 2015. The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) began in 2010 and lasted annually until 2017. The competition evaluated algorithms for large scale object detection and image classification. It utilized a subset of the vast ImageNet dataset—mentioned in the previous as an “All-Time Top Moment” and critical in the development of AI art—which at this point included over 10 million labeled images across over 10,000 categories. The competition aimed to benchmark advancements in computer vision with participants' algorithms identifying objects in unlabeled test images, producing a list of probable categories. This challenge drove significant progress in image recognition technologies, fostering innovation and providing a platform for researchers to compare their work against state-of-the-art methods in object detection and image annotation.
subjects: imagenet large scale visual recognition challenge (ilsvrc)

name: Three.js Released
desc: Three.js, a JavaScript library for creating 3D animations was initially released on April 24, 2010 by Ricardo Cabello, otherwise known as mrdoob. In 1996, Cabello started working with his brother in the demoscene when he was only twelve or thirteen years old. For the next ten-plus years, he cut his teeth in the demoscene, creating 3-D worlds in his graphics that would form the basis of his motivation to create Three.js. Three.js—along with Cinder and p5.js —would form the basis of a second wave of creative coding tools in the decade of the 2010s, following the catalyst that was Processing in 2001.

name: Cinder Launched
desc: Cinder is an open-source creative coding software tool developed by Andrew Bell and released to the public in 2010. With a C++ based programming library, Cinder is comparable to the similarly C++ based openFrameworks , which Zach Lieberman began developing around 2004 and 2005 with Theo Watson and Arturo Castro .

name: iPad Announced
desc: If the previous decade saw the launch of “smart devices” and “social media 1.0” with Apple ’s iPhone and Facebook , the 2010s saw revamped iterations of these phenomena almost immediately. 2010 saw the launch of Apple’s iPad and Instagram , redefining the second generations of devices and social. In many ways, the year demonstrated society’s transformed relationship with mass media, ushering in the rise of mass-media art by the decade’s end. After years of speculation about the Apple Tablet, Apple finally announced the iPad in January 2010. The event, conducted by Steve Jobs in one of his last great Apple announcements, showcased a category-creating tablet that surpassed many expectations in terms of the device’s instant popularity and the way it would impact art with its enhanced flexibility. Procreate was launched in 2011, enabling artists to leverage the iPad as a canvas and forever impacting digital art, particularly 1/1 practices.

name: Instagram Launches
desc: Social medial 2.0 began in earnest with Instagram . Along with Apple ’s iPad, Instagram’s launch saw the second generation of device and social, now married in an eternal embrace, with a photo-centered update that appealed to a more youthful demographic. The two cases of Facebook and Instagram demonstrate the rapid changes in taste for social media users, as after only a few years of dominance, Instagram’s rapid rise prompted Zuckerberg’s Facebook to purchase the startup in 2012 for $1 billion. Instagram would be joined by TikTok in 2016, which continued the transition on social media towards richer media, from text on Twitter to still images on Instagram and video on TikTok.
