name: onformative Founded
desc: Founded by Julia Laub and Cedric Kiefer , onformative is a studio that focuses on digital generative art and design. Based in Berlin , onformative is characterized by its unique blend of art, design and technology, producing expressive, algorithmic work. The studio engages in a wide array of projects, from interactive media installations to generative design and dynamic visuals, often collaborating with professionals across various disciplines. By focusing on an emotional approach to digital creativity, onformative continues to find the human in the digital. Their work explores a variety of materiality, showcasing the decade’s tech-led aesthetic from its very beginnings as well as an indication that digital generativity was alive and well prior to NFTs.

name: “Characteristics of pattern formation” by Jeff Jones
desc: Fully titled “Characteristics of pattern formation and evolution in approximations of Physarum transport networks,” this highly influential article would go on to inspire the work of both Sage Jenson and fxhash Founder Baptiste Crespy, ciphrd. Jones’s research analyzes the complex pattern formation and evolution exhibited by the slime mold Physarum polycephalum. Through the use of simple particle-like agents that mimic chemotaxis, this study illustrates how spontaneous and dynamic transport networks can emerge. Critically for generative art, the research highlights how adjusting model parameters can influence the complexity of emergent behaviors such as circular contractions and network path bifurcation. The study showcases a variety of pattern formations, including spots, stripes and labyrinthine structures. Jones’s work not only aligns with classical theories of biological pattern formation but also suggests potential applications in unconventional computational methods through emergent pattern formation that would be realized by artists interested in artificial life. The paper is cited by ciphrd in his work Ethereal Microcosm.

name: The Artist Is Present by Marina Abramovic at MoMA
desc: Marina Abramović creates analog, performance- and system-based work that elevates audience participation and the role of the viewer in the vein of interactive software art. Her work combines famed video art pioneer Nam June Paik ’s interest in participation with Sol LeWitt ’s instruction-based practice to think systematically about art without the use of code. Abramović’s The Artist Is Present (2010) exemplifies her systems-based approach, as the work is ultimately instruction and rules-based, as each participant in The Artist Is Present is given the following instructions: “Sit silently with the artist for a duration of your choosing.” Performed on every day the Museum was open across two and a half grueling months, The Artist is Present is a dematerialized and serial work of generative art that emphasizes participation. The piece demonstrates the similarities between digital and conceptual art. Abramović understands the power of unpredictability within systems.

name: Menstruation Machine by Sputniko!
desc: In what can be seen as a material generative system, Multimedia artist Sputniko! introduced the Menstruation Machine, a provocative wearable device designed to simulate the pain and bleeding of menstruation. The work is one of the most well-known in the decade, even appearing at MoMA the following year at the exhibition Talk to Me: Design and the Communication between People and Objects curated by Paola Antonelli . The machine, resembling a chastity belt, is equipped with electrodes and a blood-dispensing system, allowing anyone—regardless of gender—to experience a five-day menstrual cycle. Accompanied by a video narrative, the project challenges societal norms around gender and the biological experience of menstruation. By externalizing and publicizing this private process, Sputniko! opens a dialogue on the intersections of identity, technology, and the future of human biology.

name: hello world by Kazumasa Teshigawara (qubibi)
desc: Shown at the Museum of Digital Arts ( MuDA ) in Zurich several years later in 2017 and generating animated imagery in real-time, hello world explores the visual language of primordial beginnings. Its fluctuating forms mimic life, death, gender, feelings and more, expressing the transitory nature of the universe. Qubibi’s first piece of generative art is still in use by the artist today, forming the basis of the majority of his subsequent work.

name: Color of words by Gene Kogan
desc: This early work of machine learning art by the legendary Kogan explored the implicit colors associated with words and concepts. By running a set of words through a Google image search, Kogan analyzed the color distributions of the first hundred images that appeared. Using a self-organizing map (SOM) algorithm and a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), he synthesized these colors into a map of their visual representations. The project categorized the results into themes like seasons, biomes, holidays and politics. This quite early (pre-2014) instance of machine learning in creative expression highlights the lesser-known work of Kogan, how instrumental early image-classification attempts were and uncovers the hidden color palettes of language through data clustering and visualization techniques.

name: Written Images by Martin Fuchs and Peter Bichsel
desc: This book represents an attempt at a generative physical book, as each “programmed book” was a copy uniquely generated via digital printing. This innovative project incorporated contributions from over 70 media artists who created generative software, resulting in varied visual outputs. Each book featured a generative prologue by Bruce Sterling and individual artwork descriptions. The book was crowdfunded on Kickstarter and was a perhaps too-early glimpse at what a generative future may look like.

name: Media Archaeology: Approaches, Applications, and Implications by Erkki Huhtamo and Jussi Parikka
desc: Erkki Huhtamo ’s concept of “Topos” is a fascinating idea in the realm of media studies. “Topos” can be thought of as a kind of recurring theme or a common pattern that keeps showing up in different forms of media throughout history. They argue a familiar story or image keeps reappearing, even when technology changes. Huhtamo’s concept of “Topos” identifies these timeless building blocks of media culture, highlighting their adaptability across various forms of media—from ancient cave paintings to modern digital platforms. By examining these recurring themes, such as the hero’s journey, the book reveals the connections between ancient, old and new media. This study offers insights into how media shapes culture over time, uncovering the persistent patterns that endure despite technological advancements. Critically, for this Timeline, an example of “topoi” is the human urge to express creatively with systems, exploring the tension between order and randomness. Topos suggest a theory for connecting these major themes—and moments—of the Timeline. This thinking extends to the Timeline’s first moment about ancient systems cave carvings, to Islamic tiling art, Mozart, Bridget Riley , Sol LeWitt , Vera Molnár , Yoko Ono and Kim Asendorf .
subjects: media archaeology: approaches, applications, and implications

name: Len Sassaman ASCII Tribute on Bitcoin
desc: Mined on July 30 as part of Bitcoin Block 138725, this work stands as some of the earliest on-chain art and it is ASCII. The work itself is a tribute to Leonard “Len” Harris Sassaman. Sassaman was a prominent cypherpunk, cybersecurity expert and privacy advocate who passed away just a few weeks before this ASCII tribute appeared in his honor.

name: NONOTAK Formed
desc: Formed by Noemi Schipfer and Takami Nakamoto , NONOTAK merges the creative fields of visual arts and architecture with music. The duo specializes in light and sound installations, producing immersive and ethereal environments that challenge and envelop the viewer. Their work leverages Nakamoto’s expertise in space, light and sound, alongside Schipfer’s background in animated algorithmic visuals and geometric drawings, creating unique sensory experiences. NONOTAK’s minimalist aesthetic is influenced by architecture and optical art, yet harkens back to the predecessor of digital art, electronic art, which was largely based in lumino-kinetic sculpture.

name: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Unleashed
desc: Arguably the biggest development in machine learning in decades, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs or “ConvNets”) revolutionized machine vision. Their power was deployed for the first time relating to creative expression when the SuperVision algorithm from the University of Toronto used CNNs to win the ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge . Critically, ConvNets were the driving force behind the decade’s upcoming AI developments This paradigm-shifting technique enabled computers to recognize objects with near-human accuracy by using multiple layers of small neuron collections to analyze images. Each layer overlaps and refines the image representation, allowing the system to learn intricate details. Originally conceived of theoretically in the 1980s, CNN research for the thirty years was mostly quiet due to computing restraints. They only gained prominence as computing power advanced, enabling the analysis of the large datasets required. This moments serves as the main milestone in AI art developments in the decade along with GANs in 2014 and DeepDream in 2015. It also highlights the importance of 2009’s ImageNet —covered in the previous chapter—which had a lasting impact on the space due to its Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge that began in 2010.
subjects: imagenet large scale visual recognition challenge (ilsvrc)

name: Ghosts in the Machine at the New Museum, New York
desc: This exhibition examined the evolving reciprocity between humans, machines and art. Occupying the museum’s three main galleries, Ghosts in the Machine traced over fifty years of artistic engagement with technology—from the mechanical to the optical to the virtual. Curated by Massimiliano Gioni and Gary Carrion-Murayari , it featured a diverse array of contemporary and historical works that explore the anthropomorphic qualities projected onto machines. The show included kinetic artworks, experimental films and significant historical installations like Stan VanDerBeek ’s Movie-Drome, exploring how technology reshapes sensory experience and societal roles. The show, like much of generative art, aimed to reconcile the human with the mechanical, updating classic machine-based exhibitions like MoMA ’s Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age. This show featured the work of Bridget Riley , Victor Vasarely and Hans Haacke , three critical mainstream art world figures in the development of generative art.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Manolo Begins Processing Sketches
desc: Manolo Gamboa Naon (aka Manoloide) began his Processing sketches in 2012, according to himself on his github page . Considered a prodigy for his extensive, high-quality ouput, Manolo’s work can be viewed—largely unminted—on his behance page . Manolo would go on to make all of this work open-source by the end of the decade.

name: Rafaël Rozendaal, Into Time with mirrors
desc: Taking a cue from net.art, Rozendaal uses the Internet as his canvas yet his work often conveys multiple materialities. In his 2012 installation Into Time with mirrors at MIS Sao Paulo, the work utilizes broken mirrors strewn on the floor in addition to computers and projectors to portray Rozendaal’s signature bright, hard-edged style, reminiscent of a digital Mondrian.

name: Processing Foundation Begins
desc: Ben Fry , Casey Reas and Daniel Shiffman started the Processing Foundation —more than ten years after Processing’s initial release —to champion software literacy within the arts and artistic expression through technology, particularly for communities traditionally marginalized by the tech industry. Building on the legacy of Processing software, the Foundation aims to support diverse and inclusive access to technology with initiatives like fellowships, public events and summer programs. It emphasizes the philosophy of Free, Libre, Open Source Software (FLOSS) to ensure that learning and creative tools are accessible to all, fostering a space for innovation and self-determination among underrepresented groups.

name: Parallel 1 by Harun Farocki
desc: Included in Casey Reas ’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA as a standout example of computer film, this 16-minute digital video explores the evolution of computer graphics within the larger four-part series Parallel, which examines the genre of computer animation. This segment traces the stylistic history from the simplistic horizontal and vertical lines of early 1980s video games to contemporary efforts toward photorealism. Farocki highlights how initial graphical limitations, once deemed inadequate, have progressively transformed to emulate the complexities of the real world, marking a significant shift in visual representation in digital media.

name: Lauren Lee McCarthy Creates p5.js
desc: Lauren Lee McCarthy created p5.js roughly twelve years after the initial release of Processing in 2001. P5.js is a JavaScript library that revitalizes the goals of the original Processing project for today’s web environment, where JavaScript—quite different from Java, despite their similar names —has become the dominant Internet-based language. Originating from Processing, designed by Ben Fry and Casey Reas between 2000 and 2001 as a Java-based visual language for artists, the evolution to p5.js represents a shift towards more accessible web-native programming. Like Processing, p5.js has the aim of empowering artists to learn coding. Unlike Processing.js, which John Resig released in May 2008 and which translated Java-based sketches to JavaScript, p5.js operates directly in JavaScript, aligning with modern web standards and utilizing browser capabilities without requiring plugins. This development has the benefit for seamless integration of web elements and media, leveraging browser-based tools and enhancing educational and creative opportunities in digital art and design. In this sense of utilizing the web as a canvas, p5.js can be seen as continuing the traditions of net.art and further solidifies the link between net art, software art and blockchain-based art.

name: BANK by Kevin Abosch
desc: BANK by Kevin Abosch is one of the earliest works by the mixed-media and AI artist. BANK is also one of the earliest artistic explorations of the blockchain. The project was a 60-page book in 50 editions that consisted of 500 paired Bitcoin public and private keys. Published in January, these books are relics of blockchain art history.

name: Ascribe Conceptualizes Proto-NFTs
desc: Ascribe conceptualized the concept of owning digital art on a blockchain “like you own bitcoin” throughout 2013, finally launching publicly at the end of 2014. The concept for ascribe emerged from a conversation about art and blockchain between co-founders, sparked by the question, “What if you could own digital art the way you can own Bitcoin?” This idea combined art, technology and finance, leading to a collaboration with digital artist Jonathan Monaghan and the enlistment of Bruce Pon , who had a background in building banks. The team, initially calling the project “Keidom,” developed a prototype by late summer 2013, with Yanislav Malahov contracted for its creation. This early work led to one of the first recorded proto-NFT transactions for a piece of digital art by Monaghan on November 18, 2013. With help from artist Harm van den Dorpel and others, ascribe would rename itself and launch publicly roughly a year after this transcation.

name: Mothership by Jonathan Monaghan
desc: This work is considered to be a prototype for contemporary NFTs, as it is one of the earliest digital artworks to use a blockchain as a decentralized ledger. As for the work itself, Mothership is a video installation engaging in a 15-minute loop of dreamlike visuals and sound. The work navigates the realms between myth and reality, past and future, while humorously intertwining pop culture, anticipating hallmarks of future “NFT art.” Mothership also explores themes of authority, opulence and the pervasive impact of technology in our consumerist culture, with the sardonic work proving to be quite prescient with blockchain as a medium. For our story, Mothership is significant as the first work minted on the beta version of ascribe, the Bitcoin-based registration service, setting a precedent for what would evolve into what know of now as NFTs. This piece, limited to three editions and one artist’s proof, integrates the innovative use of blockchain as a decentralized ledger to authenticate digital art, while presciently commenting on the medium. As both a work and historical artefact, the piece is relatively understudied in the realm of historical NFTs.

name: Beautypi Starts ShaderToy
desc: In January, 2013, Shadertoy.com was created by Pol Jeremias and Inigo Quilez (Beautypi) as a repository for community-shared shaders. For over a decade now, ShaderToy had been a place for those interested in shaders to learn, share and experiment with the notoriously difficult form of coded expression. The community played a significant role in the development of algorithmic art as a place for thousands of users to develop for the love of coded art before it was practically feasible to sell work as NFTs. Jen Lowe and Patricio González Vivo, co-authors of The Book of Shaders , spoke to this author ( Peter Bauman ) about the importance of Shadertoy . Peter Bauman: If somebody sees an art work and is interested in it for any reason, then they learn the work was made by shaders—what would you recommend they do next if they want to dig beyond the surface level and into the process of the work?‍‍ Patricio González Vivo : I recommend reading The Book of Shaders as a primer [laughs.] Then I recommend checking out the work of Inigo and what is out there in Shadertoy . There’s a strong relationship between the shader world and the demoscene. A lot of old demosceners like Inigo Quilez , Mr. Doob and Jaume Sanchez (Clicktorelease) . They all met through shaders. I have found them in my work career around places like Samsung , Apple , Adobe and Oculus . There are all these people who were in this petri dish of the demoscene. That bunch is very interesting because the mentality was very focused on visual and technical hacking in order to make cool, flashy demos.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: Taeyoon Choi, Zach Lieberman, Jen Lowe and Amit Pitaru Co-Found the School for Poetic Computation (SFPC)
desc: After teaching for a decade at Parsons School of Design , where he also studied under Golan Levin , Zach Lieberman helped create the School for Poetic Computation in New York with Taeyoon Choi , Jen Lowe and Amit Pitaru . Co-founder Choi describes SFPC as “an independent, artist-run organization” with a flat structure and bottom-up approach. Leaning into the “poetic” part of the name, the school claims to promote “completely strange, whimsical, and beautiful work—not the sorts of things useful for building a portfolio for finding a job, but the sort of things that will surprise and delight people and help you to keep creating without a job.” The school carries on the traditions of the Bauhaus , MIT’s Media Lab and many other educational institutions to promote the creative side of technology.

name: Jerobeam Fenderson and Hansi3D Begin Oscilloscope Music
desc: Jerobeam Fenderson and Hansi3D started Oscilloscope Music, a project focusing on audiovisual oscilloscope explorations; the OsciStudio software followed in 2017. Reminiscent of Mary Ellen Bute , Ben Laposky and Herbert W. Franke ’s oscilloscope work from the early ’50s, OSCISTUDIO creates audiovisual music where the sound directly creates visuals. They achieve this by feeding the same audio signals sent to speakers into an analog oscilloscope’s X and Y inputs, generating intricate Lissajous figures. The pair’s work stands as an example of how work and equipment from digital art’s distant past could be reimagined.

name: Summer by Olia Lialina
desc: Included in Casey Reas ’s course, 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA , is a standout example of net art and the only piece appearing outside the decade of the ’90s. Summer, nearly twenty years after net.art first appeared, navigates the evolving relationship between art and Internet as speeds and loading time continued to affect the experience of her work. In this interactive piece, an animated loop shows Lialina swinging, integrated into the browser window. Each frame of the animation, though, originates from a different website, making the smoothness of the swing dependent on varying internet speeds and server functionality. This setup exemplifies Lialina’s exploration of how technological infrastructure impacts the experience of art, illustrating her thematic focus on the dependency of digital media experiences on real-time network conditions. Unlike earlier works affected unintentionally by tech evolution, Summer intentionally embeds these dynamics, reflecting the impermanent and fluctuating nature the digital. The work also underscored the reliance of the viewer on a technological layer before one can even access the work. The performance of this technological layer thus inherently becomes a part of the work, a point expertly highlighted in this work by Lialina.

name: Data-Masks (Series) by Sterling Crispin
desc: This late-early example of machine learning art explores the intersection of AI and identity through 3D-printed masks. Artist Sterling Crispin reverse-engineered facial recognition and detection algorithms, creating masks that reflect the way machines perceive human faces. Each mask, produced using genetic algorithms, mirrors the biases and patterns inherent in surveillance technology. Exhibited at ZKM Karlsruhe for GLOBALE: Infosphere in 2015, these works critique the aggressive overdevelopment of biometric surveillance, making invisible power structures visible. The series serves as both a political protest and a poetic reflection on the evolving relationship between humans and the technological "other.” It also highlights the relationship between evolutionary and genetic algorithms on early AI art.

name: Vitalik Buterin Publishes Ethereum Whitepaper
desc: Vitalik Buterin created Ethereum with the Ethereum Whitepaper , marking a pivotal shift in the story of blockchains. This new chain offered several innovations and improvements on Bitcoin and, most importantly for this story—the story of art—the chain’s introduction of smart contracts would lead the way to NFTs and digital ownership. Ethereum’s introduction of smart contracts aimed to decentralize internet applications by enabling developers to build decentralized applications (dApps). Several years later, the ERC-721 Token Standard would implement an API for tokens within smart contracts that allowed for the functionality digital artists had been seeking for decades—and what ascribe and the McCoys had envisioned—transfer and ownership of digital assets. This breakthrough had many critical predecessors but still stands as one of the more significant moments in this story of generative art. Prior to Ethereum, Buterin was already a recognized figure in the crypto community, having co-founded Bitcoin Magazine and contributed to crypto research. Alongside Buterin, key figures like Dr. Gavin Wood , who developed Ethereum’s Solidity programming language, Anthony Di Iorio , Charles Hoskinson and Joseph Lubin significantly shaped Ethereum’s early stages. Ethereum’s vision materialized with its presentation at the 2014 North American Bitcoin Conference in Miami (2014), followed by a successful ICO that raised approximately $18 million in Bitcoin, setting a robust foundation for its development.

name: Jennifer and Kevin McCoy’s Quantum
desc: NFTs Enable Digital Ownership While previous explorations of the blockchain existed prior to Jennifer and Kevin McCoy ’s Quantum —many of them can be found previously on this Timeline—none presented a complete package of what NFTs would be than the McCoys. Quantum was also, critically, publicly explained and presented the following afternoon, after it was “minted” on May 2, 2014. This legendary presentation by Kevin McCoy and Anil Dash at Rhizome ’s Seven on Seven Conference at the New Museum played a fundamental role in Quantum being more well known ten years later than work on ascribe. Quantum highlights the role of chance—fittingly—and communication in art history. What cannot be disputed is that the work played an important—if not truncated—role in priming the world for the concept of digital ownership and transfer. Another important point to highlight is that art and artists played a foundational role in the concept of digital ownership and NFTs. The idea was an artist’s and was publicly announced by an artist at a very well-respected digital art institution ( Rhizome ) and at a museum (New Museum). The work stands as an important piece of Bitcoin and Ethereum art history with its clear ties to Bitcoin (read below) and eventual mint on Ethereum for Christie’s in 2021. Kevin McCoy spoke to this author, Peter Bauman, about what is the first concept of an NFT explained in public and publicly executed : “ Monegraph was doing something special, which was unique, and in many ways warrants a first, in the sense that it was explicitly about provenance and transferable ownership via blockchain records, via blockchain transactions, and that it wasn’t just a one-off system. It was an artist conceptualizing this thing, creating a mechanism for people to do that and showing examples of that. It was the whole package and that whole package hadn’t really been assembled until that time. So the conception of NFTs that swept the world in all the downstream Ethereum-based stuff from 2017 through the 2021 hype cycle was first in Monegraph. In that sense, it’s the first. I’m proud of that fact. I’m happy with that. It’s true that’s the correct history, I think.” I wrote about this moment originally in 2023 for the Bright Moments Tokyo Timeline Poster, including it as one of the ten I chose to represent the entirety of generative art’s history, writing: A growth catalyst for generative art unparalleled in its history, NFTs unlocked the pent up demand for new media art that went unsatisfied for decades due to the complexities of the art form’s ownership.

name: Ian Goodfellow Introduces GANs
desc: In one of this story’s most relevant moments, Ian Goodfellow and his colleagues at the University of Montreal introduced the world to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), revolutionizing—and I don’t use the word lightly—the field of machine learning. GANs consist of two models: a generative model that captures the data distribution, and a discriminative model that estimates the likelihood of a sample being from the training data or the generative model. This setup creates a minimax game, driving both models to improve until the generative model produces indistinguishable data from actual data. GANs are so significant because they allowed artists to realize the dreams of the early cybernetic theorists and artists who sought to produce art autonomously from the learning and feedback of early machines. This thinking extends to artists such as Victor Vasarely , François Morellet and thinkers like Max Bense . GANs improved upon the genetic algorithms of the ’90s and ’00s that had issues scaling with larger data sets. GANs allowed for the neural network training time to greatly improve. Ultimately, GANs allowed for artists to better generate new aesthetic output that better mimicked the related training data.

name: Kathleen and Arthur Breitman Propose Tezos
desc: Arthur Breitman , writing as L.M Goodman, released two Tezos papers in 2014 that proposed and described the Tezos blockchain for the first time. The chain would go on to ICO in 2017 and play a significant role in the history of NFTs with its grassroots digital art community beginning with HEN in early 2021. Seven years before Tezos would greatly influence digital art and NFTs, Breitman’s whitepaper detailed a new decentralized ledger utilizing—like Vitalik Buterin ’s Ethereum—“smart contracts” to automate and secure digital agreements. Unlike Ethereum, Tezos was Their vision for Tezos included features for seamless upgrades and improved security measures, setting it apart from prominent blockchain projects by avoiding hard forks through on-chain governance.

name: Art Post-Internet at UCCA, Beijing
desc: Curated by Karen Archey and Robin Peckham , this exhibition was an important look at the role of networked technology—the Internet—in contemporary art. The exhibition demonstrated how the pervasiveness of the Internet informed all artistic creation. The term the show helped popularize, Post-Internet, was not meant to indicate a time past the Internet; rather, it indicated a now ubiquitous internet-aware mindset. The show was not entirely a celebration of the digital but responded to various aspects of the digital era, such as mass surveillance, the corporatization of aesthetics and the posthuman condition. Organized into themes like distribution, digital language and the physicality of networks, the exhibition featured artists like Cory Arcangel and Hito Steyerl , among others, cementing these artist’s place as leading digital thinkers to this day.

name: Is Art by Rhea Myers
desc: This piece from July 23, 2014, under three months after Quantum is another proto-NFT from 2014, yet it derives inspiration from Duchamp, 1960s Conceptualism and net.art. Other early proto-NFTs include NILIcoin and Quantum from the same year, and Mothership from 2013—all found on the Timeline. The work, published as contract code in 2014 and deployed to Ethereum in 2016, that can be toggled between states of being “art” or “not art” by anyone who sends a transaction to it. This work echoes Marcel Duchamp by reframing a smart contract as a found object. The concept draws from the legacy of 1960s Conceptual Art and 1990s net.art, both of which critically engaged with the systems of their time, using dematerialization, decentralization and interactivity as key elements. Myers’s piece explores how blockchain technology can serve as a modern platform for these ideas, questioning the essence and authentication of art by making its designation as “art” a participatory and dynamic process. The artwork thus not only interrogates the art historical context of blockchain art from its near-beginnings but also the technological and communal frameworks that support and challenge the notion of what constitutes art today. Like the McCoys—and to some extent Kevin Abosch and ascribe—this early attempt at inscribing creativity on the blockchain was rooted in net art and artist-led. Myers spoke to this author ( Peter Bauman ) for Le Random Editorials on the foundations of her work and more. Jason Bailey spoke about how this project was typical of the fragmented nature of art of the blockchain and proto-NFTs at this time. Rather than the community that would eventually form, during this time the work consisted of “individuals playing around with the concept, working on individual projects,” according to Bailey. He continues to say that there was “not much interest and not a movement; not community driven.”

name: NILIcoin by Nili Lerner
desc: Lerner’s pre-community, proto-NFTS—along with work by the McCoys and Rhea Myers were, according to Jason Bailey , the “closest thing to early NFTs” as we now know them. This is the beginning as well, for better or worse, of the association of NFTs with memes and scams. Launched in September 2014 on the Counterparty Bitcoin side-chain, NILICoin was dubbed “art coin” and allowed for the issuance of digital assets against Bitcoin. This enabled trading and ownership verification via blockchain, a clear predecessor of NFT capabilities. NILICoin had aims beyond digital asset ownership, however, as it attempted to foster an entire decentralized monetary ecosystem, unsuccessfully challenging traditional bank credit. Lerner’s work has been heavily influenced by social media and smartphones, exemplifying how those trends combined to create the conditions for NFTs.

name: “Ten Questions Concerning Generative Computer Art” by McCormack et al.
desc: In a text critical to both Philip Galanter ’s and my own understanding of generative art, Jon McCormack and his colleagues examined the complexities and evolving nature of generative computer art in their article in the April 2014 issue of Leonardo . They probe the philosophical and practical aspects of computer-generated art, posing ten pivotal questions about the identity, originality and future of generative art. These questions explore the role of machines in the creative process and challenge traditional notions of artistic authorship and creativity. The article positions generative art at a crossroads of technology and traditional artistry, contemplating its potential to redefine artistic practices in the digital age, unaware that twin revolutions—I don’t use the word lightly—were simultaneously occurring in AI and blockchain that would forever change generative art, making the questions raised by McCormack even more pertinent to consider.
subjects: ten questions concerning generative computer art

name: Akihiro Kubota’s ARTSAT1:INVADER Launches Generative Art Satellite
desc: ARTSAT project, a collaboration between Tama Art University and The University of Tokyo , launched the world’s first art satellite, ARTSAT1: INVADER. This 10 cm cube satellite, weighing 1.85 kg, was actually a work of generative art. It successfully carried out artistic missions from orbit, including generating and transmitting synthesized voice, music and poems from space. The satellite was also “cybernetic” in that it could incorporate feedback, capturing and transmitting image data and communicating with the ground via a chatbot. ARTSAT1 was in space for around six months and demonstrates humanity’s curiosity to dream about space and art—perhaps more seriously since space dominated the imagination of technologists in the ’60s.

name: Tyler Hobbs Starts Writing About Generative Art
desc: With his essay “Randomness in the Composition of Artwork,” Tyler Hobbs began a period of influential writing on generative art that continues to this day. Fittingly for Le Random and this Timeline, the first word published by Hobbs was “randomness.” These are some of the earliest attempts by the upcoming generation of generative art to describe generativity as we know it today. The essay highlights what’s exciting and compelling about generative art—emergence, surprise and endless experimentation—setting up Hobbs as a leading voice in the movement nearly a decade before an increase in his popularity. His Continuity series, also from 2014, represents the earliest state of the artist’s visual practice.
subjects: randomness in the composition of artwork

name: Stephanie Dinkins Creates AI-Powered Chatbot
desc: “Artist Stephanie Dinkins embarks on a “quest for friendship” with the humanoid android BINA48, turning her dialogues with this AI-powered chatbot into the seminal art project “Conversations with BINA48” , ‘an examination of the codification of social, cultural and future histories at the intersection of technology, race, gender and social equity.’” -Sasha Stiles

name: Diffusion Model Invented at Stanford by Jascha Sohl-Dickstein
desc: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein , a postdoc at Stanford’s Neural Dynamics and Computation Lab, invented the diffusion model, a massively significant to this day technique in machine learning. Diffusion models are the driving force behind our contemporary text-to-image models. Developed with Eric A. Weiss , Niru Maheswaranathan and the neuroscientist Surya Ganguli , the physics-based model leverages non-equilibrium thermodynamics to reverse the flow of time in a diffusion process. This novel approach transforms noise into data by training a neural network, allowing for highly detailed and accurate data generation. The diffusion model has since become a foundational tool in AI art, significantly impacting fields such as image and text generation, exemplified by its use in advanced models like DALL-E and Stable Diffusion .

name: Google’s Alexander Mordvintsev Launches DeepDream
desc: 2015 stands as a monumental year in this story—up there with 1965 (digital art’s public beginnings) and 1995 (net.art)—as the year AI art properly took off. GANs had been introduced a year earlier and served as a primary catalyst along with this seminal moment, the launch of Google ’s DeepDream. These events ensured 2015’s place in history with important work by AI legends Gene Kogan , Sougwen Chung , Alexander Mordvinstev, Mario Klingemann and more. As for DeepDream itself, On June 18, 2015, Google researchers Alexander Mordvintsev , Christopher Olah and Mike Tyka introduced it, transforming our understanding of neural networks. After a restless night, Mordvintsev conceptualized an algorithm that allowed neural networks to "dream.” By inputting images into a ConvNet and halting midway, he revealed the hidden layers' intricate patterns, producing surreal, psychedelic visuals. His breakthrough—along with the invention of GANs and advancements in text-to-image models—demonstrated the creative potential of AI and hinted at how it would come to dominate conversations in digital art. DeepDream’s high-profile launch at Google captivated the tech world, highlighting AI’s capability to generate art and offering profound insights into neural networks' inner workings.

name: From the Archives: Art and Technology at LACMA, 1967–1971 at Los Angeles County Museum of Art
desc: From the Archives: Art and Technology at LACMA , 1967–1971 offered insights into the museums influential Art & Technology Program and exhibition , which was mentioned previously on this timeline (1971). Curated by Jennifer King , the exhibition features photographs, prints, artist books and proposals from twelve artists, including Channa Horwitz and Robert Rauschenberg . Originally conceived by Maurice Tuchman in the late ’60s, the program paired artists with corporations like IBM and Disney , fostering innovative artworks using materials like Mylar and lasers. Despite bureaucratic challenges and Vietnam War controversies, the program’s legacy endures, as evidenced by this show and 2023’s Coded at LACMA. The show demonstrates not only the lengthy institutional interest from LACMA in art and technology, but also emphasizes a time when the distinction between traditional and new media artists began blurring.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982
from the archives: art and technology at lacma, 1967–1971

name: Ethereum Officially Launches
desc: Around two years after the release of Vitalik Buterin ’s Whitepaper, on July 30, 2015, Ethereum initiated its launch process with its genesis block. This release was known as “Frontier” and marked Ethereum’s experimental beginnings. A key breakthrough in this release was the first instance of a working smart contract nearly twenty years after they were theoretically proposed by Nick Szabo . Ethereum’s contracts run in the Ethereum Virtual Machine; the ERC-20 token interface followed in November 2015. These “smart contract” are automatically-executing, based on algorithmic processes and inscribed on the blockchain, distinguishing Ethereum’s capabilities from Bitcoin.

name: Patricio González Vivo and Jen Lowe Teach the World Shaders
desc: Patricio González Vivo and Jen Lowe ’s incredibly versatile open-source project, The Book of Shaders , has been published in twelve languages and applies to various environments, including Processing , openFrameworks and Three.js . The online book and toolkit have revolutionized the creative environment since their initial publications by teaching the world about the transformative power of fragment shaders. These short programs offer enhanced control and faster rendering to creative coders, game developers and engineers alike. Lowe and Gonzalez Vivo spoke to this author ( Peter Bauman ) about their book, saying: Patricio González Vivo: After finishing my MFA, I got my first job. At the same time, I was still teaching a class at Parsons.‍ Jen Lowe: He needed materials for teaching that class. Then we thought, “If you’re going to write the materials, why not make a big open-source book that’s available to everyone?” Back then, there was not anything I’m aware of that made shaders accessible.‍ Patricio González Vivo: Shaders was this very niche knowledge. There were a lot of industry trade secrets between computer science, PhDs and very specific people working in the game industry. This knowledge was very gated. By then, I had been working with OpenGL and shaders for four years. Through the friction of having to learn everything and research how things were working, I decided that it would be awesome to democratize this knowledge. By then, Jen was pregnant with our first son so I had extra anxiety.

name: Shunsuke Takawo Begins his Daily Coding
desc: Takawo began his habit of daily creative coding using Processing in 2015. By 2019, he transitioned to p5.js , sharing his work on OpenProcessing under a Creative Commons license. Through his dedicated practice, in which we has published around two-thousand sketches, he has found the ability to express himself with code as natural as that of spoken language, like his native Japanese. He told Right Click Save : “Through my #dailycoding I have come to regard programming languages as natural languages, as much as they are also sophisticated algorithms.” Takawo’s work—beyond its scope, diversity and generosity—celebrates experimentation. He employs various techniques, blending learned approaches to color and composition. His practice centers on exploring by combining different methods daily. Takawo’s daily coding work not only pushed him to continuously evolving his artistic process, but by making his work open source, he has also greatly contributed to the generative art community internationally. This moment also demonstrates the lasting strength of the forces highlighted in the previous chapter—decade—such as the role of social media in art and technology. As we can see, its role would on strengthen as a greater percentage of the population became comfortable seeing it as a way to share art.

name: Harm van den Dorpel Opens Left Gallery
desc: Left Gallery—a visionary early nft-based playform, according to Casey Reas —was started by Harm van den Dorpel and Paloma Rodríguez Carrington . Van den Dorpel got the idea after this partner, Carrington, began working at Ascribe in 2015 , the early NFT, which we touched on previously in the Timeline. Van den Dorpel explained his motivations for creating Left Gallery on Outland: “I thought this was interesting and something with great potential. If it worked for me, it could also work for other artists. I started asking around in my peer group—other artists whose work I felt was important but never had a connection to any art market. There was some possibility of financial success, but it was limited because the majority of people didn’t understand what the blockchain or a token was—the term NFT didn’t yet exist. It was then we started Left Gallery, to build a market and provide infrastructure for artists working with software.” The gallery would go on to influence Casey Reas to create a2p (artist-to-peer ) in 2019 and Feral File in 2020.

name: Drawing Operations by Sougwen Chung
desc: Drawing Operations saw Chung’s first exploration at the intersection of human and robotic collaboration in art, recalling the work of Harold Cohen yet asking modified questions. Partnering with a robotic arm named D.O.U.G._1 (Drawing Operations Unit: Generation_1), Chung created—and to this day creates with similar robots—synchronized drawing performances where the robot mimics her gestures in real-time through computer vision. This ongoing study investigates and questions the dynamics of human-robot interaction, blending behavioral empathy with artistic expression. Performed at venues such as The National Art Center in Tokyo and Redbull Studios in New York , Drawing Operations exemplifies the evolving dialogue between technology, authorship and AI.

name: Etheria Is First Ethereum NFT
desc: Released shortly after Ethereum’s mainnet launch, Etheria, the first Ethereum NFTs, consisted of a plot of virtual land. While several years before NFTs became popular, Etheria was quite modestly known until the crypto bull run of 2021. While not properly art itself, these were important pre-conditions for the upcoming art on Ethereum, beginning two years later with Curio Cards and CryptoPunks in 2017.

name: Journey through the Layers of the Mind by Memo Akten
desc: AI art pioneer Akten utilized Google ’s DeepDream algorithm, exploring the intersection of artificial intelligence and human perception. By running a neural network trained on over 20,000 image categories backwards, DeepDream generated surreal images that amplified the neural activation patterns triggered by the input. The resulting visuals, demonstrate AI’s signature dream-like aesthetic, while reflecting AI’s attempts at pattern recognition, much like Rorschach (inkblot) tests for humans. Akten’s work investigates themes of confirmation bias and cognitive projection, highlighting how both artificial and biological systems seek and affirm meaning. His later work in this decade, including his Learning to See Series (2017) used GANs and custom software to make work with a strong conceptual foundation. It invites the viewer to understand how AI learns and works so that they may reflect on our such abilities. Akten stands out in the decade for his work demonstrating the creative potential of AI—machine learning, deep learning and GANs.
subjects: journey through the layers of the mind

name: Oscar Schwartz gives a TEDx Talk on Computational Poetics
desc: “Writer and poet Oscar Schwartz gives a TEDx Talk on computational poetics, exploring the human reaction to poetry generated by machines.” -Sasha Stiles

name: Rare Pepes by Joe Looney
desc: According to Jason Bailey , 2016 saw the introduction of the first community NFTs. These communities formed during what, in hindsight, was a bear market throughout 2016 for wider crypto currencies. This shift towards a communal focus was an incredibly important step that would ignite future interest and price acceleration. To this day, many associate NFTs with communities and memes, which is essentially when that association began thanks to the Meme Economy and Rare Pepe Wallet by Joe Looney . Still Bitcoin-focused, as “NFTs” on Ethereum did not exist, the Rare Pepe project began in the Counterparty Telegram chat. Counterparty is a peer-to-peer financial platform built on Bitcoin. An anonymous user posted the first Rare Pepe, featuring Satoshi Nakamoto , and offered it for sale on the decentralized exchange, predicting it could be worth millions. Enthusiasts quickly joined, buying and creating their own Rare Pepes . The project grew rapidly, leading to the development of a dedicated wallet to view and trade these digital cards: the Rare Pepe Wallet. This wallet, according to Bailey , would go on to heavily influence Known Origin and SuperRare . Beyond contributing to early NFT and blockchain infrastructure, Rare Pepes, combining meme culture with blockchain technology, became a key use case of digital art as collectibles, influencing the rise of NFTs and the broader crypto art movement. So influential were Rare Pepes and the wallet that Bailey says: “Joe invented the future.”

name: Electronic Superhighway (2016-1966) at Whitechapel Gallery, London
desc: This major exhibition of digital art featured over 100 works exploring the impact of computer and Internet technologies on art. The title, derived from video art pioneer Nam June Paik ’s eponymous 1974 groundbreaking report, which underscored the transformative potential of global connectivity through technology and introduced the world to the term “electronic superhighway.” Curated in reverse chronological order, the exhibition started with contemporary works and ended with the 1966 Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.) with Bell Laboratories engineers. Showcasing a variety of media, it included artists like Cory Arcangel , Vera Molnár , Hito Steyerl , Trevor Paglen , Lynn Hershman Leeson and Ulla Wiggen , reflecting five decades of visual culture.

name: Noite de Processing
desc: This free and open meeting held at Garoa Hacker Clube, a hackerspace in São Paulo , provided a space from 2016 to 2024 for the creative coding community in Brazil ’s largest city to talk about art and programming. Organized by Monica Rizzolli , Alexandre Villares and João Antonio de F. P. e Ferreira , the monthly meet up is also broadcast online for the entire world to participate.
subjects: joão antonio de f. p. e ferreira

name: A Companion to Digital Art by Christiane Paul
desc: In the follow-up companion to the seminal Digital Art , Paul’s A Companion to Digital Art offered a comprehensive exploration of digital art’s evolution, aesthetics and politics. Featuring insights from both established experts and emerging scholars, the book tackled critical and theoretical issues while addressing the practical challenges of presenting, documenting, and preserving digital art amid rapid technological changes. Edited by Paul, Professor Emerita at the New School and then-Adjunct Curator at the Whitney Museum, the companion reflects a deep appreciation of digital art’s technical intricacies and its dynamic growth. It was irreplaceable to this author’s understanding of the field.

name: Zach Lieberman Begins Daily Instagram Animations
desc: Like Manolo and Takawo before him, Zach Lieberman began the practice of doing daily animations on Instagram in 2016. Working mostly in openFrameworks , the toolkit he co-created, and inspired by Reza Ali ’s daily sketches, Lieberman explored geometry, animation, gesture and graphic form on the social media giant. His stepdaughter’s feedback influenced his work, even making it a collaborative process. This daily practice allowed Lieberman to experiment and push the bounds of his ideas and techniques. By the end of the year, he had created around 1,800 sketches. Like Takawo, his work marked a significant contribution to digital art and would inspire many future artists to explore similar creative routines. The work highlights the impact that social media has had on both the consumption and creation of art in the decade following its rapid rise.

name: Spectacle, Speculation, Spam by Alan Warburton
desc: Included in Casey Reas ’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA as a standout example of computer film, Alan Warburton ’s digital video Spectacle, Speculation, Spam is a video essay he made for the Edge of Frame Weekend seminar at The Whitechapel Gallery in East London . The seminar invited artists, curators and academics “to explore where experimental animation practice sits in relation to independent animation, visual art, histories and institutions.” Preferring to focus on practical rather than theoretical papers, Warburton asked participants to cite works of art illustrating their points as opposed to papers. His presentation showcases animation’s speculative and often spam-like nature within contemporary visual culture within the broader context of what software is and can do. The video advocates for and justifies Warburton’s experimental software animation practice.

name: Factory of the Sun by Hito Steyerl at MOCA
desc: Premiering at the German Pavilion of the 2015 Venice Biennale before touring internationally, The Museum of Contemporary Art described the work as a “landmark video installation.” The piece was the talk of Venice at the time, with Google Arts & Culture describing it as “probably the most talked-about piece at the significant biennale.” Factory of the Sun blends the symbolism of sunlight with digital age critiques, employing a video game format to explore the paradox of the Internet’s utopian promise versus its oppressive transparency. The work stands in a long line of digital art that asks ethical questions about our digitizing world beyond blindly praising it—along with works by artists like CTG and Lauren Lee McCarthy . Narrated by the fictional game’s programmer, Yulia, the film oscillates between reality levels, portraying characters as motion capture laborers whose movements become light impulses. Through genres like news reportage and internet dance videos, Steyerl examines collective resistance in a surveillance-dominated virtual world, telling the surreal story of workers whose forced movements create artificial sunlight.

name: Zurich HB Flap by Andreas Gysin & Sidi Vanetti
desc: This generative-kinetic installation was the opening at exhibit at the new Museum of Digital Art ( MuDA ) Zurich , which began in 2016. The work recontextualizes the mechanical timetable from a Zurich train station into an art installation. This original split-flap display had been in operation since 1988 and was removed from its station in 2015 to be replaced by a digital model. It consists of 452 split-flap elements, each printed with destinations, times or information. In the installation, Gysin and Vanetti use software and algorithms to transform the text-based split-flap elements into abstract shapes, evolving into formal visual compositions with each flap like a pixel on a screen.

name: “So you want to build a generator” by Kate Compton
desc: Golan Levin considers this article, “ So you want to build a generator ” by Kate Compton , to be “foundational for generative art” along with Max Bense ’s “Projects of Generative Aesthetics” (1965). The “beginner-level advice essay” applies equally well to “practiced experts” and explains how to create various types of generators, including Twitterbots, level generators and art-making bots. The essay guides readers through defining their “artist-in-a-box’s” output, identifying desirable and undesirable properties, and exploring different generative methods such as distribution, parametric, tile-based, grammars, constraint solvers and simulations. The essay highlights the level of human intentionality in generative art and its so-called “autonomous” processes. It emphasizes the challenges and difficulty of understanding these high-level human creative processes and translating them into computational, generative methods. Compton’s (galaxykate0) work serves as a comprehensive resource for both novice and experienced generator builders, fostering creativity and innovation in digital art and procedural generation.
subjects: so you want to build a generator

name: inconvergent.net Publishes Work on Open-Source Algorithms
desc: Inspired by the work of artists like Jared Tarbell , Anders Hoff, also known as inconvergent, started publishing his writing about “generative algorithms, programming and more” in 2015 and 2016. These important essays and explainers of various types of algorithm and generative process would prove an important source for open-source information about foundational generative processes: flocking, reaction-diffusion, CA, etc. This open-source explanatory work carries on the tradition of artist-educators like Jen Lowe and Patricio Gonzalez Vivo’s The Book of Shaders , Casey Reas and Lauren Lee McCarthy from Processing Foundation , Zach Lieberman from openFrameworks , Golan Levin , Toxi, Takawo and more in the decade of the 2010s.

name: Neural Network Written Rap Song by Robbie Barrat
desc: 17-year-old Robbie Barrat created his first AI artwork , a rapping neural network, after a bet in his high school programming club. Barrat, from rural West Virginia, utilized open-source tools like Linux and PyBrain to teach himself coding and AI development. Tasked with proving AI’s capabilities, Barrat wrote and trained a bespoke neural network on 6,000 Kanye West lyrics, transforming it from merely rearranging words to generating original rap lines. His project highlights the potential of open-source software in democratizing AI learning, showcasing how even those far from tech hubs can contribute to and innovate within the AI field. The work also stands as Barrat’s first experiment with AI art from an early age. This is very much only the beginning of this story for Barrat.

name: Curios Cards: First Art NFT on Ethereum
desc: With the 2017 rapid increase in cryptocurrency prices, or “bull run,” the first NFTs proper appeared. Predating CryptoPunks by just over a month, Curio Cards stand as the first-art NFT project on Ethereum. While sales and popularity were modest, the works clearly anticipated the major upcoming trend of digital ownership well before the concept caught up in broader pop culture. Like Rare Pepes , this early project was free, rarity-driven and community-led. The project consisted of 30 numbered series from seven artists: Cryptograffiti , Cryptopop , Daniel Friedman , Marisol Vengas , Phneep , Robek World and Thoros of Myr . A misprinted card, “17b,” adds an unofficial 31st card to the series. Curio Cards were developed by Thomas Hunt , Travis Uhrig and Rhett Creighton . Curio Cards emphasized rarity, creating between 111 and 2,154 edition cards per series, totaling 29,700 cards. With 4,000 lost and no more able to be created, the circulating total is around 25,000. The project—like ascribe and Monegraph before it—was meant to empower artists by leveraging blockchain technology to sell their work directly, with 100% of primary sales going to the creators. Curio Cards set the stage for future NFT innovations, which would be unearthed as NFTs gained in popularity in the early 2020s. While proto-NFTs had existed on Bitcoin and its various forks like NameCoin, Curio Cards would directly influence the upcoming ERC721 standard, cementing their significance. What Curio Cards, Monegraph and ascribe had in common and clearly demonstrated was that early NFT attempts were artist-led endeavors and predated many of the negative associations surrounding NFTs. The technology broadly originated to empower artists.

name: Matt Hall and John Watkinson Release CryptoPunks
desc: The first large generative character set minted on Ethereum, CryptoPunks was released by Matt Hall and John Watkinson of Larva Labs on June 22, 2017 for free. While Curio Cards predated the project as the first art NFTs on Ethereum, CryptoPunks (or Punks) stand as the first demonstration of generative algorithm that could produce a set number of unique iterations within a set with neither the artists, collectors or platform able to know precisely what would be generated. The project is generative, clearly, because the artists introduced autonomy to a system to create work. Punks stand as generative art and introduce the world to new issues, such as the demand for algorithms to paradoxically produce endless variety in a consistent and unified output space. The 10,000 unique Punks characters would also kick off a series of projects heavily inspired by the Punks minting and community mechanics. Larva Labs would demonstrate the power of generativity again in 2019 with Autoglpyhs —later in this chapter—which would in turn inspire Art Blocks —coming in Chapter 10. Beyond their impact on digital art, Etheria , Curio Cards and CryptoPunks also provided Ethereum with a first-mover advantage on NFTs. This fact remains despite NFTs early formation occurring entirely within the Bitcoin community. It would not be until the following decade (and chapter) that the Bitcoin community would seriously reenter the NFT discussion with Ordinals.

name: “Thinking Machines: Art and Design in the Computer Age, 1959–1989” at MoMA
desc: The exhibition, along with Open Codes at ZKM, indicated renewed institutional interest in computer-generated art prior to the impact of NFTs. Curated by MoMA ’s Sean Anderson and Giampaolo Bianconi , the exhibition celebrated the role of computers and computation in art. It examined the period from the earliest computer art in the late '50s to the dawn of the Internet in the late '80s. The exhibition mostly drew upon previous machine-centered exhibitions, including ones already mentioned in this Timeline: - The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age (MoMA, 1968) - Information (MoMA, 1970) - Software ( The Jewish Museum , 1970) While broader overviews of machines had been given, the contribution of thinking machines (or computers) had yet to be properly included in the art historical narrative. The exhibition showcased more than 100 works from all six curatorial departments, highlighting the paradigmatic impact of computers on postwar art, architecture and design. Drawn largely from MoMA’s existing collection, it featured pioneering artists and designers like Beryl Korot , Alison Knowles , Vera Molnár , and John Cage , illustrating the integration of computing, systems and randomness into artistic production. The exhibition also traced the history of computer technology’s role in reshaping work, society and aesthetic hierarchies, emphasizing the lasting influence of early computational thinking. The show also draws historical linkages to kinetic art, prominently featured in the exhibit. Despite being decades overdue, the exhibition provided computer art practitioners with acknowledgement and recognition for their important contributions. While the exhibition lacked a more comprehensive overview, some of the earliest and most celebrated computer artists were featured. These included Vera Molnár, Charles Csuri and Waldemar Cordeiro . This exhibition serves as a reminder of how long institutional interest took to arrive for some artists; conversely, it also demonstrated that interest in historical computer-generated art appeared prior to the success of NFTs.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age
thinking machines: art and design in the computer age, 1959–1989

name: Open Codes at ZKM Center for Art and Media
desc: Open Codes, described by Georg Bak to Le Random in our Twitter Spaces Launch as “the exhibition of our times,” was curated by the legendary Peter Weibel with Lívia Nolasco-Rózsás , Yasemin Keskintepe and Blanca Giménez . The exhibition highlighted the importance of code in our increasingly data-driven lives. Weibel argues that in order to understand our new world, we must explore code and its various impacts artistically. The exhibition featured around 200 artistic and scientific works, encouraging visitors to engage physically and interactively with the displays. The free exhibition’s message extended beyond the purely visual, aiming to highlight the shift from a work-based society to a knowledge-based society, advocating for free civic education. Visitors experienced a blend of laboratory, lounge and co-working space, demonstrating a vision to foster creativity and communal learning. Along with MoMA ’s Thinking Machines from the same year, the exhibition carries on the tradition of exhibits from decades past, like Software at the Jewish Museum (1970).

name: Tezos ICO
desc: Tezos ICO-ed in July, 2017 with a “Proof-of-Stake” (PoS) consensus model, allowing token holders to stake—lock up their coins—to validate new blocks, for which they received additional tokens as a reward. Raising over $230 million, Tezos far surpassed its $20 million target and for a short period, became the largest ICO—an indication of the 2017 crypto-mania in valuations. Tezos, as a PoS model, differed from proof-of-work models like Bitcoin and Ethereum—at that time—in that it was more environmentally friendly, efficient and managed lower fees. These three conditions would lead to Tezos becoming the site of a bohemian digital art market in early 2021. However, its launch would not be so simple, despite the success of its ICO. The record-setting ICO was overshadowed by internal disputes. The newly formed Tezos Foundation , led by Johann Gevers , controlled the funds and was tasked with delivering Tezos tokens (XTZ) to ICO participants. However, conflicts between the Foundation and Tezos creators Kathleen and Arthur Breitman delayed token distribution and prompted class-action lawsuits. Due to these challenges, Tezos development and release were delayed to the following year, in addition to instantly damaging relations with early investors.

name: ERC20 Launches
desc: ERC-20 was the standard that governed how Ethereum tokens could be issued via smart contract. Originally released in November 2015, the ERC20 token standard would serve as the home for some of Ethereum’s first NFTs-proper, as well as ICOs launched on Ethereum.

name: Creeps & Weirdos by DADA.nyc
desc: Aligned with previous NFT attempts by the McCoys and ascribe, DADA aimed to empower artists by enabling more people to earn a sustainable living as artists. DADA’s Creeps & Weirdos collection was launched on October 31, 2017 with a Halloween theme. This global drawing program is by Beatriz Ramos , Abraham MIlano and Judy Mam . This collection, featured in Jason Bailey ’s ( Artnome ) article “ The Blockchain Art Market is Here ” in December 2017, and serving as the official image of the Rare Art Festival in January 2018, is a significant milestone in NFT history. Employing the newly launched ERC20 standard and comprising 108 unique artworks by 30 artists, Creeps & Weirdos merged the aesthetics of early crypto collectibles with rare digital art. Unlike traditional trading cards or memes, these artworks formed on a decentralized marketplace, allowing them to be bought and sold, a clear foreshadowing of modern cryptoart platforms. Each piece in the collection represented a visual conversation, emphasizing collaboration and community—two elements still crucial to NFTs. With 16,600 digital editions across five levels of scarcity, Creeps & Weirdos remains a testament to DADA’s ability to recognize the potential of blockchain and art prior to NFT-mania in the coming decade. The collection also further solidified the Ethereum blockchain as the home for NFTs, despite the initial interest forming in the Bitcoin community.
subjects: the blockchain art market is here

name: CryptoKitties Launches
desc: One of the earliest NFT projects and blockchain games that reached mania status was CryptoKitties , launching in November 2017 in the midst of a parabolic rise in the price of cryptocurrencies. Within a year, a kitty sold for 600 ETH, worth nearly $170,000 at the time but $2.2 million as of May, 2024. With over 50,000 thousand tokens selling in the first month, the game was so popular it slowed down the Ethereum network with spiking gas fees, presaging the upcoming NFT mania of 2021. Kitties played a critical role in the early adoption of NFTs—including Jason Bailey —and are of major interest to this story. The early NFT game used pieces of code (called “genes”) that defined the characteristics of a digital cartoon cat. Players could buy, collect, sell, and breed these cats, resulting in unique NFTs. The project, despite its status as an early project just months after CryptoPunks , has not maintained its value as of this writing in 2024, apparently due to an oversupply of millions of kitties bred—generatively—by enthusiastic community members. Yet CryptoKitties still played a crucial role in the story of generative art as they helped popularize, onboard and demonstrate the power of NFTs. With fewer barriers to entry and a more engaging dynamic than Punks, the project was initially more successful. It would take Jason Bailey’s, for instance, purchase of a CryptoKitty for him to understand and be convinced of the value of blockchains and NFTs.

name: “The Blockchain Art Market Is Here” by Jason Bailey (Artnome)
desc: After purchasing a CryptoKitty during the 2017 crypto bull run, Jason Bailey ( Artnome ) wrote, “The Blockchain Art Market Is Here.” The piece articulates Bailey’s prescient conviction that blockchains and NFTs would eventually have a big impact on artists and the art market, writing that he “strongly suggest[s] artists and art collectors take blockchain seriously and monitor the market.” While this idea had been expressed by artists at least back to 2014 with Kevin McCoy , Jonathan Monaghan , Nili Learner, Rhea Myers , Kevin Abosch and others, it took the popularity of CryptoKitties and its headlining grabbing numbers to actually initiate a rapid increase in adoption. The article lays out how blockchain could: revolutionize digital art sales through digital scarcity, democratize fine art investment, improve provenance and create a more ethical payment system for artists. By illustrating these points with examples like DADA.nyc’s decentralized art marketplace and CryptoKitties , Bailey leveraged the emerging attention on NFTs to increase awareness of the technology’s potential benefits—again, from an artist’s perspective. The piece, like many previous examples of writing, helped prime the public for the latest merging of art and—now blockchain—technology, foreshadowing the rise of NFTs and their impact on the art world.
subjects: the blockchain art market is here

name: Crystal Towers by Matt DesLauriers
desc: Crystal Towers by Matt DesLauriers is a data-driven generative algorithm created with Node.js, Three.js and Blender. The system takes data from skyscraper height distributions across major cities to create a series of unique black-and-white abstract compositions. The work was posted in September on Behance by DesLauriers. A few weeks later, Tyler Hobbs posted the work on Reddit ’s r/generative channel, crediting DesLauriers and encouraging other community to investigate his work, writing: “Full gallery on behance , and other interesting info posted on his Twitter at @mattdesl .” These two would go on to create some of the earliest work on Art Blocks in the following decade—and chapter.

name: LAUREN by Lauren Lee McCarthy
desc: In LAUREN , Lauren Lee McCarthy —creator of p5.js —embodies a human version of Amazon Alexa, serving as a smart home intelligence for individuals within their own residences. This week-long performance involved the installation of an entire custom-designed smarthome, including networked devices, cameras, microphones, switches, door locks and faucets. The artist remotely oversaw and controlled all aspects of the home 24/7, aiming to surpass AI by understanding and anticipating the person’s needs on a human level. The resulting relationship occupies an ambiguous space between human-machine and human-human interactions. LAUREN explores our fundamental, basic relationships with machines and whether humans can possibly know other humans as well as machines by intuition despite a lack of data. The work asks questions about this relationship in the context of our centuries-long examination of how technology in art shapes our very humanity. Beyond these deeper questions, LAUREN examines tensions between intimacy and privacy, convenience and agency, and the future role of human labor in automation.

name: R.A.R.E Art Labs Launched
desc: One of the earliest commercial NFT platforms, along with SuperRare , R.A.R.E (Rare Art Registry and Exchange) Art Labs was founded, introducing the R.A.R.E Protocol, one of the earliest crypto-economies for the digital art world. Comprising artists, developers and FinTech entrepreneurs, R.A.R.E aimed to revolutionize the relationship between art and commerce by enabling artists to monetize their digital works through blockchain verification. The R.A.R.E Protocol facilitates direct sales of digital art, allows fans to purchase verified works, and creates a marketplace for trading these digital goods. The launch positioned R.A.R.E as a pioneer in applying blockchain technology to create scarcity and value in digital art.

name: The Truelist by Nick Montfort
desc: “ Nick Montfort , poet and digital media professor at MIT, publishes The Truelist , a computer-generated book-length poem produced by a one-page, stand-alone computer program. The code used to generate the poem is included at the end of the book.” -Sasha Stiles

name: 1 the Road by Ross Goodwin
desc: “ Ross Goodwin writes 1 the Road , an experimental AI-powered novel. Inspired by Jack Kerouac ’s On the Road, Goodwin drives from New York to New Orleans accompanied by an AI program trained on poetry and sci-fi text corpora , plus a FourSquare data set. Hooked up to various sensors, the AI-in-a-laptop outputs words to a scrolling thermal printer as the road trip unfolds.”

name: “Why Love Generative Art?” by Jason Bailey on Artnome
desc: 2018, the year many threads from our long story spark an inferno after what in some ways can be seen as a flickering light, vascilating between the frenzied and nearly extinguished. While many developments that we’ll cover throughout the year led to this article, the article itself deserves a special spot for its continued use as a source and citation for explaining and introducing newcomers to generative art. In August, 2018, before Autoglyphs or Art Blocks , Artnome ’s essay did more than explain the movement of generative art to the first generation financially and technology capable of collecting it with ease. It also introduced this new generation of art collectors to Manolo, Casey Reas , Vera Molnár , Jared Tarbell and Muriel Cooper . Kate Vass spoke to this author (Peter Bauman) about the relevance of the article to her, asking him to curate 2019’s Automat und Mensch: “It was a wonderful opportunity because nobody was really interested in highlighting this history and the protagonists of the movement. I spoke to Georg and, of course, we all read the fantastic “Why Love Generative Art?” by Jason Bailey that inspired many to collect. It’s a wonderful thing when one good intention leads to many more and to people falling in love with art. Jason was already known as a contributor to this scene and Georg would not stop talking about him so our mutual willingness was to get Jason on board. Georg spoke to Jason and asked if he would be interested. Then we jumped on a call and everybody discussed it and said, “How can we do it and who is responsible for what?” We split the responsibility, with Georg mostly focusing on the historical pioneering part and Jason responsible for bringing in contemporary artists.”
subjects: automat und mensch: a history of ai and generative art

name: Rare Digital Art Festival #1, New York
desc: With the idea of Joe Looney from Rare Pepe Wallet and organized by R.A.R.E, this milestone event in NFT history kicked off in January 2018 with a huge event in this story: RARE AF #1 NYC, the first Rare Art Festival. While total attendance was low, some of the most prominent people in the burgeoning Crypto Art space appeared, including Matt Hall and John Watkinson from Cryptopunks and Beatriz Ramos from DADA NYC, in addition to Looney. According to Jason Bailey , it was a challenge getting enough artists to participate. Ramos spoke about the event on Right Click Save saying : “I remember the feeling of effervescence, of excitement — a vital energy that day that felt like the festival was a catalyst for something big. It felt like we all knew that we were on the verge of something huge that no one else was aware of, in a room with other people who share this feeling.” She continued, reflecting on the legacy of the event after four years: “I think it catalyzed the NFT movement — the creative ferment, innovation, experimentation, and community but at the same time it buried it, becoming a movement that was purely market driven. The movement in itself (which is not ideological or aesthetic) ended up transforming into the beginnings of a market. And what is left to the community is a shared sense of nostalgia for those of us who lived that moment.”

name: Landscapes and Nude Portraits by Robbie Barrat
desc: In 2017 Robbie Barrat began using Generative Adversarial Networks to make art, producing his first two significant bodies of work, Landscapes and Nude Portraits, which reached collectors in 2018. He had begun his explorations of AI in 2016, with a Bach-imitating LSTM in July and a rapping neural network in November. His initial attempt with landscapes yielded realistic but ultimately unremarkable results, highlighting the limitations of merely replicating traditional art forms with new technology. Seeking deeper engagement with the medium, Barrat then focused on nude portraits, intentionally guiding the GAN to misinterpret the overall structure while correctly learning local features. This approach underscored his interest in the creative potential of GANs, allowing the machine to produce unexpected and intriguing generative outcomes beyond pre-programmed rules. While these works remain central to his artistic exploration and explanations, they—in particular Nude Portraits—have played a remarkable role in the history of the birth of NFTs, as we will see later this year, but also its uglier speculation and mania, which ultimately drove Barrat to disavow them.

name: Christie’s First Art + Tech Summit
desc: Christie’s inaugurated its Art+Tech Summit at its London headquarters on July 18. The now-annual initiative, hosted in collaboration with Christie’s Education, aimed to explore the intersection of technology and the art world, specifically blockchain technology, following the cryptocurrency spike in price in 2018. The inaugural conference’s topic was “Exploring Blockchain – Is the Art World Ready for Consensus?” and featured thought leaders like Hans Ulrich Obrist and Jason Bailey . Infamously, Christie’s gave away 300 Robbie Barrat NFTs of “generated nude #7” on physical cards in a gift bag to attendees, placed in the bags by SuperRare in collaboration with Bailey and Barrat. Perhaps expecting greater blockchain literacy, the reception of the tokens was disappointing, as according to SuperRare ’s John Crain , “We were genuinely excited about the idea, only to find out the next day that literally no one understood what the tokenized card was for.” With SuperRare reporting only 12 of the 300 ever claimed, the remaining pieces today are known as the “Lost Robbies” and—against the initial desires or interest of the artist—sell for hundreds of thousands of dollars. One is featured in the Le Random collection.

name: SuperRare launches
desc: In April, SuperRare , one of the oldest surviving crypto art marketplaces, launched its beta smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain. Founded by a small team in Brooklyn , SuperRare aimed to make art collecting as accessible as buying stocks or posting photos online. Inspired by projects previously covered on this Timeline like CryptoPunks and Rare Pepe Wallet , SuperRare enabled select artists to issue art work on their platform. The platform quickly garnered interest, with Jason Bailey making the first purchases from Robbie Barrat ’s AI Generated Nude Portrait series. Later in the year—and this Timeline—Bailey, Barrat and SuperRare would give away 300 of these pieces in person at Christie’s First Art + Tech Summit , the infamous Lost Robbies. SuperRare was only modestly successful in its first year, facilitating over 1,124 primary sales yet only $91,000 in first-year sales volume and around 550 ETH in total volume.
