These muted figures demonstrate—even in the ninth chapter—how early we still are in this story. The platform’s release, however, marks a significant milestone in the story of generative art in this decade.

name: Tezos Mainnet Goes Live
desc: Despite legal action that delayed Tezos’s initial release by nearly a year, the chain officially launched on mainnet on September 17, 2018. The project was watched closely, as it had been one of the largest ICOs at the time. Tezos—now in the hands of its decentralized community—would spend the next 18 months steadily releasing updates and proving the viability of its consensus mechanism. It will reappear in the next decade—and chapter—in March 2020 when the first signs of creative life appear on the chain and, of course, one year later in March 2021 with the launch of Hic et Nunc.

name: Christie’s First Sale of an AI artwork
desc: This sale could in some ways be considered the initial spark that lit the fuse of the upcoming NFT craze, peaking in 2021. Kate Vass spoke to this author ( Peter Bauman ) about how this sale spurred her to put together the legendary Automat und Mensch a few months—and moments on this Timeline—later in May, 2019. The sale itself remains controversial, as it was an AI artwork, Portrait of Edmond de Belamy by Obvious but based on Robbie Barrat ’s open-source code.
subjects: automat und mensch: a history of ai and generative art

name: Programmed: Rules, Codes, and Choreographies in Art, 1965–2018 at The Whitney
desc: An indication, like in 2001, that institutions—forced apparently largely to be reactionary—are willing to show interest in digital art following a catalyst that sparks renewed public interest. This time period provided just that, as following a steep rise in cryptocurrency prices at the end of 2017 and into 2018, it is perhaps not a coincidence that the remainder of 2018 saw renewed institutional interest from entrants like The Whitney, The V&A and Christie’s. September saw the Whitney’s Programmed : Rules, Codes, and Choreographies in Art, 1965–2018.

name: Chance and Control: Art in the Age of Computers at the V&A
desc: Another indication that institutional interest renewed during the first crypto market bull run, perhaps already with the hope that cryptocurrency interest could drive interest in digital art. This is demonstrated by this show at the V&A, Chance and Control: Art in the Age of Computers, as well as Programmed: Rules, Codes, and Choreographies in Art, 1965–2018 at The Whitney .
subjects: chance and control: art in the age of computers

name: Dieter Shirley and Others Propose the ERC-721 Standard
desc: William Entriken , Dieter Shirley , Jacob Evans and Nastassia Sachs authored the ERC-721 protocol, proposed in January 2018 as Ethereum’s first NFT token standard, laying the foundation for the variety of ways NFTs remain used to this day. ERC-721 defines a set of guidelines for creating NFTs to represent unique digital assets. The protocol stipulates that, unlike fungible tokens, NFTs cannot be exchanged on a one-to-one basis due to their distinct properties. The standard facilitated the creation, transfer and management of unique digital items, enabling their increased use in creative fields such as fine art and gaming.

name: Memories of Passersby I by Mario Klingemann
desc: While first exhibited in January 2019 at Madrid’s Colección SOLO , Memories of Passersby I is an AI artwork generating an endless stream of unique, real-time portraits. A fully autonomous physical installation, the work features a neural network of multiple GANs housed in a chestnut wood cabinet, linked to two framed screens. Unlike traditional generative art, it does not rely on a database but continuously creates new images pixel by pixel, ensuring no repetition. Klingemann trained the AI using 17th- to 19th-century portraits and his surrealist aesthetic preferences. The work would go on to be sold by Sotheby’s in March 2019, a continued indication of institutional interest in AI art.

name: Progress by Tyler Hobbs at Galerîa dos Topos Léon, Mexico
desc: In Tyler Hobbs ’s first exhibition, Progress, the artist examines the profound impact of computers and technology on contemporary life, emphasizing the necessity for artists to directly engage with these tools. These programmatic works further demonstrate what this Timeline has shown for decades: interacting with computers in their native form can produce uniquely crafted artwork that is inherently infused with the essence of the latest technology. Hobbs had been creating and sharing his practice online since 2014. Progress can thus be seen as a literal marker for Hobbs’s artistic development over the previous 4-5 years. The work showcases the culmination of Hobbs’s thought and development up to this point, a key moment in generative art in the 2010s.

name: BOB by Ian Cheng
desc: Ian Cheng introduced BOB (Bag of Beliefs), a pioneering artificial life form depicted as a chimeric branching serpent. BOB represents a significant evolution in Cheng’s exploration of simulation, focusing on an individual agent’s ability to adapt to unexpected situations. Over time, BOB’s body, mind and personality evolve to manage life’s surprises, transforming them into routines. Featuring a composite AI architecture with various “demons” that drive its behavior, BOB learns rule-based beliefs from sensory experiences. This dynamic interaction between sub-personalities and external stimuli highlights the intricate relationship between technology, autonomy and human-like adaptability in generative art.

name: Meandering River by onformative
desc: This AI audiovisual installation explores the transformative forces of nature through real-time algorithmic visuals and AI-composed music. Offering a bird’s-eye view of a dynamic landscape, the project visualizes the shifting behaviors of rivers and their impact on the earth. Utilizing bespoke algorithms and shaders, the installation simulates natural phenomena such as hydraulic erosion and meander scars. The accompanying soundscape, developed with composers kling klang klong using the Google Magenta Performance RNN model, dynamically responds to the river’s simulated movements, creating an immersive experience that underscores the unpredictability and beauty of natural generativity.

name: uumwelt by Pierre Huyghe
desc: Pierre Huyghe ’s exploration of early AI technology at the Serpentine Galleries involved a transformative and autonomous art installation based on MRI scans, live animals and intense audience interaction. Huyghe used fMRI technology to capture the brain activity of an individual imagining selected images. This data was processed by a deep neural network attempting to reconstruct the images, resulting in continuously evolving visual representations displayed on large LED screens. The exhibition’s environment was dynamic, influenced by sensors detecting light, temperature, humidity, the presence of insects and even visitors' gazes. Live flies living in the gallery created unique patterns, and the space constantly morphed, embodying an ecosystem where human, animal and technological elements interacted unpredictably, reflecting Huyghe’s vision of art as a self-presenting ritual.

name: Chaos Machine by Distributed Gallery
desc: Chaos Machine demonstrates the breadth and materiality of blockchain-based generative art. Distributed Gallery unveiled the Chaos Machine—a unique crypto-jukebox artwork—during the Proof of Work exhibition at the Schinkel Pavillon in Berlin and curated by Simon Denny in September, 2018. This exhibition featured an eclectic lineup, including CryptoKitties and Harm van den Dorpel . The piece itself was constructed from oak wood, steel, slate, and glass. This 192 cm tall installation burns banknotes to play user-generated music playlists stored on the Ethereum blockchain via IPFS technology. Burning a banknote mints an NFT and prints a QR code, allowing new songs to be added to the playlist. The early material-blockchain generative work has been exhibited in multiple prestigious venues, including the Kate Vass Galerie in Zurich and the FIAC in Paris . These early experiments with NFTs by artists like Simon Denny and Robbie Barrat demonstrate how artist-led the movement was prior to the popularization of NFTs in 2021.

name: All We’d Ever Need Is One Another by Adam Basanta
desc: This mixed-media AI installation autonomously generates images, embodying a self-sustaining “art factory,” an early example of work employing material, coded and AI-generative techniques. Utilizing two flatbed scanners facing each other, the installation employs a computer script to create random settings and initiate scanning. Deep-learning algorithms then analyze the images and are “validated as art” if they match existing works by over 83%. These images were shared on social platforms and were occasionally printed live in the gallery. This work explores technological automation, object agency and the economics of art production, reflecting on the continuous, independent creation of cultural artifacts.
subjects: all we'd ever need is one another
coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: Putting the Pieces Back Together Again by Ralf Baeker
desc: This autonomous kinetic installation explores self-organization and emergent complex behavior based on a reimagination of cybernetic art in the twenty-first century. Comprising 1250 stepper motors arranged in a two-by-two-meter grid, each motor is equipped with a white acrylic pointer. These pointers move in response to alternating current, initially in random directions, reversing upon collision. This interaction creates complex, evolving patterns on the installation’s surface, reflecting non-hierarchical communication and collective behavior. Inspired by Alvin Toffler ’s notion of reassembling fragmented problems, Baecker’s work serves as a contemporary synthesis of cybernetic, kinetic and generative art, thus paying homage to three critical roots of all digital art, all mentioned many times in this Timeline.
subjects: putting the pieces back together again

name: “A Gutenberg Poetry Corpus” by Allison Parrish
desc: “ Allison Parrish creates and releases “A Gutenberg Poetry Corpus” , a public domain resource comprised of “approximately three million lines of poetry extracted from hundreds of books from Project Gutenberg.” Allison automatically filters the larger Gutenberg canon to hone in on poetry, to create a verse-specific corpus that becomes foundational to a number of important generative poetry projects.” -Sasha Stiles

name: On View by Operator
desc: One of the first works by artist duo Operator , On View captures the spirit of their practice, which uses digital tools to question—along with Lauren Lee McCarthy and Sougwen Chung —the most pressing issues facing humans and technology. Created by Operator’s Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti and commissioned by the SCAD Museum of Art, On View is an immersive experiential artwork that critiques modern society’s obsession with becoming the subject of art. The piece questions the implications of addictive interfaces, surveillance capitalism and data privacy. Utilizing TouchDesigner, real-time facial recognition, voice commands and environmental sensors, On View integrates advanced technology seamlessly into its physical spaces. This installation invites participants to critically engage with the digital architectures shaping our realities, emphasizing the need for tech literacy as technology becomes increasingly invisible.

name: Larva Labs Releases Autoglyphs
desc: A seminal event in generative art history stands as April’s release of Autoglyphs by Larva Labs . Considered the first on-chain generative art on the Ethereum blockchain, each unique glyph was created by code running directly on the blockchain, making them self-contained and independent of any central authority. Matt Hall and John Watkinson ’s Autoglyphs were inspired by the pair’s admiration for Sol LeWitt ’s Wall Drawings . The famed series would go on to inspire Erick Calderon to launch Art Blocks in November 2020, roughly 18 months after the release of Autoglyphs. Anyone could generate an Autoglyph by donating 0.2Ξ to the charity 350.org , with a total of 512 glyphs produced before the generator ceased operation. The first long-form generative series on Ethereum was thus directly inspired by the art historical legacy of rules-based systems thinking in Sol LeWitt. Its primary sales went to charity. Thus, as with the invention of NFTs themselves, the roots of long-form generative remain distant from the speculative mania and unsavory associations that would later plague NFTs broadly. Critically, Autoglyphs helped establish the concept that artwork and ownership details could be embedded on blockchains, ensuring long-term and public provenance. This project forever stands as a unique, critical link between the legacy of Conceptualism and systems-based thinking and where we stand today with on-chain art.

name: Public Key / Private Key by Jennifer and Kevin McCoy
desc: Commissioned by the Whitney for its artport site, this work is one of the first to engage with blockchain technology to make its way to a museum’s permanent collection. The work in this way is an entire reimagination of the relationship between artwork, museum and audience. Acquired by the Whitney Museum’s Christiane Paul , this piece’s incorporation of blockchain technology allow the market life of the work to continue beyond its acquisition. Fifty NFTs, dubbed digital certificates by the museum, linked to the artwork, were given to donors who could freely transfer or sell them. As these certificates change hands, the evolving list of donors is tracked on the museum’s website. Additionally, the artwork itself contains a blockchain key, making the first audience member to discover it the fifty-first donor.

name: Casey Reas Creates a2p (artist-to-peer)
desc: Casey Reas ’s precursor to Feral File was inspired by Harm van den Dorpel ’s Left Gallery from 2015. Named a2p (artist-to-peer) and built on Bitmark with Sean Moss-Pultz , it was Reas’s early exploration of blockchain, promoting peer-to-peer art trading. In each iteration, three to four curators invited 25 artists, who minted one original artwork as an edition of 10 plus one artist proof. Over a week, artists curated their collections by swapping artworks, all recorded on the blockchain, with lively discussion reminiscent of IRC chats. A2p stands as a critical moment in this history because, in many ways, it helped legitimize the blockchain for pre-blockchain generative artists. For many, a2p marked their initial foray into NFTs, inextricably linking generative art and blockchains. The platform did more than introduce; it ignited a curiosity that set the stage for the increase in interest that was to come while laying the groundwork for Reas’s Feral File.

name: Automat und Mensch at Kate Vass Galerie
desc: The exhibition Automat und Mensch: A History of AI and Generative Art in May 2019 anticipated the arrival of AI and generative art. The audacious show at Kate Vass Galerie was organized by Kate Vass and curated by Jason Bailey ( Artnome ) and Georg Bak . Vass told this author about the show : “The whole show was actually an attempt to highlight the historical perspective of generative art and the predecessors of AI.” Going back several decades, the show spotlighted the historical roots of AI and generative art: cybernetics and early robotics, as well as the computer art of pioneers like Frieder Nake and Herbert W. Franke . The show also includes contemporary artists. Bak told me : “As Kate said, our aim was to reflect on the history of AI—from early generative art to the most recent developments in AI with DeepDream and GANs . We actually had Larva Labs in the show with physical Autoglyphs . John [Watkinson] told me last time I saw him that we actually pushed him to finish Autoglyphs to get it ready for the show. It was also interesting that we actually had the first on-chain NFT in this exhibition. There were some very recent developments as well as the historical context.” Bailey spoke to this author ( Peter Bauman ) about the relevance of the exhibition five years later, saying : “I was trying to get my heroes to agree to do this. I don’t think that’s an exaggeration. I had spent twenty years looking up to people like Casey Reas , Jared Tarbell and John Maeda . I was lucky enough that I had been several years into writing the Artnome blog, where people were at least somewhat aware that I had been passionately—for no real profit or commercial purpose—writing about art and technology out of something that I love. That opened the door to at least getting responses to some emails. There was some strategy to trying to get the folks that I had been in more recent contact with who were maybe slightly better known names. Then, when you went further along, you could say, “Well, so and so has signed up.” Everyone wants to know who’s already agreed but you have to get the first few people to agree to be able to get the additional people to agree. It’s not an accident that we’re talking about it five years later. I think it’s a reflection of the attention to detail and the effort. I wouldn’t have anticipated—as someone who’d just started to curate—the effort that it took.”
subjects: automat und mensch: a history of ai and generative art

name: MACHINE HALLUCINATION by Refik Anadol
desc: This large-scale immersive audiovisual installation marked Anadol’s first major installation in New York City, and extended the machine learning practice he had begun with Archive Dreaming in 2017. Using machine learning algorithms on a vast dataset of over 100 million architectural images of New York City, Anadol created a cinematic data universe. The experience revealed the city’s collective memories and AI’s ability to re-imagine, blending architecture with perceptions of time and space. The installation offered a glimpse into the future of AI-enhanced immersive installations for which Anadol is now known after 2022’s Unsupervised at MoMA .

name: Inferno by Helena Sarin
desc: The software engineer Sarin, formerly of Bell Labs , began her experiments with GANs in early 2018. This Twitter post from March 2018 shows an example of possibly her earliest public work. Just a year later, Sarin had already began standing out with work suggesting the surreal. By the end of 2018, Sarin spoke to Jason Bailey about her practice on his Artnome blog . 2019 saw Sarin’s first exhibition, which included this work, part of her #latentDoodles series. It was showcased at the Computer Vision Art Gallery during ICCV 2019 in Seoul , Korea . The work explores the human-like quality of hand-drawn marks with the distinct patterns of computational creation. Using SNGAN trained on her sketches and doodles, Sarin upscaled and colorized the image with cycleGAN for added texture. Sarin enhances the abstract images with carefully crafted captions, adding a verbal layer that deepens the folk-like yet computationally intricate nature of her work. The work exemplifies Sarin’s master from an early of coaxing the traditional and human out of modern AI techniques.

name: CODED FIELD by Rhizomatiks
desc: This large-scale Rhizomatiks installation and dance performance, with technical and creative direction by Daito Manabe and choreography by MIKIKO , was held at the Tokyo FESTIVAL. Situated in Tokyo’s Shiba district, the project interweaves light and sound at the Daihonzan Zojoji Temple. There, architectural and topographical data were coded into a virtual space, which was then translated into dynamic light and sound emitted by balloon-shaped devices. Audience movements influenced these devices, creating an interactive experience. The work—like much in this decade—showcases many of the forebearers of digital art, including lumino-kinetic sculpture, participation and gernativity.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: The Art of Cybersecurity by Brendan Dawes
desc: This data art project that visualizes cybersecurity threat data as a series of algorithmically generated images and a 4K animation. The work features three main components: black obelisks representing threats, an organic mesh symbolizing the detection system and flowing strands illustrating the creativity enabled by neutralized threats. Each mesh shape, generated by a unique algorithm, corresponds to five different industries: media, banking, government, technology and retail. Debuted at the RSA Conference in San Francisco , the project is a key example of the renewed interest in data visualization art that was propelled—in part—in the previous decade by Ben Fry ’s work and his cocreation of Processing .

name: Rare Digital Art Festival #2, New York
desc: Running until the summer of 2022, Rare AF was the original on-chain art event that paved the way for Bright Moments , Proof of People and the variety of other Web3 native art events that now dot the yearly social calendar. In May 2019, finding enough collectors was the real challenge, echoing similar sentiment for 2024, despite a rapid jump in interest in the intervening 5 years. This 2019 iteration was the second and continued the momentum from year, featuring the space’s significant builders; however, the event would prove small until NFTs took off the following years.

name: First Contemporary and Digital Art Fair (CADAF) in New York
desc: May saw another legendary blockchain art event with the first annual Contemporary and Digital Art Fair (CADAF) in New York City. The show itself featured Artxcode’s show of algorithmic work by then-essentially unknown artists Dmitri Cherniak and Tyler Hobbs . The pair would make names for themselves the following decade and chapter with their releases on Art Blocks . Other artists whose work has been exhibited include Kevin Abosch . Panelists at the event were impressive, including Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti from Operator , Jason Bailey ( Artnome ), John Watkinson and Le Random advisor Georg Bak .

name: EONS by Mike Tyka
desc: This early example of a neural net animated narrative by Tyka blends the aesthetics of a moving painting with the structure of a music video. Created entirely using artificial neural networks, the visuals were generated with BigGAN. The animation explores the narrative potential of GANs , offering a contemplative reflection on humanity’s brief existence and our relationship with nature on geological timescales. EONS emphasizes the emotional incomprehensibility of our scientific knowledge, inviting viewers to ponder our place within the vast expanse of time.

name: Notable AI work of 2019
desc: As we close the decade, the proliferation of AI art combined with NFTs means that tracking every significant piece by every relevant artist is extremely challenging. Here are relevant works and artists deserving of recognition from the decade: Lulu xXX & Noj Barke ’s photogrammetry Erik Swahn ’s StyleGAN experiments Tom White ’s work with Convolutional Neural Network classifiers Anna Ridler ’s early training sets (e.g. Myriad) David Young ’s work with flowers and GANs Runway Palette by Cyril Diagne

name: OpenAI Releases GPT2
desc: “ OpenAI releases a paper on GPT-2 (Generative Pre-trained Transformer), an AI-powered text generation model trained on vast amounts of written text sourced via the internet; users are able to download and even fine-tune a smaller version of the model. Soon after, Gwern Branwen publishes seminal poetry experiments using GPT-2, Parrish’s Gutenberg Poetry Corpus, and Adam Daniel King releases Talk to Transformer , a no-code text generation interface.” -Sasha Stiles
subjects: language models are unsupervised multitask learners

name: POEMPORTRAITS by Es Devlin, with Ross Goodwin and Google Arts & Culture
desc: “Inspired by a conversation between Es Devlin and Hans Ulrich Obrist , and created in collaboration with Google Arts & Culture and Ross Goodwin , POEMPORTRAITS combines poetry, design and machine learning and invites participants to create interactive AI-powered poetry.” It was first shown at the Serpentine in 2017. -Sasha Stiles

name: ReRites by David Jhave
desc: “ David Jhave Johnston publishes ReRites , billed as one of the first literary works co-authored with neural networks. The project comprises AI-generated text written with a system trained on a corpus of 600,000 lines of poetry, edited by a human (Jhave Johnston).” -Sasha Stiles

name: Travesty Generator by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram
desc: “ Lillian-Yvonne Bertram publishes Travesty Generator, a poetry collection that remixes programming codes in explorations of race and gender; the collection is longlisted for the 2020 National Book Award.” -Sasha Stiles

name: Enter the Madness
desc: You thought the 2010s were wild? This decade is only a few years old, yet we’ve still never seen anything like this rapid pace of change and influx of interest. How? Why did it all come together in 2020? Perhaps that explanation starts how the decade began, with a debilitating global pandemic. But this is actually the end of the explanation, the final chapter. Refer to the previous 9 chapters of this Timeline and over 900 moments that describe and explain the technological and artistic developments that have led us here, from our earliest explorations of systems-based art-making to how digital technology and mass media art accelerated these developments in conjuncture with our digitizing lives. For more context, we suggest [watching or listening ( transcript ) to our Ch 10 Artist Discussion with Lauren Lee McCarthy , Snowfro, Ix Shells and Rafael Lozano-Hemmer .] But this 70,000-year story always had a twist coming at the end. Decades of advancements in computer science and AI research combined with our inexhaustible human capacity to intervene, experiment and create with emerging technologies led to a decade poised for disruption. Then, almost as soon as the decade began, a global pandemic hit. Increased time at home and stimulus liquidity fanned the embers we covered in chapters 1 through 9, igniting an NFT-mania. This sudden and new-found popularity for digital, on-chain and generative art would have seemed unimaginable for people who had been working in these fields for decades in relative obscurity. These quiet builders have now become the heroes of this story, which is by no means winding down with this chapter. Paradoxically, unlike a traditional narrative, this story doesn’t end here and may only be beginning. Erick Calderon, a particular hero of this chapter, told the Le Random team more about the pandemic’s impact on “2020s: Digital Art’s Normalization.” “For the last couple decades, we’ve seen this inevitable shift towards a more digital-focused world. We spend more of our lives online. And as a result, we value our digital possessions more than we did in the past. That’s something that was coming for a really long time. The pandemic just helped everyone get there, or at least for me personally. It was pre-pandemic, post-pandemic in terms of how I crossed that chasm of understanding how much our time in the digital space impacts and affects us as humans, psychologically, emotionally, all those things.” Seth Goldstein from Bright Moments also explained to me the impact of the pandemic : “It’s not an accident that we started after the pandemic. The pandemic was a really raw time where we were all alone making stuff behind our computers. Bright Moments didn’t have any legacy business to support. We didn’t have existing galleries. We just saw the opportunity to bring people together.”

name: Rafael Lima Wins Grant to Create Hicetnunc
desc: In July, Rafael Lima won a Tezos hackathon for a micro-funding project titled Hicetnunc. The grant was meant to fund a project “geared towards users in the e-sports community that [would] allow them to take part in crowdfunding.” By November of 2020, it would pivot again, “evolv[ing] into a tool for creating micro-funding DAOs for any purpose,” according to this interview with Lima . In the interview, Lima goes on to mention that future plans make include “Crypto art” and “NFT stores.” The interview also explains the origin of the name Hicetnunc, inspired by existential philosophy from readings of Paul Virilio . Lima elucidated : “It concerns an existential praxis, a structure in perceiving references and making decisions upon them.” The following year saw Hicetnunc deploy on Tezos , kicking off NFTs on the platform in earnest and starting a surprising global digital art revolution that was particularly impactful and led by artists in the Global South, including Brazilian Lima.

name: Rare AF3 Goes Virtual
desc: Scheduled to be held in the middle of the pandemic, Rare Art Festival (RareAF) transitioned to a fully virtual experience, VRAF. The festival showcased a diverse range of art forms within platforms like Cryptovoxels. With over 50 live-streamed presentations, including by Kate Vass and Fanny Lakoubay , and numerous exhibits, VRAF did a noble job of carrying on through challenging times. The challenge was not only the pandemic. A huge issue for the still growing ecosystem, extending well into 2020, was a tepid secondary market. Growing the space was of prime concern in days that must have felt quite bleak, despite a recovery in the crypto markets following a catastrophic March 2020 crash. The event reminds us of the resiliency and determination necessary to survive in this space, as in one year the mood would be quite the opposite. At least two large catalysts for growth unexpectedly appeared later in 2020: October’s launch of NBA Top Shot and November’s Art Blocks . The stage was set for one of the wildest and unexpected years in this story: 2021.

name: Decentraland and NBA Top Shot Onboard
desc: Earlier in the year at the VRAF , a huge challenge discussed was how to onboard new people interested in the possibilities enabled by NFTs for digital art. In February of 2020, Decentraland launched, which joined CryptoVoxels as an early interpretation of the metaverse. Decentraland would play a critical role in onboarding big brands and celebrities in the coming months and years, eager to buy the virtual real estate. The second onboarding surge came from NBA Top Shot, which was meant to capture ownable basketball highlights for fans to collect and trade but quickly turned into a speculative frenzy with the seeming ease at which you could make quick money. Top Shot introduced a large new crowd to NFTs—and they had capital.

name: Nifty Gateway Nurtures Early NFT Market
desc: While founded in 2018 by Duncan and Griffin Cock Foster and acquired in 2019 by Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss , Nifty Gateway accounted for much of the 2020 NFT sales. Originally meant to mass-onboard users to NFTs by introducing credit card purchases and branding them as “nifties,” Nifty Gateway played a significant role in fueling the early NFT craze in early 2021, where “Nifty Gateway accounted for $75 million of the $91 million in NFT art auctioned in February 2021,” according to data by CryptoArt.io on Forbes. Further, Nifty Gateway onboarded Beeple to NFTs and was responsible for his rapid rise in fame through a series of drops in 2020 that propelled his future astronomical prices. The platform also helped popularize other crypto-native artists like Pak, Refik Anadol , Sam Spratt and XCOPY .

name: The Rise of DAOs
desc: Along with platforms like Nifty Gateway , prior to the major NFT-led digital art mania of 2021, early DAOs such as Flamingo (October 2020) began emerging with the goal of securing on-chain digital culture through a decentralized ownership structure. Fingerprints DAO and Pleasr DAO sprung up in March 2021, while GrailersDAO began in October 2021. These DAOs not only built some of the most significant blockchain art collections, they also pioneered a novel form of decentralized communal art collecting and, ultimately, curating. Much of this story over ten chapters has been about access to art (and technology) with examples extending at least to GRAV’s efforts to bring art to the public. Revolutions in access for artists and audiences occurred decades prior but DAOs democratize and globalize access to world-class art, finally revolutionizing collector access. This decentralized asset ownership structure has also served to foster a new generation of art collector demanding the conveniences afforded of the Internet—instant transactions and instant transfer.

name: Art Blocks Brings Generative Art On Chain
desc: Art Blocks Brings Generative Art On Chain If NFTs unlocked demand, then Art Blocks, founded by Erick “Snowfro” Calderon, provided a space for demand to meet supply, creating a community where artists could manifest the technological, artistic and conceptual advancements of human history to push boundaries in art. The three genesis projects were released on November 27, including Jeff Davis ’s Construction Token , DCA’s ( Daniel Calderon Arenas ) Genesis and Snowfro’s Chromie Squiggle . Often credited with (re)launching generative art, Art Blocks was instrumental in introducing a wider audience to generative practice, especially on-chain long-form generative art. These on-chain long-form generative art roots can be traced to earlier experimentation with systems, chance and community. Art Blocks Founder Calderon was a claimer and admirer of Larva Labs ’ CryptoPunks . “As a generative artist, I thought CryptoPunks were a brilliant example of generative art,” Calderon told ArtNews . He arrived at the concept “from the day I claimed my CryptoPunks in 2017,” he told The Monty Report. After years of exploring generative art and coding, Calderon envisioned a platform where artists could upload algorithms and mint unique, blockchain-verified art pieces in the vein of CryptoPunks. Despite the influence of CryptoPunks, Art Blocks did not even have an NFT component until 2019. It also struggled to get off the ground in the early days. Calderon continued to The Monty Report: “I hit a wall in 2018 and early 2019, where I was like, ‘okay, yeah, Art Blocks isn’t going anywhere. I can’t communicate my vision. Nobody really wants to use this.’” It was then that Calderon switched focus from pitching Art Blocks to helping the broader space grow. He began integrating himself into and understanding the tiny ecosystem he was looking to disrupt. Despite these early setbacks, the platform’s auspicious November launch anticipated trends like few others. And no one, even founder Calderon, saw the enthusiasm that ensued coming, which he told to Le Random when reflecting on the 2020s . Art Blocks genuinely redefined generative art with its focus on long-form and the NFT space early on in this decade, with the platform still a force in the space today.

name: Chromie Squiggle by Snowfro
desc: Years in the making, the Art Blocks genesis project’s first iterations appeared on Twitter in September 2018 over two years before its official release on November 27, 2020. Chromie Squiggle —affectionately referred to as Squiggles—is the art project Calderon developed around his years-long pursuit of the project Art Blocks . Squiggles played a key role in Art Blocks’s development, as Calderon would walk around in 2019 with a Chromie Squiggle card to help explain the concept of generative minting. “I handed them to different people and was trying to tell them the story, and they were looking at me with their eyes crossed,” Calderon told The Monty Report. Today, the project is one of the most identifiable in all of generative art due to its recency and popularity in the broader NFT and crypto communities. Calderon writes humbly about the collection: “Simple and easily identifiable, each squiggle embodies the soul of the Art Blocks platform. Consider each my personal signature as an artist, developer, and tinkerer.”

name: Construction Token by Jeff Davis
desc: Davis has played a critical role this decade—and beyond—in creating and establishing generative art. His role became solidified when Davis released Construction Token, one of the three Art Blocks genesis projects. The other two were Chromie Squiggle by Erick Calderon (Snowfro) and Genesis by DCA (Daniel Calderon Arenas) . The following year, Davis became an advisor to Bright Moments and the only artist to release work in each of its visited cities. His influence in the space remains as both an artist and as Chief Creative Officer and Strategic Advisor at Art Blocks .

name: Composition by teamLab
desc: This light sculpture on a flat plane above the viewer continued the two-decade career of the audio and light installation artists, teamLab, from Japan . Few groups have done more to popularize and normalize dynamic, code-based art to the public on a large scale than the influential teamLab with their nearly 400k subscribers on Instagram and the millions who have experienced their work live since 2001. Their work harkens back to the roots of electronic art and, therefore, to something fundamental to digital generative art: light and its manipulation.

name: INTANGIBLE FORMS by Shohei Fujimoto
desc: This immersive, audiovisual exhibition was Fujimoto’s first solo show in North America , featuring over nine real-time, light-based installations powered by choreographed kinetic lasers, strobes, haze and moving lights. The work indicated a growing interest in immersive generative installations along with teamLab and Refik Anadol . The installations explored the universal connections between all living beings, revealing—as cybernetics did—the intricate and invisible systems that shape our reality. Set against a meditative soundscape inspired by the quiet of Shinto shrines, INTANGIBLE FORMS consists of hundreds of lasers algorithmically manipulated with the open-source toolkit openFrameworks to create the illusion of objects in space, harkening back to the roots of digital art—lumino-kinetic installation.

name: Noteworthy Code-based Work
desc: While perhaps not 2021 levels, 2020—the COVID year—still saw an overwhelming burst of digital creativity. Prior to the rise of long-form generative art the following year, most of these 2020 works would be considered short-form—or artist-curated—projects. The work we regard now may change over time, with some essential works certainly left out here. Yet code-based standouts of 2020 include: • cllm by Manolo: One of Manolo Gamboa Naon ’s most striking works and his first mint on SuperRare • Limbo by Rebecca Allen (One of the luminary’s only NFTs and a work that visualizes her career, investigating form and repetition.) • RGB-2 series by Casey Reas • I’d rather be in a dark silence than and Anthropocene by Operator • Anticlassic, Loxodography 2 2, Petal Loops and Elektroanima by Tyler Hobbs (The palettes and developing aesthetic of his upcoming QQL and Fidenza can be glimpsed from these pre-NFT collections.)
subjects: i'd rather be in a dark silence than

name: Noteworthy AI Work
desc: From about 2019, the amount of AI work increased exponentially. We highlight a few exceptional standouts only in a surely incomplete list: • Acne Studios x Robbie Barrat • Neural Decay and Neural Composition by Mario Klingemann • numpytillism, transcribing after Matisse by Helena Sarin (The legend’s genesis mint) • Bloom by Trevor Paglen (Pace exhibition)

name: I’d rather be in a dark silence than by Operator
desc: This Lumen "BCS Immersive Environment Award Winner 2021” showcases Operator ’s concept-forward explorations of systems. The piece—by the experiential artist duo of Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti —blends fashion, technology and experiential art in a postmodern, mixed media demonstration of the digital. The centerpiece is a signal-blocking trench coat, lined with military-grade fabric to protect against digital surveillance. Unveiled at Factory Berlin , the project placed participants in an immersive multisensory environment. It examines themes of data privacy and surveillance through 360° projections, soundscapes, AR filters and poetry. Operator’s work challenges the pervasive reach of surveillance technologies, offering provocative commentary on privacy in the digital age. Their work invites the viewer to consider the systems that run their lives, striking at.
subjects: i'd rather be in a dark silence than

name: DALL-E Launched
desc: We open January 2021 with a bang. This consequential deep learning model designed by OpenAI “generates”—as in creates—digital images from natural language descriptions. Utilizing a 12-billion parameter version of the GPT-3 neural network, DALL-E marked a significant advancement in AI-driven generativity. This launch opened the text-to-image race that continues today between DALL-E, Stable Diffusion and Midjourney . Although introduced at the very beginning of 2021, DALL-E and text-to-image generation did not receive mainstream attention until nearly a year later. This is because DALL-E 1 generated images autoregressively from discrete image tokens, which was computationally expensive and slow. It wasn’t until almost exactly a year later, in late December 2021, that the concept of latent diffusion models was introduced, which significantly reduced the computational requirements and decreased costs. This advancement would light the fire of mass adoption of the emerging technology.

name: Ringers by Dmitri Cherniak
desc: Released on January 31st before NFT mania had properly taken hold, this iconic project would go on to be acquired by LACMA , sold at Sotheby’s and cemented in history as the crown jewel in one of the most notorious former collections. This Art Blocks Curated project stands as a massively significant part of a span that saw long-form generative art’s best-known releases, from Snowfro’s Chromie Squiggle in November 2020 through Tyler Hobbs ’s Fidenza in June 2021. The collection helped establish the Canadian Cherniak as one of generative art’s rising superstars, propelling him to collaborations with MoMA on their postcards project and one of the most recognizable pieces in generative art: The Goose. While the project’s aesthetics on an individual level may not be universally considered innovative, the power of Ringers —and all generative systems—was in its ability to create a system that could produce 1,000 outputs. Taken as a whole, Ringers demonstrates, like Sol LeWitt and many others, the power of simplicity executed masterfully and thoughtfully.

name: Archetype by Kjetil Golid
desc: Released on February 27, Golid’s Archetype was another early 2021 project that would later assume legendary status after a relatively quiet release on Art Blocks Curated. This long-form generative art project is rooted in the concept of rectangle partitioning. The algorithm divides and subdivides rectangles into intricate grids, creating varied compositions with six main properties: Framed, Shading, Scene, Palette, Coloring Strategy and Layout. With 600 minted pieces, Archetype shines in its display of the algorithm’s flexibility, producing consistently aesthetic works, from orderly grids to chaotic patterns.

name: First Tezos NFTs Minted
desc: In February 2021, NFTs arrived on the Tezos blockchain, years in the making and just in time. Although perhaps some earlier NFTs were created as part of a November 2020 giveaway, the first Objkt.com -listed NFTs begin appearing in early February, including this piece, which may be the first Tezos NFT . These early February pre- HEN -launch works include pieces by artists like Mario Klingemann , who minted work on Tezos in late February.

name: Hicetnunc (HEN) Founded by Rafael Lima
desc: On March 1, Hicetnunc (HEN) officially launched its mainnet along with the OBJKT Swap Protocol on Tezos, which enabled NFT transactions. With low monetary barriers to entry and no gatekeepers, Hicetnunc exploded onto the digital art scene as a marketplace, fostering a loyal following of digital creatives from around the globe but particularly the Global South. Before HEN, many established generative artists were skeptical of NFTs and avoided associations with them. As respected artists such as Mario Klingemann became some of the earliest adopters, HEN gained instant legitimacy. The platform rapidly became popular with a near-utopian, frenzied community. This explosion of creativity brought generative art from South America , with its illustrious legacy, to the entire world. This author, Peter Bauman , wrote about critical moments throughout generative art history in South America on a collaboration with Bright Moments.

name: Everydays: The First 5000 Days by Beeple
desc: If two local catalysts propelled the NFT mania of 2021, they were the pandemic and this March 11 record-breaking Beeple sale. The macro-catalysts include the pre-conditions for NFTs that Casey Reas has spoken about and so much of this Timeline has been devoted to, including the rise of mass-media art in the ’80s, mobile technology and blockchains. Developments in systems thinking and abstraction throughout art history were also critical. However, in terms of more proximate causes for NFT-mania, this sale did more than almost any single event to bring attention to NFTs and the art made on them. The traditional art world, while often appearing noble, is largely dictated by economics. This single—largely economic—event may have therefore done more for mainstream adoption of digital art than any other individual digital art effort in decades. The flip side to the positive attention this sale may have brought to the space is the undoubted increase in financialization and speculation that it also ignited. Art Blocks founder Erick Calderon spoke to Le Random about the challenges of hyperfinancialization in the decade.

name: Mark Cuban Enters NFTs
desc: While ultimately not a mainstream success, Cuban’s NFT viewing gallery, Lazy, demonstrated the Web3 and NFT world’s rapid rise in prominence, especially after the March Beeple sale. Cuban purchased Lazy less than two weeks after Beeple’s record-breaking sale.

name: Social Codes by Feral File
desc: Originally minted on Bitmark, Social Codes was a group online exhibition by Feral File and curated by artist Casey Reas in March before NFT-mania has properly taken off. The exhibition’s timing was perfect, as interest in the artists featured was rising rapidly. The ten artists included Dmitri Cherniak , LIA, Andrew Benson , Raven Kwok , Anna Carreras , Manolo Gamboa Naon , Maya Man , Frederik Vanhoutte , Saskia Freeke and Dave Whyte (Bees and Bombs) . Each artwork was created using custom software, and meant to showcase the power of code as a medium for artistic expression. Social Codes provided a cohesive space for these rapidly emerging digital artists to make work, curated by the legendary creator of Processsing itself. The show was thus a critical stamp of approval for some of the earliest generative art on the blockchain, increasingly, long-form generative art.

name: Subscapes by Matt DesLauriers
desc: By April 23, when Matt DesLauriers released Subscapes, 2021-as-we-know-it was already taking shape with the Beeple sale , Art Blocks and HEN in the rearview mirror. Yet Subscapes on Art Blocks Curated was another generative art project that, in just a few month’s time, would reach legendary status. The hype for these early Art Blocks reached a peak a few months later, at the end of August, recording hundreds of ETH in volume per day. Comprising 650 unique on-chain iterations, each piece visualizes an otherworldly landscape inspired by topographic maps and hand drawn strokes. The outputs paradoxically appear at once natural, alien and mechanical, demonstrating DesLauriers’s mastery of his digital aesthetic.

name: Fidenza by Tyler Hobbs
desc: After the dust settled in a chaotic generative art summer of 2021, Tyler Hobbs ’s Fidenza in the end remains perhaps the most celebrated. This versatile and aesthetically diverse generative algorithm stood out for its recognizable elegance. Rooted in the flow field algorithm for which the project is now nearly synonymous, Fidenza generates intricate, (mostly) non-overlapping curves that are layered with thick, curved rectangles, creating complex, organic compositions. The algorithm allows for a wide range of variations in turbulence, scale, and color, producing outputs that range from serene, flowing patterns to bold, chaotic structures. Hobbs spoke to this author, Peter Bauman , about his evolving views on “algorithmic aesthetics” : “This is the way I like to precisely define where the art is now: it’s the potential output space of the generative procedure combined with the curation model. That is to say, I think what the artist has really crafted is that output space and all the things that can happen in it. Obviously, they don’t necessarily have control over exactly what happens but to a certain extent they do because they’re also able to choose the curation model. For example, with Fidenza, I was developing it with the knowledge that every single output could be part of the final result set. That potential output space was designed with that curation model in mind—versus QQL , where I know that it’s going to undergo heavy curation, sometimes really extreme curation. The algorithm can have a completely different type of output space and be successful and to ignore the curation model would be an oversight. So I think that’s where the art really lies but I think the results are probably the best way to judge the success of those other things—the tangible, observable effects. I think the art has already been, in some ways, created before those final outputs are even seen.”

name: Bright Moments Opens in Venice Beach
desc: In May, Bright Moments , co-founded by Seth Goldstein and Louie Ryan , began its journey. In a few short years, the ambitious organization traveled to ten—eight—cities around the world, organized a collection of 1,000 contemporary works and created a 10k NFT collection, CryptoCitizens . The journey began at Bright Moments’ genesis location, Venice Beach , California . Starting as a community space for people to enjoy themselves around NFTs in person, Bright Moments from the beginning was able to incorporate a sense of playful seriousness into the physical appreciation of digital art. The location also serves as the beginning of the community that Bright Moments would build over the course of the next few years, bringing many of the prominent names from this chapter together in places across the planet. What Bright Moments in general and this event in particular signified was the increasing overlap of generative art, performance and real-life experience. Bright Moments made generative art something communal and experiential in a way it perhaps hadn’t been since Jasia Reichardt ’s 1968 Cybernetic Serendipity or the early 1980s SIGGRAPH computer art fairs. In December 2021, Bright Moments would travel to its first location outside of California with its New York event. The exhibition featured work by Tyler Hobbs and Emily Edelman , among others, signaling the beginnings of a rising global community. Goldstein and Bright Moments artist and Art Blocks founder spoke to Le Random about the power of participation and community in art , fostered by Bright Moments.

name: Dreaming at Dusk by Itzel Yard (Ix Shells)
desc: In May, the self-taught coder Yard created the generative work Dreaming at Dusk for an NFT auction supporting the Tor Project. The artwork, derived from the private key of the first onion service, raised 500 ETH (approximately $2 million USD), marking a historic moment for both the artist and the organization. The work commemorates a piece of Internet history, harkening back to the days of net.art. The sale made Yard the highest-selling woman NFT artist on Foundation.

name: Sotheby’s Natively Digital Sale
desc: In June, Sotheby’s held its first-ever curated NFT auction, Natively Digital, marking a pivotal moment in the integration of digital art within the traditional art world. It’s no surprise that early forays from the art world came from the auction houses; however, museums like the Whitney and Buffalo AKG demonstrated interest in artistic interventions with blockchain technology years prior. This is thanks to the efforts of curators Christiane Paul and Tina Rivers Ryan , respectively. Perhaps a long-term disservice, the sale did muddle NFTs together as a “genre,” as co-curator and On NFTs author Robert Alice featured a diverse collection of 27 NFTs, including works from pioneering crypto artists and contemporary creators. The auction highlighted the historical breadth of digital ownership and scarcity, showcasing both historic NFTs and more contemporary digital art. Natively Digital solidified Sotheby’s role in this early NFT market and underscored the growing significance of blockchain-based art in the global art ecosystem. The sale was even flagged by artist Casey Reas as a critical moment. Despite these positives, leaning into the NFT aspect while being less sensitive to artistic practices and their potentially rich connective tissue remains a lost opportunity.

name: ICA Miami Makes Early NFT Acquisition
desc: In July, the Institute of Contemporary Art in Miami ( ICA Miami ) acquired its first NFT , CryptoPunk 5293, as a gift from trustee Eduardo Burillo . The acquisition marks one of the very first by a museum anywhere, although the first was likely the Whitney several years earlier with Jennifer and Kevin McCoy ’s Public Key / Private Key . Predating even this was MAK in Austria’s 2015 purchase with Bitcoin of the Harm van den Dorpel proto-NFT, Event Listeners. Created by Larva Labs in 2017 and covered extensively in this chapter and the previous one, the acquisition further solidified the CryptoPunk series as culturally relevant. The acquisition marked a significant moment for the museum, highlighting its commitment to exploring contemporary art’s most emerging landscape. This early adoption of NFT art reflected an ongoing interest by ICA Miami to recognize the growing influence of blockchain technology in the art world.

name: CENTURY by Casey Reas
desc: Released as the so-called “Generative Art Summer” on Art Blocks was just beginning, the six-month stretch in the middle of 2021 marked a turning point. Interest and sales in generative art reached levels never seen before. What would have seemed unimaginable just a few months earlier peaked in late August 2021. CENTURY, a body of work Reas began in 2012, paid homage to 20th-century art movements, particularly inspired by Ellsworth Kelly ’s 1950s works. Reas’s creation draws on concrete and non-objective art, color-field painting, and minimalism, the systems-thinking precursors to the Conceptual movement of the ’60s and ’70s that link directly to generative art’s history and are discussed in chapters 4 and 5. CENTURY as a series consisted of work that appeared to be “cut” and "reassembled” with viewer keyboard inputs, echoing Kelly’s practice of rearranging his paintings yet showcasing the ability of the digital to include interactivity. The collection is designed to be viewed on large screens and in motion, emphasizing its infinitely animating live code capabilities.

name: Rituals - Venice by Aaron Penne x Boreta
desc: In September, Aaron Penne and Boreta released this infinitely generative audiovisual artwork with Bright Moments . The project is designed to evolve over 9 million years, combining randomized processes with meditative soundscapes and visuals. The work generates unique harmonies and patterns that continually shift over time. In 2022, it won the Lumen Prize NFT Award, as the project consisted of 1,000 unique NFTs, with the first 200 minted live at Bright Moments Gallery in Venice , CA, that September. This live minting event was one of the first by Bright Moments to capture what would become its raison d'être: the ability to connect collectors and artists in a deeply personal experience, blending digital and physical spaces and permanently linking the artwork to the moment of its creation on the blockchain but also in physical space and time.

name: Facebook Embraces the Metaverse
desc: In October, Facebook rebranded as Meta , signaling its strategic shift toward building a private metaverse—a virtual world blending social experiences, augmented reality and immersive environments. The moments is significant for this Timeline because it signifies that we are likely not even at the beginning in terms of people realizing the importance of digital ownership. When virtual reality becomes increasingly mixed with our physical reality, it’s not a far logical jump to suspect we will want these worlds customized to our specific aesthetic preferences, including the display of art work. Whether this company achieves its vision of a metaverse is unclear or even questionable, despite the fact that it’s extremely well capitalized and rich with personal data. The moment, however, signifies a step in the direction towards reality in what previous decades felt like science fiction. This particular announcement came at the Connect 2021 conference, where CEO Mark Zuckerberg outlined Meta’s vision to evolve beyond 2D screens, creating interconnected digital spaces where users can interact, work and play in new, immersive ways. This rebranding marked a significant transformation in the company’s focus, positioning Meta as a major player in any attempts to create a new virtual world. What that ultimately unlocks for digital fine art and its ownership suggests a bright future.

name: Fx(hash) Launches
desc: In late October, fxhash launched in beta. In early November, they released Project 0, FXHASH Generative Logo, the long-form generative art platform on Tezos’s genesis. Fxhash capitalized on the energy of NFTs, the vibrant Tezos art community, a pre-existing model in Art Blocks and a healthy dose of criticism from artists of the Ethereum blockchain. At this time in 2021, Ethereum was still PoW and came with significant environmental concerns attached. Its popularity also meant relatively extraordinarily high fees, which served to exclude artists from developing economies. From the beginning, fxhash aimed to provide artists with intuitive tools to create and sell their long-form generative art while offering collectors and curators a secure marketplace to explore and acquire these unique digital works. The platform quickly became a central hub for the generative art community, enabling global artists to earn a living from their creations and fostering a vibrant ecosystem. Fxhash’s launch marked a significant step forward in this story and the accessibility of software-based generativity. The first project—meant to be more of a proof of concept—and token minted on fxhash were created by ciphrd (Baptiste Crespy). FXHASH Generative Logo served as the platform’s logo, symbolizing the blockchain-enabled algorithmic process that generates unique outputs from individual hashes.

name: Mario Klingemann Creates Botto
desc: In October, Mario Klingemann launched Botto , a decentralized autonomous artist governed by a DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization). This decentralized autonomous artist was designed to generate and sell art based on community feedback mechanisms of the DAO. Simon Hudson, the project’s first hire, led the BottoDAO from launch day until September 2026. Utilizing AI models and governed by the BottoDAO, Botto creates thousands of images weekly, with community members voting to select and auction the final artwork as NFTs. This project challenges traditional notions of authorship, harkening back to Harold Cohen and his AARON , which was similarly intended to be an immortal artist. While both AARON and Botto can operate somewhat independently of direct human control, Botto is guided instead by collective input and decentralized governance, meaning its future as a continuing artist is not limited by a single individual’s wishes or passing. The project’s roots lie in Gene Kogan ’s Abraham .ai from 2017.

name: RGB Elementary Cellular Automaton by ciphrd
desc: A few days after the platform’s official launch, fxhash founder ciphrd released the first collection proper: RGB Elementary Cellular Automaton (RBG). Inspired by Stephen Wolfram ’s Elementary Cellular Automaton, the project is the quintessential study of a rule-based generative system. Recognizing the importance of this work, Le Random acquired RGB #1 from the artist himself.

name: Monogrid by Kim Asendorf
desc: In October, Asendorf released one of the projects for which he is most identified: Monogrid on HEN . This collection of 256 unique real-time animations was minted on Tezos with each 1/1 edition exploring the dance of density, color and motion within a grid of rectangles. The series demonstrated Asendorf’s own “pixel sorting” technique, which he introduced as open source in 2012 and has significantly impacted the creating coding community. The process involves “separating a vertical or horizontal line of pixels in an image and sorting their positions into a different order” with shaders. Monogrid evolves from low-density pixel grids to complex—mind bending—with animations dynamically altering the visual structure infinitely and in real time. This layered experiential work highlights Asendorf’s mastery of real-time generative art.

name: Unstable Presence by Rafael Lozano-Hemmer at SFMOMA
desc: This October mid-career retrospective was co-produced by the Musée d’Art Contemporain de Montréal and SFMOMA . Unstable Presence displayed work from the decades-long career of Lozano-Hemmer. Known for his large-scale, participatory installations, the artist explores where technology, architecture and audience interaction meet. The exhibition featured a series of works that emphasized the transient nature of physical presence within natural and technological environments. By engaging viewers through interactive and performative installations, Unstable Presence, like much of Lozano-Hemmer’s work, highlights the poetic and political dimensions of our interactions with space, offering a unique commentary on the fluid nature of the ephemeral and the enduring.

name: Gene Kogan Creates BrainDrops, Long-Form AI Art Platform
desc: In November, artist and AI educator Gene Kogan co-founded BrainDrops , a transformative NFT platform dedicated to AI-generated art. BrainDrops quickly became a central hub for artists and enthusiasts exploring the creative potential of AI. The platform launched in November 2021 with Kogan’s own Brain Loops; Roope Rainisto ’s Life in West America , later its best-known release, followed in February 2023. Kogan spoke to this author and Le Random for our talk, covering the previous decade. BrainDrops continues to foster a vibrant community, offering educational resources and innovative tools, solidifying its role and strengthening the image of the much-derided AI-generated art in the eyes of the NFT and fine art worlds.

name: theVERSEverse Founded
desc: In November, a group of women poets established theVERSEverse NFT poetry gallery. The group celebrates poetry and text’s long-standing role in the history of generative expression, drawing from the legacies of artists like Hugo Ball , Christopher Strachey and Yoko Ono . The poets of theVERSEverse are Ana María Caballero , Sasha Stiles, Kalen Iwamoto and Elisabeth Sweet . The gallery creates literary experiences that reimagine how we consume text-based creativity in a world increasingly confronted with zeros and ones. As this Timeline has referenced many times, text—with its set rules—has often predated visual aleatoric experimentation, a legacy theVERSEverse excitingly highlights. Le Random is grateful that the poets have a strong connection to our Editorials and this Timeline. Stiles is the only other co-author of this Timeline, writing dozens of the 1000+ moments . Stiles also spoke to this author, Peter Bauman (Monk Antony) and Le Random’s Collection Lead Conrad House to discuss her digital poetry practice and the historical roots of generative text for Le Random Editorials. Sweet has authored two articles on Le Random Editorials. The first was our fifth-ever piece, “Generations of Verse,” which examined the history of generative text. The second, “machine rêverie,” is a fantastic conversation with artist ‍aurèce vettier . Ana María Caballero has contributed a piece to Le Random Editorials. When prompted to use an Editorial page as a blank canvas, she chose to share the details of her project, Paperwork .

name: Garden, Monoliths by Zancan
desc: On December 9, Michael Zancan released what would become one of fxhash ’s most revered projects, Garden, Monoliths. Just examining this single day gives an indication of the burning flames of interest that were raging during this particular time period in generative art. GM—as the project is affectionately known—is rooted in L-systems and based on the artist’s own “Grass.js” algorithm developed during a period of natural inspiration. The project features intricate vector-based designs that blend the density and organic patterns of nature with the rigidity of monolithic forms. Each artwork emerges as either a “Garden” or “Monolith,” representing variations of Zancan’s now signature style that combines delicate line strokes with occasional transparent fills, harkening back to the days of 1970s plotter artists experimenting with the organic. This includes the “grass” work of artists Colette and Charles J. Bangert as well as Grace C. Hertlein . This author, Peter Bauman , spoke to Colette Bangert about her naturalism-inspired work that would go on to deeply inform projects like GM, even if indirectly. Bangert said: “There was always the changing sky, seasonal ground and what I saw in between as I looked, walked, traveled and lived. Sometimes there were other people, other art. Mostly it was just me daily seeing and creating marks on a surface, then seeing what was there and once in a while that seeing went out into the world to be seen. The work itself, over the years, I named landscape as a way to understand and show connections to the world of the trees, sky, ground, green—or not look of the land—I’ve seen daily, even as the world climate changes everything. It’s colors, lines, forms and places daily, year by year, as I also change and grow onward.” December 9 on fxhash alone saw the releases of Zancan, Erik Swahn ’s Farbteiler, Loren Bednar , ge1doot, Michael Connolly (xiiixiii) , Owen Moore , Rudxane ’s Tych, collections by wblut, Loackme and many more. The period was simply an explosion of pent-up creativity that was finally released. For those lucky enough to be around the Discord chatrooms on days like this, there was an electricity and excitement that was never sustainable but demonstrated the potential of the space to move people.

name: HEN Discontinued
desc: In November, HEN founder Rafael Lima unexpectedly pulled the plug on the platform he created amid internal debate and pressure. Displaying the resiliency of decentralized Web3 organizations, HEN was quickly ported to alternative front-ends that were able to continue operations as usual. The resourcefulness and agility of the community is exemplified by Tezos members such as NftBiker , who started providing collecting and art tools, as part of a maturing ecosystem. This also saw the prominence of platform objkt.com increase. The community front-end Teia was formally launched in February 2022.

name: objkt.com Founded
desc: Co-founded by Timothy Mc Alister and launched as an NFT platform on the Tezos blockchain, objkt.com quickly becoming the largest digital art marketplace for NFTs on Tezos, akin to OpenSea on Ethereum. Initially starting as an auction site, it expanded into a full marketplace, especially after HEN ’s usability challenges and instability following the departure of its founder. One of the earliest releases was a collaboration with artist and illustrator George Goodwin on the early Tezos PFP project Tezzards, helping to congeal the early Tezos art community. The platform played a pivotal role in shaping the Tezos art ecosystem, providing a decentralized space for artists and collectors to engage, mint, trade and showcase their work.

name: Latent Diffusion Models Introduced
desc: Unlike DALL-E , which generated images autoregressively from discrete image tokens, Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) operated in latent space and were the step that enabled text-to-image technology to go mainstream. Instead of working directly with pixels like Diffusion Models , LDMs first compress the image into a simpler, lower-dimensional space (called the latent space) using a pre-trained autoencoder. This compressed version of the image retains the essential information but is much less detailed. The diffusion model then works in this simpler space, which makes the process faster and less resource-intensive. Once the model has generated the image in the latent space, it’s converted back into a full, high-resolution image. Once this capability was introduced, text-to-image modeling became much less expensive and therefore widely available—and impactful.

name: IGÚN by Minne Atairu
desc: This Lumen Global South Award Winner from 2021 is a generative art project that employs GANs to reimagine the lost bronze casting traditions of the Benin Kingdom, disrupted by the British invasion of 1897. Using datasets of looted ceremonial heads and other artifacts, Atairu creates AI-generated interpolations that explore the cultural and artistic absence inflicted by colonialism and its lasting scars. This mixed media collection also demonstrates the trend of how AI elements in art may eventually become ubiquitous. In addition to GANs, the work utilizes AR and 3D printing, reconstructing and reinterpreting these historical objects with the latest technology. IGÚN offers a dynamic vision that bridges past and present, while raising awareness of cultural restitution and historical memory. The project is a powerful demonstration of how systems thinking can be supplemented by AI to produce enduring artistic statements.

name: The Shell Record by Anna Ridler
desc: Centered on the history of shells as a medium of exchange, this standout AI project was created using a dataset of shells collected from the Thames in early 2021. The project, comprising moving images generated by a GAN trained on these shells, reflects on themes of value, trade and the history of shells as one of humanity’s earliest forms of currency. The piece is not static, as the work is bought and sold, it evolves, expanding its dataset and altering its visual presentation. By training her own dataset, this work embeds the natural history of the Thames into the digital realm and the blockchain as only AI could. The difficulty, time and effort of projects like this also involve countless artist choices—yes, even for an AI work, Mr Chiang.

name: Generativemasks by Takawo
desc: Honed over the course of several years through Takawo’s “dailycoding” practice beginning in 2015, Generativemasks features symmetrical geometric patterns that speak to generative art’s lush digital and material history. Alluding to the styles of indigenous Japanese culture, the collection highlights generative art’s ancient roots by one of its foremost contemporaries.
