name: A Community Finds its Voice
desc: In the beginning of 2022, a nascent on-chain generative art community began to find its voice as organizations like Right Click Save , TENDER and Waiting To Be Signed joined Outland—first publishing November 30, 2021—in giving voice to artists and collectors with suddenly much to say. In 2021, these voices had been fairly insular, mostly kept to Art Blocks , fxhash and DAO Discord channels. Led by Editor-in-Chief Alex Estorick , Right Click Save is part of ClubNFT, which was founded by Jason Bailey ( Artnome ) and had artist Danielle King as its CFO. Together with Outland—led by Editor-in-Chief Brian Droitcour —they served as invaluable platforms for digital art’s written discourse in these critical early years.

name: Memories of Qilin by Emily Xie
desc: In March, this generative long-form Art Blocks Curated project was inspired by traditional East Asian art and folklore. Through code, Xie recreates the fluidity and movement found in classical paintings, drawing inspiration from the colors and forms of woodblock prints. The project evokes religious themes and mythological imagery—dragons, phoenixes and the qilin, a symbol of prosperity. Programmed in p5.js , Memories of Qilin merges ancient cultural heritage with modern digital techniques—a project typical of a day where the roles of religion and art are blurring.

name: Fx(hash) 1.0 Launches
desc: While its beta debut was in late October 2021 , April 2022 saw fxhash officially launch with version 1.0. The latest version greatly improved the user experience, including on a security level, overall platform upgrades and the ability to collaborate on a single contract. The upgrade was successful at eliminating many of the bugs of the beta version of fxhash, which included issues with unverified scam artist mints. The release brought fxhash out of its most feral, Wild West beginnings. Also critical to the early success of fxhash was the curatorial platform Tender, which cultivated early community voices such as Trinity and Will from podcast Waiting To Be Signed. Their careful effort cultivating serious discussion around work was an under-appreciated factor in the success of the early fxhash community.

name: Fx(hash) Generative Art Minting at Art Basel Hong Kong
desc: In May, fxhash launched its first live minting event, Art Basel Hong Kong . The event was also one of the first public generative art minting experiences to engage the broader community as well as the traditional art world. With some of the top artists minting on fxhash at the time, the event was an earnest attempt to demonstrate the delights of minting a random work of generative art. This author, Peter Bauman , went to the event in person and wrote this related piece shortly after on fxtext.

name: Collapse of Terra Network
desc: In May, the cryptocurrency market experienced one of its worst runs to date. It was caused by the sudden catastrophic collapse of the cryptocurrency and Web3 organization Terra, which included LUNA and stable coin UST. The event sent shockwaves through the entire Web3 community and portended a more muted period in the space after unprecedented levels of interest and hysteria in the previous 18 months. Central to this downfall were UST, Terra’s algorithmic stablecoin, and the Anchor protocol, which offered unsustainably high yields to attract deposits. As concerns over the stability of the system grew, a massive run on UST ensued, leading to the dramatic devaluation of Terra’s native token, LUNA. The implosion wiped out billions in value, exposing critical vulnerabilities in decentralized finance (DeFi) and raising questions about transparency and investor protection in the crypto space.

name: Verse Launches
desc: In June, Verse , founded by Jamie Gourlay and Augustinas Malinauskas , launched with the goal of bringing order and legitimacy to the chaotic NFT art market. Verse introduced a curated, elevated approach to NFT sales, led by former Tate Britain curator Leyla Fakhr and Creative Director Dr Mimi Nguyen . The platform’s first exhibition, This Is Tomorrow, featured works selected by a panel including Simon Denny and Tyler Hobbs . Verse describes its opening as the beginning of an aim “to encourage the collaboration between artists and curators, and create a space where artists can showcase works that may not have been ownable to collectors before NFTs.” Since its launch, Verse—along with Art Blocks , fxhash and others—helped shape a decade where creatives’ tools and access were expanded like never before.

name: Phillips Holds Ex-Machina: A History of Generative Art
desc: In July, the auction house Phillips presented this respectable online auction, curated by Georg Bak , and exhibition tracing the evolution of generative art. The event featured works from early pioneers like Vera Molnar and Herbert W. Franke , alongside contemporary artists such as Snowfro and Dmitri Cherniak . The exhibition, which traveled from Paris to London , showcased the various connections between pioneers of computational art. The exhibition did well to highlight the rich history of generative art within both traditional and NFT markets at a time when this history was less well known.
subjects: ex-machina: a history of generative art

name: QQL by Tyler Hobbs and Dandelion Wist Mané
desc: In September, Tyler Hobbs and Dandelion Mané introduced their co-creative QQL, a collaborative generative art project, empowering collectors to curate their own unique pieces from the pair’s versatile algorithm. The collection was novel in the way a highly successful artist was willing to experiment with a demonstration one of the core principles of generativity—cession of control but also authorship. The question of authorship extends ideas of groups such as GRAV who de-emphasized the individual creator, stressing collective creation. The project itself consisted of 999 Mint Passes, holders of which could then mint their selected outputs. This allowed for hundreds of community members to contribute to a dynamic, evolving collection underscoring communal engagement. The project anticipated the increased creative exploration of co-creation , which this author, Peter Bauman , wrote about for Right Click Save in early 2023. This shift included the launch of fxparams in March, 2023, which showed that the wider community was interested in exploring and embracing co-creative art.

name: Ethereum Adopts Proof-of-Stake Mechanism
desc: In September, Ethereum released the Bellatrix upgrade to initiate “The Merge” process of transitioning from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake. The relevance of the Merge for this story is that many artists refused to engage with Ethereum previously due to its ecological impact in particular. This shift significantly reduced the network’s energy consumption by approximately 99%, addressing those growing concerns over the environmental impact of its technology. The Merge also aimed to enhance the network’s scalability and security by replacing energy-intensive mining with a system where validators stake their Ether to participate in block creation.

name: Dear Machine, paint for me at Kate Vass Galerie
desc: This October exhibition curated by Georg Bak and Kate Vass featured works by pioneers and contemporary artists alike, including Frieder Nake , Alexander Mordvintsev and Ganbrood . The exhibition showcased a broad spectrum of algorithmic art, from early generative works to modern AI-driven pieces, demonstrating the evolving role of machines in the creative process and the collaboration between artist-programmers and their digital tools since the ideas of Shannon, Bense and Moles.

name: Unsupervised by Refik Anadol, MoMA
desc: In November, Refik Anadol unveiled Unsupervised at the Museum of Modern Art ( MoMA ), a groundbreaking AI-driven installation that reimagines over 200 years of the museum’s collection. Using a machine-learning model trained on MoMA’s publicly available data, Anadol’s work continuously generates new, immersive digital forms, reflecting the museum’s environment in real-time. Unsupervised explores the intersection of technology and creativity, offering viewers a visionary reinterpretation of modern art through a dynamic, ever-changing display. The installation is also tokenized on the blockchain, highlighting the integration of digital art within contemporary museum practices. The following year, the piece would be donated to the museum by 1OF1, led by Ryan Zurrer , with the RFC Collection, in an indication of the museum’s interest in emerging technologies.

name: Bright Moments Mexico City
desc: In early April, Bright Moments held their first international event, renting Kraftwerk in Berlin for 10 nights of communal celebrating. A few months later in July, the team reassembled in London , marking the mid-way point in its journey thus far. In November, the production packed up and moved to Mexico City, which saw the anticipated release of 100 Untitled Spaces by Erick Calderon (Snowfro). These opportunies provided critical opportunities for both the existing community to meet and socialize, but also attracted newcomers to the space with its more laid and contemporary approach to a traveling art exhibition.

name: FTX Collapses
desc: In November, as this author was attending the previously mentioned Bright Moments Mexico City , news began breaking of the collapse of the FTX crypto exchange and Alameda Research. Once one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, FTX precipitously collapsed in a matter of days, stunning the industry and giving a further black eye to anything related to crypto or NFTs. The downfall began when a report revealed the financial instability of Alameda Research, FTX’s sister company, leading to a market panic. Binance—the Chinese-based company considered FTX’s main rival—initially considered rescuing FTX but withdrew after reviewing its finances. FTX filed for bankruptcy on November 11, with CEO Sam Bankman-Fried resigning amid accusations of fraud. The collapse triggered a broader crisis in the cryptocurrency market, with FTX owing billions to creditors and sparking a major loss of confidence in the industry, the cloud of which remains to this writing.

name: Midjourney Launched
desc: In July, Midjourney moved to an open beta, making the text to image AI generator available to the public on its V3, with V1 appearing in February 2022. The Discord-accessible image generator founded by David Holz joined DALL-E and the following month’s entrant Stable Diffusion to disrupt animation and photography with Artificial Intelligence.

name: Proof of People London
desc: In July, Proof of People (PoP), a Web3 arts festival, debuted in London . PoP was organized by Vertical Crypto Art, a blockchain art curation house founded by Micol Ap. PoP in London and later New York served similar roles during this time as Bright Moments —and earlier SIGGRAPH art shows—bringing a disparate digital art community together in person. For decades, artists and collectors have spoken of the importance of such in-person events.

name: Stable Diffusion Released
desc: In August, just a few weeks after the public release of Midjourney , Stability AI publicly released Stable Diffusion, a text-to-image model co-developed with researchers from LMU Munich and Runway ML. The release marked a the third significant text-to-image generative AI model in less than a year. Combined, these models played a significant role is expanding access to creative tools. Stable Diffusion in particular achieved this as the model operates on under an open-source license. As with the other generative AI tools released in this whirlwind period, within months, the model garnered over 10 million users, sparking both widespread interest, curiosity and fear in these emerging technologies.

name: Rafael Lozano-Hemmer: Common Measures by Rafael Lozano-Hemmer at Pace
desc: In September, Lozano-Hemmer had his first solo exhibition at Pace since joining the gallery. Common Measures featured three major installations showcasing his use of digital technologies, including AI, robotics and projection mapping. Lozano-Hemmer’s poetic work utilizes software and systems to engage audiences in interactive experiences that explore social, political and scientific themes. This exhibition continued his exploration of the intersection between architecture and performance, drawing on traditions of public-facing work in the vein of GRAV, phantasmagoria and animatronics.

name: Menstrualverse by Sputniko!
desc: Sputniko!’s Menstrualverse challenges the representation of gender in virtual realities by introducing the artists’s famed Menstruation Machine (2010 and found on this Ttimeline) as a wearable avatar accessory in Decentraland. The wearable enabled users to publicly perform menstruation in the Metaverse so as not to transpose its taboo from physical to virtual worlds. Ironically, these attempts to expand gender expression, resulted in the wearable being rejected by Decentraland due to safety and age standards. Menstrualverse raises critical questions about identity, autonomy and the future of bodily performance in digital spaces, harkening back to the questions and ideas of artists such as Copper Giloth and Rebecca Allen . The work questions whether the Metaverse will reflect or erase biological realities—and their prejudiced taboos.

name: Takawo Founds Japan Generative Art Foundation (JGAF)
desc: Shunsuke Takawo founded the Japan Generative Art Foundation (JGAF) to advance the understanding and appreciation of generative art in his home country. The foundation’s mission is to introduce and cultivate this computational art form through exhibitions and educational programs, fostering a broader engagement with contemporary digital creativity. JGAF also aims to create opportunities for artists and build an international network dedicated to generative art, positioning itself as a pivotal force in promoting generativity globally. The project was funded by sales from Takawo’s Generativemasks .

name: Peer to Peer Presented by Buffalo AKG and Feral File
desc: In November, Buffalo AKG and Casey Reas ’s Feral File presented the online exhibition Peer to Peer. The show served as a promising indication of the growing overlap between art associated with blockchain technology and major contemporary art institutions. The show, curated by Dr. Tina Rivers Ryan —now at Artforum—featured thirteen new works from global artists, utilizing AI, 3D modeling and smart contracts to reimagine themes from the museum’s collection. As the first American museum survey of blockchain art, it highlighted the emerging role of museums in a decentralized art world. Proceeds from the exhibition support the museum’s new media art gallery and digital technology lab, with works remaining accessible through Feral File. The show featured work of LaTurbo Avedon , Mitchell F. Chan , Entangled Others , Simon Denny , Amir H. Fallah , Sarah Friend , Auriea Harvey , Rhea Myers , Osinachi , Casey Reas, Anne Spalter , Itzel Yard (Ix Shells) and Sarah Zucker . The following year, the exhibition would again be in the news as all 16 of the works were acquired as NFTs by Buffalo AKG’s Dr. Ryan.

name: Buffalo AKG Acquires NFTs
desc: In December, following the Peer to Peer online exhibition, the Buffalo AKG acquired tokenized editions of all sixteen featured artworks, marking the first major NFT collection in a U.S. art museum. Curated by Dr. Tina Rivers Ryan , the exhibition highlighted global artists exploring blockchain technology, reinforcing the museum’s 160-year legacy of engaging with emerging artistic movements. The acquisition includes works by LaTurbo Avedon , Mitchell F. Chan , Entangled Others , Simon Denny , Amir H. Fallah and others, cementing Buffalo AKG’s role in the acceptance of creative exploration in emerging technologies.

name: First Ordinal Inscription
desc: In December, engineer Casey Rodarmor created Inscription 0 of the new Bitcoin protocol Ordinals. Within months, the community had grown significantly, especially as marketplaces like Imagine Art and Generative appeared in 2023. Ordinals reignited an apparently dormant interest in the possibilities of digital ownership—beyond currency—on Bitcoin. This reminds of the previous decade’s earliest NFT ideas, which featured essentially the only options available at the time: Bitcoin and its forks, like Namecoin. Bitcoin’s place in this history was secure before Ordinals, but certainly makes it even more relevant now. The reason: Bitcoin now had its own cultural artifacts, which, like NFTs or artifacts of any kind, varied in quality.

name: Coded: Art Enters the Computer Age, 1952-1982 at LACMA
desc: Unlike many of the previous exhibitions at major museums that celebrated art and technology, Coded did not go so far as to showcase any contemporary practitioners of code-based art; however, the show was instrumental in recontextualizing and legitimizing four decades of history in art and technology. Coded highlighted how artists from 1952 to 1982 harnessed early computing technology. The exhibition, featuring 100 works by pioneers like Vera Molnár , Frieder Nake and Stan VanDerBeek , institutionalizes the evolution of generative practices and digital systems aesthetics. This landmark showcase, curated with historical precision by Leslie Jones , illustrates the foundational role of algorithmic, systems thinking and programming in the history of art. Anne and Michael Spalter provided work for the show through their Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection. The show was also largely supported by digital art patrons Carl & Marilynn Thoma , whose Thoma Foundation funds nearly every major digital art exhitition in the United States . Ultimately, Coded provided much absent contextualization to a movement long overlooked, while signaling the upswing in digital art’s evolving relationship with institutions.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: SFMOMA Acquires First NFT
desc: In January, following closely behind the heels of Buffalo AKG , the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art ( SFMOMA ) acquired its first NFT just a few weeks after Buffalo’s acquisition. This embrace of the latest from the digital art movement was part of a global embrace of NFTs by modern art institutions around the world in 2023. The piece itself, Final Transformation #2 (2022) was by Lynn Hershman Leeson , known for her exploration of technology’s impact on humanity. The artist created the NFT as part of her ongoing engagement with digital media and film. The work featured an excerpt from her 1997 film Conceiving Ada and a nod to her installation Room #8 (2006–18). It was generously donated by the artist. This acquisition marks SFMOMA’s commitment to integrating digital innovation into its esteemed collection.

name: OpenAI Releases GPT-4
desc: In March, OpenAI achieved a major advancement in artificial intelligence functionality and adoption. GPT-4’s enhanced reasoning, creativity and problem-solving abilities surpassed its predecessors. The model’s prominence and entrance into the social and creative milieu were dizzying. The large language model handles tasks like composing complex texts, interpreting images and interactive dialogue, showcasing a significant leap in AI capabilities that could be applied towards creative ends. While predictive text isn’t new ( Google Translate 2006, Siri 2011, etc), the sophistication jump from these early examples to GPT4 caught all non-AI researchers off guard. A technology that for decades—since perhaps the ’60s—was thought to be right around the corner, 5 years away, suddenly was actually here. ChatGPT, which GPT-4 was folded into, reached 100 million users in 2 months, beating platforms like Instagram and TikTok by significant margins. Not without its drawbacks or critics, the technology and its peers nonetheless will shape the future of content and art for the foreseeable future.

name: Centre Pompidou Acquires NFTs
desc: In February, the Centre Pompidou became the first major institution outside of North America dedicated to modern and contemporary art to acquire a collection of NFTs. Just two months prior, Buffalo AKG acquired 16 works as NFTs from their online exhibition Peer to Peer. Nonetheless, the Pompidou’s acquisition must be considered historic and included works from thirteen artists, including Larva Labs —the CryptoPunks and Autoglyph creators Matt Hall and John Watkinson — Jonas Lund , Fred Forest and emerging figures such as aaajiao and Émilie Brout & Maxime Marion. The collection, consisting of eighteen projects, explored how blockchain technology and artistic creation could reinforce each other as well as the museum’s commitment to contemporary technological innovation. The acquisition highlighted the museum’s interest in the emerging technologies that expanded the definition of art in the digital age. Another major modern art museum would announce NFT acquisitions just three days later.

name: LACMA Announces NFT Acquisition
desc: In February, just three days after Centre Pompidou ’s NFT acquisition announcement, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art ( LACMA ) announced their own significant acquisition of NFTs. The move was a further indication of the growing acceptance of blockchain-based work in the world’s largest art institutions. This collection included a gift from prominent collector Cozomo de’ Medici featuring noteworthy new media artists such as Monica Rizzolli , Dmitri Cherniak , Justin Aversano , Cai Guo Qiang, Matt DesLauriers and Claire Silver . It also saw works enter through individual donations by John Gerrard and Tom Sachs ’s Rocket Factory. Work by Erick Calderon also entered the collection in this bundle. The previous year, LACMA, in collaboration with of all people, Paris Hilton , launched a fund to acquire digital art by women, including works by Nancy Baker Cahill , Shantell Martin and Krista Kim . LACMA also partnered with Cactoid Labs to commission digital artists to create pieces inspired by the museum’s collection. This series featured works by Monica Rizzolli, Ix Shells, Jen Stark , Emily Xie , Sarah Zucker , 0xDEAFBEEF, William Mapan and Tyler Hobbs . The growing collection reflects LACMA’s lasting commitment to exploring new media and expanding its collection to include cutting-edge forms of artistic expression. The bundle acquisition underscores the growing recognition of blockchain-based art within the traditional art world, especially juxtaposed to the acquisitions by Buffalo AKG and Centre Pompidou.

name: Human Unreadable by Operator
desc: This 2023 Lumen Prize Metaversal Generative Art Award Winner and Art Blocks Curated long-form generative art project fused code, choreography and cryptography into a visceral, three-act experience. This author, Peter Bauman , spoke to artist duo Operator’s Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti about the project in “Operator on Human Unreadable” at Le Random Editorials. The work challenges the clean, universal aesthetics of modernism by introducing vulnerability, risk and the human body into the digital realm in the vein of pioneers like Analivia Cordeiro and Rebecca Allen . Each piece in the collection is driven by on-chain choreographic data, creating a dialogue between human expression and technical systems. Human Unreadable invites audiences to engage with the chaotic and embodied aspects of human experience, probing the possibilities of human-machine collaboration on the blockchain, while liberating the movement from the screen . “As Conceptualism liberated the ’60s art world from the canvas. Operator ’s Human Unreadable liberates the on-chain generative art world from the screen.” -Peter Bauman

name: Bright Moments in Tokyo and Buenos Aires
desc: In May and November of 2023, Bright Moments continued its global tour with vibrant events in Tokyo and Buenos Aires . In Tokyo, the experience included nightly minting at a skyscraper by Shibuya Crossing, personalized gallery tours in a traditional Japanese house, and a grand reveal at one of the city’s renowned nightclubs. The Le Random team of thefunnyguys and this author, Peter Bauman , spoke at the Tokyo event on ten moments from this very Timeline. The set the stage and context for the artist talks. Buenos Aires followed with equally immersive events, further solidifying Bright Moments' commitment to connecting digital spaces with real-world communities. Le Random’s thefunnyguys and Bauman spoke at this event as well, describing ten moments in generative art history from the South America and the world. These city-wide experiences not only showcased the unique cultural essence of each culturally iconic location but also strengthened the global generative art community through shared, in-person experiences, harkening back to the early-80s computer art community SIGGRAPH nurtured in North America or the similar organization a continent away in Ars Electronica . What made Bright Moments was that it was truly and intentionally a global endeavor.

name: Code Chronicles at bitforms
desc: In March, bitforms gallery in New York presented Code Chronicles, curated by Aleksandra Artamonovskaja now Head of Art at Tezos ( Trilitech ). This exhibition featured generative artworks by eight pioneering artists, demonstrating the links between on-chain generativity and its code-based predecessors. Artists included LIA, Sara Ludy , Ana Maria Caballero, Maya Man , Helena Sarin , Sarah Ridgley , Sarah Friend and Ivona Tau . Listen to Le Random’s chat with LIA about beginning her career in the ’90s for our Timeline Ch 7 talk. The show explored the intersection of digital identity, memory and generative processes, highlighting how these hyper-emerging technologies were impacting digital expression. Each piece emphasized the dynamic relationship between artist and algorithm, reflecting on themes of impermanence and the blurred distinctions between human creativity and machine intelligence. The show demonstrated a thoughtful link between the gallery world and artists exploring on-chain.

name: Generative Platforms Explode
desc: In a demonstration of the growing popularity of the generative coded movement, lerandom.art . With the proliferation of generative AI tools in 2022 ( DALL-E , Midjourney and Stable Diffusion ), it’s not surprising to see platforms arise to service the growing field. These included Fellowship by Alejandro Cartegena, BrainDrops by Gene Kogan , Emergent Properties , K011 and SkaldaAI . Cartegena, a photographer with work in SFMOMA , co-founded Fellowship in 2021 as an NFT photography platform, which since transitioned to an AI focus. In December 2022, Johann König relaunched EXPANDED.ART—formerly Misa, which had been founded in July, 2021—as a physical gallery in Berlin and online marketplace. It focuses on integrating Web3 technology, contextualizing digital pioneers and supporting female and non-binary artists. Another vibrant platform that’s appeared during this time is Highlight , co-founded by Nat Emodi , which affords artists several minting options and chains. Around this time, Bitcoin Ordinals also began growing its community. This followed the first ordinal inscription , which took place in December 2022, kicking high levels of the possibilities of digital ownership beyond currency on Bitcoin. This reminds of the previous decade’s earliest NFT ideas, which featured essentially the only options available at the time: Bitcoin and its forks, like Namecoin. Bitcoin’s place in this history was secure before Ordinals, but certainly makes it even more relevant now. Two Ordinals platforms arose: Imagine Art and Generative. Finally, several “Open Minting” platforms appeared around this time that aimed to enable creators with an ever-expanding suite of mixed-media digital tools. These platforms included the previously mentioned Highlight, which proved to be the most enduring. Others are Alba , EditArt , Mint256 , Prohibition and Re-tain . This interest in platform growth between 2022 and 2023 demonstrated the deep impact these emerging technologies had on a variety of new media practices and interventions.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: MoMA Announces NFT Acquisitions
desc: In October, along with its MoMA Postcard launch, a major breakthrough in on-chain generative art history took place when The Museum of Modern Art ( MoMA ) expanded its digital art collection to include NFTs. The acquisitions included works by Refik Anadol and Ian Cheng , underscoring MoMA’s commitment to artists exploring emerging technologies, building on a legacy of innovative exhibitions like The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age (1968), Information (1970) and Thinking Machines (2017).
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: MoMA Postcard Launched
desc: In October, MoMA introduced the MoMA Postcard project, an enormous stamp of approval from a global modern art museum on the creative application of emerging technologies. The blockchain-based initiative encouraged global collaboration in digital art through the creation of free art works. The project began with 15 artists creating digital postcards, each evolving as it traveled across continents. This collective effort highlighted the potential of web3 technologies to foster co-creativity, community, and new forms of artistic expression. MoMA Postcard was an encouraging sign that major institutions would not take decades to begin taking these emergent art forms seriously. The participative element also highlighted blockchain art’s ability to engage globally in simple yet meaningful ways, emphasizing the accessibility and collaborative spirit at the core of the digital art movement.

name: Fx(hash) 2.0 Launches
desc: In December, fxhash launched its long-awaited version 2.0, which incorporated Ethereum minting capabilities in addition to Tezos. Fxhash founder ciphrd spoke to this author, Peter Bauman , about the launch. Also joining were Paul Schmidt and Charlie Middleton. “We didn’t want to be positioned as a tool that opens up any creativity while limiting our artists in terms of reach because, well, some collectors only collect on Tezos or Ethereum. There is a crossover between those collector groups, but essentially, there are also a lot of differences between these blockchains. It’s in that regard that we wanted to integrate Ethereum into the platform.”

name: AGH 1 in Berlin
desc: In December, the real-time generative art trio AGH, consisting of Kim Asendorf , Andreas Gysin and Leander Herzog , debuted their collective show, AGH 1 , in Berlin , organized and co-curated by Grailers with support from Fingerprints and Highlight . The group, known for their shared focus on digital aesthetics and real-time code-based art, used this platform to challenge traditional art narratives and glorify the intrinsic beauty of computational processes. Their work celebrates the digital, emphasizing its inherent qualities such as motion, interactivity and adaptability. They aim to create a new, responsive art form that reflects the technological possibilities of the contemporary digital age. The three artists spoke to this author, Peter Bauman (Monk Antony) about the event for Le Random Editorials.

name: Grande Dame Vera Molnár Passes
desc: In December, the art world and, especially the generative and digital art communities, bid farewell to the Grande Dame, Vera Molnár , a pioneering figure in generative, systems and algorithmic art. This author, Peter Bauman , wrote “Molnár’s Paris,” taking a look at the artist’s storied life spent mostly in the French capital. Born in 1924, but moving to Paris in 1947 after WWII, the Hungarian artist was a trailblazer in merging human creativity with computational precision, coining the term and concept machine imaginaire to describe her innovative approach. Molnár’s work, spanning over six decades, explored the symbiosis between hand-drawn elements and algorithmic systems, with intense and prolonged interest, leaving a lasting mark on what the digital could achieve.

name: The Best of Times
desc: 2024 was a big year. It’s so hard to tell living through it; it’s hard to hear clearly in the din of noise. It was also a year of contrasts. It was the best of times, it was—you know. Let’s start with the good news—the age of wisdom, the epoch of belief, the season of Light. Digital art had a moment in 2024—actually it had several moments. The first was February to March. February saw the Pompidou, Whitney and MOMI all open major historical generative art exhibitions with shows on Vera Molnár , Harold Cohen and Auriea Harvey , respectively. Later in the month, MoMA announced a blockchain-based exhibition with Feral File that included artists like Yoko Ono and Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst —their names will come up again. Just a few weeks later, Tina Rivers Ryan —a renowned digital curator whose Electric Op also appears this year—announced she would be taking over as editor at Artforum , one of contemporary art’s premier publications. This came just after Taschen released its mammoth On NFTs book by Robert Alice studio during Bright Moments and NFT Paris . It was a big couple of months for media and digital art—a proper moment. It would have been the highlight of many prior years on this Timeline. But 2024 was only really getting started. Did I mention that Herndon and Dryhurst had big years? Besides the aforementioned MoMA show, they also participated in the Whitney Biennial and took over the entirety of Serpentine North for this author’s work of the year, The Call . By the middle of the year, we were treated to one of the year’s most unique events, the historic Generative Art Summit in Berlin that celebrated the form from its analog roots to its turn to digital computation. Organized by Dr. Susanne Paech from the HWF Foundation, the conference included some of the most impactful figures in generative art over the last sixty years: artists, thinkers, writers, gallerists, academics and curators. It won’t be possible to repeat the event in the same way beyond the logistical challenges due to the availability of the attendees moving forward. This author was lucky to be a part of it and speak on behalf of Le Random with Dr Paech and thefunnyguys. The second half of the year included more major exhibitions. First up were MUDAM’s Radical Software and Buffalo AKG ’s Electric Op in September. November saw LACMA ’s Digital Witness —part of Getty’s much larger art and technology themed event PST ART —and perhaps the event of the year, Tate’s Electric Dreams . Institutions like MoMA, Tate , Pompidou, LACMA, Whitney, Serpentine, Artforum and more demonstrated serious and impactful commitment and interest to digital art in 2024. Without question, this second half of the year was another moment. In fact, that’s exactly how Tina Rivers Ryan explained it to me in early 2025. Now for the not-so-great news—the age of foolishness, the epoch of incredulity, the season of Darkness. 2024 saw both the legacy and digital art worlds struggle in seeming coordination with museums laying off staff, commercial galleries closing and auction houses struggling. At the same time, the digital and Web3 world saw galleries close, marketplaces shutdown and free-minting platforms gain in popularity. Yet some marketplaces thrived in 2024, including Verse and Fellowship in particular, while Art Blocks , Highlight and fxhash completed partial pivots to continue their great work. 2024 was a Dickensian year—about the haves and have nots. The history books will and should remember it as a year of Light for digital art—certainly it had its moments as Tina Rivers Ryan described to me in early 2025. But for many, the lights turned out and perhaps for good. In the spirit of this Timeline’s broad perspective, 2024 was undoubtedly a momentous year. It was perhaps the year you could say with confidence that the digital, Web3 and legacy art worlds were as connected as ever.

name: Auriea Harvey at MOMI
desc: Auriea Harvey ’s My Veins Are the Wires, My Body Is Your Keyboard at Museum of the Moving Image presented a landmark survey of Harvey’s career, opening in February. The exhibition was curated by Regina Harsanyi and explored Harvey’s oeuvre, dating back to her seminal early work in net art in the 1990s. It also included interactive media and digital sculpture, showcasing the depth of the artist’s career. Featuring archival material, interviews and newly commissioned works, the exhibition examined themes of digital materiality, intimacy and technological embodiment. It was accompanied by a publication with contributions from scholars and artists, reflecting on Harvey’s impact on digital and interactive art. We spoke to Harvey for our Timeline chat on the 1990s. The show also received extensive critical acclaim and served to introduce thousands to the work of a net art legend.
subjects: my veins are the wires, my body is your keyboard

name: Harold Cohen: AARON at Whitney
desc: Opening just one day after MOMI’s Harvey exhibition, famed curator Christiane Paul ’s Harold Cohen: AARON at The Whitney Museum’s looked at another seminal media art pioneer. This author spoke to curator Christiane about the show , which showcased the work of the symbolic AI artmaking program AARON developed by Harold Cohen (1928–2016). Originally conceived in the late 1960s and early 1970s at UC San Diego , AARON was an ongoing experiment in translating artistic knowledge—even an entire practice, a self portrait—into code. The exhibition featured Cohen’s plotter-generated drawings, painting-machine works and live demonstrations of AARON in action . Positioned against the rise of modern AI tools like DALL-E and Midjourney , the show provided much-needed historical context on AI-driven creativity, authorship and collaboration, emphasizing Cohen’s vision of full machine autonomy in art.

name: Vera Molnár Survey at Pompidou
desc: The third landmark survey of a new media pioneer at a major global museum in the space of a month, the Centre Pompidou presented Speak to the Eye. Emblematic of an artist gaining recognition too close to passing, the show nonetheless was a welcome celebration of the grande dame of generative art, perhaps our most venerated figure— Vera Molnár . The show spanned the legend’s career from early hand-drawn geometric abstractions—her machine imaginaire —to her sustained and forever-important serial algorithmic compositions. The show did well at demonstrating Molnár’s systematic emphasis—how she explored ideas and of form, order and controlled randomness throughout her life. It was obssession that would have resulted in a complete and storied practice with or without the computer. But the computer was the artist’s superpower and one of the loves of her life. The exhibition even examined Molnár’s late experiments with AI-generated art, which she revealed to aurèce vettier . The show at France ’s preeminent modern art institution was a show befitting the career of an all-time great, not only in French, generative or digital art. To mark the occasion, I wrote about “Molnár’s Paris.”

name: Taschen Releases On NFTs by Robert Alice
desc: February 22nd in Paris marked the launch of Taschen’s On NFTs, an early major art historical survey of the NFT ecosystem, authored by artist and researcher Robert Alice . The book features academic essays and richly illustrated profiles of 101 key artists—many of whom were in Paris for the week—connecting NFTs to broader art history and positioning the medium within a lineage of algorithmic, conceptual and digital art. The launch came during a busy and memorable week in Parisian digital art history, which also witnessed Bright Moments and NFT Paris , with the Vera Molnár show opening at the Pompidou the following week.

name: Agoria Exhibits and Performs at Musée d’Orsay
desc: Also in February, electronic musician and digital artist Agoria brought Le Code d’Orsay to the Musée d’Orsay in a surreal convergence of one of the world’s great, historic collections, contemporary generative art, blockchains and biology. The exhibition also featured Σ Lumina , an interactive steel sculpture co-created with Johan Lescure , which produced shadows in the shape of scannable QR codes. These codes could then be used to mint an NFT on fxhash using the Tezos blockchain. Delightfully, the work incorporated visitors’ breaths to alter the visual composition in real time. If a world-class-museum-worthy work of art wasn’t enough, Agoria also composed an original tribute to the museum, which he performed during a DJ set in its historic nave amongst ancient statues.

name: Bright Moments and NFT Paris
desc: In its second-to-last stop on its global tour, Bright Moments brought its traveling community and immersive minting and art experience to NFT Paris , transforming a café into a hub for generative and AI-based art, organized by artist Emily Edelman . This iteration of Bright Moments would be the last to feature new artist live minting projects. Standouts included Lauren Lee McCarthy’s Seeing Voices and Linda Dounia ’s Flore Perdue . I spoke to both artists about the projects leading up to the event.

name: Sound Machines by MoMA and Feral File
desc: This online blockchain-based exhibition by MoMA and Feral File brought together seven artists to explore the intersections of sound, technology and art. Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst ’s Play from Memory examined human and machine learning in music, while Yoko Ono ’s SOUND PIECE V (1996/2024) created an on-chain archive of laughter. Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley ’s CANCEL YOURSELF (2024) reimagined agency through an interactive soundscape and 0xDEAFBEEF’s PAYPHONE (2024) explored telephony and tokenization. Honoring MoMA’s legacy of sound art, extending to great curators like Barbara London , the exhibition showcased how new technologies—from generative AI to blockchains—can reimagine auditory experience.

name: Tina Rivers Ryan Named Editor of Art Forum
desc: In March, Artforum announced art historian, curator, and longtime contributor Tina Rivers Ryan as its new Editor in Chief. Ryan, known for her expertise in digital and video art, served as curator at the Buffalo AKG . Ryan closed the year and her time at the reopened Buffalo AKG with the fantastic Electric Op . The move was a major step forward for digital art, as one of its biggest proponents now heads one of its most renowned publications.

name: Whitney Biennal Includes Mat & Holly
desc: The 2024 Whitney Biennial took on the topic of AI, without actually fully committing to its investigation. It did, however, include Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst ’s xhairymutantx, an interactive piece built around a generative model that investigates themes of identity, digital presence and the malleability of training data. Presented both in the museum’s sixth-floor gallery and online via artport, the project manipulates Herndon’s visual likeness. Viewers are able to distort her recognizable red hair and features through AI-generated transformations dictated by prompting. The work subverts traditional text-to-image models by limiting the viewer to the world of the artist’s creation rather than the generalities of a generic deep generative model. It was interactive and gave users permission to enjoy using generative AI—many perhaps for the first time.

name: Bright Moments Concludes
desc: At the end of April, during the opening of the Venice Biennale , Bright Moments concluded its three-year global journey. To mark the occasion, it organized and released the Finale Collection , a unique generative art project uniting over sixty artists on a single contract. This final act celebrates community, transformation, and reflection, encapsulating the project’s evolution across nine cities. The collection, minted on a single contract, mirrors Bright Moments’ ethos—blending digital and physical, randomness and curation—as it brings together pioneering artists and collectors one last time. Beyond the collection was the actual event, Bright Moments Venice itself. Taking place in a 14th-century scuola architectural complex over three days, the event brought out mixed emotions as it was simultaneously a celebration and a farewell as the organization reached its final destination with an unclear future. Befitting the local, the event included a Bright Moments documentary as well. Beyond the Biennale and Bright Moments, there were several other relevant exhibitions at the same time, including Christoph Büchel ’s Monte di Pietà, Memo Akten ’s Boundaries , Huemin and Ganbrood ’s The Dream Cathedral and Sam Spratt ’s The Monument Game.

name: NFC Lisbon
desc: This annual Lisbon crypto culture event in May draws a broad crowd from across the crypto industry. It’s also a celebration of NFTs and t his author gave a talk at the event, titled “The 70,000 Year History of Generative Art.”

name: Digital Art Mile at Art Basel
desc: Also in June was another major European digital art event—this time a satellite event of exhibitions and programming organized by ArtMeta during Art Basel , Basel . Le Random co-organized a day of talks that included this author interviewing Analívia Cordeiro live and thefunnyguys giving the keynote address. The “mile” consisted of two venues within a fifteen-minute walk of the Art Basel venue proper. First was space25, a three-story space curated by AI gallerists Fellowship . Second was space31, which featured several digital galleries such as fxhash and was presented by the Tezos blockchain.

name: Generative Art Summit Berlin
desc: Early July saw a third major European summer digital art event and this was the most spectacular and historic. Organized by Dr. Susanne Paech from the HWF Foundation and held at Akademie der Künste in Berlin , The Generative Art Summit Berlin was a once-in-a-lifetime event. It brought together nearly every living historical pioneer able to travel, including Frieder Nake , Larry Cuba and Joan Truckenbrod . This author and thefunnyguys were interviewed by Dr. Paech, demonstrating the Summit’s willingness to embrace the new. It explored generative art’s various faces across decades, from early analog experiments to AI-driven creativity. Hosted by the Foundation Herbert W. Franke , himself a critical figure, the show brought together past and present in a way that may be impossible to achieve again in the future. It was a special week in Berlin.

name: Getty PST
desc: In September, Getty’s PST ART: Art & Science Collide began, exploring art and science through 50+ exhibitions, public programs and research initiatives across Southern California . This included at UCLA , where artists Lauren Lee McCarthy and Casey Reas, along with Chandler McWilliams, presented an exhibition and a research project as part of the program , which I got to speak to them about. I also spoke to Getty Research Institute’s Nancy Perloff about another show as part of the program, Sensing the Future : Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.) . Listen here ( transcript ) or on your favorite podcast platform. Finally, the later-discussed Digital Witness at LACMA was also part of the broader Getty PST ART, which is why Tina Rivers Ryan mentioned it when describing the “moment” digital art had at the end of 2024.

name: Radical Software MUDAM
desc: In September, easily one of 2024’s most important shows opened: Radical Software: Women, Art & Computing 1960–1991. Curated by Michelle Cotton , the show surveyed the history of digital art from a feminist perspective, highlighting women pioneers in computational art’s history. The exhibition also uncovered and/or brought to the fore much vital research, as evidenced by the diversity of the show. It featured over 100 works by 50 artists from fourteen countries and spanned from 1960s–1991, covering early mainframe experiments to the rise of personal computing. It emphasized how artists often collaborated with scientists and engineers to create the newest digital works across drawing, film, performance and text. Positioned within the second wave of feminism, the exhibition challenges conventional tech-art narratives, celebrating women’s overlooked contributions to digital creativity before the internet’s public emergence. For this and many other reasons, Tina Rivers Ryan mentioned this specifically to me as key to digital art’s “moment” at the end of 2024.

name: Electric Op at Buffalo AKG
desc: In September, one of the most important shows of the year opened with Electric Op . Six years in the making, according to curator Tina Rivers Ryan , the show examines how Op art, video, and digital media evolved together, shaping the way images are created and perceived. The show demonstrates the historical genealogy of digital art, building on previous attempts by curators such as Margit Rosen ’s bit international at ZKM in 2008. Featuring more than 100 works by nearly ninety artists from the past six decades, the exhibition explored how artists use of geometric abstraction and optical illusions led directly to engagement with new technologies, like the computer. What’s daring about the show is that it brings the story to the present, when most historical surveys end around 1990. By showcasing how contemporary artists like LoVid carry forward the legacy of Op art, the exhibition demonstrates its resonance with the present and past. Electric Op juxtaposes contemporary digital art luminaries such as Cory Arcangel and Rafael Lozano-Hemmer with historical figures like Bridget Riley and Vera Molnar, repositioning Op art as a key movement in the Information Age—if not the first as Ryan argues. I spoke to four of the exhibiting artists at Electric Op , including Arcangel and Lozano-Hemmer . They reflect on their unique practices and contributions to the show. Another example of the “moment” digital art had at the end of 2024.

name: The Call at Serpentine
desc: In October, digital art continued its strong autumn with this author’s work of the year, The Call at Serpentine by Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst . Berlin-based duo Herndon and Dryhurst collaborated with Serpentine Arts Technologies to present The Call, an immersive installation exploring AI as a tool for collective creativity. The show serves as a moving example of what Dryhurst has described as protocol art, where the work’s emphasis lies in its underlying systems of coordination, governance and interaction rather than a single static output. Inspired by choral traditions, the project develops new protocols for training AI, incorporating recordings from fifteen UK community choirs. The installation unfolds across three thematic spaces, each reflecting key aspects of AI: compute, data, and model. The Hearth —a striking organ-like instrument powered by GPU fans—symbolizes computation, filling the space with hymns generated by AI. The Wheel presents spatialized recordings of participating choirs, referencing ancient religious structures while reflecting contemporary data collection practices. In The Oratory , visitors actively engage, singing into a microphone that triggers an AI-generated choral response, mirroring the participatory nature of both collective singing and AI training. By reframing AI as a communal rather than individual process, The Call examines data ownership, artistic authorship and the potential for AI to function as a shared cultural and technological language. The show clearly belongs with digital art’s 2024 fall “moment.”

name: V&A’s Digital Art Book and Inaugural Digital Art Season
desc: October was a big month for digital art, especially in London . In addition to Serpentine ’s The Call , October included the Victoria and Albert Museum’s (V&A) inaugural Digital Art Season to partly coincide with Frieze London as well. Included in the V&A’s programming was the launch of the museum’s new historical digital art book, Digital Art: 1960s to Now , edited by curators Melanie Lenz , Corinna Gardner and Pita Arreola . I was able to attend this launch along with wonderful talks by Arreola and artist Kyle McDonald . The following day at the V&A was FEMG3N, the third installment of FEMGEN, featuring a discussion with artists Licia He and Anna Ridler, writer Charlotte Kent and curator Melanie Lenz, alongside a talk by myself on the contributions of women in generative art. I highlighted Eudice Feder and Joan Shogren for their barely-known contributions and wonderful stories. Founded in 2022 by Micol Apruzzese and Alex Estorick , FEMGEN fosters inclusivity in digital art, celebrating female and nonbinary artists working with generative systems. The V&A also showed a screening of Gary Hustwit ’s generative documentary Eno on legendary musician Brian Eno . Besides Frieze London and all of its ancillary events, October in London also saw the Lumen Prize 2024 Awards Presentation. It was a busy month for digital art in one of its world capitals and clearly part of 2024’s digital art “moment.”

name: Lawrence Lek Wins 2024 Artist Award at Frieze London
desc: In October during Frieze London , it’s notable to point out that the fair’s main award went to an AI artist in 2024, Lawrence Lek . For winning the award, Lek debuted Guanyin : Confessions of a Former Carebot, a multimedia installation blending AI and Buddhist mythology. This author spoke to Lek about his unique, narrative AI films , which barely—or don’t—incorporate the technology at all but asks some of the most evocative questions on the subject.

name: YCAM InterLab Camp vol.5: Homo Codens
desc: A busy October for digital art ended with a small digital art event in Yamaguchi, Japan , showcasing how this 2024 was not restricted to Europe and the United States ; this was a global movement. Held at the wonderful Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM) , which was featured previously on this Timeline as a major moment in Japanese digital art history when the facility opened in 2003. I was fortunate to be invited to speak at the event , organized by Shunsuke Takawo , called InterLab Camp vol.5: Homo Codens—How Will Humanity Draw in the AI Era? It was an intensive workshop that explored generative art, AI-assisted creativity and how coding as an expressive tool continues to expand. Participants came from all walks of life and participated in hands-on sessions, discussions and collaborative projects. It showed the passionate roots of creative coding, where market forces and “floor prices” were the last things on anyone’s minds.
subjects: yamaguchi center for arts and media (ycam)

name: LACMA Digital Witness
desc: At the end of November, another event in Getty’s PST ART opened, perhaps the most significant— Digital Witness : Revolutions in Design, Photography, and Film. The show is the successor show to LACMA ’s 2023 Coded: Art Enters the Computer Age, 1952–1982 . Digital Witness picks up essentially where Coded left off, exploring the previous four decades of digital image manipulation and tracing its impact on photography, graphic design and visual effects. Featuring over 150 works by nearly 200 creators, the exhibition examines technology’s impact on digital aesthetics, realism and storytelling, highlighting the accessibility and influence of editing tools today. In this sense, the show is less about generativity per se but is still an important exhibition of digital art’s history. Tina Rivers Ryan mentioned the show specifically when referring to the end of 2024 and its “moment” for digital art.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: Tate’s Electric Dreams
desc: If Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst ’s The Call is my work of the year. The exhibition of the year is Tate’s Electric Dreams . The show at Tate Modern is a major exhibition celebrating the early pioneers of optical, kinetic, programmed and digital art from the 1950s and Japan ’s Gutai to the dawn of the internet age. What’s striking about the show is it’s Tate’s—one of the world’s most visited museums'—first focus on digital art since Tate Modern opened twenty-four years earlier, in 2000. In other words, this is a big moment for digital art. I had the pleasure of speaking to the show’s curator, Val Ravaglia , who curated it with Odessa Warren and Kira Wainstein , twice about the show. First, in a written piece where we discuss historic challenges to artist’s working with technology and much more. Then in Part 2, a video interview, we some of the specific curatorial concerns of the show, especially display . I also interviewed three legendary exhibiting artists from the show: Rebecca Allen, Analívia Cordeiro and Eduardo Kac, who exemplify the aims of the show . Yes, I thought the show was important. More about this landmark show. It brings together over 150 works by more than 70 artists from across Asia , Europe and the Americas, showcasing the geographic diversity of digital art’s roots. It explores how artists intervened with emerging technologies in various ways to create immersive environments with just optical illusions, interactive installations and machine-generated imagery. These innovators experimented with light, motion and perception, responding to the increasing presence of technology in daily life. While touching on similar roots to Buffalo AKG ’s and Tina Rivers Ryan ’s Electric Op , Electric Dreams has a broader focus and incorporates more of digital art’s twentieth-century roots. For example, the exhibition highlights key artistic movements and moments going back to Gutai, ZERO , New Tendencies and a special section dedicated to Jasia Reichardt’s , of course, legendary Cybernetic Serendipity . Of particular focus for Ravaglia was showcasing how artists reclaimed machines from military and corporate contexts to explore new creative possibilities. Works range from early experiments with video synthesizers like the Sandin Image Processor and algorithmic art to psychedelic environments and home computer-generated imagery. Importantly, the show juxtaposes historical analog artists including Atsuko Tanaka , Otto Piene and Julio Le Parc with pioneering digital practitioners like Nam June Paik , Harold Cohen , Rebecca Allen and Suzanne Treister . Electric Dreams was a major museum’s historical retrospective on digital art and its roots—exactly the kind of dialogue with the public that digital art needs to be having moving forward.

name: Light: Rafaël Rozendaal at MoMA
desc: Among the final moments of 2024 is another of the world’s great museums and perhaps the most renowned modern art institution showcasing generative algorithms on its giant Garden Lobby screen with Light: Rafaël Rozendaal . I spoke to Rozendaal about the opportunity and his illustrious career. Known for treating code like paint, Rozendaal transforms the browser—and MoMA ’s 25-foot screen—into a fluid canvas. His minimalist animations, designed to be accessible to anyone, anywhere, embody lightness in both concept and execution, with each piece occupying mere kilobytes. The exhibition highlights Rozendaal’s pioneering approach to generative art, emphasizing resolution-independent, future-proof works. By immersing viewers in shifting colors and forms, Light offers a digital meditation in a world of increasing complexity.
